meta.title: Mathematics Atlas
meta.scope: Selected foundational through graduate mathematics; broad coverage without a claim of completeness.
methodology: Formulas, definitions, identities, theorems, methods and models are included when they illuminate useful recurring structures.
Mathematical links have an explicit relation and explanation. Pattern membership is a classification; sharing a pattern does not imply equivalence.
Metaphors are teaching devices with explicit formula mappings, a shared structure, a transfer question and limits. They do not establish a mathematical equivalence or a learning prerequisite.
Generalization is directed from simpler to more general; derivation from tool to consequence; application from idea to use. Equivalence, analogy and duality can be explored both ways.
Prerequisites are an editorial learning scaffold, not a complete syllabus or formally proved dependency graph.

Learning suggestions prioritize covered prerequisites, connections to known formulas, breadth of mathematical links and optional target goals. Metaphor and pattern edges do not increase mathematical connectivity scores. Suggestions are planning heuristics, not an assessment of mastery.

Explanations are original synthesis. Linked primary sources are further reading; source granularity ranges from an exact result to a relevant course or book. This is not a formal verification or an exhaustive proof collection.
Importance and pattern frequencies are relative to this curated collection, not universal rankings of all mathematics.

nodes.name: Derivative
nodes.intuition: Zooming into a differentiable graph reveals a straight line. Its slope converts a tiny input change into the leading output change.
nodes.conditions: f is real-valued on an open interval containing x; the displayed finite two-sided limit must exist.
nodes.example: For f(x)=x², f′(3)=6: a small increase h near 3 changes the square by about 6h.

patterns.why: The difference quotient approaches the coefficient of the best local linear model.
The slope is defined by a limit of measurements at shrinking scales.

nodes.name: Linearity of differentiation
nodes.intuition: Independent contributions to a quantity have independent contributions to its rate of change. Fixed scaling factors pass straight through differentiation.
nodes.conditions: a and b are real or complex constants; f and g are differentiable at the point in question.
nodes.example: The derivative of 3x²−2sin x is 6x−2cos x.

patterns.why: Differentiation preserves addition and scalar multiplication.
A complicated expression can be differentiated one component at a time.

nodes.name: Power rule
nodes.intuition: A power law loses one power of x when converted from a total amount to a marginal change. The exponent becomes the multiplier.
nodes.conditions: For arbitrary real α take x>0; for nonnegative integer α the rule holds for every real x, with the derivative of x⁰ treated as 0.
nodes.example: The derivative of a cube's volume s³ with respect to side length s>0 is 3s².

patterns.why: The derivative of a degree-α power scales with degree α−1.
The exponent tells how sensitively a power responds locally.

nodes.name: Derivative of an exponential
nodes.intuition: Exponential functions reproduce their own shape when differentiated. Only the scale factor changes, making them natural modes for constant-coefficient differential equations.
nodes.conditions: a is a real or complex constant; x is real.
nodes.example: If a population is P(t)=100e^{0.02t}, its instantaneous growth is 0.02P(t).

patterns.why: Exponentials turn a constant relative rate into a function.
Differentiation multiplies this shape by a constant instead of changing its shape.

nodes.name: Logarithmic derivative
nodes.intuition: Taking a logarithm turns absolute change into relative change. It also turns the derivative of a product into a sum of relative rates.
nodes.conditions: f is a real differentiable function with f(x)≠0 on the interval considered.
nodes.example: For f(x)=x³ with x>0, f′/f=3/x; a 1% small relative change in x gives about a 3% change in f.

patterns.why: The logarithm converts multiplicative variation into additive variation.
The ratio f′/f normalizes change by the present size.

nodes.name: Derivatives of sine and cosine
nodes.intuition: The rate of a circular coordinate is the other coordinate, with a sign recording the direction of rotation. Differentiation therefore cycles through oscillatory shapes.
nodes.conditions: x is real and angles are measured in radians.
nodes.example: For y(t)=sin(2t), y′(t)=2cos(2t) and y″(t)=−4y(t).

patterns.why: Circular rotation moves sine and cosine into one another.
Repeated differentiation repeats a four-step cycle.

nodes.name: Product rule
nodes.intuition: A product changes because either factor can change. The product of both tiny changes is smaller than the first-order terms and disappears in the derivative.
nodes.conditions: f and g are differentiable at the point considered.
nodes.example: For rectangle area A(t)=w(t)h(t), A′=w′h+wh′.

patterns.why: The two terms isolate change in one factor at a time.
The second-order product of increments is discarded in the limiting first-order model.

nodes.name: Quotient rule
nodes.intuition: A ratio increases when its numerator grows and decreases when its denominator grows. The squared denominator adjusts both effects to the same scale.
nodes.conditions: f and g are differentiable at the point, and g is nonzero there.
nodes.example: For average speed v=d/t with variable d(t) and t>0, v′=(td′−d)/t².

patterns.why: Numerator and denominator changes make separate signed contributions.
Normalization by the changing denominator creates the g² factor.

nodes.name: Chain rule
nodes.intuition: Change passes through a chain of transformations. The outer sensitivity multiplies the inner sensitivity, with the outer derivative evaluated at the intermediate value.
nodes.conditions: g is differentiable at x, and f is differentiable at g(x), with the composition defined nearby.
nodes.example: For f(g(x))=sin(x²), the derivative is 2x cos(x²).

patterns.why: The derivative of a composition combines the derivatives of its stages.
Composing the two local linear models multiplies their slopes.

nodes.name: Derivative of an inverse function
nodes.intuition: Undoing a locally expanding map contracts by the reciprocal amount. The inverse rate is measured at the corresponding original input.
nodes.conditions: f is continuously differentiable near x₀, f′(x₀)≠0, and y lies in a neighborhood where the local inverse exists.
nodes.example: Since (exp x)′=exp x, the inverse logarithm has derivative 1/y for y>0.

patterns.why: Forward and inverse local sensitivities are reciprocal.
The inverse derivative converts rates back into the original coordinate.

nodes.name: Implicit differentiation
nodes.intuition: A constraint forces changes in x and y to cancel. Their partial sensitivities determine the compensating slope without solving the constraint explicitly.
nodes.conditions: F is C¹ near (x₀,y₀), F(x₀,y₀)=0 and F_y(x₀,y₀)≠0; the formula holds for the resulting local graph.
nodes.example: For x²+y²=1 with y≠0, the tangent slope is y′=−x/y.

patterns.why: The tangent constraint is F_x dx+F_y dy=0.
The formula gives the tangent direction along a level curve.

nodes.name: Mean value theorem
nodes.intuition: Some instantaneous slope matches the average slope over the whole interval. This connects local rates to global changes without requiring the derivative to be continuous.
nodes.conditions: a<b; f:[a,b]→R is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b).
nodes.example: For f(x)=x² on [1,3], the average slope is 4 and it occurs at c=2.

patterns.why: A global average rate is attained by a local rate.
Control of all local slopes bounds the total change.

nodes.name: L'Hôpital's rule
nodes.intuition: Near a common zero, the ratio of two vanishing quantities can be controlled by the ratio of their local rates. It is a theorem about a limit, not an algebraic identity between ratios.
nodes.conditions: On (a,a+δ), f and g are differentiable, g and g′ are nonzero, f(x)→0 and g(x)→0; the derivative ratio has a limit in the extended real line. This entry states the one-sided 0/0 version.
nodes.example: lim as x→0⁺ of (eˣ−1)/x equals lim eˣ/1=1.

patterns.why: The conclusion concerns a limiting ratio under explicit existence assumptions.
Comparing local rates resolves an indeterminate global ratio.

nodes.name: Local linear approximation
nodes.intuition: A tangent line predicts sufficiently small changes with an error smaller than the input step. The little-o term states exactly what 'locally straight' means.
nodes.conditions: f is differentiable at the interior point a; o(|h|)/|h|→0 as h→0.
nodes.example: √(4+h)=2+h/4+o(|h|), so √4.04 is approximately 2.01.

patterns.why: The leading correction is linear in h.
The error shrinks faster than the first-order scale.

nodes.name: Taylor's theorem with Lagrange remainder
nodes.intuition: Matching successive derivatives builds a polynomial that captures more of the local shape. A derivative at an intermediate point measures exactly what the polynomial misses.
nodes.conditions: n is a nonnegative integer; f is C^{n+1} on an interval containing the segment from a to a+h; ξ lies between those endpoints.
nodes.example: If |f″|≤M nearby, the tangent-line error has magnitude at most M h²/2.

patterns.why: The local behavior is decomposed into successively higher powers.
The first two terms are the tangent model, followed by curvature and higher corrections.
The remainder is bounded by a constant times |h|^{n+1}.

nodes.name: Taylor series of an analytic function
nodes.intuition: An analytic function is completely encoded near a point by all of its derivatives there. The coefficients are local measurements that reconstruct the function within a convergence neighborhood.
nodes.conditions: f is real analytic at a, and x is inside a neighborhood where its Taylor series equals f; being infinitely differentiable alone is insufficient.
nodes.example: For eˣ at a=0, every derivative equals 1, giving 1+x+x²/2!+⋯.

patterns.why: The function is expressed in the monomial basis.
The infinite expansion requires convergence to the function, not merely existence of derivatives.
The coefficients encode an infinite sequence of local derivatives.

nodes.name: Exponential power series
nodes.intuition: Factorials make successive contributions small enough for every complex input. The coefficients also ensure that differentiating the series gives the same series.
nodes.conditions: z is any complex number; the series converges absolutely everywhere and uniformly on compact sets.
nodes.example: At z=1, the partial sum through n=5 is 2.71666…, approaching e.

patterns.why: This series constructs the exponential from repeated multiplication and addition.
Successive coefficients satisfy a_{n+1}=a_n/(n+1).
Factorial decay yields unlimited radius of convergence.

nodes.name: Sine and cosine power series
nodes.intuition: Odd and even powers separate the two coordinates of oscillation. Alternating signs encode the reversal that occurs after two derivatives.
nodes.conditions: z is any complex number; both series converge absolutely and locally uniformly.
nodes.example: For small real x, sin x=x−x³/6+O(x⁵), so replacing sin x by x has cubic leading error.

patterns.why: Odd powers make sine odd; even powers make cosine even.
The exponential series splits into even and odd parts.
The derivatives cycle, fixing the coefficient signs and factorials.

nodes.name: Logarithm power series
nodes.intuition: A logarithm accumulates the reciprocal rate 1/(1+x). Integrating a geometric expansion turns its constant coefficients into reciprocal integers.
nodes.conditions: The stated real identity holds for |x|<1, and also at x=1 by a separate endpoint convergence argument; x=−1 is excluded.
nodes.example: At x=1, the convergent alternating series 1−1/2+1/3−⋯ equals log 2.

patterns.why: Integrating the geometric series produces the logarithm.
The expansion resolves multiplicative growth into additive power corrections.
Endpoint behavior needs a separate convergence check.

nodes.name: Riemann integral
nodes.intuition: Break an interval into small pieces, estimate each contribution as height times width, and add them. Integrability means all sufficiently fine tagged partitions agree in the limit.
nodes.conditions: a<b; f is bounded and Riemann integrable on [a,b]; P has a=x₀<⋯<x_m=b, ξ_i∈[x_{i−1},x_i], and mesh ‖P‖=max Δx_i.
nodes.example: For f(x)=x on [0,1], the accumulated triangular area is 1/2.

patterns.why: Local contributions are added over an interval.
A partition-independent limit replaces the finite sum.
Addition of integrands adds their contributions.

nodes.name: Linearity of integration
nodes.intuition: Accumulating a sum gives the sum of the separate accumulations. Fixed gains can be applied before or after the accumulation.
nodes.conditions: f and g are Riemann integrable on the finite interval [a,b]; α and β are constants.
nodes.example: The integral of 2x+3 on [0,1] is 2·(1/2)+3·1=4.

patterns.why: The integral is a linear functional on its integrable domain.
An integrand can be split into simpler parts.

nodes.name: Fundamental theorem of calculus
nodes.intuition: Accumulation and instantaneous change undo one another. Summing all local changes leaves only the difference between endpoint values.
nodes.conditions: For the first identity, f is continuous on [a,b] and x∈(a,b); for the second, G is C¹ on [a,b].
nodes.example: Integrating the rate 2x from 1 to 3 gives 3²−1²=8.

patterns.why: Differentiation and accumulation are inverse operations up to an additive constant.
An integral over the interval is determined by values at its endpoints.
Local changes telescope to a total change.

nodes.name: Integration by parts
nodes.intuition: A derivative can be moved from one factor to the other if its sign is reversed and the endpoint contribution is retained. This is the main bridge from differentiation rules to weak and variational methods.
nodes.conditions: u and v are C¹ on the finite interval [a,b]; the formula also extends to absolutely continuous functions under the corresponding integrability conditions.
nodes.example: Taking u=x and v′=eˣ gives ∫₀¹xeˣ dx=1.

patterns.why: The derivative transfers between paired factors with a minus sign.
Moving the derivative produces a boundary contribution.
The product rule separates into two integrals.

nodes.name: Substitution in an integral
nodes.intuition: Changing the integration coordinate changes the widths of the pieces being added. The derivative of the coordinate map provides the width conversion.
nodes.conditions: g is C¹ on [a,b] and f is continuous on an interval containing g([a,b]); oriented limits are used, so g need not be monotone.
nodes.example: With u=t², ∫₀¹2t cos(t²) dt=∫₀¹cos u du=sin 1.

patterns.why: g′ converts infinitesimal lengths between coordinates.
The integrand is composed with the coordinate map.
The same signed accumulation is expressed using different pieces.

nodes.name: Average value of a function
nodes.intuition: Spread a function's total accumulation evenly across its interval. The resulting constant has exactly the same integral.
nodes.conditions: a<b are finite and f is integrable on [a,b].
nodes.example: The average value of x² on [0,3] is (1/3)·9=3.

patterns.why: Total contribution is divided by total interval length.
The integral is the continuous analogue of a sum.
Normalization by length makes the average have the same units as f.

nodes.name: Mean value theorem for integrals
nodes.intuition: For a continuous profile, its average height occurs somewhere on the profile. A single rectangle of that height has the same signed area.
nodes.conditions: a<b are finite; f:[a,b]→R is continuous.
nodes.example: For f(x)=x² on [0,3], one valid point is c=√3.

patterns.why: The average value is attained by the continuous function.
A total integral can be represented by a constant contribution times length.

nodes.name: Improper integral on a half-line
nodes.intuition: An infinite region is handled by accumulating over finite regions and asking whether the running total settles. An infinite domain does not by itself imply an infinite total.
nodes.conditions: f is locally Riemann integrable on [a,∞); convergence means that the displayed limit exists and is finite. Absolute convergence is the stronger condition ∫_a^∞|f|<∞.
nodes.example: ∫₁^∞x^{−p} dx=1/(p−1) for p>1, and diverges for p≤1.

patterns.why: Convergence is a limit of finite integrals.
The tail is included by progressively enlarging the region.
Power-law tails have a sharp integrability threshold.

nodes.name: Gaussian integral
nodes.intuition: Squaring a one-dimensional Gaussian integral turns it into a radially symmetric area integral. Polar coordinates then replace a difficult antiderivative with a simple radial accumulation.
nodes.conditions: a is real and strictly positive; the integral is absolutely convergent.
nodes.example: With a=1/2, the integral is √(2π), giving the normalization of the standard normal density.

patterns.why: Rotational symmetry simplifies the product integral.
Polar coordinates make x²+y² into r².
Rescaling x by √a explains the a^{−1/2} factor.

nodes.name: Arc length of a parametrized curve
nodes.intuition: A velocity vector gives the distance traveled per unit parameter. Accumulating its magnitude gives total length, independent of how quickly the curve is traced.
nodes.conditions: γ:[a,b]→Rⁿ is piecewise C¹; the formula gives length with multiplicity along the traversal.
nodes.example: For γ(t)=(R cos t,R sin t), 0≤t≤2π, the length is 2πR for R>0.

patterns.why: The norm of each tangent displacement measures local length.
Infinitesimal lengths are integrated.
Orientation-preserving regular reparametrizations preserve the length.

nodes.name: Composite trapezoidal quadrature
nodes.intuition: Replace each curved segment by the line between its endpoint values. The resulting trapezoid uses the average endpoint height, so curvature controls the error.
nodes.conditions: a<b, n≥1 is an integer, h=(b−a)/n; the displayed error bound assumes f∈C²([a,b]) and the maximum is over [a,b].
nodes.example: For f(x)=x² on [0,1] with n=2, T₂=3/8, while the exact integral is 1/3.

patterns.why: Every panel uses the arithmetic mean of its endpoint heights.
Piecewise linear interpolation replaces the curved graph.
The error bound is O(h²) as the mesh shrinks.

nodes.name: Composite Simpson quadrature
nodes.intuition: Each pair of panels is integrated using a quadratic interpolant through three samples. Symmetry also makes the rule exact for cubics.
nodes.conditions: a<b; n≥2 is even, h=(b−a)/n, I=∫_a^b f; the error bound assumes f∈C⁴([a,b]) and the maximum is over [a,b].
nodes.example: For f(x)=x³ on [0,1] with two panels, S₂=(1/6)(0+4/8+1)=1/4 exactly.

patterns.why: Normalized quadrature weights form a weighted average of samples.
Each local approximation is a parabola.
Symmetric sampling cancels an odd-order error term.

nodes.name: Newton's root-finding method
nodes.intuition: Follow the tangent line to where it crosses zero, then repeat using a fresh tangent. A good local linear model can turn a moderately accurate guess into a much better one.
nodes.conditions: Each iterate requires f′(x_n)≠0. Local quadratic convergence holds for f∈C² near a simple root r with f′(r)≠0 and x₀ sufficiently close; arbitrary starting points need not converge.

patterns.why: Each step solves the tangent approximation of f(x)=0.
The next estimate is built from the current estimate.
A root is a fixed point of the Newton update map.

nodes.name: Integral form of the Taylor remainder
nodes.intuition: The missing part of a Taylor polynomial is an accumulated higher derivative. Nearby and distant points contribute with a polynomial weight determined by repeated integration.
nodes.conditions: n≥0 is an integer; f∈C^{n+1} on an interval containing a and x, using oriented integration when x<a.
nodes.example: With n=0, the formula is f(x)=f(a)+∫_a^x f′(t)dt, the fundamental theorem.

patterns.why: The error integrates derivative information over the full segment.
Repeated integration by parts builds the successive Taylor coefficients.
A finite polynomial and an exact integral account for the whole function.

nodes.name: Partial derivative
nodes.intuition: Change one coordinate while holding the others fixed. The result measures sensitivity along a coordinate axis, which is only one of many possible directions.
nodes.conditions: f is defined on an open subset of Rⁿ containing x; e_i is the ith standard basis vector; the finite limit must exist.
nodes.example: For f(x,y)=x²y, ∂_x f=2xy and ∂_y f=x².

patterns.why: The limit measures first-order change along one axis.
Different coordinates contribute separate sensitivities.

nodes.name: Gradient
nodes.latex: \nabla f=(\partial_1 f,\ldots,\partial_n f),\qquad D_v f=\nabla f\cdot v
nodes.intuition: The gradient assembles scalar sensitivities into one vector. In Euclidean coordinates it points in the direction of fastest first-order increase, with magnitude equal to that maximal rate.
nodes.conditions: f:U⊂Rⁿ→R is differentiable at x. D_v f is the derivative along vector v; interpreting a rate per unit distance requires ‖v‖₂=1.
nodes.example: For f(x,y)=x²+y², ∇f=(2x,2y), so the steepest increase points radially outward.

patterns.why: The dot product converts a small displacement into predicted change.
The Euclidean inner product identifies a linear functional with a vector.
Negating the gradient gives the steepest local descent direction in the Euclidean norm.

nodes.name: Directional derivative
nodes.intuition: Probe the function along a chosen straight path through a point. Different directions reveal different rates even at the same location.
nodes.conditions: f is defined near x∈Rⁿ, v∈Rⁿ, and the finite limit exists. For differentiable f it equals Df(x)[v]; directional derivatives in every direction alone do not imply differentiability.
nodes.example: For f(x,y)=x²+y² at (1,0), the direction (0,1) gives rate 0, while (1,0) gives rate 2.

patterns.why: The chosen tangent direction determines the measured change.
For differentiable functions, the rate is a linear function of the direction.

nodes.name: Total derivative
nodes.intuition: One linear map must approximate the change for every sufficiently small displacement. This unifies all directions into a single local model.
nodes.conditions: f maps an open subset of Rⁿ into Rᵐ; Df(x) is a linear map, and the remainder divided by ‖h‖ tends to zero as h→0 through arbitrary directions.
nodes.example: For f(x,y)=(x+y,xy), Df(x,y)[h,k]=(h+k,yh+xk).

patterns.why: A linear map captures the full first-order response.
The approximating map is additive and homogeneous in the displacement.

nodes.name: Jacobian matrix
nodes.latex: J_f(x)=\left[\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial x_j}(x)\right]_{\substack{1\le i\le m\\1\le j\le n}}
nodes.intuition: Every output can respond to every input, so sensitivities form a table. Matrix multiplication then predicts all output changes at once.
nodes.conditions: f=(f₁,…,f_m):U⊂Rⁿ→Rᵐ has the displayed partial derivatives; it represents the total derivative when f is differentiable.
nodes.example: For f(x,y)=(x²−y²,2xy), J_f=[[2x,−2y],[2y,2x]].

patterns.why: Rows separate outputs and columns separate input directions.
When total differentiability holds, the Jacobian maps small input changes to output changes.
Jacobians describe local coordinate transformations.

nodes.name: Multivariable chain rule
nodes.intuition: Local changes pass through a sequence of linear transformations. Matrix multiplication automatically sums over every intermediate route by which one input affects an output.
nodes.conditions: g:U⊂Rⁿ→Rᵐ is differentiable at x, f:V⊂Rᵐ→Rᵏ is differentiable at g(x), and g maps a neighborhood of x into V.
nodes.example: For z=f(x(t),y(t)), dz/dt=f_x x′+f_y y′.

patterns.why: The derivative respects the order of composed transformations.
Linear local maps combine by matrix multiplication.
The matrix product sums contributions through intermediate coordinates.

nodes.name: Hessian matrix
nodes.intuition: The Hessian measures how the gradient changes. Its quadratic form describes bending in each direction, distinguishing bowls, peaks and saddles.
nodes.conditions: For this entry f is C² on an open subset of Rⁿ; the Hessian is then symmetric.
nodes.example: For f(x,y)=x²−y², H=diag(2,−2), showing opposite curvatures and a saddle at the origin.

patterns.why: The second-order change is one half of hᵀHh.
Directional curvature depends on how the displacement is oriented.
Curvature helps classify stationary points and choose scaled updates.

nodes.name: Second-order multivariable Taylor expansion
nodes.intuition: A tangent plane supplies the leading prediction, and a quadratic bowl or saddle corrects for curvature. Cross terms capture interactions between coordinates.
nodes.conditions: f:U⊂Rⁿ→R is C² in a neighborhood of x; h→0 with x+h∈U.
nodes.example: For f(x,y)=xy at (0,0), the linear term vanishes and the quadratic term is exactly hk.

patterns.why: The gradient term is the first local approximation.
The Hessian captures the next-order correction and cross-coordinate interaction.
Value, slope and curvature account for successively finer structure.

nodes.name: Equality of mixed partial derivatives
nodes.intuition: For a sufficiently smooth function, infinitesimal changes in two coordinate directions can be taken in either order. The resulting symmetry is what makes the Hessian a symmetric matrix.
nodes.conditions: f is C² on an open subset of Rⁿ; weaker versions exist, but equality can fail when the relevant regularity is absent.
nodes.example: For f(x,y)=x²y³, both f_xy and f_yx equal 6xy².

patterns.why: Interchanging the two derivative directions leaves the result unchanged.
The two partial-derivative operators commute on C² functions.

nodes.name: Inverse function theorem
nodes.intuition: If the local linear model loses no directions, the nonlinear map can be undone in a small neighborhood. The inverse changes according to the inverse linear model.
nodes.conditions: f:U⊂Rⁿ→Rⁿ is C¹, U is open, and det Df(a)≠0; the theorem guarantees a C¹ local inverse between suitable neighborhoods, not global injectivity.
nodes.example: The map (x,y)↦(eˣ cos y,eˣ sin y) has nonzero Jacobian determinant and local inverses, though periodicity prevents one global inverse.

patterns.why: Invertibility of the linear approximation guarantees local nonlinear invertibility.
A nonsingular map supplies valid local coordinates.
Forward and inverse derivatives undo each other.

nodes.name: Implicit function theorem
nodes.intuition: When a constraint can respond independently to each dependent variable, it can locally solve for those variables. The derivative is the compensation needed to keep the constraint unchanged.
nodes.conditions: F:U⊂Rⁿ×Rᵐ→Rᵐ is C¹, F(a,b)=0, and D_yF(a,b) is invertible; a unique local C¹ graph y=g(x) exists near (a,b).
nodes.example: For F(x,y)=x²+y²−1 near (0,1), the upper circle is the local graph y=√(1−x²).

patterns.why: A linear solve predicts how dependent coordinates must move.
The zero set becomes a smooth local surface.
The constraint selects a valid collection of local independent coordinates.

nodes.name: Multiple integral as accumulation over cells
nodes.intuition: The same height-times-width idea works with area or volume cells. Every cell contributes its local value multiplied by how much space it occupies.
nodes.conditions: Ω⊂Rⁿ is bounded and Jordan measurable; the formula is understood using fine rectangular partitions and a Riemann-integrable extension by zero to a bounding rectangle, with tagged cells Q_i.
nodes.example: On a unit square, integrating f(x,y)=x+y gives 1.

patterns.why: Local density is multiplied by cell volume and added.
Fine partitions approach a partition-independent total.
Cell volumes express the geometry of the underlying domain.

nodes.name: Multivariable change of variables
nodes.intuition: A coordinate change reshapes small volume elements. The determinant measures their volume expansion, while the absolute value removes orientation from ordinary volume.
nodes.conditions: U⊂Rⁿ is open, T:U→T(U) is a C¹ diffeomorphism, and f is nonnegative measurable or integrable on T(U); the corresponding integrals may be infinite in the nonnegative case.
nodes.example: For T(u,v)=(2u,3v), each area element is multiplied by |det diag(2,3)|=6.

patterns.why: The same integral is rewritten in a different coordinate system.
The Jacobian determinant gives local volume scaling.
Volume responds to all local stretching directions together.

nodes.name: Integration in polar coordinates
nodes.intuition: A thin polar cell has radial width dr and sideways width r dθ. The factor r records how the same angular slice becomes wider farther from the origin.
nodes.conditions: D⊂(0,∞)×(α,α+2π) is measurable, its polar image is Ω, and f is nonnegative measurable or integrable; the ray seam and origin may be added or removed as measure-zero sets.
nodes.example: The area of a radius-R disk is ∫₀^{2π}∫₀^R r dr dθ=πR².

patterns.why: Cartesian position is replaced by radius and angle.
Rotational symmetry often removes angular dependence.
Angular lengths scale proportionally with radius.

nodes.name: Line integrals of scalar and vector fields
nodes.intuition: A scalar line integral accumulates density along length. A vector line integral accumulates the component aligned with travel, so reversing direction changes its sign.
nodes.conditions: γ:[a,b]→Rⁿ is piecewise C¹; f and F are continuous along its image. Integrals include traversal multiplicity.
nodes.example: A constant tangential force of magnitude 3 along a straight path of length 2 does work 6.

patterns.why: Contributions are integrated along a path.
The tangent norm or dot product measures how the path samples the field.
Regular parametrizations produce the same oriented or length-weighted integral.

nodes.name: Fundamental theorem for line integrals
nodes.intuition: Moving through a potential field accumulates exactly the total change in potential. Different routes between the same endpoints give the same result.
nodes.conditions: φ is C¹ on an open set containing the piecewise C¹ path γ:[a,b]→Rⁿ.
nodes.example: For φ(x,y)=x²+y², every path from (0,0) to (1,2) has gradient line integral 5.

patterns.why: Path accumulation collapses to endpoint values.
Closed-loop work is zero for a gradient field.
The chain rule differentiates φ∘γ along the path.

nodes.name: Divergence
nodes.intuition: Divergence measures the local excess of outward flow over inward flow. Positive divergence describes expansion or a source; negative divergence describes compression or a sink.
nodes.conditions: F:U⊂Rⁿ→Rⁿ is C¹; the local flux interpretation uses the outward flux per unit volume of shrinking regular neighborhoods.
nodes.example: For F(x)=x in Rⁿ, div F=n: every coordinate direction contributes one unit of expansion.

patterns.why: Directional expansion rates add to a total local source strength.
Divergence enters balances between stored amount and net outgoing flow.
It converts infinitesimal boundary flux into a volume density.

nodes.name: Curl in three dimensions
nodes.intuition: Curl measures infinitesimal circulation around each axis. Its component through a small oriented surface records the local tendency of the flow to turn.
nodes.conditions: F is a C¹ vector field on an open subset of oriented Euclidean R³, using a right-handed coordinate system.
nodes.example: For F=(−y,x,0), curl F=(0,0,2), consistent with rotation around the z-axis.

patterns.why: Each component measures circulation in a perpendicular coordinate plane.
Local circulation density becomes boundary circulation after integration.
The coordinate formula represents an oriented geometric vector independent of rotations of a right-handed frame.

nodes.name: Laplacian
nodes.intuition: The Laplacian adds curvature in all coordinate directions. It measures whether a value sits below or above its nearby average, which makes it the natural operator for diffusion and equilibrium.
nodes.conditions: f is C² on an open subset of Euclidean Rⁿ; other metrics require their corresponding Laplace–Beltrami operator.
nodes.example: For f(x,y)=x²+y², Δf=4; for f(x,y)=x²−y², Δf=0.

patterns.why: For smooth functions, nearby spherical averages differ from the central value at second order by a constant times Δf.
It is the trace of the second-derivative quadratic form.
The Euclidean Laplacian is invariant under orthogonal changes of coordinates.

nodes.name: Flux through a parametrized surface
nodes.intuition: The cross product of two surface tangent vectors gives an oriented area element. Only the normal component of the field passes through that element.
nodes.conditions: r:D⊂R²→R³ is a regular C¹ parametrization, injective except on permitted boundary seams; F is continuous on the surface and the orientation agrees with r_u×r_v. Piecewise surfaces are summed over compatible patches.
nodes.example: For an upward horizontal unit square and F=(0,0,5), the flux is 5.

patterns.why: Two tangent directions determine area and its normal orientation.
Local normal flux is summed over the surface.
The cross product supplies the area conversion from parameter coordinates.

nodes.name: Green's theorem in the plane
nodes.intuition: When local circulations are added over a region, contributions on internal edges cancel. Only the circulation around the outer boundary and any hole boundaries remains.
nodes.conditions: D is a bounded planar region with piecewise smooth boundary; P,Q are C¹ on an open neighborhood of its closure; ∂D is positively oriented, with the region on the left.
nodes.example: Taking P=−y/2 and Q=x/2 makes the circulation equal the area of D.

patterns.why: A boundary integral equals an integral of local interior circulation.
Internal contributions cancel during summation.
Cancellation leaves only the net boundary effect.

nodes.name: Stokes' theorem for curl
nodes.intuition: Local circulation across a surface adds up to circulation around its edge. Interior boundaries disappear because adjacent pieces traverse them in opposite directions.
nodes.conditions: S is an oriented piecewise smooth compact surface in R³ with piecewise smooth boundary; F is C¹ near S; boundary orientation follows the right-hand rule.
nodes.example: For F=(−y/2,x/2,0), either side over the unit disk equals π.

patterns.why: The surface curl integral is determined by boundary circulation.
Local oriented circulation adds with cancellation of internal edges.
Compatible orientation keeps the geometric equality independent of parametrization.

nodes.name: Divergence theorem
nodes.intuition: All interior inflows and outflows cancel when a region is assembled. What remains is the net flow crossing its outer boundary.
nodes.conditions: Ω⊂Rⁿ is bounded with piecewise C¹ boundary, F is C¹ on a neighborhood of its closure, and n is the outward unit normal.
nodes.example: For F(x)=x in a three-dimensional ball, 3·volume equals radius times surface area.

patterns.why: An interior source integral equals boundary flux.
Net production inside a region must appear as outgoing flux.
Local expansion is integrated over volume.

nodes.name: Generalized Stokes' theorem
nodes.intuition: The same boundary principle governs intervals, surfaces and higher-dimensional spaces. Exterior differentiation is the operation whose accumulated effect is read on the boundary.
nodes.conditions: M is a compact oriented smooth n-manifold with smooth boundary; ω is a C¹ differential (n−1)-form on M; ∂M has the induced boundary orientation. The dimension n is a positive integer.
nodes.example: For M=[a,b] and the 0-form ω=f, the statement is ∫_a^b f′(x)dx=f(b)−f(a).

patterns.why: Exterior differentiation inside M corresponds to restriction to its boundary.
Integration pairs differentiation of forms with taking boundaries of domains.
The statement is coordinate-independent and uses orientation rather than a chosen coordinate grid.

nodes.name: Green's first identity
nodes.intuition: Integration by parts extends to a region in space by replacing endpoint terms with normal flux through the boundary. It converts second derivatives into a pairing of first derivatives.
nodes.conditions: Ω⊂Rⁿ is bounded with C¹ boundary; u and v are C² on a neighborhood of its closure; ∂_n v=∇v·n uses the outward normal.
nodes.example: If v=u and u=0 on the boundary, ∫uΔu=−∫|∇u|².

patterns.why: The cost of moving a spatial derivative is a boundary normal derivative.
The Laplacian pairs with a gradient inner product after integration.
Choosing u=v produces the Dirichlet energy.

nodes.name: Green's second identity
nodes.intuition: Swap two functions in Green's first identity and subtract. The symmetric gradient terms cancel, exposing the precise boundary obstruction to self-adjointness of the Laplacian.
nodes.conditions: Ω⊂Rⁿ is bounded with C¹ boundary; u and v are C² on a neighborhood of its closure; n is outward.
nodes.example: If u=v=0 on the boundary, ∫uΔv=∫vΔu.

patterns.why: It compares an operator acting on either side of an integral pairing.
Suitable boundary conditions make the Laplacian symmetric under exchange of u and v.
Boundary data exactly accounts for the failure of the interior pairings to agree.

nodes.name: Curl of a gradient and divergence of a curl
nodes.intuition: Certain differential constructions automatically erase the next kind of circulation or source. Each term cancels with its opposite after swapping mixed derivatives.
nodes.conditions: f is C² and F is a C² vector field on an open subset of R³. The converses require additional topological hypotheses and are not asserted here.
nodes.example: Every smooth potential field ∇f has zero curl, even though an arbitrary curl-free field on a domain with holes need not have a global potential.

patterns.why: These pairs of differential operators compose to zero.
Equality of mixed partials causes the cancellation.
A field represented as a curl has no local divergence sources.

nodes.name: Reynolds transport theorem
nodes.intuition: A total can change because its density changes inside the region or because the region's boundary moves across material. The theorem separates those two contributions.
nodes.conditions: Ω(t) is a bounded C¹ domain transported by a sufficiently smooth velocity field v, and ρ is C¹ in space and time; boundary orientation is outward. The formula is local in times where the smooth flow remains a diffeomorphism.
nodes.example: For an expanding interval [0,R(t)] and density 1, the derivative of its length is R′(t), entirely from boundary motion.

patterns.why: A moving control volume requires accounting for material crossing its boundary.
Interior time change and moving-boundary flux make separate terms.
Pulling the moving region back through its flow gives a fixed integration domain.

nodes.name: Limit of a sequence
nodes.intuition: Convergence means that any requested accuracy eventually holds forever. The threshold may depend on the requested accuracy, but every later term must satisfy it.
nodes.conditions: x_n and L are real numbers; replace absolute value by a metric to define convergence in a metric space.
nodes.example: For x_n=1/n and L=0, choosing N>1/ε ensures |x_n|<ε whenever n≥N.

patterns.why: The quantifiers make eventual closeness precise.
Every positive error scale must eventually be reached.

nodes.name: Cauchy criterion for convergence
nodes.latex: x_n\text{ converges in }\mathbb R\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists N\ \forall m,n\ge N:\ |x_m-x_n|<\varepsilon
nodes.intuition: A sequence can be recognized as convergent without knowing its destination: its late terms must crowd together. Completeness of the number system turns that internal agreement into an actual limit.
nodes.conditions: The equivalence holds for real sequences, and more generally in complete metric spaces; a Cauchy sequence need not converge inside an incomplete space.
nodes.example: Rational approximations to √2 are Cauchy in Q but have no limit in Q; they do converge in R.

patterns.why: Pairwise tail closeness replaces reference to an unknown limit.
The criterion uses only distances between points.

nodes.name: Monotone bounded sequence theorem
nodes.intuition: A quantity that only increases and cannot escape above must approach its least upper bound. Completeness rules out an unreachable gap just below that bound.
nodes.conditions: x_n is a nondecreasing real sequence bounded above; a dual statement holds for nonincreasing sequences bounded below.
nodes.example: The partial sums of ∑_{n=1}∞2^{−n} rise toward 1 without exceeding it.

patterns.why: Monotonicity plus a bound guarantees a limit.
Nonnegative increments produce increasing partial totals.

nodes.name: Limit superior and limit inferior
nodes.intuition: Remove earlier terms and track the largest and smallest values still possible. These tail envelopes identify the eventual upper and lower levels even when the sequence oscillates.
nodes.conditions: x_n is a real or extended-real sequence; tail suprema and infima are taken in the extended real line.
nodes.example: For x_n=(−1)^n+1/n, limsup x_n=1 and liminf x_n=−1.

patterns.why: Tail envelopes generalize limits to oscillatory sequences.
Upper and lower asymptotic behavior are tracked separately.

nodes.name: Comparison test for nonnegative series
nodes.intuition: A smaller nonnegative accumulation cannot overflow when a larger one stays finite. A known series can therefore serve as an upper budget for an unknown one.
nodes.conditions: The inequality holds for all sufficiently large n; changing finitely many finite terms does not affect convergence.
nodes.example: Because 1/(n²+1)≤1/n², the first series converges with the convergent p-series of exponent 2.

patterns.why: Termwise bounds become bounds on partial sums.
Bounded increasing partial sums converge.

nodes.name: Ratio test
nodes.latex: L=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right|:\qquad L<1\Rightarrow\sum a_n\text{ absolutely converges},\quad L>1\Rightarrow\sum a_n\text{ diverges}
nodes.intuition: Successive terms that eventually shrink by a fixed factor below one fit under a geometric series. If they grow by a factor above one, they cannot even approach zero.
nodes.conditions: a_n is nonzero for all sufficiently large n, the displayed limit exists in [0,∞], and the case L=1 is inconclusive.
nodes.example: For a_n=z^n/n! with fixed z≠0, the ratio |z|/(n+1) tends to 0.

patterns.why: The comparison uses the relative size of consecutive terms.
The limiting ratio controls a geometric tail.
Each term is compared directly with its predecessor.

nodes.name: Root test and power-series radius
nodes.latex: L=\limsup_{n\to\infty}|a_n|^{1/n},\quad L<1\Rightarrow\sum a_n\text{ absolutely converges};\qquad R^{-1}=\limsup_{n\to\infty}|c_n|^{1/n}
nodes.intuition: The nth root extracts the effective exponential scale of a term. Applying that scale test to c_n z^n identifies exactly the open disk where a power series converges.
nodes.conditions: For ∑a_n, L>1 gives divergence and L=1 is inconclusive. For ∑c_n z^n, R is its radius of convergence, with 1/0=∞ and 1/∞=0; boundary points require separate analysis.
nodes.example: For ∑z^n, limsup|c_n|^{1/n}=1, so the convergence radius is 1.

patterns.why: Roots isolate the geometric growth rate of coefficients.
A limsup yields a convergence criterion even with irregular terms.
Taking nth roots is equivalent to averaging logarithmic size over n.

nodes.name: Alternating series error bound
nodes.intuition: Alternating over- and underestimates squeeze the answer between successive partial sums. The first omitted term gives a direct accuracy certificate.
nodes.conditions: b_n≥0 is nonincreasing and b_n→0; S_N is the partial sum through n=N.
nodes.example: Approximating log 2 by its first N alternating harmonic terms has error at most 1/(N+1).

patterns.why: Monotone shrinking oscillations converge by squeezing.
Positive and negative contributions cancel in a controlled order.

nodes.name: Cauchy product of absolutely convergent series
nodes.intuition: To multiply two expansions, combine all pairs whose indices have the same total. Absolute convergence makes this regrouping safe.
nodes.conditions: a_n and b_n are real or complex, and both series converge absolutely; the displayed product series then converges absolutely.
nodes.example: Multiplying ∑z^n/n! by ∑w^n/n! groups terms into the exponential addition law e^z e^w=e^{z+w}.

patterns.why: Pairwise combinations are grouped by the combined index.
The inner sum enumerates all ways to split n into two nonnegative indices.
Absolute convergence permits rearranging and grouping infinite contributions.

nodes.name: Uniform convergence
nodes.intuition: One common stage of approximation must work at every input. This prevents a hidden bad region from moving around as the sequence advances.
nodes.conditions: f_n and f are real- or complex-valued functions on the same set E; the supremum may initially be infinite, but it must tend to zero.
nodes.example: x^n→0 on [0,1) pointwise, but not uniformly, because values arbitrarily near 1 remain near 1.

patterns.why: Convergence controls the worst error over the entire domain.
The supremum norm measures distance between functions.

nodes.name: Weierstrass M-test
nodes.latex: |f_n(x)|\le M_n,\quad\sum_n M_n<\infty\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\sum_n f_n(x)\text{ converges uniformly and absolutely}
nodes.intuition: If every function is bounded by one term of a fixed convergent numerical series, every input shares the same small tail. The numerical series pays for all approximation errors at once.
nodes.conditions: The bound holds for every x in a common set E and each n, with M_n≥0; the numerical sum is finite.
nodes.example: On |x|≤R, |x^n/n!|≤R^n/n!, proving uniform convergence of the exponential series on every bounded disk.

patterns.why: A common summable tail gives uniform convergence.
The worst possible contributions still have finite total size.

nodes.name: Passing a uniform limit through a finite integral
nodes.intuition: The worst height error times interval length bounds the total area error. Uniformly accurate profiles therefore have accurate accumulated totals.
nodes.conditions: a<b are finite; f_n are Riemann integrable on [a,b] and converge uniformly to f; then f is Riemann integrable.
nodes.example: If two profiles differ everywhere by at most 0.01 on an interval of length 5, their integrals differ by at most 0.05.

patterns.why: Uniform convergence justifies interchanging a limit and a finite integral.
A global error is bounded by local worst error times total length.
The estimate scales linearly with the size of the domain.

nodes.name: Termwise differentiation of a function series
nodes.intuition: Differentiating an infinite sum is safe when the derivative tails are controlled uniformly and the original values settle at one anchor point. Control of values alone would not prevent rapidly oscillating slopes.
nodes.conditions: On a finite interval [a,b], f_n∈C¹; ∑f_n′ converges uniformly, and ∑f_n(x₀) converges at some x₀∈[a,b]. Then ∑f_n converges uniformly to a C¹ function and the identity holds on (a,b).
nodes.example: On every compact interval, the exponential series and its derivative series satisfy these conditions, giving (eˣ)′=eˣ.

patterns.why: A uniform bound on derivative tails permits the interchange.
The finite linearity of differentiation extends to a controlled infinite sum.
Integration of the derivative series reconstructs the function from one point.

nodes.name: Banach contraction theorem
nodes.latex: d(Tx,Ty)\le q\,d(x,y),\quad0\le q<1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad T x^*=x^*,\qquad d(T^n x_0,x^*)\le\frac{q^n}{1-q}d(x_1,x_0)
nodes.intuition: A map that consistently shrinks distances brings all repeated trajectories to one common self-consistent state. Geometric shrinkage also gives an explicit error bound.
nodes.conditions: T maps a nonempty complete metric space X into itself and has the displayed global contraction constant q; x₁=T x₀; the fixed point is unique. The displayed error bound is stated for integers n≥1.
nodes.example: T(x)=(x+2)/3 on R has q=1/3 and unique fixed point 1.

patterns.why: The limit solves x=T(x).
The theorem controls repeated application of one update.
A geometric tail bound makes the iterates Cauchy and quantifies convergence.

nodes.name: Integral with respect to a measure
nodes.latex: \int f\,d\mu=\sup_{\substack{0\le s\le f\\s\ {\rm simple}}}\int s\,d\mu,\qquad\int\sum_{j=1}^m a_j{\bf1}_{E_j}\,d\mu=\sum_{j=1}^m a_j\mu(E_j)
nodes.intuition: Approximate a nonnegative function from below by finitely many value levels. Each level contributes its height times the measure of the set where it occurs.
nodes.conditions: For the first formula f≥0 is measurable on a measure space; for the second, a_j≥0 and the measurable E_j are pairwise disjoint. Signed or complex integration requires integrability of |f|, unless a specified one-sided extended integral is used.
nodes.example: Counting measure turns the integral into a sum; a probability measure turns it into an expectation.

patterns.why: Values are weighted by the measure of the sets carrying them.
Simple functions separate the range into finitely many levels.
Taking a supremum of lower approximations defines the full integral.

nodes.name: Monotone convergence theorem
nodes.intuition: Build a nonnegative function by adding content without ever removing it. The total integral then grows to the integral of the completed function, even if that total is infinite.
nodes.conditions: f_n are nonnegative measurable functions on a measure space and increase pointwise almost everywhere to f; equality is in [0,∞].
nodes.example: For any nonnegative measurable f, the truncated functions min(f,n) have integrals increasing to ∫f.

patterns.why: Monotone approximation permits exchanging limit and integral.
Adding nonnegative content cannot hide cancellation.

nodes.name: Fatou's lemma
nodes.intuition: Nonnegative mass can disappear in a pointwise limit by escaping or concentrating, so equality is not guaranteed. The integral of what remains cannot exceed the limiting lower total.
nodes.conditions: f_n are nonnegative measurable functions on a common measure space; extended values are permitted.
nodes.example: For f_n=n·1_(0,1/n) on (0,1), each integral is 1 but the pointwise limit is 0, giving a strict inequality.

patterns.why: A one-sided inequality survives without a common dominating function.
Nonnegativity prevents cancellations that would break the lower-bound argument.

nodes.name: Dominated convergence theorem
nodes.latex: f_n\to f\ {\rm a.e.},\quad |f_n|\le g\in L^1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\to0,\quad\int f_n\,d\mu\to\int f\,d\mu
nodes.intuition: Pointwise convergence controls the eventual value at each location, while one integrable envelope prevents mass from hiding in narrow spikes or distant tails. Together they allow limits to pass through accumulation.
nodes.conditions: f_n are measurable real- or complex-valued functions, f_n→f almost everywhere, and a single nonnegative integrable g bounds |f_n| almost everywhere for every n.
nodes.example: On [0,1], x^n→0 almost everywhere and |x^n|≤1, so ∫₀¹x^n dx→0.

patterns.why: A common integrable bound justifies interchanging limit and integral.
The envelope prevents uncontrolled contributions to the total.

nodes.name: Fubini's theorem
nodes.intuition: An absolutely integrable total can be accumulated by rows or by columns. Absolute integrability prevents positive and negative contributions from depending on the chosen summation order.
nodes.conditions: (X,μ) and (Y,ν) are σ-finite measure spaces; f is measurable and ∫|f| d(μ×ν)<∞. Inner integrals exist for almost every outer variable.
nodes.example: On [0,1]², integrating x+y in either order gives 1.

patterns.why: A product domain is integrated one coordinate at a time.
The grouping order of an absolutely integrable total does not affect its value.
Exchanging the order of the two integrations preserves the result.

nodes.name: Tonelli's theorem
nodes.intuition: For nonnegative contributions, regrouping cannot create ambiguous cancellation. Repeated integration is valid even before knowing whether the total is finite.
nodes.conditions: (X,μ) and (Y,ν) are σ-finite measure spaces, and f:X×Y→[0,∞] is measurable; all equalities allow the value +∞.
nodes.example: Tonelli permits squaring ∫e^{−x²}dx as a nonnegative double integral before its value has been computed.

patterns.why: Only nonnegative mass is accumulated.
The integral over a product is assembled from slices.
Monotone simple approximations support the interchange, including infinite totals.

nodes.name: Lp norm of a function
nodes.intuition: Measure function size by aggregating powers of its magnitude. Larger p places more emphasis on peaks, while p=∞ records the largest size outside negligible sets.
nodes.conditions: f is measurable; Lp consists of functions with finite displayed norm, identified when equal almost everywhere. For p≥1 these are norms; p<1 is not included.
nodes.example: On a probability space, ‖X‖₂=√E|X|² is a root-mean-square size.

patterns.why: On normalized measure spaces, the norm is a power mean of |f|.
‖f−g‖_p measures distance between functions.
Multiplying a function by a scalar scales its norm by the scalar's magnitude.

nodes.name: Hölder's inequality
nodes.intuition: Two functions can be paired safely when the integrability demanded of one compensates for that of the other. Reciprocal exponents describe this balance.
nodes.conditions: 1≤p,q≤∞ with 1/p+1/q=1 and 1/∞=0; f∈Lp(μ), g∈Lq(μ) on a common measure space.
nodes.example: For p=q=2, the integral pairing is bounded by the product of root-square sizes, the Cauchy–Schwarz case.

patterns.why: The conjugate exponent q supplies natural bounded pairings against Lp functions.
Convex power inequalities underlie the bound.
Both sides scale identically in f and g.

nodes.name: Minkowski's inequality
nodes.intuition: The size of a combined function cannot exceed the sum of the separate sizes. This makes Lp function spaces obey the same triangle geometry as ordinary vectors.
nodes.conditions: 1≤p≤∞, and f,g∈Lp on the same measure space.
nodes.example: With counting measure and p=2, this becomes the Euclidean triangle inequality for finite vectors.

patterns.why: The inequality makes the Lp distance satisfy the triangle axiom.
Lp unit balls are convex for p≥1.
Bounding separate components bounds their sum.

nodes.name: Convolution
nodes.intuition: Slide one profile across another and add the products of their overlapping values. With a nonnegative normalized kernel, convolution is a moving weighted average.
nodes.conditions: For the basic setting f,g∈L¹(Rⁿ), the integral exists almost everywhere and f*g∈L¹; more general exponent conditions are supplied by Young's inequality.
nodes.example: Convolving two uniform densities on [0,1] produces the triangular density of their independent sum.

patterns.why: A nonnegative kernel with integral one assigns normalized local weights.
Successive translation-invariant linear filters combine by convolution.
All decompositions x=(x−y)+y contribute to the result.

nodes.name: Young's convolution inequality
nodes.intuition: The integrability of two profiles controls the size of their combined convolution. A normalized L¹ smoothing kernel cannot increase any Lp norm.
nodes.conditions: 1≤p,q,r≤∞ with the displayed relation and 1/∞=0; f∈Lp(Rⁿ), g∈Lq(Rⁿ); convolution is defined almost everywhere under these conditions.
nodes.example: If g≥0 and ∫g=1, then ‖f*g‖₂≤‖f‖₂.

patterns.why: A normalized smoothing kernel averages translations without enlarging Lp size.
The exponent relation matches the dimensional scaling of convolution.
Convexity and Hölder-type estimates control the averaged magnitude.

nodes.name: Approximate identities and mollification
nodes.intuition: Average over neighborhoods that shrink toward each point. The approximation becomes smooth while recovering the original function in an integral norm.
nodes.conditions: ρ≥0 is C∞ with compact support in Rⁿ and ∫ρ=1; ε→0⁺; f∈Lp(Rⁿ), 1≤p<∞. Pointwise recovery everywhere is not asserted.
nodes.example: Mollifying the corner of |x| rounds it; on compact intervals the smoothed versions approach the original function.

patterns.why: The kernel gives a localized weighted average.
ε^{−n} preserves total kernel mass as its width shrinks.
Shrinking averages converge in Lp for finite p.

nodes.name: Weak derivative
nodes.intuition: Move the derivative onto smooth test functions and ask which function reproduces the resulting measurements. This preserves differentiation even when a classical slope fails at some points.
nodes.conditions: Ω⊂Rⁿ is open and u,v∈L¹_loc(Ω); a weak derivative is unique up to equality almost everywhere.
nodes.example: The function |x| has weak derivative sign(x), although its classical derivative fails at x=0.

patterns.why: The derivative is defined by its action inside an integral pairing.
Compact support removes boundary terms from integration by parts.
The definition behaves well under suitable integral-norm limits.

nodes.name: Sobolev norm
nodes.intuition: A Sobolev space measures both the amount of a function and the amount of its variation. Functions can be compared through integrated derivative information instead of requiring every derivative to be pointwise smooth.
nodes.conditions: Ω⊂Rⁿ is open, k≥0 is an integer and 1≤p<∞; all derivatives in the sum are weak derivatives in Lp. Multi-index α has nonnegative integer components and |α| is its total order.
nodes.example: For k=1,p=2, the squared norm is ∫|u|²+∫|∇u|², combining amplitude and gradient energy.

patterns.why: The norm defines a distance that controls values and derivatives.
Derivative orders contribute separately to total regularity.
At p=2 the squared norm comes from a Hilbert-space inner product.

nodes.name: Derivative of a distribution
nodes.intuition: A generalized function is described by how it responds to test functions. Its derivative is defined by shifting differentiation to the test function with a minus sign.
nodes.conditions: T is a distribution on an open Ω⊂Rⁿ, meaning a continuous linear functional on C_c∞(Ω); φ belongs to that test-function space.
nodes.example: The Heaviside step function satisfies H′=δ₀ as a distribution: a jump becomes a concentrated point mass.

patterns.why: Differentiation is defined through the dual action on test functions.
The derivative is a linear operation on distributions.
Jump and boundary effects survive as singular distributions.

nodes.name: Riesz representation in a real Hilbert space
nodes.intuition: Every continuous linear measurement of a Hilbert-space vector is an inner product with one specific vector. Geometry therefore represents the entire continuous dual space.
nodes.conditions: H is a real Hilbert space and H* denotes its bounded linear functionals; completeness is essential for this general statement.
nodes.example: For L², the functional f↦∫fg with fixed g∈L² is represented by the function g.

patterns.why: Vectors represent continuous linear functionals.
The representing vector has exactly the norm of the measurement.
The proof identifies the one direction orthogonal to the functional's kernel.

nodes.name: Norm-preserving Hahn–Banach extension
nodes.intuition: A bounded linear measurement on a subspace can be extended to the whole space without making its worst-case sensitivity larger. Existing linear information need not become distorted when the domain grows.
nodes.conditions: X is a real normed vector space, M⊂X is a linear subspace, and ℓ is a bounded linear functional on M; the extension L is linear and bounded. It need not be unique.
nodes.example: For any nonzero vector x, there is a norm-one functional L with L(x)=‖x‖.

patterns.why: Linear functionals provide measurements that detect vector size.
The unit ball supplies the convex bound respected by the extension.
The functional's norm is preserved when extending its domain.

nodes.name: Norm of a bounded linear operator
nodes.intuition: The operator norm is the largest possible amplification of an input of unit size. Successive transformations amplify by at most the product of their separate worst cases.
nodes.conditions: T:X→Y and S:Y→Z are bounded linear maps between normed spaces; the first supremum is finite by boundedness.
nodes.example: For a real matrix acting with Euclidean norms, ‖A‖₂ is its largest singular value.

patterns.why: It records worst-case multiplicative amplification.
Amplification under composition is submultiplicative.
The norm depends on the chosen input and output geometries.

nodes.name: Neumann series for an inverse
nodes.intuition: The geometric-series idea survives when the ratio is a linear operator. Repeated corrections Aⁿ sum to an inverse if each application is small enough.
nodes.conditions: A is a bounded linear operator on a Banach space and ‖A‖<1; the series converges in operator norm.
nodes.example: The solution of x=b+Ax is b+Ab+A²b+⋯ under the same contraction condition.

patterns.why: Successive powers describe repeated propagation or correction.
A geometric norm bound proves convergence.
The inverse identity uses multiplication and addition in an operator algebra.

nodes.name: Arzelà–Ascoli compactness
nodes.intuition: A family cannot evade convergence if neither its height nor its rate of spatial variation runs away. These two controls guarantee a uniformly convergent subsequence.
nodes.conditions: K is a compact metric space; f_n∈C(K,R) are uniformly bounded and equicontinuous; the limit f is continuous. The whole sequence need not converge.
nodes.example: Functions on [0,1] bounded by 1 with a common Lipschitz constant 2 satisfy the hypotheses.

patterns.why: Compactness extracts a convergent subsequence.
Uniform control is expressed in the supremum metric on functions.
A common Lipschitz bound is one sufficient way to control local variation uniformly.

nodes.name: Weierstrass polynomial approximation
nodes.intuition: Polynomials can approximate every continuous profile on a closed finite interval as closely as desired. The approximating polynomial need not be the function's Taylor polynomial.
nodes.conditions: a<b are finite and f is real-valued and continuous; the polynomial can depend on f and ε.
nodes.example: The corner function |x| on [−1,1] can be uniformly approximated by polynomials despite failing to have a derivative at 0.

patterns.why: Polynomial combinations form a dense collection of building blocks.
Arbitrarily small uniform error is possible.
The approximation family is closed under addition and multiplication.

nodes.name: Parseval's identity for Fourier series
nodes.intuition: A function's squared size is exactly the sum of squared sizes of its orthogonal frequency components. Changing to Fourier coordinates preserves energy.
nodes.conditions: f∈L²([−π,π]); Fourier coefficients use the displayed normalization. The equality concerns L² energy and does not assert pointwise convergence of the series.
nodes.example: For f(x)=cos x, only coefficients at k=±1 equal 1/2, so normalized energy is 1/4+1/4=1/2.

patterns.why: Cross-frequency terms vanish in the inner product.
Energy is preserved when passing to Fourier coefficients.
All L² energy is accounted for by the complete Fourier basis.

nodes.name: Bessel's inequality
nodes.intuition: Projecting onto orthogonal directions can only capture energy already present. If the directions are incomplete, some energy may remain outside their span.
nodes.conditions: x belongs to an inner product space and (e_n) is an orthonormal sequence; the squared-coefficient series is nonnegative and bounded by ‖x‖².
nodes.example: In R³, projecting (1,2,3) onto the first two coordinate axes captures 1²+2²=5 of the total energy 14.

patterns.why: Different projection components have no cross terms.
The captured components leave an orthogonal residual.
Squared norm splits into projection energy and residual energy.

nodes.name: Poincaré inequality with zero boundary values
nodes.intuition: A function fixed to zero at the boundary cannot become large without changing somewhere. Its gradient therefore controls its entire amplitude in an integral sense.
nodes.conditions: Ω⊂Rⁿ is bounded and open; H₀¹ is the closure of C_c∞(Ω) in H¹; a finite constant C_Ω depends on Ω. Without a boundary or zero-mean condition, nonzero constants invalidate such a bound.
nodes.example: On (0,L), the sharp constant is L/π and equality is attained by sin(πx/L).

patterns.why: Boundary constraints control interior size.
The domain's size influences the constant.
Gradient energy bounds the squared L² amplitude.

nodes.name: Integration against a pushforward measure
nodes.intuition: Transport the mass through a map, then measure a quantity at the destination. The same answer comes from measuring the composed quantity before moving the mass.
nodes.conditions: T:X→Y is measurable between measurable spaces, μ is a measure on X, and g:Y→[0,∞] is measurable or g is integrable against T#μ. No inverse or differentiability of T is required.
nodes.example: If a die outcome X is squared, averaging g(X²) uses the distribution obtained by pushing the die measure through T(x)=x².

patterns.why: A map transfers the integration measure to its output space.
Testing after transport equals testing a composed function before transport.
Moving measures and composing test functions are dual operations.

nodes.name: Radon–Nikodym density
nodes.intuition: When one measure never assigns mass to a set the other regards as negligible, it can be described by a density relative to that reference measure. The density is a local conversion factor between ways of weighting space.
nodes.conditions: μ and ν are σ-finite positive measures on the same measurable space, with ν absolutely continuous with respect to μ; dν/dμ is a nonnegative measurable function unique μ-almost everywhere.
nodes.example: A probability distribution with a Lebesgue density p satisfies P(A)=∫_A p(x)dx.

patterns.why: The derivative is the factor converting reference mass into target mass.
Integrals under one measure can be rewritten using another measure and a density.
Measures are characterized by their integrals against measurable tests.

nodes.name: Riesz–Thorin interpolation
nodes.intuition: Bounds at two endpoint integrability scales control every intermediate scale. Reciprocal exponents interpolate arithmetically while the operator bound interpolates geometrically.
nodes.conditions: 0<θ<1; 1≤p_j,q_j≤∞ on σ-finite measure spaces, with 1/∞=0; T is a complex-linear operator on L^{p₀}+L^{p₁} whose endpoint operator norms are at most finite positive M₀,M₁.
nodes.example: If T is a contraction on both L¹ and L∞, it is a contraction on every intermediate Lp.

patterns.why: Reciprocal exponents are weighted arithmetic averages.
The norm estimate is a weighted geometric mean, linear after taking logs.
The theorem expresses a log-convex interpolation principle.

nodes.name: Weak formulation of the Dirichlet Poisson problem
nodes.intuition: Ask the equation to hold after averaging against every test function. Moving a derivative onto the test function lets the solution have only square-integrable first derivatives.
nodes.conditions: Ω⊂Rⁿ is bounded and open, f∈L²(Ω), and H₀¹ encodes homogeneous Dirichlet boundary values; this is the weak form of −Δu=f. It has a unique solution under these hypotheses.
nodes.example: On (0,1) with f=1, u(x)=x(1−x)/2 satisfies the weak equation and vanishes at both endpoints.

patterns.why: Every test function gives an integral measurement of the equation.
The gradient pairing is the bilinear form associated with Dirichlet energy.
The test space incorporates zero boundary values.

nodes.name: Lax–Milgram theorem
nodes.intuition: A bilinear energy that controls every direction can convert any bounded linear forcing into one unique response. Coercivity supplies both solvability and a stability estimate.
nodes.conditions: H is a real Hilbert space; a is bilinear with |a(u,v)|≤M‖u‖‖v‖ and a(v,v)≥α‖v‖² for M<∞ and α>0; ℓ∈H*. The theorem asserts existence and uniqueness of the displayed u; a need not be symmetric.
nodes.example: For a(u,v)=∫∇u·∇v on H₀¹ of a bounded domain, Poincaré supplies coercivity and gives the Dirichlet Poisson solution.

patterns.why: The bilinear form identifies a state with its response to every test vector.
A positive quadratic lower bound prevents nearly invisible directions.
The forcing norm controls the solution norm quantitatively.

nodes.name: Complex derivative
nodes.intuition: The same complex multiplier must describe small changes arriving from every direction in the plane. This is far more restrictive than checking a slope along the real axis alone.
nodes.conditions: f is defined on an open subset of C containing z; the finite limit must exist through arbitrary nonzero complex increments. Holomorphic means complex differentiable at every point of an open set.
nodes.example: For f(z)=z², f′(z)=2z; for f(z)=conjugate(z), quotients along real and imaginary increments disagree.

patterns.why: The local model is multiplication by one complex scalar.
The model respects the rotation structure of complex multiplication.
All directions of approach must give the same limit.

nodes.name: Cauchy–Riemann equations
nodes.intuition: The two output coordinates must cooperate as one complex multiplication. These equations say that local stretching and turning are identical in every direction.
nodes.conditions: For the stated equivalence, u and v are C¹ on an open U⊂R² and the equations hold throughout U.
nodes.example: For z²=(x²−y²)+i(2xy), u_x=v_y=2x and u_y=−v_x=−2y.

patterns.why: The Jacobian is constrained to the matrix of a complex multiplier.
The constrained matrix represents rotation and uniform scaling when the derivative is nonzero.
The real derivative must respect multiplication by i and therefore be complex linear.

nodes.name: Holomorphic functions have harmonic components
nodes.intuition: A holomorphic function packages two equilibrium fields whose gradients fit together. Their second derivatives cancel in exactly the way required for harmonicity.
nodes.conditions: f is holomorphic on an open subset of C; u and v are its real and imaginary parts. Two arbitrary harmonic functions do not necessarily form such a pair.
nodes.example: For f(z)=z², u=x²−y² and v=2xy each have zero Laplacian.

patterns.why: Cauchy–Riemann symmetry forces cancellation in the Laplacian.
One complex function separates into two coupled real harmonic fields.
Each component inherits the mean-value property of harmonic functions.

nodes.name: Complex contour integral
nodes.intuition: The curve's complex tangent multiplies the function value at each point. The real and imaginary totals encode two coupled planar line integrals.
nodes.conditions: γ:[a,b]→C is piecewise C¹ and f is continuous along γ; orientation and traversal multiplicity are retained.
nodes.example: Around the positively oriented unit circle, ∮dz/z=∫₀^{2π}i dt=2πi.

patterns.why: Complex contributions are added along an oriented path.
A parametrization converts the contour integral to an ordinary interval integral.
The field is sampled along the curve and multiplied by its tangent.

nodes.name: Cauchy's integral theorem
nodes.intuition: A holomorphic field has no net contour accumulation around a loop that can be contracted within its domain. Singularities or holes are the places where nonzero circulation can survive.
nodes.conditions: f is holomorphic on a simply connected open domain U⊂C and γ is a closed piecewise C¹ curve in U.
nodes.example: ∮_γ e^z dz=0 for every closed piecewise C¹ curve in C.

patterns.why: The integral around a boundary vanishes when no interior singularity obstructs it.
Contour accumulation is unchanged under allowable path deformations.
Holomorphicity enforces cancellation of the real planar curl contributions.

nodes.name: Cauchy's integral formula
nodes.intuition: Values on a surrounding contour determine every value inside it. The kernel weights boundary information according to the interior point being reconstructed.
nodes.conditions: f is holomorphic on a neighborhood of the closed disk D(a,R), γ is its positively oriented boundary circle, and |z−a|<R.
nodes.example: For f(ζ)=ζ² and γ the circle |ζ|=2, ∮ζ²/(ζ−1)dζ=2πi.

patterns.why: Boundary data determines the interior holomorphic function.
A weighted contour integral reconstructs a point value.
Point evaluation is represented by pairing with the Cauchy kernel.

nodes.name: Cauchy's formula for derivatives
nodes.intuition: Boundary values encode every local derivative inside the contour. Repeated differentiation changes only the kernel and a factorial coefficient.
nodes.conditions: n≥0 is an integer; f is holomorphic near a closed disk, γ is its positively oriented boundary, and z lies strictly inside.
nodes.example: For f(ζ)=e^ζ around the unit circle, ∮e^ζ/ζ³ dζ=πi.

patterns.why: All local derivative information is recovered from boundary values.
Each derivative raises the kernel power and multiplies its coefficient.
Derivative evaluation is an integral pairing with a singular kernel outside the contour path.

nodes.name: Cauchy estimates
nodes.intuition: A holomorphic function cannot vary rapidly deep inside a disk unless it becomes large on the surrounding circle. Boundary distance controls the allowed derivative scale.
nodes.conditions: f is holomorphic on a neighborhood of the closed disk of radius R>0 centered at a; n≥0 is an integer.
nodes.example: If an entire function is bounded by M on every circle, |f′(a)|≤M/R for every R, so f′(a)=0.

patterns.why: Boundary size bounds interior derivatives.
The n-th derivative is controlled by inverse radius to the n-th power.
Taking a radius limit can force derivatives to vanish.

nodes.name: Laurent expansion on an annulus
nodes.intuition: Allowing negative powers extends Taylor expansion to regions with a missing center. The coefficients separate the outward analytic part from the part carrying the obstruction inside the hole.
nodes.conditions: f is holomorphic on r<|z−a|<R, with 0≤r<R≤∞; r<ρ<R and the coefficient circle is positively oriented. The series converges absolutely and uniformly on compact subannuli.

patterns.why: Positive and negative powers describe different parts of the analytic behavior.
The annulus specifies the convergence region.
Contour integrals recover the expansion coefficients.

nodes.name: Residue and the simple-pole formula
nodes.intuition: A residue is the one Laurent coefficient that survives a full turn of contour integration. For a simple denominator zero, it is the numerator divided by the local denominator slope.
nodes.conditions: For the first formula, f has an isolated singularity at a and a_{−1} is its Laurent coefficient. For the second, g and h are holomorphic near a, h(a)=0 and h′(a)≠0; g(a)=0 gives a removable singularity and residue 0.
nodes.example: For f(z)=1/(z²+1), the residue at z=i is 1/(2i).

patterns.why: One selected Laurent coefficient controls contour accumulation.
A simple zero satisfies h(z)≈h′(a)(z−a).
Contour integration selects the single power with exponent −1.

nodes.name: Residue theorem
nodes.intuition: Most of a meromorphic function cancels around a closed contour. The remaining integral is completely determined by finitely many local singular coefficients inside.
nodes.conditions: D is a bounded Jordan domain with piecewise C¹ boundary oriented positively; f is meromorphic on a neighborhood of its closure, has no poles on the boundary, and the sum is over its finitely many poles in D.
nodes.example: Closing 1/(1+z²) by a large upper semicircle and checking the arc tends to zero gives ∫_R dx/(1+x²)=π.

patterns.why: A boundary integral reads off interior singularities.
Each isolated pole contributes independently.
The contour integral sums local residues.

nodes.name: Argument principle
nodes.intuition: Following how a function winds around zero along a boundary counts what happens inside. Zeros add turns and poles subtract turns, each according to its order.
nodes.conditions: D is a bounded Jordan domain with positively oriented piecewise C¹ boundary; f is meromorphic near its closure and has no zeros or poles on the boundary; N_D and P_D count multiplicities.
nodes.example: For f(z)=z⁵−1 on |z|=2, the integral divided by 2πi equals 5.

patterns.why: Zeros and poles are counted with integer multiplicity.
Boundary winding determines an interior count.
The logarithmic derivative detects changes in argument.

nodes.name: Rouché's theorem
nodes.intuition: A smaller boundary perturbation cannot push a function's boundary image through zero. Its winding, and hence the number of enclosed zeros, stays unchanged.
nodes.conditions: D is a bounded Jordan domain with piecewise C¹ boundary; f and g are holomorphic on a neighborhood of its closure; zeros are counted with multiplicity.
nodes.example: On |z|=2, |3z+1|≤7<32=|z⁵|, so z⁵+3z+1 has five zeros in the disk.

patterns.why: The zero count is invariant under a boundary-safe deformation.
The conclusion preserves an integer number of zeros.
A boundary magnitude comparison controls an interior root count.

nodes.name: Maximum modulus principle
nodes.intuition: A nonconstant holomorphic function cannot create an isolated magnitude peak in the interior. The largest magnitude on a bounded region is controlled by the boundary.
nodes.conditions: D⊂C is a bounded connected open set, f is continuous on its closure and holomorphic in D. A local interior maximum of |f| implies that f is constant on D.
nodes.example: For f(z)=z² on the closed unit disk, the maximum magnitude is 1 and occurs on the unit circle.

patterns.why: Interior magnitude is bounded by boundary magnitude.
A nonconstant holomorphic function cannot have an interior local maximum of its modulus.
Mean-value structure rules out a strict interior magnitude peak.

nodes.name: Liouville's theorem for entire functions
nodes.latex: f\text{ entire},\quad\sup_{z\in\mathbb C}|f(z)|<\infty\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f\text{ is constant}
nodes.intuition: Holomorphicity everywhere leaves no place for global boundedness to coexist with nontrivial variation. Large circles squeeze every derivative to zero.
nodes.conditions: f is holomorphic on all of C and bounded in modulus by one common finite constant.
nodes.example: e^z is nonconstant and entire, so it cannot be bounded on all of C even though |e^{it}|=1 on the imaginary axis.

patterns.why: Bounds on arbitrarily large surrounding circles constrain the interior.
Letting the circle radius tend to infinity forces zero derivative.
Cauchy's first-derivative bound decays like inverse radius.

nodes.name: Schwarz lemma
nodes.intuition: A holomorphic self-map of the unit disk that fixes its center cannot move a point farther from that center. Achieving the full allowed stretch forces the map to be a rotation.
nodes.conditions: f is holomorphic from the open unit disk into itself with f(0)=0. Equality at a nonzero interior point or |f′(0)|=1 implies f(z)=e^{iθ}z for a real θ.
nodes.example: f(z)=z² fixes 0 and satisfies |z²|≤|z| for |z|<1.

patterns.why: Fixing the origin anchors the comparison.
Distance to the center cannot increase.
Rotations are precisely the equality cases.
