nodes.name: Poisson integral on the unit disk
nodes.intuition: A harmonic interior value is a weighted average of boundary values. Close boundary points receive stronger weight as the evaluation point approaches the circle.
nodes.conditions: g is a continuous real-valued 2π-periodic function on the unit-circle boundary; the formula gives its unique harmonic extension continuous on the closed disk.
nodes.example: For boundary data g(t)=cos(nt), n≥0, the extension is rⁿcos(nθ).

patterns.why: The Poisson kernel is nonnegative and has normalized integral one.
Boundary data determines the harmonic solution inside.
Angular Fourier modes are damped by r^{|n|}.

nodes.name: Mean-value property of harmonic functions
nodes.intuition: At equilibrium, a value equals the average of every sufficiently small surrounding sphere and ball. A point cannot sustain a mismatch with all of its neighbors.
nodes.conditions: u∈C²(Ω), Δu=0, Ω⊂Rⁿ is open with n≥2, and the closed ball B_r(x) lies in Ω; |∂B_r| denotes surface measure and |B_r| volume.
nodes.example: For u(x,y)=x²−y², the average around a circle centered at the origin is 0, equal to u(0,0).

patterns.why: The value is exactly the normalized surrounding integral.
Spherical averages treat every direction equally.
A central interior value is read from the surrounding boundary.

nodes.name: Schwarz reflection principle
nodes.intuition: Real boundary values make reflection across the real axis compatible with holomorphic structure. Reflecting both the input and the output extends the function through that boundary.
nodes.conditions: U⊂C is a domain symmetric under conjugation; f is holomorphic on U∩{Im z>0}, continuous on its union with U∩R, and real-valued on U∩R. Then the displayed F is holomorphic on U.
nodes.example: A polynomial with real coefficients obeys f(conjugate z)=conjugate f(z), so reflection recovers its lower-half-plane values.

patterns.why: Conjugation symmetry continues matching real boundary data.
Boundary values allow analytic information to pass into the reflected region.
Conjugating before and after evaluation preserves holomorphic orientation.

nodes.name: Möbius transformation
nodes.intuition: A fractional linear map combines translations, scalings, rotations and inversion. On the extended complex plane it is an invertible coordinate change that preserves circles or lines and the cross-ratio of four points.
nodes.conditions: a,b,c,d∈C with ad−bc≠0; T acts on the Riemann sphere using the usual infinity conventions. The derivative formula applies at finite z with cz+d≠0.
nodes.example: T(z)=(z−i)/(z+i) maps the upper half-plane onto the unit disk.

patterns.why: The transformation supplies a reversible complex coordinate change.
Generalized circles and cross-ratios are preserved.
Composition corresponds to multiplication of 2×2 coefficient matrices up to nonzero scalar factors.

nodes.name: Principal complex logarithm
nodes.intuition: A logarithm records both radial size and accumulated angle. Choosing an angular range requires a cut, because traveling once around zero changes the logarithm by 2πi.
nodes.conditions: The principal holomorphic branch is defined on C∖(−∞,0]; Arg takes values in (−π,π). There is no single-valued continuous logarithm on the entire punctured plane.
nodes.example: Log(i)=iπ/2; the two logarithms of −1 immediately above and below the cut approach iπ and −iπ.

patterns.why: The logarithm locally inverts complex exponentiation.
Modulus and argument become additive radial and angular coordinates.
A full turn changes the chosen logarithm by the period 2πi.

nodes.name: Identity theorem for holomorphic functions
nodes.intuition: Analytic structure lets exact agreement on a sufficiently rich small set propagate throughout a connected domain. This gives uniqueness of analytic continuation whenever an extension exists.
nodes.conditions: Ω⊂C is a connected open set; f,g are holomorphic on Ω; E⊂Ω has an accumulation point lying inside Ω. Finite samples or accumulation only at the boundary do not suffice.
nodes.example: If an entire function agrees with e^z at z=1/n for every positive integer n, it equals e^z everywhere.

patterns.why: An interior accumulation of zeros forces all local Taylor coefficients to vanish.
Agreement extends successively through overlapping analytic neighborhoods along a path.
Nonzero holomorphic functions have isolated zeros with integer orders.

nodes.name: Separation of variables for a first-order ODE
nodes.intuition: Separate the part depending on the state from the part depending on time. Each side then accumulates its own rate, leaving an implicit relation for the trajectory.
nodes.conditions: a and b are continuous, y is a differentiable solution with y(t₀)=y₀, and b is nonzero throughout the interval of state values used. Constant solutions at zeros of b must be considered separately.
nodes.example: For y′=ty with y(0)=1, separation gives log y=t²/2 and y=e^{t²/2}.

patterns.why: The right-hand side factors into a time part and a state part.
Integrating 1/b(y) changes the state coordinate to one with a prescribed time rate.
Both sides are integrated from the initial condition.

nodes.name: Integrating factor for a linear ODE
nodes.intuition: Multiply the equation by exactly the factor that turns its left side into one product derivative. Integrating then collects the initial value and all later forcing.
nodes.conditions: The equation is y′+p(t)y=q(t), with continuous p,q on an interval containing t₀ and y(t₀)=y₀; μ(t₀)=1 and μ never vanishes.

patterns.why: An exponential of accumulated p solves μ′=pμ.
The rescaled variable μy absorbs the homogeneous dynamics.
The forcing contributes through an integral weighted by the integrating factor.

nodes.name: Constant relative growth or decay
nodes.intuition: A fixed percentage rate compounds continuously. Equal time intervals multiply the state by the same factor, whether the process grows or decays.
nodes.conditions: a is a real constant, t is real, and y(t₀)=y₀; this is the unique solution of the stated linear initial value problem.
nodes.example: With a=−log 2, a positive quantity halves every unit of time.

patterns.why: Constant logarithmic rate integrates to an exponential.
The rate is proportional to the current amount.
Evolution over two time intervals multiplies the corresponding exponential factors.

nodes.name: Logistic growth
nodes.intuition: Growth is nearly exponential when the state is small, then slows as the state approaches a limiting capacity. The current size and the remaining fraction of capacity jointly determine the rate.
nodes.conditions: r>0, K>0, y(t₀)=y₀>0 and t≥t₀; y≡0 is a separate equilibrium solution. The parameters are constant in this model.
nodes.example: Starting at y₀=K/2 gives y(t)=K/[1+e^{−r(t−t₀)}].

patterns.why: The constant states 0 and K are equilibria.
For 0<y<K, log[y/(K−y)] increases linearly in time.
The rate combines a linear growth term and a quadratic saturation term.

nodes.name: Constant-coefficient second-order linear equation
nodes.intuition: Exponential trial solutions turn derivatives into powers of one number. A differential equation therefore becomes a polynomial equation whose roots determine the possible modes.
nodes.conditions: a,b,c are real constants with a≠0; the formula describes all complex-valued solutions, with conjugate coefficients chosen for real solutions when roots are nonreal.
nodes.example: For y″−y=0, the roots are ±1 and y=C₁eᵗ+C₂e^{−t}.

patterns.why: Independent homogeneous modes can be superposed.
Exponentials retain their shape under differentiation.
The characteristic polynomial replaces the differential operator.

nodes.name: Underdamped harmonic oscillator
nodes.intuition: A restoring force creates oscillation while damping steadily reduces its amplitude. The solution separates an exponential envelope from a periodic core.
nodes.conditions: m,k>0, c≥0 and c²<4mk are constants; there is no external forcing; A,B are fixed by initial data.
nodes.example: For m=k=1 and c=0, x(t)=Acos t+Bsin t is undamped oscillation.

patterns.why: An exponential envelope multiplies a sinusoidal mode.
Damping causes exponential amplitude decay.
The characteristic quadratic determines damping and oscillation regimes.

nodes.name: Variation of parameters for a linear system
nodes.intuition: Use the homogeneous evolution as a changing coordinate frame. In that frame, the forcing simply accumulates before being mapped back to the original state.
nodes.conditions: x′=A(t)x+b(t), with continuous matrix A and vector b on an interval; Φ solves Φ′=AΦ and is invertible there; x(t₀)=x₀.
nodes.example: For constant A, the formula becomes x(t)=e^{A(t−t₀)}x₀+∫_{t₀}^t e^{A(t−s)}b(s)ds.

patterns.why: The substitution x=Φc removes homogeneous dynamics.
Forcing is integrated in the moving frame.
Initial-state and forcing responses add independently.

nodes.name: Abel–Liouville identity for the Wronskian
nodes.intuition: The volume spanned by solution vectors changes at a rate given by the trace of the system matrix. If the vectors start independent, a continuous linear evolution never makes them dependent at a finite time.
nodes.conditions: A(t) is a continuous n×n real or complex matrix on an interval and Φ′=AΦ; Φ need not initially be invertible for the determinant identity itself.
nodes.example: For y″+p(t)y′+q(t)y=0, the two-solution Wronskian is W(t₀)e^{−∫_{t₀}^t p(s)ds}.

patterns.why: The determinant records volume amplification.
The scalar volume solves W′=(tr A)W.
A zero trace makes the solution-volume determinant constant.

nodes.name: Picard iteration for an initial value problem
nodes.intuition: Guess a trajectory, read the rates it would generate, and integrate those rates to produce a better trajectory. On a short enough interval this self-consistency update is a contraction.
nodes.conditions: f is continuous on [t₀−h,t₀+h]×B̄(y₀,b), bounded there by M and Lipschitz in y with constant L; choose hM≤b and hL<1, and start from the constant function y₀. The iterates converge uniformly to the unique local solution. Here h>0 and b>0.
nodes.example: For y′=y, y(0)=1, iterations from 1 produce 1+t, then 1+t+t²/2, and successive exponential partial sums.

patterns.why: The ODE solution is a fixed point of its integral equation.
The previous trajectory generates the next approximation.
Integrating the rate imposes the initial condition automatically.

nodes.name: Gronwall's inequality
nodes.intuition: If error can grow only in proportion to the error already present, its worst growth is exponential. An integral inequality becomes an explicit time-dependent bound.
nodes.conditions: t∈[t₀,T]; u and b are continuous and nonnegative, and A≥0 is a constant.
nodes.example: Two solutions of an ODE with Lipschitz constant L satisfy a separation bound δe^{L(t−t₀)} when their initial separation is δ.

patterns.why: Accumulated proportional growth produces an exponential bound.
The hypothesis bounds the whole growth history by an integral.
The estimate controls errors between approximations or nearby solutions.

nodes.name: Explicit Euler method
nodes.intuition: Move forward using the slope available at the current state, then recompute. Each step is a tangent prediction, so small local errors accumulate across the interval.
nodes.conditions: h>0 and y′=f(t,y); global error is O(h) on a fixed finite interval when f is C¹ near the solution, uniformly Lipschitz in y there, and sufficiently small steps stay in that neighborhood. Stability still depends on the equation and step size.
nodes.example: For y′=λy, the method gives y_n=(1+hλ)^n y₀; for real λ<0, asymptotic decay requires |1+hλ|<1.

patterns.why: A tangent line supplies the next-state estimate.
Each time step updates the state from the previous one.
Under smoothness and stability control, the fixed-interval error shrinks linearly with h.

nodes.name: Classical fourth-order Runge–Kutta method
nodes.intuition: Estimate slopes at the beginning, twice near the middle, and near the end of a step. A carefully weighted average cancels the first several orders of error.
nodes.conditions: The method approximates y′=f(t,y). On a fixed finite interval it has global error O(h⁴) for, for example, C⁵ f that is uniformly Lipschitz in y near the solution, with sufficiently small steps staying there.
nodes.example: For y′=y and one step from y₀=1, the update is 1+h+h²/2+h³/6+h⁴/24.

patterns.why: The final slope uses weights 1,2,2,1 normalized by 6.
Intermediate states and later time steps are built from earlier estimates.
The stage weights achieve fourth-order global convergence under regularity assumptions.

nodes.name: Fourier series and Fourier coefficients
nodes.intuition: Resolve a periodic function into pure angular frequencies. Each coefficient measures alignment with one oscillation, and orthogonality makes those coefficients separately recoverable.
nodes.conditions: f is a 2π-periodic L² function; the displayed convergence is in L². For piecewise C¹ periodic f, the pointwise sum equals the average of the two one-sided limits, which may differ from the assigned value at a jump.
nodes.example: For f(x)=3+2cos x, the only nonzero coefficients are f̂₀=3 and f̂₁=f̂_{−1}=1.

patterns.why: Distinct integer frequencies have zero inner product over a full period.
Frequency modes provide a complete L² coordinate system.
Each coefficient is an average of f times an oscillatory test function.

nodes.name: Fejér summation by averaging Fourier partial sums
nodes.intuition: Averaging successive Fourier approximations smooths their oscillatory errors. This recovers uniform convergence for every continuous periodic function, even when ordinary partial sums need not converge uniformly.
nodes.conditions: f is a continuous real- or complex-valued 2π-periodic function and S_n is the symmetric Fourier partial sum using frequencies −n,…,n.
nodes.example: For f(x)=cos x, σ_Nf=[N/(N+1)]cos x, which converges uniformly to cos x.

patterns.why: The method takes an arithmetic mean of all partial sums up to N.
A positive approximation kernel yields uniform convergence.
Equivalent triangular frequency weights taper the high-frequency cutoff.

nodes.name: Regular Dirichlet Sturm–Liouville problem
nodes.intuition: A spatial differential operator has preferred modes just as a matrix has eigenvectors. Self-adjoint boundary conditions make modes with different eigenvalues orthogonal in the correct weighted geometry.
nodes.conditions: a<b are finite; p∈C¹([a,b]) is strictly positive, q,w are real continuous with w>0; y(a)=y(b)=0; y_m,y_n are real nonzero eigenfunctions of this same problem.
nodes.example: With p=w=1 and q=0 on (0,L), y_n=sin(nπx/L) and λ_n=(nπ/L)².

patterns.why: Distinct eigenvalues yield zero weighted inner product.
Eigenfunctions supply modes for expanding solutions.
Common boundary conditions eliminate integration-by-parts boundary terms.

nodes.name: Unilateral Laplace transform
nodes.intuition: Measure a time profile against exponentially damped oscillations. The exponential kernel is chosen so that time differentiation becomes algebraic multiplication plus initial data.
nodes.conditions: f is piecewise continuous on finite subintervals of [0,∞) and of exponential order a, meaning |f(t)|≤Ce^{at} for sufficiently large t; absolute convergence holds for complex s with Re s>a.
nodes.example: For f(t)=e^{at}, F(s)=1/(s−a) when Re s>a.

patterns.why: The kernel combines exponential damping and oscillation.
Transforms of sums are sums of transforms.
The transform combines the full nonnegative-time history with a parameterized weight.

nodes.name: Laplace transform of a derivative
nodes.intuition: The transform transfers a time derivative onto its exponential kernel. The boundary at time zero remains visible, so the transformed equation remembers the initial condition.
nodes.conditions: f∈C¹([0,∞)), and f and f′ are of exponential order; Re s is sufficiently large that both transforms converge and e^{−st}f(t)→0.
nodes.example: Transforming y′+ay=0 with y(0)=y₀ gives (s+a)Y(s)=y₀.

patterns.why: The initial-value term is the surviving integration-by-parts boundary contribution.
Time differentiation becomes multiplication by the transform variable.
The derivative is transferred from the signal to the exponential test kernel.

nodes.name: Laplace convolution theorem
nodes.intuition: A causal response combines every earlier input with the effect of the elapsed time since that input. Laplace transformation turns this history accumulation into a simple product.
nodes.conditions: f and g are piecewise continuous on finite nonnegative-time intervals and of exponential orders a and b; the identity holds for Re s>max(a,b), where the relevant double integral is absolutely convergent.
nodes.example: Convolving f(t)=1 and g(t)=1 on t≥0 gives t; their transforms multiply to 1/s² for Re s>0.

patterns.why: Serial causal linear filters multiply in the transform representation.
Every earlier time contributes to the current output.
The identity e^{−s(u+v)}=e^{−su}e^{−sv} separates the double integral.

nodes.name: Heat or diffusion equation
nodes.intuition: A location changes according to its mismatch with its spatial surroundings. Positive diffusivity smooths local peaks and fills local valleys.
nodes.conditions: κ>0 is a constant; a classical solution has one continuous time derivative and two continuous spatial derivatives. An initial condition and, on bounded domains, boundary conditions are needed to specify an evolution problem.
nodes.example: On a periodic line, u(t,x)=e^{−κk²t}cos(kx) is a decaying mode for integer k.

patterns.why: The Laplacian drives values toward nearby averages.
Total mass is conserved under no-flux boundaries or sufficient decay at infinity.
Time scales like length squared divided by diffusivity.

nodes.name: Gaussian heat kernel
nodes.intuition: Diffusion replaces each point by a Gaussian-weighted average of the initial profile. As time grows, the averaging window spreads with width proportional to the square root of time.
nodes.conditions: x∈Rⁿ, n≥1, κ>0 and t>0; for f∈L¹(Rⁿ), u is a smooth heat-equation solution for positive times and u(t,·)→f in L¹ as t↓0.
nodes.example: In one dimension, G_t is the normal density with mean 0 and variance 2κt.

patterns.why: The nonnegative kernel has total integral one.
Spatial width grows like √t while height decreases like t^{−n/2}.
Quadratic distance appears inside an exponential.

nodes.name: L² energy decay for heat flow
nodes.intuition: Diffusion reduces squared amplitude by spending spatial variation. A flat profile has no gradient energy left to dissipate.
nodes.conditions: Ω is bounded with C¹ boundary, κ>0, and u is a sufficiently smooth real solution of the heat equation with homogeneous Dirichlet or homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions; these make the boundary energy flux vanish.
nodes.example: For a Neumann problem, the mean stays constant while the squared deviation from that mean decreases.

patterns.why: Squared amplitude and squared gradients form the two energies.
Heat evolution descends a spatial energy landscape.
Integration by parts converts the interior Laplacian into dissipation after boundary cancellation.

nodes.name: Wave equation
nodes.intuition: Spatial curvature creates acceleration, so a disturbance overshoots and propagates instead of merely flattening. Initial displacement and initial velocity jointly determine the motion.
nodes.conditions: c>0 is constant and u is twice continuously differentiable in time and space for a classical solution; initial and, where relevant, boundary data specify the problem.
nodes.example: In one dimension, cos(kx)cos(ckt) solves the equation for real k.

patterns.why: Appropriate closed or homogeneous-boundary systems conserve wave energy.
The dynamics balance quadratic kinetic and gradient energies.
Linear wave modes can be superposed.

nodes.name: D'Alembert's formula
nodes.intuition: Initial displacement splits equally into left- and right-moving copies. Initial velocity contributes through the interval that can influence the point by time t.
nodes.conditions: For the whole-line equation u_tt=c²u_xx with c>0, t≥0, f∈C²(R), g∈C¹(R), u(x,0)=f(x) and u_t(x,0)=g(x); the formula gives the classical solution.
nodes.example: If initial velocity is zero, u(x,t) is the arithmetic mean of f(x−ct) and f(x+ct).

patterns.why: The displacement contribution averages two translated initial values.
The initial velocity is integrated over the domain of dependence.
The motion separates into left- and right-traveling waves.

nodes.name: Conservation of wave energy
nodes.intuition: A wave exchanges kinetic activity with stored spatial deformation. When no forcing or boundary work adds energy, their total remains constant.
nodes.conditions: c>0; Ω is bounded with C¹ boundary; u is a sufficiently smooth real solution of u_tt=c²Δu with homogeneous Dirichlet or homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions.
nodes.example: A single standing wave alternates between maximum displacement and maximum speed while this total stays fixed.

patterns.why: The total energy is invariant in time.
The energy is a sum of squared velocity and squared spatial gradient.
Kinetic and deformation contributions trade energy.

nodes.name: Constant-velocity transport
nodes.intuition: The entire profile moves with one velocity without changing its shape. Following a point carried by that motion makes the observed value constant.
nodes.conditions: v∈Rⁿ is constant and f∈C¹(Rⁿ); the formula is the classical whole-space solution with u(0,x)=f(x).
nodes.example: In one dimension, f(x)=e^{−x²} and v=2 gives a Gaussian bump centered at x=2t with unchanged width.

patterns.why: A frame moving at velocity v removes time dependence.
Values are constant along transported trajectories.
The profile is composed with the inverse translation x↦x−tv.

nodes.name: Method of characteristics
nodes.intuition: Choose paths that move with the transport field. Along those paths, the spatial derivative and time derivative merge into one ordinary derivative.
nodes.conditions: b is C¹ in space and time on the local region, f is continuous and u is a C¹ solution; characteristic ODEs are considered over times where their flow exists.
nodes.example: For u_t+xu_x=0, characteristics satisfy x(t)=x₀eᵗ and u(t,x)=u(0,xe^{−t}).

patterns.why: Moving along the flow converts the PDE into pathwise ODEs.
The chain rule differentiates u along a characteristic.
Forcing is integrated along the transported path.

nodes.name: Duhamel's principle
nodes.intuition: Every instant of forcing launches a homogeneous response that evolves for the remaining time. Add all those responses to the freely evolved initial state.
nodes.conditions: S(t) is a strongly continuous semigroup of bounded operators on a Banach space X with generator A, u₀∈X, and f:[0,T]→X is continuous; the vector-valued integral gives the mild solution of u′=Au+f. Additional regularity is needed for a classical time derivative.
nodes.example: With S(t)=e^{−at}, the formula solves y′+ay=f(t) by an exponentially weighted history integral.

patterns.why: Responses to independent forcing increments add.
All earlier forcing contributions are integrated.
The semigroup evolves each contribution through the remaining interval.

nodes.name: Poisson boundary value problem
nodes.intuition: A source distribution determines the curvature required of an equilibrium field. Boundary values anchor the otherwise underdetermined potential.
nodes.conditions: This entry defines the classical Dirichlet problem on a bounded domain: seek u∈C²(Ω)∩C(closure Ω) for specified interior source f and boundary data g. Existence and regularity require suitable domain and data hypotheses; the weak formulation supplies one precise alternative.

patterns.why: Interior sources and boundary data jointly determine the field.
The Laplacian encodes a divergence balance for gradient flux.
Under the appropriate Dirichlet setting, the solution minimizes an energy minus source-work functional.

nodes.name: Euler–Lagrange equation
nodes.intuition: An optimal or stationary curve must resist every small admissible deformation to first order. Integration by parts turns that global stationarity requirement into a local differential equation.
nodes.conditions: L is C², y is C², and variations are C¹ with zero endpoint values on a finite interval. The equivalence is between the differential equation and vanishing first variation; stationarity alone does not imply a minimum.
nodes.example: For L=½m(y′)²−V(y), the equation is my″+V′(y)=0.

patterns.why: The equation is a necessary first-order condition for a smooth extremum.
Derivatives are transferred from the perturbation using integration by parts.
Fixed endpoints eliminate the boundary term, leaving an interior condition.

nodes.name: Beltrami identity
nodes.intuition: If the integrand does not explicitly depend on the position along the independent variable, one combination of value and slope remains constant. This reduces a second-order variational equation to a first integral.
nodes.conditions: L(y,v) is C² and independent of the independent variable t; y is a C² solution of the Euler–Lagrange equation on an interval.
nodes.example: For arc length L=√(1+(y′)²), the identity gives 1/√(1+(y′)²)=C, implying a constant slope for a smooth stationary graph.

patterns.why: The displayed quantity stays constant along a stationary curve.
Absence of explicit t-dependence expresses translation symmetry in t.
A second-order equation is reduced to a conserved first-order relation.

nodes.name: Hamilton's equations
nodes.latex: p=\partial_{\dot q}L,\qquad H=p\cdot\dot q-L,\qquad\dot q=\partial_pH,\quad\dot p=-\partial_qH
nodes.intuition: Describe motion using position and momentum instead of position and velocity. One scalar Hamiltonian then generates both rates through paired derivatives with opposite signs.
nodes.conditions: L(q,v,t) is C² for q,v∈Rⁿ and its velocity Hessian is nonsingular in the region considered, so v can be expressed locally in terms of (q,p,t); H uses that substitution and the trajectory obeys Euler–Lagrange.
nodes.example: For H(q,p)=p²/(2m)+V(q), Hamilton's equations give q̇=p/m and ṗ=−V′(q).

patterns.why: Position and momentum are conjugate variables linked by a Legendre transformation.
If H has no explicit time dependence, it is constant along its own flow.
An invertible velocity-to-momentum map rewrites the dynamics.

nodes.name: Noether conservation law for a configuration symmetry
nodes.intuition: A continuous change of coordinates that leaves the Lagrangian unchanged produces a quantity the motion cannot change. The conserved quantity pairs momentum with the infinitesimal symmetry direction.
nodes.conditions: L(q,v,t) is C²; a smooth one-parameter configuration transformation Q_ε with generator ξ leaves L(Q_ε(q),DQ_ε(q)v,t)=L(q,v,t), with time fixed; q is a C² Euler–Lagrange solution. This version assumes exact invariance, not invariance only up to a total derivative.
nodes.example: Translation symmetry in one coordinate gives conservation of the corresponding momentum component; rotational symmetry gives angular momentum.

patterns.why: The Lagrangian is unchanged by a continuous family of transformations.
The associated momentum pairing stays constant in time.
Momentum evaluates the infinitesimal configuration displacement.

nodes.name: Second variation of a one-dimensional functional
nodes.intuition: The first variation measures slope in the space of curves, and the second variation measures curvature there. Its sign tests whether small perturbations tend to raise or lower the functional.
nodes.conditions: J[y]=∫_a^b L(t,y,y′)dt on a finite interval; L is C² near the curve, y,η are C¹ and η(a)=η(b)=0; all L derivatives are evaluated at (t,y(t),y′(t)). A smooth local minimum requires this quantity to be nonnegative for every admissible η, but nonnegativity alone is not sufficient.
nodes.example: For J[y]=½∫(y′)²dt, δ²J=∫(η′)²dt, strictly positive for nonzero fixed-endpoint perturbations.

patterns.why: The perturbation and its derivative enter through a quadratic form.
Its sign gives a necessary second-order condition for a minimum.
It measures curvature of a functional along directions in a function space.

nodes.name: Dirichlet Rayleigh–Ritz principle
nodes.intuition: The lowest-frequency mode is the nonzero shape with the least gradient energy per unit squared amplitude. Restricting the search to trial shapes gives computable upper bounds on that eigenvalue.
nodes.conditions: Ω⊂Rⁿ is bounded, connected and has Lipschitz boundary; λ₁ is the first eigenvalue of −Δ with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions. The minimum is attained by a first eigenfunction.
nodes.example: On (0,L), sin(πx/L) attains the quotient (π/L)².

patterns.why: The lowest eigenvalue is an energy minimum.
The quotient compares two quadratic functionals.
Multiplying u by a nonzero scalar leaves the quotient unchanged.

nodes.name: Probability axioms
nodes.intuition: Probability assigns a consistent amount of mass to events. Splitting an event into disjoint pieces preserves its total mass.
nodes.conditions: Events belong to a sigma-algebra on a sample space; the A_i are pairwise disjoint.
nodes.example: For a fair die, each of six disjoint outcomes has mass 1/6.

patterns.why: The entire sample space has total mass one.
Disjoint pieces contribute additive probability.

nodes.name: Conditional probability
nodes.intuition: Conditioning restricts attention to the outcomes still possible and rescales their mass to one.
nodes.conditions: A and B are events with P(B)>0; conditioning on probability-zero events requires a different construction.
nodes.example: Among even die rolls, the chance of rolling 6 is (1/6)/(1/2)=1/3.

patterns.why: Renormalization makes the surviving mass sum to one.
The event B changes what is known about A.

nodes.name: Law of total probability
nodes.intuition: Split a complicated chance calculation into cases, then average the answers using the chances of those cases.
nodes.conditions: The B_i form a finite or countable measurable partition with P(B_i)>0; zero-mass pieces may be omitted.
nodes.example: A machine chosen with probabilities .6 and .4 has defect rates .01 and .03, giving .018 overall.

patterns.why: Case-specific probabilities are weighted by case probabilities.
A partition replaces one event calculation with disjoint cases.

nodes.name: Bayes' rule
nodes.intuition: Evidence reweights competing explanations by how well each predicts it. The denominator puts the revised weights back on a common probability scale.
nodes.conditions: The hypotheses form a finite or countable partition, the displayed conditionals exist, and P(E)>0.
nodes.example: With prior odds 1:1 and a likelihood ratio of 3, the posterior probability is 3/4.

patterns.why: Observed evidence revises the probability of explanations.
Normalization turns likelihood-weighted prior mass into posterior mass.

nodes.name: Independence of random variables
nodes.intuition: Knowing one variable leaves the probability law of the other unchanged.
nodes.conditions: The identity must hold for every measurable A and B; pairwise independence need not imply mutual independence of three or more variables.
nodes.example: Two independent fair dice give P(X=1,Y=1)=1/36.

patterns.why: The joint law factors into its marginal laws.
Separate sources of uncertainty combine without dependence.

nodes.name: Union bound
nodes.intuition: Adding all failure probabilities gives a safe upper bound even when failures overlap.
nodes.conditions: A_i is a finite or countable family of events; the upper bound may exceed one and may be loose.
nodes.example: If five checks each fail with probability at most .01, any failure has probability at most .05.

patterns.why: Individual risk contributions are added.
Overlap is counted more than once, creating the inequality.

nodes.name: Expectation
nodes.intuition: Expectation is an average whose weights are probabilities. It compresses a distribution into the balance point of its mass.
nodes.conditions: X is measurable and integrable: E|X|<infinity; nonnegative X also admits an extended expectation.
nodes.example: A fair six-sided die has expectation 3.5 even though no individual outcome equals 3.5.

patterns.why: Values are weighted by the probability mass assigned to them.
An integral accumulates contributions across all outcomes.

nodes.name: Linearity of expectation
nodes.intuition: An average of a sum equals the sum of the averages, even when the summands depend on one another.
nodes.conditions: The number of summands is finite, all X_i are integrable, and a_i,b are deterministic real constants.
nodes.example: The expected number of heads in ten possibly dependent fair coin tosses is five.

patterns.why: Addition and deterministic scaling commute with expectation.
Each contribution can be averaged separately.

nodes.name: Probability as an indicator expectation
nodes.intuition: Turn a yes-or-no event into a number. Counts then become sums of indicators, so expected counts become sums of probabilities.
nodes.conditions: The second formula is for a finite family, or a countable family with nonnegative terms and possibly infinite expectation.
nodes.example: Expected fixed points in a random permutation of n objects equal n times 1/n, hence one.

patterns.why: Indicators translate event occurrence into numerical counts.
Expected counts add without independence assumptions.

nodes.name: Variance
nodes.intuition: Variance measures average squared distance from the balance point. Squaring makes deviations in opposite directions reinforce rather than cancel.
nodes.conditions: X is real and E[X^2]<infinity.
nodes.example: A Bernoulli(p) variable has variance p(1-p).

patterns.why: Squared deviations are averaged over the distribution.
The squared distance expands into a second moment minus a squared mean.

nodes.name: Variance under affine change
nodes.intuition: Moving every value by the same amount preserves spread; multiplying distances by a scales squared spread by a squared.
nodes.conditions: X has finite variance and a,b are real constants.
nodes.example: Converting a measurement from meters to centimeters multiplies its variance by 10,000.

patterns.why: Variance has squared units.
Translation changes the mean while leaving variance fixed.

nodes.name: Variance of a sum
nodes.intuition: Total uncertainty contains each variable's own spread and every pair's tendency to move together.
nodes.conditions: A finite collection of real random variables with finite second moments; the covariance terms vanish for pairwise uncorrelated variables.
nodes.example: Two unit-variance variables with correlation .5 have sum variance three.

patterns.why: Expanding a square produces diagonal and cross terms.
The total splits into individual variation and shared variation.

nodes.name: Covariance
nodes.latex: \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb EX)(Y-\mathbb EY)]=\mathbb E[XY]-\mathbb E[X]\mathbb E[Y]
nodes.intuition: Covariance detects whether two centered quantities tend to have matching signs. It measures shared linear fluctuation, not every kind of dependence.
nodes.conditions: X and Y are real and square-integrable.
nodes.example: If Y=2X+3, their covariance is twice Var(X).

patterns.why: Centered products are averaged across outcomes.
Zero covariance means centered variables are orthogonal in L2.

nodes.name: Pearson correlation
nodes.intuition: Correlation is the cosine between centered random variables. Dividing by their lengths removes measurement units.
nodes.conditions: Both variables have finite, strictly positive variance; the bound follows from Cauchy-Schwarz.
nodes.example: If Y=-3X+2 and Var(X)>0, correlation is -1.

patterns.why: Normalized inner products encode angles.
Positive rescaling leaves correlation unchanged.

nodes.name: Covariance under a linear map
nodes.intuition: A linear transformation carries an uncertainty ellipsoid into another ellipsoid. The same map acts on both sides because covariance compares pairs of directions.
nodes.conditions: X is a finite-dimensional real random vector with finite second moments; A and b are deterministic and dimensionally compatible.
nodes.example: For a scalar a, this reduces to Var(aX)=a^2 Var(X).

patterns.why: Uncertainty changes predictably when coordinates change.
The covariance matrix controls variance in every direction.

nodes.name: Conditional expectation
nodes.latex: Z=\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G]\iff Z\text{ is }\mathcal G\text{-measurable},\quad \mathbb E[Z\mathbf1_A]=\mathbb E[X\mathbf1_A]\ \forall A\in\mathcal G
nodes.intuition: Conditional expectation is the average compatible with the information available. It matches the original variable's averages on every event that information can distinguish.
nodes.conditions: X is integrable; G is a sub-sigma-algebra. Z is integrable and unique almost surely. For square-integrable X it is the L2 projection onto G-measurable variables.
nodes.example: Given a die's parity, the predicted roll is 3 for odd and 4 for even.

patterns.why: Information groups outcomes, and each group receives its conditional average.
In L2 the unpredictable residual is orthogonal to all known square-integrable quantities.

nodes.name: Tower property
nodes.latex: \mathbb E[\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G]\mid\mathcal H]=\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal H],\quad \mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal G
nodes.intuition: Averaging first with finer information and then with coarser information gives the same answer as using the coarser information directly.
nodes.conditions: X is integrable and H is a sub-sigma-algebra of G; equality holds almost surely.
nodes.example: A population mean equals the weighted mean of subgroup means.

patterns.why: Nested conditional averaging collapses to the coarser operator.
Averages of correctly weighted averages preserve the overall mean.

nodes.name: Law of total variance
nodes.intuition: Total variation splits into average variation within groups and variation between group means.
nodes.conditions: X is square-integrable; conditioning means conditioning on the sigma-algebra generated by Y.
nodes.example: For a two-stage experiment, separate randomness remaining after the first stage from randomness in the first-stage prediction.

patterns.why: Overall spread separates into within-group and between-group parts.
The prediction and its residual have zero cross term.

nodes.name: Jensen's inequality
nodes.intuition: For a convex transformation, averaging before transforming costs no more than transforming first and averaging. Curvature determines how variability changes the result.
nodes.conditions: X is integrable and takes values in an interval where phi is convex; assume phi(X) is integrable. Reverse the inequality for concave phi.
nodes.example: Taking phi(x)=x^2 gives (E[X])^2<=E[X^2].

patterns.why: A convex graph lies above its supporting averages.
The inequality compares the order of averaging and transformation.

nodes.name: Markov's inequality
nodes.intuition: A nonnegative quantity cannot be large too often without making its average large.
nodes.conditions: X>=0 almost surely, E[X]<infinity, and a>0.
nodes.example: If a nonnegative waiting time has mean 2, the chance it exceeds 10 is at most .2.

patterns.why: The mean limits the amount of mass that can lie far to the right.
A moment bound becomes a probability bound.

nodes.name: Chebyshev's inequality
nodes.intuition: Finite variance limits how often observations can lie many standard deviations from their mean, regardless of the distribution's shape.
nodes.conditions: X has mean mu and finite variance sigma^2; t>0.
nodes.example: At most 1/9 of the probability can be at least three standard deviations from the mean.

patterns.why: Squared deviation converts a two-sided event into a nonnegative variable.
Only distance measured relative to standard deviation matters.

nodes.name: Exponential Chernoff bound
nodes.intuition: Exponentials magnify large values, allowing a moment bound to detect rare tails. Optimizing the magnification makes the bound as tight as this method allows.
nodes.conditions: X is real; optimize over positive lambda for which the moment generating function is finite. The bound is valid but can be uninformative.
nodes.example: For a standard normal and a>0, choosing lambda=a gives P(X>=a)<=exp(-a^2/2).

patterns.why: An exponential converts additive deviations into multiplicative penalties.
Choosing the best tilting parameter sharpens the bound.

nodes.name: Hoeffding's inequality
nodes.intuition: Independent bounded fluctuations cancel reliably: a large collective deviation becomes exponentially unlikely.
nodes.conditions: X_i are independent and a_i<=X_i<=b_i almost surely, with finite deterministic bounds; t>0 and sum_i(b_i-a_i)^2>0.
nodes.example: For n independent values in [0,1], the sample mean deviates by epsilon with probability at most 2 exp(-2n epsilon^2).

patterns.why: Tail probabilities decay at an exponential rate.
Independent bounded averages concentrate as sample size grows.

nodes.name: Strong law of large numbers
nodes.intuition: Long averages stabilize around the distribution's balance point. Random observations collectively become a dependable numerical summary.
nodes.conditions: X_1,X_2,... are iid real variables with E|X_1|<infinity; almost-sure convergence is an infinite-sequence statement, not a finite-sample error bound.
nodes.example: The running fraction of heads converges almost surely to p for independent Bernoulli(p) trials.

patterns.why: Repeated observations produce a stable empirical mean.
The assertion concerns the limiting behavior of an infinite sequence.

nodes.name: Central limit theorem
nodes.intuition: After their mean is removed and their size is standardized, sums of many iid finite-variance contributions approach one common bell shape.
nodes.conditions: X_i are iid real variables, E[X_i]=mu, and 0<Var(X_i)=sigma^2<infinity. Convergence is in distribution; no universal sample-size threshold guarantees accuracy.
nodes.example: For fair coin counts, (heads-n/2)/(sqrt(n)/2) approaches a standard normal distribution.

patterns.why: The theorem describes fluctuations of sample averages.
The square-root normalization preserves a nontrivial limiting spread.
The Gaussian law emerges as a distributional limit.

nodes.name: Moment generating function
nodes.intuition: One function stores moments as its derivatives. Exponentials also turn independent addition into multiplication.
nodes.conditions: For the derivative identity, M_X is finite on an open interval containing zero; k is a nonnegative integer.
nodes.example: For X~Poisson(lambda), M_X(t)=exp(lambda(e^t-1)).

patterns.why: Derivatives extract numerical features of the distribution.
The exponential kernel converts independent sums into products.

nodes.name: Characteristic function
nodes.intuition: A probability distribution can be encoded by how strongly its values align with each frequency. This transform always exists because the complex exponential has unit magnitude.
nodes.conditions: X is any real random variable and t is real; the product identity requires X and Y to be independent.
nodes.example: A centered normal with variance sigma^2 has characteristic function exp(-sigma^2 t^2/2).

patterns.why: The transform determines the entire probability law.
Independent sums become products of frequency responses.

nodes.name: Cumulant generating function
nodes.intuition: Taking the logarithm extracts additive features of a law. Mean and variance are the first two of these cumulants.
nodes.conditions: The real MGF is finite on an open interval containing zero; independent cumulant generating functions add on their common domain.
nodes.example: For a normal law, K(t)=mu*t+sigma^2*t^2/2, so all cumulants above order two vanish.

patterns.why: A logarithm turns transform products into sums.
Cumulants separate additive contributions to a distribution.

nodes.name: Probability generating function
nodes.intuition: Store the probabilities of a count as coefficients of a power series. Products then describe sums of independent counts.
nodes.conditions: N takes nonnegative integer values; the series converges absolutely for |z|<=1. The derivative at 1 is a left limit and may be infinite.
nodes.example: For Bernoulli(p), G(z)=1-p+pz; n independent trials give (1-p+pz)^n.

patterns.why: Power-series coefficients encode individual count probabilities.
Multiplication collects ways to obtain the same total count.

nodes.name: Bernoulli distribution
nodes.intuition: The smallest random model records whether an event occurs. Its mean is exactly the probability of occurrence.
nodes.conditions: 0<=p<=1, with endpoint values interpreted by their degenerate distributions; the power formula is unambiguous for 0<p<1.
nodes.example: A random success indicator with success probability .7 has mean .7.

patterns.why: One binary choice is the elementary building block.
The long-run fraction of ones estimates p.

nodes.name: Binomial distribution
nodes.intuition: Count successes in independent repetitions of the same yes-or-no experiment. The binomial coefficient counts which repetitions succeeded.
nodes.conditions: n is a nonnegative integer, k=0,...,n, and 0<=p<=1; use the degenerate interpretation at endpoints.
nodes.example: Exactly three heads in five fair flips has probability 10/32.

patterns.why: The binomial coefficient counts success arrangements.
Independent binary trials generate the count law.

nodes.name: Poisson distribution
nodes.intuition: Poisson counts describe events scattered independently at a fixed average intensity. The single parameter sets both mean count and variance.
nodes.conditions: lambda>0; lambda=0 is the point mass at zero. A Poisson model is an assumption, not a consequence of merely knowing an average rate.
nodes.example: At mean count two, the probability of no events is e^-2.

patterns.why: The random variable records how many events occur.
The exponential factor normalizes factorial-weighted count probabilities.

nodes.name: Geometric waiting time
nodes.intuition: To wait k trials for the first success, first observe k-1 failures and then one success. Repeated failure does not change the remaining waiting-time law.
nodes.conditions: Independent Bernoulli(p) trials with 0<p<=1; T counts the successful trial, so its support begins at one.
nodes.example: A fair coin takes two tosses on average to produce the first head.

patterns.why: After a failure, the experiment restarts in the same state.
Waiting probabilities decay geometrically.

nodes.name: Negative binomial distribution
nodes.intuition: Count failures before the r-th success. The last trial must succeed, while the earlier trials can arrange the remaining successes in many ways.
nodes.conditions: r is a positive integer, 0<p<=1, k is a nonnegative integer, and trials are independent with success probability p; K counts failures.
nodes.example: With r=2 and p=1/2, exactly one preceding failure has probability 1/4.

patterns.why: The combinatorial factor counts allowed success positions.
Waiting for r successes adds r independent one-success waiting periods.

nodes.name: Hypergeometric distribution
nodes.intuition: Sampling without replacement changes the remaining composition after each draw. Counting subsets handles this dependence exactly.
nodes.conditions: N,K,n are integers with 0<=K,n<=N; max(0,n-(N-K))<=k<=min(n,K). Every n-subset is equally likely.
nodes.example: In a five-object population with two marked objects, two draws contain both marked objects with probability 1/10.

patterns.why: Favorable subsets are divided by all equally likely subsets.
Sampling without replacement introduces dependence.

nodes.name: Continuous uniform distribution
nodes.intuition: A uniform density assigns probability in proportion to interval length. Its balance point is the midpoint.
nodes.conditions: a<b are finite real numbers; endpoint density values have no effect on probabilities.
nodes.example: If X is uniform on [0,10], the chance X lies in [2,5] is .3.

patterns.why: Reflection about the midpoint leaves the law unchanged.
Expectations are normalized integrals over the interval.

nodes.name: Exponential waiting time
nodes.latex: f_T(t)=\lambda e^{-\lambda t}\mathbf1_{\{t\ge0\}},\quad P(T>s+t\mid T>s)=e^{-\lambda t}
nodes.intuition: An exponential clock has a constant instantaneous event rate. Surviving a while gives no extra information about the remaining wait.
nodes.conditions: lambda>0 and s,t>=0; E[T]=1/lambda.
nodes.example: At rate two events per unit time, the chance of waiting longer than one unit is e^-2.

patterns.why: Survival decays exponentially with elapsed time.
The conditional remaining wait has the original law.

nodes.name: Normal distribution
nodes.intuition: The bell curve weights values by an exponential penalty on squared distance from the center. Independent normal contributions remain normal when added.
nodes.conditions: mu is real, sigma>0, and x is real; the density integrates to one.
nodes.example: A standard normal has mu=0 and variance one.

patterns.why: The log density is a negative quadratic.
The density is symmetric around its mean.
Exponentiating a squared-distance penalty produces Gaussian tails.

nodes.name: Gamma distribution
nodes.intuition: The gamma family extends waiting for several arrivals from integer event counts to a continuous shape parameter.
nodes.conditions: alpha>0 and lambda>0 is the rate; Gamma(alpha)=integral_0^infinity t^(alpha-1)e^-t dt. Variance is alpha/lambda^2.
nodes.example: The waiting time for three arrivals in a rate-two Poisson process is Gamma(3,2), with mean 1.5.

patterns.why: Integer shapes arise by adding independent exponential waiting times.
Changing the rate rescales time.

nodes.name: Beta distribution
nodes.intuition: Beta densities describe uncertain proportions and adapt naturally to accumulated successes and failures.
nodes.conditions: alpha,beta>0, 0<p<1; density is zero outside [0,1]. The mean is alpha/(alpha+beta).
nodes.example: Beta(1,1) is uniform on [0,1], while Beta(2,2) favors central proportions.

patterns.why: The random quantity is itself a possible probability or proportion.
Powers become linear sufficient-statistic terms after taking logs.

nodes.name: Multivariate normal density
nodes.intuition: A multivariate Gaussian replaces distance on a line with distance shaped by a covariance ellipsoid. Its contour surfaces are ellipsoids.
nodes.conditions: x,mu in R^d and Sigma is symmetric positive definite; singular Gaussian laws exist but lack this density on all of R^d.
nodes.example: For Sigma=I, the coordinates are independent standard normals after centering.

patterns.why: The exponent is a covariance-weighted quadratic distance.
Whitening converts the ellipsoid into a spherical normal law.

nodes.name: Density under a change of variables
nodes.intuition: Probability mass stays constant when coordinates change; the density compensates for how the map stretches volume.
nodes.conditions: X has a density on an open subset of R^d; g is a C1 diffeomorphism onto its image with nonzero Jacobian determinant. Formula holds almost everywhere, and density is zero outside the image.
nodes.example: If X>0 and Y=log X, then f_Y(y)=f_X(e^y)e^y.

patterns.why: The Jacobian converts density between coordinate systems.
The probability assigned to corresponding regions is preserved.

nodes.name: Tail integral formula
nodes.intuition: An average height can be computed by adding the fractions that rise above each horizontal level.
nodes.conditions: X is a nonnegative measurable real variable and N is nonnegative integer-valued; both sides may be infinite. Tonelli's theorem justifies the interchange.
nodes.example: For geometric waiting time T, summing its survival probabilities gives E[T]=1/p.

patterns.why: Each level contributes the probability that the variable reaches it.
A nonnegative value is decomposed into stacked indicator layers.

nodes.name: Density of an independent sum
nodes.intuition: To obtain a total z, combine every possible first contribution x with the matching second contribution z-x.
nodes.conditions: X and Y are independent real variables with densities; the convolution gives a density almost everywhere.
nodes.example: Adding two independent uniform [0,1] variables produces a triangular density on [0,2].

patterns.why: All decompositions of the same total contribute.
The operation composes independent additive uncertainty.

nodes.name: Markov chain transition law
nodes.intuition: The current state carries all information needed for the next-step probability law. Each matrix row lists the possible next states and their chances.
nodes.conditions: A finite or countable state space; the displayed version is time-homogeneous. Conditional equality holds almost surely for attainable histories.
nodes.example: A two-state weather model can assign tomorrow's probabilities using only today's weather.

patterns.why: The same one-step rule generates the entire sequence.
State transitions are chosen according to probability weights.

nodes.name: Chapman-Kolmogorov equation
nodes.intuition: To cross several time steps, sum over every possible intermediate state. Matrix multiplication is weighted case-splitting.
nodes.conditions: A time-homogeneous finite or countable Markov chain, with nonnegative integer m,n; sums over states are nonnegative and convergent.
nodes.example: Two-step reachability is computed by multiplying the transition matrix by itself.

patterns.why: Successive transitions compose by matrix multiplication.
Each intermediate state contributes its conditional probability weighted by its chance.

nodes.name: Stationary distribution
nodes.intuition: A stationary law is a probability distribution that looks the same after another transition. Inflow and outflow balance in aggregate.
nodes.conditions: P is a stochastic matrix. A finite chain has at least one stationary law; a finite irreducible chain has a unique one. Convergence from every initial law also needs aperiodicity.
nodes.example: For a symmetric two-state chain, pi=(1/2,1/2) is stationary.

patterns.why: The probability update leaves pi unchanged.
Probability flow redistributes mass without changing the stationary profile.

nodes.name: Detailed balance
nodes.intuition: Every pair of states exchanges equal stationary probability flow. This stronger balance makes time-reversed trajectories statistically identical.
nodes.conditions: P is stochastic and pi is a probability vector. Detailed balance implies stationarity; stationarity need not imply detailed balance.
nodes.example: An undirected weighted random walk is reversible with pi_i proportional to the weighted degree.

patterns.why: Forward and reversed transitions have matching probability flow.
Pairwise balance implies global mass balance.

nodes.name: Discounted Markov reward equation
nodes.intuition: Long-term value is immediate reward plus a discounted average of future value. The same equation is both a recursive forecast and a linear system.
nodes.conditions: P is a finite stochastic matrix, r is a finite real reward vector, and 0<=gamma<1; the Neumann series converges and the inverse exists.
nodes.example: For one state with reward two and gamma=.9, v=2/(1-.9)=20.

patterns.why: Value is unchanged by the Bellman update.
P averages successor-state values.
The series adds discounted rewards over time.

nodes.name: Fundamental matrix of an absorbing chain
nodes.intuition: Count every possible visit to transient states before absorption. Row sums then give the expected number of steps remaining.
nodes.conditions: A finite chain with transient-state submatrix Q and eventual absorption with probability one from each transient state; equivalently rho(Q)<1.
nodes.example: With one transient state that persists with probability q<1, expected time to absorption is 1/(1-q).

patterns.why: Summing k-step visit probabilities counts expected visits.
The matrix geometric series packages all possible path lengths.

nodes.name: Poisson process increments
nodes.intuition: A Poisson process scatters events through time at constant intensity. Nonoverlapping time intervals receive independent counts.
nodes.conditions: lambda>0, s,t>=0, N(0)=0, and the counting process has stationary independent increments with the displayed Poisson laws.
nodes.example: At rate three per hour, a two-hour increment is Poisson(6).

patterns.why: Counts increase by adding arrivals across intervals.
Disjoint intervals contain independent random counts.

nodes.name: Independent thinning of a Poisson process
nodes.intuition: Independently labeling each arrival splits one Poisson stream into independent Poisson streams with proportionally reduced rates.
nodes.conditions: N is a rate-lambda Poisson process; each arrival independently receives label one with probability p in [0,1], independently of N. N_2 counts the remaining arrivals.
nodes.example: Randomly retaining one quarter of rate-eight arrivals gives a rate-two retained stream.

patterns.why: One event stream splits into disjoint labeled streams.
Independent retention multiplies the rate by p.

nodes.name: Martingale property
nodes.intuition: A martingale is a forecast that has no predictable one-step drift. New information may move it, but its current value already averages those possible changes.
nodes.conditions: (F_n) is a filtration; M_n is F_n-measurable and E|M_n|<infinity for every n. A martingale need not have independent increments.
nodes.example: A centered sum of independent integrable zero-mean increments is a martingale.

patterns.why: The current value is the conditional average of the next value.
Expected value is preserved over deterministic time steps.

nodes.name: Optional stopping for bounded times
nodes.intuition: Choosing when to stop using only information already revealed cannot change a martingale's expected value when the stopping horizon is bounded.
nodes.conditions: M_n is an integrable discrete-time martingale and T is a stopping time with 0<=T<=N almost surely for a deterministic finite N. Unbounded stopping needs additional hypotheses.
nodes.example: Stop a fair random walk at a target or after 100 steps, whichever comes first; expected stopped position remains the initial position.

patterns.why: Expected value survives an admissible random stopping rule.
A stopping decision cannot look into future increments.

nodes.name: Brownian motion covariance and increments
nodes.intuition: Brownian motion accumulates infinitesimal independent fluctuations. Two times share exactly the randomness accumulated before the earlier time.
nodes.conditions: Standard Brownian motion starts at zero, has continuous paths, and has independent Gaussian increments; 0<=s<=t.
nodes.example: W_4 has standard deviation two, while Cov(W_1,W_4)=1.

patterns.why: Independent increments build the entire path.
Variance grows linearly in elapsed time.

nodes.name: Brownian scaling
nodes.intuition: Speeding Brownian time by a factor c stretches its typical displacement by the square root of c.
nodes.conditions: W is standard Brownian motion and c>0; equality is in law as processes, not pathwise equality for one realization.
nodes.example: A time interval four times longer has twice the standard deviation.

patterns.why: Time and displacement use different scaling exponents.
The rescaled process has the same Brownian law.

nodes.name: Ito isometry
nodes.intuition: Independent infinitesimal noise increments make cross terms disappear. The variance of accumulated noise is the accumulated squared noise amplitude.
nodes.conditions: W is Brownian relative to the filtration, H is predictable, and E[integral_0^T H_t^2 dt]<infinity for finite T.
nodes.example: For deterministic H_t=2, the integral has variance 4T.

patterns.why: Nonoverlapping martingale increments have zero expected cross products.
Local variance contributions add through time.

nodes.name: Ito's formula
nodes.intuition: Random paths retain a second-order contribution that ordinary smooth paths lose. The extra curvature term comes from Brownian quadratic variation.
nodes.conditions: X is a continuous Ito process with progressively measurable b,sigma and locally finite integral(|b|+sigma^2)dt; f is C^{1,2}. Derivatives are evaluated at (t,X_t), and localization gives the formula up to the process lifetime.
nodes.example: For f(x)=x^2 and X=W, d(W_t^2)=2W_t dW_t+dt.

patterns.why: A Taylor expansion retains the quadratic noise term.
Brownian increments have nonzero accumulated squared variation.

nodes.name: Geometric Brownian motion
nodes.intuition: Multiplicative noise becomes additive after taking logarithms. The variance correction ensures the original process has the stated mean drift.
nodes.conditions: X_0>0 is deterministic, mu is real, sigma>=0, and W is standard Brownian motion.
nodes.example: For mu=0, X_t has constant expectation X_0 although its log has drift -sigma^2/2.

patterns.why: Logarithms turn proportional changes into additive increments.
Both drift and noise amplitude are proportional to current size.

nodes.name: Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process
nodes.intuition: A restoring force pulls the process toward a central value while noise continually perturbs it. Old disturbances fade exponentially.
nodes.conditions: kappa>0, sigma>=0, theta and deterministic x_0 are real; W is standard Brownian motion.
nodes.example: Its variance tends to sigma^2/(2*kappa), giving a stable noise level around theta.

patterns.why: The deterministic drift pulls toward its equilibrium theta.
The solution adds exponentially weighted past noise.

nodes.name: Fokker-Planck equation
nodes.intuition: The random trajectory description and the evolving probability-density description encode the same diffusion. Drift transports probability and noise spreads it.
nodes.conditions: Assume a nonexplosive Ito diffusion with coefficients for which the SDE is well-defined. The law satisfies this equation weakly against smooth compactly supported test functions; a classical density formula additionally requires the displayed derivatives to exist.
nodes.example: With b=0 and sigma=1, this is the heat equation for a Brownian density.

patterns.why: The equation redistributes probability through a flux.
The density equation is adjoint to the generator acting on observables.

nodes.name: Empirical distribution function
nodes.intuition: Replace an unknown population distribution by equal mass on the observed data points. The empirical CDF counts the fraction below a threshold.
nodes.conditions: n>=1 and X_i are real observations. IID sampling is needed for the usual population-convergence interpretation, but not for the definition.
nodes.example: For observations 1,2,2,5, the empirical probability of a value at most two is 3/4.

patterns.why: Each observation receives equal empirical weight.
The CDF counts observations satisfying a threshold event.

nodes.name: Unbiased sample variance
nodes.intuition: Estimating the center from the same data uses one independent direction. Dividing by n-1 compensates for the resulting downward bias.
nodes.conditions: For unbiasedness, X_i are iid with finite variance sigma^2 and n>=2; the descriptive formula can be computed for arbitrary real observations.
nodes.example: For observations 1 and 3, the sample variance is two.

patterns.why: Spread is measured with squared residuals.
Centering removes the one-dimensional constant component.

nodes.name: Standard error of the sample mean
nodes.intuition: Averaging n independent equal-variance measurements divides uncertainty by the square root of n. The estimated standard error substitutes the sample spread.
nodes.conditions: X_i are independent with common finite variance sigma^2; the first formula is exact. S/sqrt(n) is the customary plug-in estimate under iid sampling, n>=2.
nodes.example: Quadrupling the number of independent observations halves the mean's standard error.

patterns.why: Independent averaging reduces variability.
The square-root law determines how precision grows with sample size.

nodes.name: Bias-variance decomposition
nodes.intuition: Squared estimation error separates into random wobble around the estimator's own mean and systematic displacement from the target.
nodes.conditions: theta is a fixed real target and T has a finite second moment.
nodes.example: An estimator with bias two and variance three has mean squared error seven.

patterns.why: Total error separates into variance and squared bias.
Centered random fluctuation has zero inner product with a constant.

nodes.name: Least squares
nodes.intuition: Choose the prediction vector closest to the observations in squared Euclidean distance. This turns fitting a model into a geometric projection problem.
nodes.conditions: X is a finite real n-by-p matrix and y in R^n. A minimizer always exists; coefficients are unique exactly when X has full column rank.
nodes.example: With only a constant predictor, the fitted value is the arithmetic mean of the observations.

patterns.why: The fitted parameters minimize a defined loss.
At a solution, the residual is perpendicular to every model direction.
The objective is a sum of squared deviations.

nodes.name: Least-squares normal equations
nodes.intuition: The best fit leaves no residual component that any predictor could explain. Setting the objective's gradient to zero expresses exactly that condition.
nodes.conditions: For any real finite X,y, the normal equations characterize all least-squares minimizers. The inverse formula requires full column rank; solving by QR or SVD is generally preferable numerically.
nodes.example: For X equal to the all-ones column, the equation becomes n*beta_hat=sum_i y_i.

patterns.why: X-transpose times the residual is zero.
Quadratic minimization reduces to solving a linear system.

nodes.name: Simple linear regression coefficients
nodes.latex: \widehat b=\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\overline x)(y_i-\overline y)}{\sum_i(x_i-\overline x)^2},\qquad \widehat a=\overline y-\widehat b\,\overline x
nodes.intuition: A best-fitting line uses shared centered movement divided by the predictor's own spread. Its intercept makes it pass through the data's center.
nodes.conditions: Finite real data, n>=2, and the x_i are not all equal; an intercept is included and squared residuals are minimized.
nodes.example: For points (0,1),(1,3),(2,5), the fitted line is y=1+2x.

patterns.why: The fitted line passes through the point of sample means.
The slope balances a cross-product sum against a squared-distance sum.

nodes.name: Gauss-Markov covariance bound
nodes.intuition: Among linear unbiased fits, ordinary least squares has the smallest variance in every parameter direction when errors have equal variance and no correlation.
nodes.conditions: y=X beta+epsilon with fixed full-column-rank X, E[epsilon]=0 and Cov(epsilon)=sigma^2 I. The competing estimator is Ay with AX=I; no normality assumption is needed.
nodes.example: Any unbiased linear estimate of a contrast c^T beta has variance at least sigma^2 c^T(X^T X)^-1 c.

patterns.why: OLS is optimal within the stated class of estimators.
The competing estimator's extra component adds a positive-semidefinite covariance.

nodes.name: Weighted least squares
nodes.intuition: Residuals are measured in a geometry that values some directions more heavily. Precision weighting gives reliable measurements greater influence.
nodes.conditions: W is real symmetric positive definite and X has full column rank. For generalized least squares with known error covariance Sigma, choose W=Sigma^-1.
nodes.example: For a constant model and diagonal W, the fitted constant is the weighted mean sum(w_i y_i)/sum(w_i).

patterns.why: A constant fit becomes a precision-weighted mean.
W changes the metric used to measure errors.

nodes.name: Ridge regression
nodes.intuition: A quadratic penalty trades some fit quality for smaller, more stable coefficients. It particularly suppresses directions the data measure weakly.
nodes.conditions: X,y are finite real arrays and lambda>0; all displayed coefficients are penalized, so the inverse exists even if X is rank deficient.
nodes.example: For X=I, every coefficient shrinks from y_i to y_i/(1+lambda).

patterns.why: Fit error and coefficient size are balanced in one objective.
Adding positive curvature stabilizes the quadratic problem.

nodes.name: Lasso regression
nodes.intuition: An absolute-value penalty makes small coefficients expensive relative to their benefit, allowing some fitted coefficients to become exactly zero.
nodes.conditions: Finite real X,y and lambda>0; minimizers exist, but coefficient uniqueness needs further conditions. All displayed coefficients are penalized.
nodes.example: For X=I, the solution soft-thresholds each observation at lambda.

patterns.why: The method balances residual fit against coefficient magnitude.
The objective remains convex despite corners that promote zeros.

nodes.name: Maximum likelihood estimation
nodes.intuition: Choose the model parameter that assigns the observed data the greatest probability density or mass. Taking logs converts independent contributions into an additive score.
nodes.conditions: The sum formula assumes iid data with density or mass f_theta relative to a fixed dominating measure. The argmax may be empty or nonunique; likelihood is a function of theta, not a probability distribution over theta.
nodes.example: For Bernoulli data with p allowed in [0,1], the MLE is the observed success fraction.

patterns.why: Parameters maximize the model's support for the observed sample.
Log likelihood adds contributions that multiply in the likelihood.

nodes.name: Maximum a posteriori estimation
nodes.intuition: A posterior mode combines fit to the observations with a preference encoded by the prior. In log form, the prior becomes a penalty.
nodes.conditions: A prior density or mass and likelihood are specified, the posterior is proper, and a maximizer exists. Density modes depend on the chosen parameterization.
nodes.example: A centered Gaussian prior on regression coefficients gives a quadratic penalty and a ridge-type MAP estimate.

patterns.why: A posterior mode minimizes a sum of losses.
Data and prior assumptions jointly determine the estimate.

nodes.name: Likelihood score
nodes.intuition: The score measures which parameter directions would make an observation more plausible. At the true model its average directional push cancels.
nodes.conditions: The definition needs differentiability and positive f_theta at x. The zero-mean identity additionally needs parameter-independent support and differentiation under the normalization integral, with integrable derivatives.
nodes.example: For N(mu,sigma^2) with known sigma, the score for mu is (x-mu)/sigma^2.

patterns.why: A derivative measures local changes in log likelihood.
Normalization forces the expected score to vanish under regularity.

nodes.name: Fisher information
nodes.intuition: Information is both score variability and average curvature of log likelihood. A sharply changing likelihood distinguishes nearby parameters more precisely.
nodes.conditions: For the first expression the score exists and has finite second moments. The Hessian identity needs common parameter-independent support, twice differentiable densities, and justified first and second differentiation under the integral.
nodes.example: For one normal observation with known variance sigma^2, information about its mean is 1/sigma^2.

patterns.why: Information is a second-moment matrix and curvature matrix.
It quantifies local distinguishability of model parameters.

nodes.name: Cramer-Rao lower bound
nodes.intuition: An unbiased estimator cannot fluctuate arbitrarily little if the data barely distinguish nearby parameter values.
nodes.conditions: A scalar parameter lies in an open interval; n iid observations have differentiable densities on common support, 0<I_1(theta)<infinity, and differentiation passes under integrals of both f_theta and T f_theta. T is unbiased for theta and has finite variance.
nodes.example: The sample mean of normal data with known variance attains the bound sigma^2/n.

patterns.why: More Fisher information permits a smaller variance bound.
Cauchy-Schwarz limits how strongly an estimator can align with the score.

nodes.name: Method of moments
nodes.intuition: Fit a distribution by matching a few population summaries to their empirical counterparts.
nodes.conditions: A p-parameter model has the displayed finite moments. Solving the equations requires identifiability and may give no solution, several solutions, or a parameter outside the model.
nodes.example: For an exponential rate lambda, matching the first moment gives lambda_hat=1/Xbar when Xbar>0.

patterns.why: Sample moments estimate population averages.
A parameter-to-moments map is inverted to recover parameters.

nodes.name: Neyman-Fisher factorization
nodes.intuition: A sufficient statistic compresses the data while preserving everything relevant to the parameter in the likelihood.
nodes.conditions: For a dominated statistical model, the existence of nonnegative measurable factors g_theta and parameter-independent h is equivalent to sufficiency of T, with the usual almost-everywhere conventions.
nodes.example: For iid Bernoulli observations, the total number of successes is sufficient for p.

patterns.why: The statistic retains all parameter-relevant information.
The likelihood separates into a parameter-bearing factor and a parameter-free factor.

nodes.name: Rao-Blackwell improvement
nodes.intuition: Average away fluctuations that carry no additional information about the parameter. Conditioning on a sufficient summary preserves unbiasedness while reducing noise.
nodes.conditions: U is an unbiased square-integrable estimator of theta in a dominated model; S is sufficient and the conditional expectation is taken using a parameter-independent conditional law given S.
nodes.example: For iid Bernoulli data, conditioning the first observation on the success count produces the sample mean.

patterns.why: Conditional averaging removes irrelevant random variation.
The estimator's variance cannot increase.

nodes.name: Beta-binomial conjugate update
nodes.intuition: A beta prior and binomial data combine by adding evidence to two running counts. The posterior mean blends the prior mean with the observed success rate.
nodes.conditions: p~Beta(alpha,beta), alpha,beta>0; given p, s~Binomial(n,p), n is a nonnegative integer and 0<=s<=n.
nodes.example: Starting with Beta(1,1), three successes in four trials gives Beta(4,2) and posterior mean 2/3.

patterns.why: Each new success or failure increments one parameter.
Posterior mean is a weighted blend of prior mean and empirical proportion.

nodes.name: Normal-normal conjugate update
nodes.intuition: Independent Gaussian information combines by adding precision. The posterior center is an average weighted by how precisely each source is known.
nodes.conditions: mu~N(mu_0,tau_0^2), tau_0^2>0; conditionally iid x_i~N(mu,sigma^2) with known sigma^2>0. The posterior is N(mu_n,tau_n^2).
nodes.example: Equal prior and data-mean precision place the posterior mean halfway between their centers.

patterns.why: The posterior mean is precision weighted.
Multiplying Gaussian densities adds their quadratic log penalties.

nodes.name: Posterior predictive distribution
nodes.intuition: Predict by averaging all parameter-specific predictions over the remaining parameter uncertainty.
nodes.conditions: The posterior is proper and the new outcome is conditionally independent of observed data given theta; the displayed densities use appropriate dominating measures, with sums for discrete theta.
nodes.example: Under a beta posterior, the next Bernoulli success probability equals the posterior mean of p.

patterns.why: Predictions are mixed using posterior weights.
Uncertainty about parameters remains part of predictive uncertainty.

nodes.name: Student t pivot
nodes.intuition: Replacing an unknown population spread by an estimated spread adds uncertainty. The t distribution accounts for that extra randomness exactly in the normal model.
nodes.conditions: X_i are iid N(mu,sigma^2), sigma^2>0, n>=2, and S^2 uses divisor n-1.
nodes.example: For n=10 normal observations, the standardized mean using S follows t with nine degrees of freedom.

patterns.why: Standardization removes the unknown location and scale.
Estimating the denominator changes the reference distribution.

nodes.name: Chi-squared pivot for normal variance
nodes.intuition: The centered sample occupies n-1 orthogonal Gaussian directions. Its squared standardized length has a chi-squared distribution.
nodes.conditions: X_i are iid N(mu,sigma^2), sigma^2>0, n>=2, and S^2 is the unbiased sample variance; chi^2_k is the sum of k independent squared standard normals.
nodes.example: A sample of six normal observations gives a five-degree-of-freedom reference law for variance inference.

patterns.why: Independent Gaussian residual coordinates contribute separate squared lengths.
A chi-squared variable is a sum of squared standard normals.

nodes.name: Exact t interval for a normal mean
nodes.latex: C(X)=\left[\overline X-t_{n-1,1-\alpha/2}\frac S{\sqrt n},\ \overline X+t_{n-1,1-\alpha/2}\frac S{\sqrt n}\right],\quad P_\mu(\mu\in C(X))=1-\alpha
nodes.intuition: Invert the t pivot to obtain all mean values compatible with the observed standardized error at a chosen coverage level.
nodes.conditions: IID normal observations with unknown mean and positive variance, n>=2, and 0<alpha<1. t_{nu,q} is the q quantile. Coverage refers to repetitions of the random interval construction.
nodes.example: Choosing alpha=.05 produces a procedure with 95% coverage under the normal model.

patterns.why: An acceptance region for a test becomes a confidence set for parameters.
Interval width is a quantile times the estimated standard error.

nodes.name: Delta method
nodes.latex: \sqrt n(T_n-\theta)\xrightarrow d\mathcal N(0,\Sigma)\ \Longrightarrow\ \sqrt n(g(T_n)-g(\theta))\xrightarrow d\mathcal N(0,J\Sigma J^\top)
nodes.intuition: A smooth transformation acts almost linearly on sufficiently small estimation errors. Its derivative pushes the limiting uncertainty into new coordinates.
nodes.conditions: T_n is R^d-valued with the stated limit; g maps a neighborhood of theta to R^k and is differentiable at theta, with Jacobian J=Dg(theta). A zero derivative can give a degenerate first-order limit.
nodes.example: For a positive mean estimator, the asymptotic variance of its logarithm is divided by the square of the true mean.

patterns.why: The Jacobian approximates the transformation near the target.
Covariance is transported through the local linear map.

nodes.name: Bootstrap estimate of standard error
nodes.intuition: Treat the observed data as a provisional population, resample it, and measure how much the statistic varies across those simulated samples.
nodes.conditions: For the iid nonparametric bootstrap, independently generate B>=2 samples of size n with replacement from the empirical distribution and recompute T. This estimates the conditional bootstrap spread; accuracy for population inference requires additional model and statistic assumptions.
nodes.example: Resample a dataset repeatedly to estimate the sampling uncertainty of its median.

patterns.why: Simulation creates repeated versions of the sampling experiment.
A statistic is repeatedly applied to resampled versions of the data.

nodes.name: Neyman-Pearson likelihood-ratio test
