nodes.intuition: Spend the allowed false-positive probability on observations that favor the alternative most strongly. This maximizes power for two fully specified models.
nodes.conditions: Simple hypotheses H0:f0 and H1:f1 use a common dominating measure; c>=0 and gamma in [0,1] are selected for the desired size when attainable. Randomization handles ties.
nodes.example: Distinguishing two known normal means with common variance reduces to a threshold on the sample mean.

patterns.why: The test maximizes power subject to a type-I error budget.
Likelihood ratios rank how strongly outcomes distinguish two models.

nodes.name: Wilks' likelihood-ratio limit
nodes.intuition: Compare the best unrestricted fit with the best fit obeying the null constraints. Locally quadratic likelihoods turn their difference into a squared projection length.
nodes.conditions: IID observations in a regular identifiable p-dimensional smooth model; the true parameter is interior, the null is a smooth p0-dimensional embedded submodel, Fisher information is nonsingular, both MLEs are consistent, and the likelihood admits its usual local quadratic expansion. Boundary and singular cases are excluded.
nodes.example: Testing one regular scalar restriction gives an asymptotic chi-squared law with one degree of freedom.

patterns.why: A local quadratic likelihood expansion controls the limit.
The difference measures a squared distance to the constrained model.

nodes.name: Tail-area p-value
nodes.intuition: A p-value measures how unusual the observed test statistic is under the specified null when larger values count as more extreme.
nodes.conditions: A simple null law P0 and a test statistic T are fixed before observing x. The superuniform bound holds for alpha in [0,1]; discrete tests can be conservative. This is not a posterior probability of the null.
nodes.example: Under a continuous null, a prechosen upper-tail test rejects at level .05 when p<=.05.

patterns.why: Tail probability maps a statistic onto a common [0,1] scale.
Evidence is evaluated relative to a specified null model.

nodes.name: Pearson chi-squared goodness-of-fit statistic
nodes.intuition: Compare observed category counts with expected counts after normalizing each squared error by its expected size.
nodes.conditions: (O_1,...,O_k) is multinomial(n,p), k is fixed, each known p_i>0, and n->infinity. Estimating probabilities from data changes the limiting degrees of freedom and requires additional analysis.
nodes.example: For a fair die, the statistic compares six observed counts with n/6 and has five asymptotic degrees of freedom.

patterns.why: The statistic adds standardized squared discrepancies.
Category frequencies are compared with model counts.

nodes.name: ANOVA sum-of-squares decomposition
nodes.intuition: Overall scatter equals scatter remaining inside groups plus scatter explained by different group centers.
nodes.conditions: Finite real observations partitioned into nonempty groups of sizes n_j; ybar is the overall mean and ybar_j the group mean. The identity needs no distributional assumptions.
nodes.example: If every observation equals its group mean, all variation lies in the between-group term.

patterns.why: Variation separates into within-group and between-group parts.
Within-group residuals sum to zero, canceling the cross term.

nodes.name: Logistic regression model
nodes.intuition: A linear predictor becomes an unrestricted log-odds score, while the logistic function maps it to a valid probability.
nodes.conditions: x,beta are finite real vectors and Y is binary. The formula specifies a conditional model; iid observations or conditional independence are extra assumptions for the usual summed likelihood.
nodes.example: Increasing a predictor by one multiplies the odds by exp(beta_j), holding the other predictors fixed.

patterns.why: Linear changes in log odds become multiplicative changes in odds.
A nonlinear link transforms a linear score into a probability.

nodes.name: Exponential family and log partition function
nodes.intuition: Many familiar distributions share a linear score in selected data summaries, followed by exponential reweighting and normalization.
nodes.conditions: h>=0 and T are measurable; eta lies where the normalizing integral is finite and positive. Interior natural parameters with justified differentiation satisfy grad A=E[T] and Hess A=Cov(T).
nodes.example: Bernoulli has T(x)=x and A(eta)=log(1+exp eta).

patterns.why: A log partition function normalizes exponential weights.
T collects the data summaries that carry parameter information.

nodes.name: Expectation-maximization algorithm
nodes.intuition: Alternate between averaging over unknown hidden variables and refitting the model to that averaged complete-data objective.
nodes.conditions: The observed likelihood is positive and finite; conditional expectations and the selected maximizer exist, with compatible support for the EM lower-bound argument. Exact EM does not decrease observed log likelihood, but does not guarantee a global optimum.
nodes.example: Gaussian-mixture EM alternates soft component membership weights with weighted mean and covariance updates.

patterns.why: The E-step averages over latent explanations.
The M-step improves an objective touching the current likelihood.
Alternating updates repeatedly refine the same model.

nodes.name: Kalman measurement update
nodes.intuition: Correct a prior estimate using the part of a measurement it failed to predict. The gain balances prior uncertainty against measurement noise.
nodes.conditions: Prior state X~N(m,P), P positive semidefinite; observation y=HX+epsilon with independent epsilon~N(0,R), R positive definite. These are exact conditional mean and covariance formulas.
nodes.example: For a scalar with equal prior and measurement variances, the updated mean is their midpoint.

patterns.why: The scalar case is a precision-weighted blend of prior and measurement.
The posterior can become the prior for the next measurement.

nodes.name: Principal component variance maximization
nodes.intuition: Find the direction in which a centered cloud varies most. Further orthogonal directions reveal successively less variance; principal components are uncorrelated, but need not be statistically independent.
nodes.conditions: Sigma is a real symmetric positive-semidefinite covariance or sample-covariance matrix. A maximizing unit eigenvector exists; it is not unique if the largest eigenvalue is repeated.
nodes.example: For covariance diag(9,1), the first principal direction is the first coordinate and explains 90% of total variance.

patterns.why: The first component maximizes retained variance under a unit-length constraint.
A symmetric covariance matrix supplies perpendicular component directions.

nodes.name: Convex function inequality
nodes.intuition: Along every segment, a convex function stays below the chord joining its endpoint values. Mixing choices cannot cost more than mixing their costs.
nodes.conditions: f is real-valued on a convex subset of a real vector space; x,y are in its domain and t in [0,1].
nodes.example: The squared norm is convex; applying the formula to x and -x gives its minimum at zero.

patterns.why: The inequality compares the cost of an average with the average cost.
Every line segment obeys the same upward-curvature condition.

nodes.name: First-order characterization of convexity
nodes.intuition: Every tangent plane of a differentiable convex function is a global lower bound. A zero gradient therefore certifies global optimality.
nodes.conditions: f is differentiable on an open convex subset of R^n; the displayed inequality for every x,y is equivalent to convexity.
nodes.example: For f(x)=x^2, the difference between the graph and its tangent at a is (x-a)^2.

patterns.why: A first-order approximation supports the whole graph from below.
Local derivative information becomes a global inequality.

nodes.name: Second-order characterization of convexity
nodes.intuition: A smooth function is convex precisely when it curves upward or stays flat in every direction.
nodes.conditions: f is twice continuously differentiable on an open convex subset of R^n; positive semidefiniteness is required at every point in the domain.
nodes.example: For f(x)=x^T A x with symmetric A, convexity is equivalent to A being positive semidefinite.

patterns.why: Directional curvature is a Hessian quadratic form.
Nonnegative curvature on every line characterizes convexity.

nodes.name: Strong convexity inequality
nodes.intuition: Strong convexity gives a uniform bowl shape. Moving away from a minimizer must raise the objective at least quadratically.
nodes.conditions: mu>0, f is differentiable on a convex domain, and the inequality holds for all x,y there. A minimizer, if it exists, is unique.
nodes.example: A quadratic with Hessian at least mu*I is mu-strongly convex.

patterns.why: A positive curvature floor strengthens ordinary convexity.
Objective error controls squared distance from the minimizer.

nodes.name: Descent lemma
nodes.intuition: If the gradient cannot change too quickly, the graph cannot rise faster than a quadratic above its tangent. This supplies a safe model for choosing steps.
nodes.conditions: f is differentiable on a convex domain and its gradient is L-Lipschitz there in Euclidean norm, L>0; the segment from x to y stays in the domain. Convexity of f is not required.
nodes.example: For a quadratic with Hessian operator norm at most L, the bound follows directly from its expansion.

patterns.why: The quadratic term bounds the error of the tangent approximation.
A quadratic upper model controls finite steps.

nodes.name: Gradient descent
nodes.intuition: Move against the local direction of fastest increase. The step size controls how far the local slope can safely guide the next move.
nodes.conditions: f is differentiable and eta_k>0. For an L-Lipschitz gradient on R^n, a fixed 0<eta<2/L gives descent unless the gradient is zero; convergence to a global minimum needs further structure such as convexity.
nodes.example: For f(x)=x^2/2, choosing eta=1 sends any starting point directly to zero.

patterns.why: The gradient uses a local linear model of the objective.
Each point is updated from the previous point by the same rule.

nodes.name: Convex gradient descent error bound
nodes.intuition: For smooth convex objectives, repeated safe gradient steps reduce objective error at a guaranteed inverse-iteration rate.
nodes.conditions: f:R^n->R is convex with L-Lipschitz gradient, L>0, and has a minimizer x*. Use constant step 1/L and integer k>=1.
nodes.example: The bound guarantees that doubling the iteration budget halves this worst-case error estimate.

patterns.why: The bound quantifies approach to the optimum.
A step-size choice produces a certified objective guarantee.

nodes.name: Newton step for optimization
nodes.intuition: Fit a local quadratic bowl and step toward its minimizer. Curvature corrects for directions with very different scales.
nodes.conditions: f is twice differentiable and the Hessian is invertible at the current iterate; positive definiteness makes d a descent direction. A damping or line-search choice may be needed; unrestricted full steps need not converge.
nodes.example: A full step solves any strictly convex quadratic exactly in exact arithmetic.

patterns.why: The method optimizes a local second-order model.
The inverse Hessian rescales the gradient by local curvature.

nodes.name: Coordinate descent
nodes.intuition: Improve one coordinate at a time while holding the others fixed. A large optimization problem becomes a sequence of one-dimensional problems.
nodes.conditions: The selected one-dimensional minimum must exist. Cyclic or random coordinate selection and suitable smoothness or convexity assumptions are needed for convergence guarantees.
nodes.example: For a diagonal positive quadratic, one exact coordinate sweep finds the minimizer.

patterns.why: A multivariable problem is broken into coordinate subproblems.
Repeated local updates accumulate into a full fit.

nodes.name: Stochastic gradient descent
nodes.latex: x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta_kg_k,\quad g_k=\nabla f_{I_k}(x_k),\quad \mathbb E[g_k\mid x_k]=\nabla F(x_k),\quad F=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nf_i
nodes.intuition: Use a randomly chosen contribution to estimate the full gradient. Each step is noisy but much cheaper when the objective has many terms.
nodes.conditions: Each f_i is differentiable, I_k is uniform on {1,...,n} independently of past randomness given x_k, and eta_k>0. The formula alone gives no convergence guarantee; step sizes, variance, and objective geometry matter.
nodes.example: Choose one observation at each step to update a large regression fit.

patterns.why: The noisy gradient is correct on average.
Random subsampling replaces a full deterministic calculation.

nodes.name: Heavy-ball momentum
nodes.intuition: Keep part of the previous displacement so consistent directions accumulate speed. Momentum can damp alternating motions but can also overshoot.
nodes.conditions: f is differentiable, eta>0, and typically 0<=beta<1. These choices alone do not guarantee convergence; for a positive quadratic with largest Hessian eigenvalue L, stability holds for eta<2(1+beta)/L.
nodes.example: On a narrow quadratic valley, memory of previous motion can reduce slow progress along the shallow direction.

patterns.why: The next state depends on two successive positions.
Past movement contributes to the current step.

nodes.name: Lagrange multiplier stationarity
nodes.intuition: At a constrained optimum, no feasible infinitesimal direction can improve the objective. The objective gradient must therefore lie among the normals to the constraints.
nodes.conditions: f and h_j are C1 near a local constrained optimum x*, and the constraint gradients there are linearly independent. These equations are necessary, not generally sufficient.
nodes.example: Optimizing a quadratic on the unit sphere produces an eigenvector equation.

patterns.why: The objective gradient is perpendicular to feasible tangent directions.
Constraint gradients describe the normal directions of the feasible surface.

nodes.name: Lagrangian dual function
nodes.intuition: Attach prices to constraint violations and minimize the priced objective. Each choice of nonnegative inequality prices gives a lower-bound candidate.
nodes.conditions: The primal is min f0 subject to f_i<=0 and h_j=0; lambda_i>=0 and nu_j are free. The infimum uses the common domain, and g may equal minus infinity.
nodes.example: For a linear program, a finite dual value forces cancellation of the free primal variable's coefficient.

patterns.why: Constraint prices create a second optimization problem.
The infimum converts an objective family into lower bounds.

nodes.name: Weak duality
nodes.intuition: Any valid dual bound lies below every feasible primal cost. A small gap between one of each certifies near optimality.
nodes.conditions: The primal uses inequalities f_i<=0 and equalities h_j=0; g is the Lagrangian infimum and lambda>=0. Convexity is unnecessary; compare well-defined extended optimal values.
nodes.example: A feasible solution of cost ten and dual bound nine proves the unknown optimal cost lies between nine and ten.

patterns.why: Primal solutions and dual bounds constrain the same optimal value.
A gap gives an explicit certificate of solution quality.

nodes.name: Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions
nodes.intuition: Optimality balances the objective gradient with active constraint normals. A constraint receives a nonzero price only if it is tight.
nodes.conditions: For differentiable convex f0,f_i on R^n and affine equalities, any feasible triple satisfying KKT is globally optimal. If a strict feasible point exists (Slater), KKT is also necessary at every attained finite optimum. Nonconvex necessity needs a constraint qualification and gives no global certificate.
nodes.example: For min x^2 subject to x>=1, x=1 and multiplier two satisfy stationarity and complementary slackness.

patterns.why: Primal variables and constraint prices meet in a common certificate.
Only active boundary constraints can carry nonzero multipliers.

nodes.name: Slater's strong-duality condition
nodes.intuition: A genuinely feasible interior point prevents a convex problem's constraints from pinching off the geometry needed for exact dual bounds.
nodes.conditions: The f_i and f0 are finite convex functions on R^n, equalities are affine, and the primal optimal value is finite. The displayed strict-feasibility condition is sufficient; more general versions use relative interiors.
nodes.example: A feasible convex program with strictly slack inequalities admits an attained dual optimum even if the primal infimum is approached only as a limit.

patterns.why: Strict feasibility keeps inequalities away from a pathological boundary intersection.
The condition guarantees equality of primal and dual optimal values.

nodes.name: Linear programming duality
nodes.intuition: A resource-allocation optimum can be described either by choosing activities or by assigning prices that bound their value.
nodes.conditions: Finite real A,b,c; the displayed equality and attainment hold when the primal is feasible and its optimal value is finite. Without those assumptions, infeasibility or unboundedness must be handled separately.
nodes.example: A primal solution and a feasible price vector with equal objectives certify optimality immediately.

patterns.why: Activity variables and resource prices form paired problems.
Both objectives and constraints are linear.

nodes.name: Convex quadratic program
nodes.latex: \min_x\ \tfrac12x^\top Qx+c^\top x\quad\text{subject to }Gx\le h,\ Ax=b,\qquad Q\succeq0
nodes.intuition: A quadratic cost measures smooth tradeoffs while linear constraints describe allowed choices. This includes many fitting and allocation problems.
nodes.conditions: Q is symmetric positive semidefinite and all arrays are finite real with compatible dimensions. Semidefinite Q can allow nonuniqueness or an unbounded objective; Q positive definite gives a unique optimum on any nonempty closed feasible polyhedron.
nodes.example: Nonnegative least squares is a quadratic program with Q=2X^T X and constraints beta>=0.

patterns.why: Curvature is encoded by one constant matrix.
Positive-semidefinite curvature and linear constraints form a convex problem.

nodes.name: Convex subgradient
nodes.intuition: At a corner, several slopes may support the graph from below. The subdifferential stores all of them.
nodes.conditions: f is a proper convex function on R^n, possibly taking +infinity, and f(x) is finite; a boundary point can have an empty subdifferential.
nodes.example: For f(x)=|x|, the subdifferential at zero is the entire interval [-1,1].

patterns.why: A subgradient defines a global supporting affine function.
Generalized slopes extend gradients to nonsmooth functions.

nodes.name: Proximal operator
nodes.intuition: Move toward lower cost while paying for distance from the current point. The quadratic tether makes many difficult updates well-defined and stable.
nodes.conditions: g is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex on R^n; eta>0. The minimizer exists and is unique.
nodes.example: For g the indicator of a nonempty closed convex set, the proximal operator is Euclidean projection onto that set.

patterns.why: The update itself solves a small minimization problem.
A quadratic distance limits how far the update moves.

nodes.name: Soft thresholding
nodes.intuition: Shrink each coordinate toward zero by a fixed amount, stopping at zero. Small coordinates disappear entirely.
nodes.conditions: v is a finite real vector, lambda>=0, and sign(0)=0; this minimizes one-half ||x-v||^2+lambda||x||_1.
nodes.example: Thresholding (3,-.4,0) at one gives (2,0,0).

patterns.why: The separable objective splits into independent scalar minimizations.
The formula exactly solves an absolute-value-penalized quadratic.

nodes.name: Proximal gradient method
nodes.intuition: Use a gradient step for the smooth part and a proximal step for the nonsmooth part. Each part is handled by the operation suited to its structure.
nodes.conditions: For the standard convex convergence guarantee, f is convex with L-Lipschitz gradient on R^n, g is proper closed convex, a minimizer of f+g exists, and 0<eta<=1/L.
nodes.example: For squared-error loss plus an L1 penalty, one iteration is a gradient step followed by soft thresholding.

patterns.why: Smooth and nonsmooth terms are treated separately.
Two simple operators form one complete update.

nodes.name: Projected gradient method
nodes.intuition: Take a downhill step and then return to the nearest feasible point. Projection enforces the constraint after each update.
nodes.conditions: C is a nonempty closed convex subset of R^n. For the standard convex convergence guarantee, f has an L-Lipschitz gradient, is convex, has a minimizer on C, and 0<eta<=1/L.
nodes.example: For nonnegative variables, projection clips negative coordinates to zero.

patterns.why: Projection chooses the closest feasible correction.
An unconstrained step is composed with constraint enforcement.

nodes.name: Log-sum-exp
nodes.intuition: Log-sum-exp is a smooth maximum that lets several strong alternatives contribute. Subtracting the largest input computes it without unnecessarily large exponentials.
nodes.conditions: x is a finite real vector, n>=1. It obeys max_i x_i<=LSE(x)<=max_i x_i+log n; the base is e.
nodes.example: LSE(0,0)=log 2, reflecting two equally weighted alternatives.

patterns.why: Logarithms summarize sums of exponential scores.
Its Hessian is a positive-semidefinite categorical covariance.

nodes.name: Softmax weights
nodes.intuition: Turn arbitrary real scores into positive weights that sum to one. A score difference becomes a log probability ratio.
nodes.conditions: x is a finite real vector and n>=1; the formula uses the natural exponential. Adding the same constant to every score changes no probability.
nodes.example: Scores (0,log 3) give probabilities (1/4,3/4).

patterns.why: The output weights can form an expectation or weighted mean.
Common shifts of all scores leave the normalized probabilities unchanged.

nodes.name: Legendre-Fenchel conjugate
nodes.intuition: Describe a function by how much a linear slope can exceed it. This switches from positions to supporting-slope information.
nodes.conditions: f is a proper extended-real function on R^n; f* may take +infinity. The conjugate is convex and lower-semicontinuous even when f is not convex.
nodes.example: For f(x)=||x||^2/2, the conjugate is f*(y)=||y||^2/2.

patterns.why: Positions and slopes give paired representations.
A supremum defines the transformed function.

nodes.name: Fenchel-Young inequality
nodes.intuition: A function value and its dual value always cover the linear pairing. Equality means the primal point and dual slope support each other perfectly.
nodes.conditions: f is proper closed convex; x is in its effective domain. The inequality uses extended-real values; equality requires finite values and is equivalent to the subgradient condition.

patterns.why: The inequality links a function to its conjugate.
Equality identifies a supporting slope.

nodes.name: Bregman divergence
nodes.intuition: Measure how far the function rises above its tangent at y. Curvature creates a notion of discrepancy adapted to the chosen function.
nodes.conditions: h is differentiable and strictly convex on an open convex domain containing x,y. D_h>=0 and vanishes only at x=y, but it is generally neither symmetric nor a metric.

patterns.why: The generating function determines how discrepancies are measured.
The divergence is the error in a tangent-plane approximation.

nodes.name: Mirror descent
nodes.intuition: Choose a geometry that matches the variables, then take a local improvement step measured in that geometry. Probabilities and Euclidean coordinates can therefore use different natural updates.
nodes.conditions: C is convex, h is differentiable and strictly convex at the evaluated interior points, eta_k>0, and the displayed minimum is attained. Boundary values can use a lower-semicontinuous extension; convergence needs additional assumptions on f, h, and steps.
nodes.example: Negative-entropy geometry on the simplex produces multiplicative exponential-weight updates from an interior starting point.

patterns.why: A Bregman divergence replaces Euclidean squared distance.
The objective is represented by its current gradient.

nodes.name: Finite-game minimax theorem
nodes.intuition: Randomized strategies allow two opposing players to agree on one worst-case value. Neither player benefits from knowing which optimization order is used.
nodes.conditions: A is a finite real m-by-n payoff matrix, and Delta_m,Delta_n are probability simplexes; payoff is bilinear and both players may randomize.
nodes.example: In matching pennies, each player uses probabilities (1/2,1/2), giving value zero for the usual plus/minus-one payoff.

patterns.why: The max-min and min-max problems have the same value.
Mixed strategies turn pure outcomes into expected payoffs.

nodes.name: Self-information
nodes.intuition: An unlikely outcome carries more surprise than a likely one. Logarithms make the surprise of independent outcomes add.
nodes.conditions: x is an outcome of a discrete law with p(x)>0; natural logs give nats, and log base two gives bits. A zero-probability event has infinite formal self-information.
nodes.example: An outcome of probability 1/8 carries three bits of self-information.

patterns.why: Products of probabilities become sums of surprise.
Rarity sets the amount of surprise attributed to an outcome.

nodes.name: Shannon entropy
nodes.intuition: Entropy is average surprise. It measures how uncertain a random outcome is before observing it.
nodes.conditions: X has a finite or countable discrete law; use 0 log 0=0. Natural logs give nats; a countable law may have infinite entropy.
nodes.example: A fair binary outcome has entropy log 2 nats, or one bit.

patterns.why: Individual surprises are averaged using their probabilities.
The mean surprise quantifies uncertainty about the outcome.

nodes.name: Cross entropy
nodes.intuition: Evaluate outcomes generated by p using probabilities supplied by q. The excess average surprise measures the mismatch between them.
nodes.conditions: p and q are probability vectors on the same finite alphabet, with q_i>0 whenever p_i>0 for finite cross entropy; otherwise it is +infinity. Terms with p_i=0 contribute zero.
nodes.example: A model assigning 1/2 to each of two outcomes incurs log 2 nats per observation under any binary source.

patterns.why: Model surprise is averaged under the true or empirical outcome law.
Total predictive surprise separates into inherent uncertainty and mismatch.

nodes.name: Kullback-Leibler divergence
nodes.intuition: KL divergence measures the extra expected log loss from using q when p describes the outcomes. It is directional, so reversing the arguments changes the question.
nodes.conditions: p,q are probability vectors on the same finite alphabet; zero p_i contributes zero, while p_i>0 and q_i=0 gives +infinity. KL is not generally symmetric and is not a metric.
nodes.example: For Bernoulli(1/2) versus Bernoulli(1/4), KL equals one-half log(4/3).

patterns.why: The divergence quantifies predictive mismatch.
A log ratio compares two probability assignments.

nodes.name: Gibbs' inequality
nodes.intuition: On average, a distribution assigns its own outcomes at least as well as any competing distribution under log loss.
nodes.conditions: p,q are probability vectors on the same finite alphabet, with the usual zero-mass and infinite-divergence conventions.
nodes.example: The cross entropy of p with q cannot be smaller than the entropy of p.

patterns.why: Convexity of negative log proves the inequality.
The true distribution uniquely minimizes expected log loss.

nodes.name: Entropy chain rule
nodes.intuition: Describe X first, then the uncertainty still remaining about Y. The two stages account for the full joint uncertainty.
nodes.conditions: X,Y have finite alphabets; conditional distributions are used only at positive-mass x. All entropies use the same logarithm base.
nodes.example: Two independent fair bits have joint entropy two bits, one from each stage.

patterns.why: Joint uncertainty splits into marginal and conditional uncertainty.
Conditional entropy averages remaining uncertainty over observed X.

nodes.name: Mutual information
nodes.intuition: Mutual information measures how much knowing one variable reduces uncertainty about the other. It detects dependence beyond linear correlation.
nodes.conditions: X,Y have finite alphabets; the product law p_Xp_Y is positive on the support of the joint law. All logs use the same base.
nodes.example: If Y=X is a fair bit, mutual information is one bit; independent variables have zero mutual information.

patterns.why: The quantity measures shared predictive information.
Subtracting joint uncertainty reveals the uncertainty counted twice.

nodes.name: Conditional mutual information
nodes.latex: I(X;Y\mid Z)=\sum_zp(z)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{XY\mid z}\|p_{X\mid z}p_{Y\mid z}),\quad I(X;Y,Z)=I(X;Z)+I(X;Y\mid Z)
nodes.intuition: Measure the dependence left between X and Y after accounting for Z. Averaging over Z makes this a conditional information quantity.
nodes.conditions: X,Y,Z have finite alphabets; only z with p(z)>0 enter conditional distributions.
nodes.example: Two variables can be independent marginally yet become dependent after conditioning, as in the XOR construction.

patterns.why: Dependence is evaluated within each condition and then averaged.
The information chain rule separates information already explained by Z.

nodes.name: Data-processing inequality
nodes.intuition: Processing an observation cannot create new information about its source when the processor sees only that observation.
nodes.conditions: X,Y,Z have finite alphabets and satisfy conditional independence X independent of Z given Y, equivalently the indicated Markov chain.
nodes.example: Coarsening a recorded measurement to a rounded value cannot increase its information about the original source.

patterns.why: A downstream representation cannot add missing source information.
The inequality applies when one channel is composed after another.

nodes.name: Fano's inequality
nodes.intuition: If a decoder usually reconstructs a finite label correctly, little uncertainty can remain about that label. Conversely, large conditional entropy forces errors.
nodes.conditions: X takes K>=2 possible values, Y has a finite alphabet, Xhat=g(Y), and P_e=P(Xhat!=X); use 0 log 0=0 and one common log base.
nodes.example: For binary X, the bound reduces to H(X|Y)<=h(P_e).

patterns.why: Remaining entropy limits achievable decoding accuracy.
Separate whether an error occurred from which wrong label occurred.

nodes.name: Maximum entropy on a finite alphabet
nodes.intuition: If only the number of possible outcomes is fixed, spreading probability equally creates the most uncertainty.
nodes.conditions: p is a probability vector on a specified alphabet of n>=1 outcomes, with natural logs and 0 log 0=0.
nodes.example: A fair six-sided die has entropy log 6 nats, the largest possible for six outcomes.

patterns.why: All labels receive the same weight at the maximum.
Entropy is maximized under normalization alone.

nodes.name: Differential entropy
nodes.intuition: Differential entropy summarizes a density's spread in continuous coordinates. Unlike discrete entropy, its value depends on the units used.
nodes.conditions: X has a Lebesgue density f; assume integral |f log f| is finite for a finite well-defined value, with 0 log 0=0. Differential entropy can be negative.
nodes.example: A uniform density on an interval of length a has differential entropy log a.

patterns.why: The negative log density is averaged under the density itself.
Changing coordinate units shifts the entropy.

nodes.name: Gaussian maximum entropy at fixed variance
nodes.intuition: With a fixed variance, the Gaussian spreads probability as unpredictably as possible under differential entropy.
nodes.conditions: X is real with a density, finite variance sigma^2>0, and a well-defined finite differential entropy. Equality holds exactly for a Gaussian density with that variance, up to almost-everywhere equality.
nodes.example: A unit-variance density has entropy at most one-half log(2*pi*e) nats.

patterns.why: The Gaussian solves an entropy maximization problem.
The fixed second moment becomes a quadratic log-density constraint.

nodes.name: Gibbs distribution
nodes.intuition: Exponential weights balance low cost against diversity. Increasing beta concentrates mass on lower-energy choices.
nodes.conditions: There are finitely many finite real energies E_i and beta>0. The displayed law uniquely minimizes sum_i p_i E_i-(1/beta)H(p) over the probability simplex.
nodes.example: If two energies are equal, they receive equal weights for every beta.

patterns.why: Energy differences become probability ratios through exponentials.
The distribution balances mean energy against entropy.

nodes.name: Entropy variational formula for log-sum-exp
nodes.intuition: A smooth maximum is the best weighted average score plus a reward for keeping the weights spread out.
nodes.conditions: x is a finite real vector, Delta_n is the probability simplex, and H uses natural logs with 0 log 0=0. The unique maximizing weights are softmax(x).
nodes.example: For n equal scores a, the optimum is uniform and the value is a+log n.

patterns.why: Log-sum-exp and negative entropy are convex-conjugate partners.
The objective combines an expected score with entropy.

nodes.name: Evidence lower bound identity
nodes.intuition: An approximate latent distribution creates a lower bound on log evidence. The missing amount is exactly its KL divergence from the true posterior.
nodes.conditions: 0<p(x)<infinity; q is a probability density or mass absolutely continuous with respect to the posterior, and both displayed right-hand terms are finite. KL nonnegativity then gives L(q)<=log p(x).
nodes.example: Choosing q equal to the exact posterior makes the bound tight.

patterns.why: Log evidence separates into a tractable objective and an approximation gap.
Improving the lower bound minimizes posterior mismatch.

nodes.name: Capacity of a discrete memoryless channel
nodes.intuition: Choose the input distribution that makes the output as informative about the input as possible. This value governs reliable long-block communication.
nodes.conditions: A fixed finite-input, finite-output memoryless channel p(y|x), with no additional input constraint. C is the supremum of achievable rates with error tending to zero; natural-log information gives nats per use.
nodes.example: A noiseless channel with n symbols has capacity log n nats per use.

patterns.why: The sender chooses an input law to maximize information transfer.
Mutual information measures the usable information per channel use.

nodes.name: Real Gaussian channel capacity
nodes.intuition: For additive Gaussian noise, useful information grows logarithmically with signal-to-noise ratio. A Gaussian input makes best use of the allowed average power.
nodes.conditions: One real memoryless channel use is Y=X+Z, with independent Z~N(0,N), N>0, and E[X^2]<=P, P>=0. The formula is in nats per real use; divide by log 2 for bits.
nodes.example: At P=N the capacity is one-half bit per real channel use.

patterns.why: Information grows as the logarithm of the variance ratio.
The result maximizes information subject to a second-moment budget.

nodes.name: Kraft inequality
nodes.intuition: Each binary codeword occupies a branch of a binary tree. Prefix-free words must occupy disjoint branches, so their total tree mass cannot exceed one.
nodes.conditions: For a finite collection of positive integer lengths ell_i, a binary prefix code with those lengths exists exactly when the inequality holds. Every uniquely decodable binary code also satisfies it.
nodes.example: Lengths (1,2,2) satisfy equality and are realized by codewords 0,10,11.

patterns.why: Codewords consume disjoint portions of a binary tree.
The available tree mass sums to one.

nodes.name: Entropy bound for binary prefix coding
nodes.intuition: Entropy sets the ideal average description length. Integer codeword lengths cost less than one additional bit per symbol for an optimal binary prefix code.
nodes.conditions: A finite alphabet with at least two positive-probability symbols; H(p) uses natural logs. The minimum is over binary prefix codes for single symbols, with average length measured in bits.
nodes.example: For probabilities (1/2,1/4,1/4), lengths (1,2,2) achieve the entropy exactly at 1.5 bits.

patterns.why: Code efficiency is measured by probability-weighted average length.
Entropy is the fundamental lower bound on expected description length.

nodes.name: Fourier transform
nodes.intuition: Measure how strongly a signal aligns with each oscillation. Frequency coordinates can expose structure hidden in its time or spatial values.
nodes.conditions: f is a complex-valued Lebesgue-integrable function on R for this ordinary integral definition; xi is real. This branch consistently uses the 2-pi frequency convention.
nodes.example: A normalized probability density has Fourier value one at frequency zero.

patterns.why: A signal is represented by frequency content rather than point values.
The integral transforms sums and scalar multiples linearly.

nodes.name: Fourier inversion
nodes.intuition: Reassemble a signal by adding its frequency contributions with their phases. Under suitable integrability, the frequency description loses no information.
nodes.conditions: Assume f and its Fourier transform are in L1(R). The identity holds almost everywhere and at every continuity point of f; broader L2 inversion uses an L2 limit rather than this absolute integral.
nodes.example: The transform and inverse transform of a Gaussian recover the original Gaussian.

patterns.why: The signal is rebuilt from its oscillatory components.
Analysis into frequencies is paired with synthesis from frequencies.

nodes.name: Fourier convolution theorem
nodes.intuition: Convolution mixes shifted copies in the original coordinates. In frequency coordinates, each frequency is simply scaled by a multiplier.
nodes.conditions: f,g belong to L1(R); their convolution belongs to L1 and the displayed identity holds at every real xi with the chosen Fourier convention.
nodes.example: Convolving a signal with a smoothing kernel suppresses frequencies where the kernel's transform is small.

patterns.why: Cascading convolution operations becomes multiplication of frequency responses.
The frequency representation simplifies an integral operation.

nodes.name: Fourier translation rule
nodes.intuition: Moving a signal changes the phase of each frequency while preserving its spectral magnitude.
nodes.conditions: f in L1(R), a real, with the 2-pi Fourier convention.
nodes.example: A delayed pulse has the same magnitude spectrum as the original pulse.

patterns.why: Translation preserves the magnitude of every Fourier component.
A time shift becomes a complex exponential phase factor.

nodes.name: Fourier modulation rule
nodes.intuition: Multiplying by a pure oscillation moves the whole spectrum to a new center frequency.
nodes.conditions: f in L1(R) and nu real; the modulation uses the same 2-pi convention as the transform.
nodes.example: A narrow baseband signal can be shifted to a carrier band by complex modulation.

patterns.why: A multiplicative time-domain operation becomes frequency translation.
The spectrum's shape is preserved under the shift.

nodes.name: Fourier scaling rule
nodes.intuition: Compressing a signal in time spreads it in frequency. The amplitude factor compensates for the change in integration scale.
nodes.conditions: f in L1(R) and a is a nonzero real number; negative a also reverses orientation.
nodes.example: The signal f(2t) is twice as narrow in time and its spectrum is one-half fhat(xi/2).

patterns.why: Time and frequency widths change reciprocally.
A substitution in the integral produces the Jacobian factor.

nodes.name: Fourier differentiation rule
nodes.intuition: Differentiation amplifies rapid oscillations more strongly than slow ones. In frequency coordinates, a derivative is multiplication by frequency.
nodes.conditions: For this statement assume f is a Schwartz function (smooth with all derivatives rapidly decreasing); weaker hypotheses can also justify integration by parts and vanishing boundary terms.
nodes.example: A second derivative transforms to -(2*pi*xi)^2 fhat(xi).

patterns.why: A differential operator becomes pointwise multiplication.
Frequency components remain separate under a linear derivative.

nodes.name: Plancherel identity
nodes.intuition: Changing from time to frequency coordinates preserves total squared magnitude. Energy is redistributed among frequencies, not changed.
nodes.conditions: f belongs to L2(R), and its transform is defined by the unique L2 extension of the L1-intersection-L2 transform. The 2-pi convention makes the equality have no extra factor.
nodes.example: A filter that removes frequencies cannot increase L2 energy when its multiplier has magnitude at most one.

patterns.why: Total squared magnitude is preserved by the transform.
The transform behaves like a continuous orthonormal coordinate change.

nodes.name: Fourier transform of a Gaussian
nodes.intuition: A Gaussian remains Gaussian under the Fourier transform, with reciprocal width. Its shape is balanced between localization in both domains.
nodes.conditions: a>0 is real and the 2-pi transform convention is used.
nodes.example: When a=1, exp(-pi*t^2) is its own Fourier transform.

patterns.why: The Gaussian family is preserved by Fourier transformation.
A wider Gaussian in one domain becomes narrower in the other.

nodes.name: Discrete Fourier transform
nodes.latex: X_k=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}x_ne^{-2\pi i kn/N},\qquad x_n=\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}X_ke^{2\pi i kn/N}
nodes.intuition: A finite vector can be represented by its alignment with N discrete oscillations. Orthogonality makes the representation exactly reversible.
nodes.conditions: N>=1 is an integer, x in C^N, and indices n,k run from zero to N-1. The forward transform is unnormalized and the inverse uses 1/N.
nodes.example: X_0/N is the arithmetic mean of the original vector.

patterns.why: A finite signal changes to a discrete frequency basis.
Discrete complex exponentials form an orthogonal basis.

nodes.name: Parseval identity for the DFT
nodes.intuition: The DFT redistributes squared length across orthogonal frequency directions. Its normalization determines the single factor of N.
nodes.conditions: x in C^N with N>=1 and the unnormalized forward DFT used in discrete-fourier-transform.
nodes.example: For the all-ones vector, the only nonzero coefficient is X_0=N; both sides equal N.

patterns.why: Total squared signal magnitude is unchanged after normalization.
The identity compares sums of squared component magnitudes.

nodes.name: Circular convolution and the DFT
nodes.intuition: Wrap finite sequences around a circle and sum all pairs producing the same cyclic index. The DFT diagonalizes this cyclic mixing.
nodes.conditions: x,y in C^N and N>=1; indices are taken modulo N. Ordinary linear convolution requires enough zero-padding to avoid circular wraparound.
nodes.example: For lengths a and b, zero-padding to N>=a+b-1 allows circular convolution to reproduce their linear convolution.

patterns.why: Frequency-wise multiplication composes cyclic convolution operations.
The rule respects cyclic shifts.

nodes.name: Radix-two FFT butterfly
nodes.intuition: Split a transform into even-index and odd-index inputs, solve the two smaller transforms, and reuse their results to reconstruct the full transform.
nodes.conditions: N=2^m with integer m>=1; E and O are the length-N/2 DFTs of even and odd subsequences, and 0<=k<N/2. Recursing gives O(N log N) arithmetic operations.
nodes.example: An eight-point DFT splits into two four-point DFTs, then four two-point DFTs.

patterns.why: A large transform is reduced to smaller transforms of the same form.
Even and odd subsequences provide reusable partial results.

nodes.name: Shannon sampling theorem
nodes.intuition: Exact bandlimiting makes regularly spaced samples contain the whole signal. Shifted sinc functions reconstruct the continuous curve between samples.
nodes.conditions: T>0, f in L2(R), and fhat vanishes outside [-1/(2T),1/(2T)]. Use the continuous bandlimited representative and sinc(0)=1; the full series converges in L2 and uniformly. A truncated finite reconstruction is an approximation.
nodes.example: A signal with no frequencies above B can be reconstructed from all samples at spacing T=1/(2B), for B>0.

patterns.why: Shifted sinc functions rebuild the signal from sample values.
Bandlimiting restricts the information that must be encoded by samples.

nodes.name: Autocorrelation of a stationary process
nodes.intuition: Compare a signal with a delayed version of itself and average the product. This reveals persistence and repeated structure across time lags.
nodes.conditions: X is a complex second-order wide-sense stationary process, so the mean is constant and covariance depends only on lag. For zero mean, autocorrelation equals autocovariance.
nodes.example: A stationary centered Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process has an autocorrelation that decays exponentially with lag magnitude.

patterns.why: Lagged products are averaged over the probability law.
Stationarity removes dependence on absolute time.

nodes.name: Wiener-Khinchin relation
nodes.intuition: Time-lag dependence and frequency power contain the same second-order information. Integrating the power spectrum recovers the process variance in the zero-mean case.
nodes.conditions: X is zero-mean, mean-square continuous, and wide-sense stationary with finite variance and integrable autocorrelation. Then S is a nonnegative spectral density; more general stationary processes require a spectral measure.
nodes.example: Exponentially decaying autocorrelation corresponds to a Lorentzian-shaped power spectrum.

patterns.why: Lag structure is transformed into frequency power.
Integrated spectral density equals total variance.

nodes.name: Fourier uncertainty principle
nodes.intuition: A nonzero signal cannot be arbitrarily concentrated in both time and frequency. Narrowing one representation imposes a minimum spread on the other.
nodes.conditions: For a simple sufficient hypothesis, f is a Schwartz function with ||f||_2=1. mu_t and mu_xi are the means under |f|^2 and |fhat|^2; the Fourier convention uses 2*pi. Shifted and modulated Gaussian functions attain equality.
nodes.example: A Gaussian pulse achieves the smallest possible product of variance-defined time and frequency widths.

patterns.why: Localization is constrained across paired time and frequency descriptions.
Spread is quantified by second moments about the two centers.

nodes.name: Linear map
nodes.intuition: A linear map respects mixing: transforming a mixture gives the same result as mixing the transformed ingredients. This is the exact version of the local approximation used by derivatives.
nodes.conditions: V and W are vector spaces over the same field; T:V→W; the law holds for every u,v in V and every pair of scalars a,b.
nodes.example: Differentiation on polynomials sends 3p+2q to 3p′+2q′.

patterns.why: The defining law preserves linear combinations.
The map preserves addition and scalar multiplication.

nodes.name: Matrix multiplication
nodes.intuition: Each output-to-input connection is the sum over possible intermediate coordinates. Multiplying matrices therefore records the composition of linear maps.
nodes.conditions: A is m×n and B is n×p over the same field; the sum is finite.

patterns.why: The intermediate coordinate is summed out when maps are composed.
All paths through an intermediate index contribute additively.

nodes.name: Basis and unique coordinates
nodes.intuition: A basis is a smallest complete set of directions: every vector can be assembled from it in exactly one way. Coordinates are instructions relative to this chosen set.
nodes.conditions: V is finite-dimensional over a field; b₁,…,bₙ is a basis precisely when the displayed existence and uniqueness hold.
nodes.example: The polynomial 2−3t+t² has coordinates (2,−3,1) in the basis (1,t,t²).

patterns.why: A vector separates into uniquely weighted basis directions.
The coefficients depend on the selected basis.

nodes.name: Rank–nullity theorem
nodes.intuition: Input directions split into directions the map erases and independent directions visible at the output. These two counts exhaust the input dimension.
nodes.conditions: T:V→W is linear over a field and V is finite-dimensional; W may be larger or infinite-dimensional.
nodes.example: A rank-2 linear map from a five-dimensional space has a three-dimensional kernel.

patterns.why: Input dimension separates into lost and transmitted dimensions.
The total count of independent input directions is accounted for.

nodes.name: Dimension of a sum of subspaces
nodes.intuition: Adding two spaces counts their shared directions twice. Subtracting the intersection corrects the overlap.
nodes.conditions: U and W are finite-dimensional subspaces of one vector space over a field.
nodes.example: Two distinct planes through the origin in three dimensions meet in a line, so their sum has dimension 2+2−1=3.

patterns.why: The overlap is subtracted after adding the two dimensions.
A basis of the intersection can be extended to bases of both spaces.

nodes.name: Change of basis and similarity
nodes.intuition: One matrix converts new coordinates to old, the operator acts, and the inverse converts back. Similar matrices describe the same transformation in different coordinates.
nodes.conditions: T is an endomorphism of a finite-dimensional vector space; P is invertible and its columns are the new basis vectors expressed in the old basis.
nodes.example: Swapping coordinate axes conjugates diag(2,5) into diag(5,2).

patterns.why: The matrix changes while the linear map stays fixed.
Trace, determinant and eigenvalues survive similarity.

nodes.name: Determinant
nodes.intuition: The determinant is the signed volume multiplier of a linear map. The alternating sum removes combinations that collapse volume into lower dimensions.
nodes.conditions: A is an n×n matrix over a commutative field or ring; signed-volume interpretation is for real Euclidean space.
nodes.example: The diagonal matrix diag(2,3) multiplies oriented area by 6.

patterns.why: For real matrices its absolute value scales volume.
Swapping two input directions reverses orientation and the determinant sign.

nodes.name: Multiplicativity of determinant
nodes.intuition: Sequential transformations multiply their volume factors. A composition can preserve full dimension only if both square factors do.
nodes.conditions: A and B are n×n matrices over the same commutative ring; the volume interpretation assumes real entries.
nodes.example: A stretch by 3 followed by one by 4 along the same axis has volume multiplier 12.

patterns.why: Volume factors compose multiplicatively.
Each determinant is a global scaling of oriented volume.

nodes.name: Inverse by the adjugate
nodes.intuition: Cofactors assemble a matrix whose multiplication cancels all cross terms, leaving det(A) times the identity. Dividing by that factor reverses the transformation.
nodes.conditions: A is square over a field with det A≠0; adj A is the transpose of the cofactor matrix. This identity is conceptual, not the preferred numerical algorithm.
nodes.example: For A=[[a,b],[c,d]], its inverse is [[d,−b],[−c,a]]/(ad−bc).

patterns.why: Cofactors encode complementary minors to reconstruct the inverse.
Invertibility means multiplication can be undone within the matrix algebra.

nodes.name: Cramer’s rule
nodes.intuition: Replacing one column by the target vector measures how much of that column direction the solution needs. The ratio compares the new oriented volume to the original one.
nodes.conditions: A is an invertible n×n matrix over a field; Aᵢ(b) replaces its ith column with b.
nodes.example: For 2x+y=5 and x−y=1, determinant ratios give x=2 and y=1.

patterns.why: The solution is resolved into individual coordinates.
Each coordinate is a ratio of oriented volumes.

nodes.name: Trace
nodes.intuition: Trace adds the self-to-self contributions of a map. Although diagonal entries depend on coordinates, their sum equals the eigenvalue sum and remains unchanged by a basis change.
nodes.conditions: For the eigenvalue sum, A is complex square, or real with eigenvalues counted over C, including algebraic multiplicities. For cyclicity A is m×n and B is n×m over a commutative field.
nodes.example: A=[[2,7],[0,5]] has trace 7, matching eigenvalues 2 and 5.

patterns.why: Local diagonal contributions are added.
Similarity preserves the sum despite changing coordinates.

nodes.name: Inner product
nodes.intuition: An inner product measures alignment while extending the dot product to abstract vector spaces. It also supplies lengths and perpendicularity.
nodes.conditions: Displayed formula is the standard inner product on Rⁿ or Cⁿ. Throughout these entries the first slot is conjugate-linear, the second linear; an abstract inner product is conjugate-symmetric and positive definite.
nodes.example: For real vectors (1,2) and (3,4), the inner product is 11.

patterns.why: The second slot respects linear combinations.
Self-pairing gives squared length and zero pairing gives orthogonality.

nodes.name: Norm axioms and induced norm
nodes.intuition: A norm is a consistent way to assign size to vectors. Scaling multiplies size, and taking a detour cannot beat a direct route.
nodes.conditions: The axioms hold for all vectors and scalars in a real or complex vector space; the final formula is the Euclidean norm and is not the only possible norm.
nodes.example: The Euclidean norm of (3,4) is 5, while its ℓ¹ norm is 7.

patterns.why: Multiplying a vector by a scalar multiplies its size by the scalar magnitude.
d(x,y)=‖x−y‖ turns any norm into a distance.

nodes.name: Cauchy–Schwarz inequality
nodes.intuition: Alignment cannot exceed the product of lengths. Equality means the two vectors contain the same direction, up to a scalar.
nodes.conditions: x and y belong to a real or complex inner-product space; equality holds exactly when they are linearly dependent, including a zero vector.

patterns.why: The inequality bounds alignment using lengths.
Nonnegativity of a squared residual proves the bound.

nodes.name: Parallelogram law
nodes.intuition: The total squared lengths of a parallelogram’s diagonals equal twice the total squared lengths of adjacent sides. Cross terms cancel between the two diagonals.
nodes.conditions: The identity holds for norms induced by real or complex inner products. Conversely, a norm satisfying it for all x,y comes from an inner product.
nodes.example: For x=(1,0), y=(0,1), the two diagonal squares are 2+2=4.

patterns.why: Adding opposite cross terms isolates the squared lengths.
Replacing y by −y exchanges diagonals without changing the total.

nodes.name: Polarization identity over the reals
nodes.intuition: You can recover angles from distance measurements alone. The difference of the two diagonal squares isolates the interaction between the vectors.
nodes.conditions: x,y lie in a real inner-product space and the norm is the induced one. Complex inner products require additional terms involving iy.
nodes.example: For x=(1,0), y=(1,1), the formula gives (5−1)/4=1.

patterns.why: Length information determines the bilinear pairing and conversely.
A difference of quadratic evaluations extracts the mixed term.

nodes.name: Orthogonal projection
nodes.intuition: Projection keeps the components pointing along a chosen subspace and discards perpendicular components. The retained point is the closest point of the subspace.
nodes.conditions: q₁,…,qₖ is an orthonormal basis of a finite-dimensional subspace U of a real or complex inner-product space; Q has those vectors as columns in orthonormal coordinates.
nodes.example: Projection of (3,4) onto the x-axis is (3,0).

patterns.why: The residual x−Pᵤx is perpendicular to every allowed direction.
The projection uniquely minimizes distance to U.

nodes.name: Orthogonal decomposition and energy split
nodes.intuition: A signal splits into the part a subspace can express and an unexplained perpendicular remainder. Their squared sizes add without cross terms.
nodes.conditions: U is a finite-dimensional subspace of an inner-product space, or a closed subspace of a Hilbert space; Pᵤ is its orthogonal projection.
nodes.example: For x=(3,4) projected onto the x-axis, 25=9+16.

patterns.why: Every vector separates into two perpendicular components.
Squared length is fully accounted for by the two components.

nodes.name: Gram–Schmidt orthogonalization
nodes.intuition: Each new vector is cleaned of directions already represented. Normalizing the remainder produces a new independent unit direction.
nodes.conditions: v₁,…,vₙ is a linearly independent finite list in an inner-product space; q₁=v₁/‖v₁‖. Independence ensures no denominator is zero.
nodes.example: Starting from (1,0) and (1,1), the second residual is (0,1).

patterns.why: The kth step uses only previously constructed directions.
Subtracting projections removes all previous components.

nodes.name: QR factorization
nodes.intuition: A linear transformation becomes an orthonormal coordinate frame followed by triangular mixing. This separates geometry from the bookkeeping of dependent coordinates.
nodes.conditions: A is m×n over R or C with m≥n and full column rank; the reduced Q is m×n, and R is invertible n×n. Requiring positive real diagonal entries makes this reduced factorization unique.
nodes.example: The columns (1,0) and (1,1) yield Q=I and R=[[1,1],[0,1]].

patterns.why: A matrix separates into orthogonal and triangular factors.
Q preserves Euclidean inner products on its input space.

nodes.name: Bessel’s inequality for an orthonormal list
nodes.intuition: Looking along only some perpendicular directions cannot reveal more energy than the vector contains. Missing directions account for the gap.
nodes.conditions: q₁,…,qₖ is a finite orthonormal list in an inner-product space; equality holds iff x belongs to its span.
nodes.example: For x=(3,4,12) and the first two coordinate directions, 9+16≤169.

patterns.why: Perpendicular components contribute independently.
Observed energy plus residual energy equals total energy.

nodes.name: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
nodes.intuition: An eigenvector is a direction the transformation leaves on its own line. Along that direction the full transformation behaves like multiplication by a single number.
nodes.conditions: A is a square matrix over a field; λ is in the chosen scalar field and v is nonzero. A real matrix may have no real eigenvalues.
nodes.example: For diag(2,5), the coordinate axes are eigenvectors with eigenvalues 2 and 5.

patterns.why: The transformation is scalar multiplication along an eigenvector.
The eigenvector line is invariant under the map.

nodes.name: Characteristic polynomial
nodes.intuition: Subtracting a proposed scalar action tests whether some direction is annihilated. The determinant records exactly when that failure of invertibility occurs.
nodes.conditions: A is n×n over a field; roots and eigenvectors are considered over that field or a stated extension. Over C the polynomial has n roots counting multiplicity.

patterns.why: A matrix question becomes a polynomial root question.
The roots separate the possible scalar actions.

nodes.name: Cayley–Hamilton theorem
nodes.intuition: Every square matrix obeys its own characteristic equation. High powers can therefore be rewritten using only finitely many lower powers.
nodes.conditions: A is an n×n matrix over a commutative field; p_A(t)=det(tI−A), and polynomial evaluation uses matrix powers with constant term times I.
nodes.example: If p_A(t)=t²−5t+6, then A²=5A−6I.

patterns.why: The polynomial relation reduces later matrix powers to earlier ones.
Polynomial relations constrain the algebra generated by A.

nodes.name: Diagonalization
nodes.intuition: A suitable coordinate system uncouples the transformation into separate stretch factors. Repeated application then becomes ordinary scalar exponentiation.
nodes.conditions: A is n×n over a field and has a basis of eigenvectors; P consists of those eigenvectors. The power formula holds for integers k≥0, and for negative k if every eigenvalue is nonzero.
nodes.example: A matrix with eigenvalues 2 and 3 and two independent eigenvectors has powers controlled by 2ᵏ and 3ᵏ.

patterns.why: An eigenvector basis removes coupling between coordinates.
The transformation splits into one-dimensional scalar actions.

nodes.name: Spectral theorem in finite dimensions
nodes.latex: A=U\Lambda U^*,\quad U^*U=I;\qquad A^*A=AA^*\iff\text{such a decomposition exists}
nodes.intuition: A normal complex matrix has independent perpendicular modes. For Hermitian matrices these modes have real strengths, making quadratic energy especially transparent.
nodes.conditions: A is a complex n×n matrix: unitary diagonalization is equivalent to normality. If A=A*, all eigenvalues are real; a real symmetric matrix has an orthogonal diagonalization. A general real normal matrix need not be real-diagonalizable.
nodes.example: The symmetric matrix [[2,1],[1,2]] has orthogonal eigenvectors (1,1), (1,−1) with eigenvalues 3 and 1.

patterns.why: Distinct modes can be chosen perpendicular.
A normal operator separates into independent eigenvalue actions.
Self-adjoint symmetry guarantees real observable values.

nodes.name: Rayleigh quotient
nodes.intuition: The Rayleigh quotient measures the strength of a Hermitian transformation in one direction. In an eigenbasis it is a weighted average of the eigenvalues.
nodes.conditions: A is a nonempty Hermitian matrix, x≠0, and λmin, λmax are its smallest and largest eigenvalues. Equality occurs in the corresponding extreme eigenspaces.
nodes.example: For diag(2,8) and x=(1,1), R_A(x)=5.

patterns.why: Squared eigenbasis coordinates form nonnegative weights summing to one after normalization.
The minimum and maximum over directions are extreme eigenvalues.

nodes.name: Courant–Fischer min–max principle
nodes.intuition: To find the kth-smallest mode, choose the best k-dimensional space against its worst direction. Dimensional constraints force that space to encounter the kth eigenvalue.
nodes.conditions: A is n×n Hermitian with λ₁≤…≤λₙ, and 1≤k≤n; S ranges over k-dimensional complex subspaces (real subspaces for real symmetric A).
nodes.example: For diag(1,4,9), the best two-dimensional subspace has worst Rayleigh quotient 4.

patterns.why: A nested optimization isolates each eigenvalue.
Subspace dimension forces intersection with eigenspaces.

nodes.name: Singular value decomposition
nodes.intuition: Every finite matrix can be understood as orthogonal changes of coordinates surrounding independent nonnegative stretches. Unlike eigenvectors, the input and output directions may live in different spaces.
nodes.conditions: A is m×n over R or C; U and V are orthogonal or unitary square matrices, and Σ is rectangular diagonal with nonnegative singular values. Include zeros with the usual dimensional padding.
nodes.example: A rank-one matrix has one positive singular value and acts through one input direction and one output direction.

patterns.why: The matrix splits into independent input-output modes.
Left and right singular directions form orthonormal systems.
Different coordinate changes are allowed at the input and output.

nodes.name: Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse
nodes.intuition: The pseudoinverse reverses the directions a map actually transmits and leaves erased directions at zero. It chooses the smallest solution among equally good fits.
nodes.conditions: A is a finite real or complex matrix with SVD A=UΣV*; Σ⁺ has transposed shape. A⁺b is the unique minimum-Euclidean-norm least-squares solution.
nodes.example: For diag(2,0), A⁺=diag(1/2,0).

patterns.why: Visible and null directions receive different treatment.
The result minimizes residual norm and then solution norm.

nodes.name: Eckart–Young–Mirsky low-rank approximation
nodes.intuition: The best rank budget is spent on the largest independent stretches. No alternative k-dimensional representation can hide the next singular direction.
nodes.conditions: A is m×n real or complex, σ₁≥…≥σmin(m,n)≥0 and 0≤k<min(m,n); ‖·‖₂ is the spectral norm. The same truncation minimizes Frobenius error, whose square is Σᵢ>kσᵢ²; minimizers need not be unique.
nodes.example: For diag(5,2,1), the best rank-one spectral error is 2.

patterns.why: Truncation solves a precise minimum-error problem.
Discarded singular modes determine the residual.

nodes.name: Polar decomposition
nodes.intuition: A square transformation separates into a pure nonnegative stretch followed by a length-preserving motion. This extends magnitude times phase from complex numbers to matrices.
nodes.conditions: A is a square real or complex matrix; H is the unique positive semidefinite square root. U can be chosen orthogonal or unitary; it is unique when A is invertible, but may not be unique otherwise.
nodes.example: For A=−2I, H=2I and U=−I.

patterns.why: Stretch and isometry are isolated into two factors.
U preserves lengths while H determines directional stretching.

nodes.name: Jordan normal form
nodes.intuition: When independent eigenvectors are missing, chains of generalized eigenvectors describe the remaining coupling. The extra nilpotent pieces record how far the map is from diagonal.
nodes.conditions: A is a finite square matrix over C, or over a field where its characteristic polynomial splits. Each Nα has ones on a block’s superdiagonal and is nilpotent; block ordering is arbitrary.
nodes.example: The matrix [[2,1],[0,2]] is a single Jordan block and cannot be diagonalized.

patterns.why: The operator separates into generalized eigenvector chains.
Nilpotent steps move down a finite chain before reaching zero.

nodes.name: Quadratic form
nodes.intuition: A quadratic form measures size or energy with direction-dependent weights and interactions. Its matrix records both individual squared contributions and pairwise cross terms.
nodes.conditions: x is real and A is real symmetric; every real quadratic polynomial homogeneous of degree two has such a unique symmetric matrix. Complex Hermitian forms use x*Ax instead.
nodes.example: q(x,y)=2x²+2xy+3y² has matrix [[2,1],[1,3]].

patterns.why: Only degree-two interactions appear.
Positive definite forms define ellipsoids and modified squared lengths.

nodes.name: Sylvester’s law of inertia
nodes.intuition: A real quadratic form has intrinsic counts of positive, negative and flat directions. Coordinate changes can reshape the expression but cannot change those counts.
nodes.conditions: A is real symmetric and P is invertible; the integers p,q,r are unique, although P is not. This is congruence, not similarity, so individual eigenvalue magnitudes need not be preserved.
nodes.example: x²−y²+0z² has inertia (1,1,1) under any invertible real coordinate change.

patterns.why: The positive, negative and null dimension counts survive congruence.
The form separates into positive squares, negative squares and zeros.

nodes.name: Cholesky factorization
nodes.latex: A=LL^*,\qquad L\text{ lower triangular with positive diagonal}
nodes.intuition: A positive definite quadratic energy can be converted into an ordinary sum of squares by a triangular coordinate transform. Positivity makes each successive square root possible.
nodes.conditions: A is Hermitian positive definite over C, or real symmetric positive definite; then L exists uniquely with positive real diagonal entries. Semidefinite matrices require qualifications and may have nonunique factors.

patterns.why: A positive matrix is expressed through a triangular factor and its adjoint.
x*Ax equals ‖L*x‖².

nodes.name: Schur complement
nodes.intuition: Eliminating one block of variables changes the interactions among the remaining variables. The Schur complement is the effective matrix after that elimination.
nodes.conditions: The block matrix is square, A is square and invertible, and all block sizes are compatible over a field. S need not be invertible for the determinant identity.
nodes.example: Eliminating x from 2x+y=b₁ and x+3y=b₂ leaves coefficient 3−1/2=5/2 on y.

patterns.why: Block elimination separates one subsystem from its residual.
The correction CA⁻¹B follows influence through the eliminated variables.

nodes.name: Matrix exponential
nodes.intuition: The exponential turns a constant infinitesimal linear rule into its finite-time motion. Eigenvector directions evolve like ordinary scalar exponentials.
nodes.conditions: A is a fixed finite square real or complex matrix, t is real or complex, and the series converges absolutely in every matrix norm. The ODE statement uses real time with x(0)=x₀; e^(A+B)=e^Ae^B is guaranteed when A and B commute.
nodes.example: For A=[[0,−1],[1,0]], e^(tA) is a rotation through angle t.

patterns.why: Continuous repeated linear action is encoded by the exponential series.
e^(sA)e^(tA)=e^((s+t)A) combines time intervals.

nodes.name: Kronecker product
nodes.intuition: The Kronecker product lets two coordinate systems vary independently. Its block structure represents the product of two linear actions.
nodes.conditions: A,B,C,D are finite matrices over one field and AC and BD are defined; the first formula defines the Kronecker product.
nodes.example: I₂⊗B places two copies of B along the block diagonal.

patterns.why: Independent actions combine while preserving their separate multiplication rules.
The large matrix retains the two-factor structure.

nodes.name: Tensor product universal property
nodes.intuition: A tensor product packages two-input bilinear behavior into one-input linear behavior. It creates a space in which every bilinear operation can be treated as an ordinary linear map.
nodes.conditions: V,W,Z are vector spaces over a common field; the displayed correspondence is natural and bijective. The induced linear map b̃ is unique for each bilinear b.
nodes.example: A bilinear expression Σᵢⱼaᵢⱼvᵢwⱼ becomes a linear functional on the tensors eᵢ⊗fⱼ.

patterns.why: Bilinearity in separate slots becomes linearity on a new space.
The universal property factors every bilinear map through the canonical tensor map.

nodes.name: Dual space and pullback of linear functionals
nodes.intuition: A forward map of vectors pulls measurements backward. To measure the output, first apply the map and then the output measurement.
nodes.conditions: T:V→W is linear over a field; V* and W* are algebraic dual spaces. Here T* denotes the dual map, not the Hermitian adjoint unless an inner-product identification is supplied.
nodes.example: If T scales vectors by 3, it also multiplies every pulled-back linear measurement by 3.

patterns.why: Vectors move forward while linear measurements move backward.
The construction reverses order: (ST)*=T*S*.

nodes.name: Adjoint of a linear map
nodes.intuition: The adjoint transfers a linear action from one side of an inner-product measurement to the other. In orthonormal coordinates this reverses rows and columns and conjugates entries.
nodes.conditions: T maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner-product spaces; matrices are expressed in orthonormal bases. The adjoint exists uniquely; infinite-dimensional unbounded operators need domain qualifications.
nodes.example: A real column vector viewed as a map has its transpose as adjoint.

patterns.why: The same pairing can be computed by moving the map to the other input.
The construction depends on the chosen inner products.

nodes.name: Gram determinant and volume
nodes.intuition: All lengths and pairwise angles together determine the volume spanned by a list of vectors. The volume vanishes exactly when the directions are dependent.
nodes.conditions: v₁,…,vₖ are vectors in a real Euclidean space with k≤its dimension; Volₖ is the unsigned volume of their parallelepiped. The determinant is nonnegative.
nodes.example: For v₁=(1,0) and v₂=(1,2), G=[[1,1],[1,5]] has determinant 4, so area is 2.

patterns.why: The pairing matrix determines a geometric volume.
Squaring removes orientation and yields a nonnegative determinant.

nodes.name: Matrix geometric series
nodes.intuition: Repeated feedback can be added one pass at a time. When repeated powers decay, all indirect effects sum to a single inverse.
nodes.conditions: A is a finite square real or complex matrix with spectral radius ρ(A)<1. The series converges in every matrix norm; ‖A‖<1 in a submultiplicative norm is sufficient but not necessary.
nodes.example: For A=(1/2)I, the sum is 2I.

patterns.why: Each power represents one additional pass through the same map.
Decay of the spectrum makes infinitely many passes summable.

nodes.name: Sherman–Morrison rank-one update
nodes.intuition: Changing a matrix along one input-output interaction changes its inverse by another rank-one term. The denominator checks whether the update destroys invertibility.
nodes.conditions: A is invertible and square over R or C; u,v have compatible dimensions and 1+v*A⁻¹u≠0. A* notation on v means conjugate transpose.
nodes.example: For A=I and u=v=e₁, the updated inverse changes the first diagonal entry to 1/2.

patterns.why: A simple rank-one perturbation remains simple after inversion.
An existing inverse can be updated when one new interaction is added.

nodes.name: Group axioms
nodes.intuition: A group abstracts reversible actions that can be composed. You may regroup a sequence of actions, do nothing, and undo any action.
nodes.conditions: G is a set with a closed binary operation; associativity holds for all a,b,c, one identity e exists, and every a has an inverse. Commutativity is not assumed.
nodes.example: Rotations of a square form a group; all rigid symmetries of the square form a larger noncommutative group.

patterns.why: Group multiplication composes actions.
Invertible transformations preserve the structure being acted on.

nodes.name: Group homomorphism
nodes.intuition: A homomorphism translates one system of actions into another while preserving how actions combine. It can forget distinctions, but must forget them consistently.
nodes.conditions: G,H are groups and φ:G→H; the law holds for every a,b in G. The group operations may use different notation.
nodes.example: det:GLₙ(R)→R× sends matrix composition to multiplication of determinants.

patterns.why: The map preserves the operation defining a group.
Translation commutes with combining two actions.

nodes.name: Kernel and image of a homomorphism
nodes.intuition: The kernel is exactly the information a map erases, while the image is exactly what it can express. Group laws make the erased information compatible with quotienting.
nodes.conditions: φ:G→H is a group homomorphism; the kernel is normal in G, and the image is a subgroup of H.
nodes.example: For reduction Z→Z/5Z, the kernel is 5Z and the image is all five residue classes.

patterns.why: The map separates erased information from surviving output.
Kernel and image inherit subgroup structure.

nodes.name: Quotient group
nodes.intuition: A quotient treats certain transformations as invisible. Each new element is a whole class of old elements that differ only by an invisible action.
nodes.conditions: N is a normal subgroup of G. Normality is essential for the displayed multiplication to be independent of the chosen representatives.
nodes.example: Z/12Z models addition of hours on a clock.

patterns.why: The group law descends to equivalence classes.
Changing representatives within a coset leaves the quotient element unchanged.

nodes.name: First isomorphism theorem
nodes.intuition: Once you identify precisely the differences a homomorphism erases, what remains is a perfect copy of its output. This turns information loss into a structural description.
nodes.conditions: φ:G→H is any group homomorphism; the quotient is by its normal kernel, and the induced map is a well-defined group isomorphism onto the image.
nodes.example: The map Z→{1,−1}, n↦(−1)ⁿ has kernel 2Z, so Z/2Z is isomorphic to {1,−1}.

patterns.why: The original group is reduced by exactly its invisible part.
The remaining quotient and image have identical group laws.

nodes.name: Lagrange’s theorem for finite groups
nodes.intuition: A subgroup tiles its finite group with equal-size cosets. The total number of elements is the number of tiles times the size of one tile.
nodes.conditions: G is a finite group and H is a subgroup; [G:H] counts left cosets. The converse divisibility claim is false: a divisor of |G| need not occur as a subgroup order.
nodes.example: A subgroup of a group with 15 elements can only have order 1,3,5 or 15.

patterns.why: Equal-size cosets partition the whole group.
Translation bijects every coset with the subgroup.

nodes.name: Group action
nodes.intuition: An abstract group becomes concrete by letting it move objects. The action law says the group’s multiplication agrees with doing those moves in sequence.
nodes.conditions: G is a group, X a set, and the action is a map G×X→X satisfying both laws for all g,h,x. Each g necessarily acts by a bijection.
nodes.example: The permutation group Sₙ acts on n coordinate positions by reordering them.

patterns.why: Multiplication matches successive moves of an object.
The action exposes orbits and properties constant along them.

nodes.name: Orbit–stabilizer theorem
nodes.intuition: The number of genuinely different positions equals the number of available actions divided by the number that leave the object where it is. Stabilizers measure redundant ways to reach the same position.
nodes.conditions: G is finite and acts on X; Gₓ={g:g·x=x}. The orbit-coset bijection remains valid for infinite groups, but the displayed numeric division is the finite version.
nodes.example: The 8 symmetries of a square act on its 4 vertices; a chosen vertex has a stabilizer of size 2.

patterns.why: Equivalent actions are grouped into equally sized stabilizer cosets.
Fixed-object symmetries quantify redundant motion.

nodes.name: Burnside’s orbit-counting lemma
nodes.intuition: To count objects up to symmetry, average how many objects each symmetry leaves unchanged. The average exactly removes overcounting from different stabilizer sizes.
nodes.conditions: A finite group G acts on a finite set X; Fix(g)={x:g·x=x} and X/G is the set of orbits.
nodes.example: Two-colorings of three labeled positions modulo all permutations have (8+3·4+2·2)/6=4 orbits, determined by the number of red positions.

patterns.why: The answer is an arithmetic mean of fixed-point counts.
Configurations related by the group action are identified.
Double counting pairs (g,x) with g·x=x proves the formula.

nodes.name: Class equation
nodes.intuition: Conjugation groups elements by how they sit inside the symmetry system. Central elements are alone in their classes; every other class is counted by its centralizer.
nodes.conditions: G is finite; gᵢ is one representative from each noncentral conjugacy class, Z(G) is the center, and C_G(g)={h:hg=gh}.
nodes.example: For S₃, the class sizes are 1,3,2, so 6=1+3+2.
