patterns.why: Conjugacy classes partition the group.
Conjugation preserves the algebraic role of an element.

nodes.name: Sylow theorems
nodes.latex: |G|=p^a m,\quad p\nmid m:\qquad |P|=p^a,\quad n_p\equiv1\pmod p,\quad n_p\mid m
nodes.intuition: The largest possible prime-power pieces of a finite group always exist, and symmetry makes them conjugate. Their possible number is sharply restricted by arithmetic.
nodes.conditions: G is finite, p is prime, a≥1 and p does not divide m. A Sylow p-subgroup P exists; every p-subgroup lies in one; all Sylow p-subgroups are conjugate. nₚ counts them, and nₚ=1 iff the Sylow subgroup is normal.
nodes.example: In a group of order 15, n₅ divides 3 and is 1 modulo 5, so the order-5 subgroup is unique and normal.

patterns.why: All maximal p-subgroups are related by conjugation.
Orbit counts impose congruence and divisibility restrictions.

nodes.name: Cayley’s theorem for groups
nodes.intuition: Every abstract group can be realized as actual permutations. Letting the group move its own elements gives a faithful concrete model.
nodes.conditions: G is any group; Sym(G) is the group of all bijections of the underlying set. For finite |G|=n, this embeds G into Sₙ.
nodes.example: A cyclic group of order 3 becomes the permutations generated by the cycle (123).

patterns.why: Abstract multiplication is represented by permutation composition.
The regular action remembers every group element distinctly.

nodes.name: Order of a power in a cyclic subgroup
nodes.intuition: Taking k steps at a time around a cycle may visit only part of it. The greatest common divisor measures how many interlaced smaller cycles appear.
nodes.conditions: g has finite order n≥1 in a group and k is an integer; gcd(n,0)=n.
nodes.example: If g has order 12, then g⁸ has order 12/gcd(12,8)=3.

patterns.why: Repeated application returns to the identity after a predictable number of steps.
The gcd measures how the original cycle splits.

nodes.name: Direct product of groups
nodes.intuition: Two independent symmetry systems can run side by side. The paired system keeps both states and composes each component separately.
nodes.conditions: G and H are groups; the order formula is the finite version. No commutativity of either factor is required.
nodes.example: Two independent binary switches form Z/2Z×Z/2Z, with four states.

patterns.why: Each coordinate retains its own group law.
Independent choices multiply cardinalities.

nodes.name: Structure theorem for finite abelian groups
nodes.latex: G\cong\mathbb Z/d_1\mathbb Z\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathbb Z/d_r\mathbb Z,\qquad 1<d_1\mid d_2\mid\cdots\mid d_r
nodes.intuition: Every finite commuting symmetry system can be built from independent cyclic counters. Divisibility-ordered counter lengths give a unique structural description.
nodes.conditions: G is a finite abelian group; the integers dᵢ are uniquely determined, with an empty sum for the trivial group. General finite nonabelian groups do not admit this description.
nodes.example: Z/2Z×Z/6Z is already in invariant-factor form.

patterns.why: The whole group splits into canonical cyclic building blocks.
Commutativity is the key condition allowing the classification.

nodes.name: Ring structure and distributivity
nodes.intuition: A ring lets addition and multiplication cooperate. Distributivity is the rule that makes expanding, collecting and evaluating algebraic expressions consistent.
nodes.conditions: A ring has an abelian additive group, associative multiplication, and the two displayed distributive laws. We use rings with identity; multiplication need not commute.
nodes.example: Square matrices form a ring: multiplication distributes over addition even though AB may differ from BA.

patterns.why: Two operations are linked by distributivity.
Multiplication by a fixed element is additive.

nodes.name: Quotient ring
nodes.intuition: An ideal specifies algebraic differences to ignore while keeping both addition and multiplication meaningful. Quotienting can enforce equations by declaring their left-hand sides zero.
nodes.conditions: R is a ring with identity and I is a two-sided ideal; commutative rings automatically have two-sided ideals. Operations are independent of representative choices.
nodes.example: R[x]/(x²+1) is a way to construct complex arithmetic from real polynomials.

patterns.why: Both ring operations descend to equivalence classes.
Different representatives of one residue class yield the same result.

nodes.name: Maximal ideals and fields
nodes.latex: R/I\text{ is a field}\iff I\text{ is maximal}
nodes.intuition: A maximal ideal removes just enough information that every surviving nonzero element becomes invertible. No intermediate proper quotient remains.
nodes.conditions: R is a commutative ring with identity and I is a proper ideal. A field here has distinct zero and one.
nodes.example: The ideal (5) is maximal in Z, giving the field Z/5Z; (6) is not maximal.

patterns.why: Field invertibility is characterized by the ideal structure of the original ring.
Larger ideals correspond to smaller quotient structures.

nodes.name: Polynomial division algorithm
nodes.intuition: Repeatedly canceling the highest power leaves a remainder too small to divide further. This is long division with degree playing the role of size.
nodes.conditions: f,g are polynomials over a field and g≠0; q and r exist uniquely. Over a general coefficient ring, the conclusion still holds when the leading coefficient of g is a unit.
nodes.example: Dividing x³−1 by x−1 gives q=x²+x+1 and r=0.

patterns.why: Each cancellation strictly lowers the remaining degree.
A polynomial splits into a multiple plus a bounded-degree remainder.

nodes.name: Polynomial remainder and factor theorem
nodes.intuition: A zero of a polynomial is exactly a removable linear factor. Evaluation tells you the remainder after dividing by that factor.
nodes.conditions: f is a polynomial over a field and a is in that field; q is the unique quotient. The displayed statement also holds over a commutative ring with identity.
nodes.example: Since f(2)=0 for f(x)=x²−3x+2, the factor x−2 divides f.

patterns.why: A root separates off a linear factor.
Evaluation connects polynomial operations with scalar arithmetic.

nodes.name: Lagrange interpolation
nodes.intuition: Build one polynomial for each data point that is one there and zero at all the others. Adding these selectors with the desired heights fits every point exactly.
nodes.conditions: x₀,…,xₙ are distinct elements of a field and y₀,…,yₙ are arbitrary; p is the unique polynomial of degree at most n with p(xᵢ)=yᵢ.
nodes.example: The data (0,1),(1,3) give p(x)=1+2x.

patterns.why: The interpolant is a linear combination of data values.
Cardinal basis polynomials separate the interpolation constraints.

nodes.name: Tower law for field extensions
nodes.intuition: Choosing coordinates in two stages multiplies the number of independent scalar directions. A basis over an intermediate field expands into a basis over the smaller field.
nodes.conditions: F⊆K⊆L are fields and both degrees on the right are finite. The extension degree is vector-space dimension.

patterns.why: Independent choices of basis factors multiply dimensions.
A two-stage field construction is resolved through an intermediate field.

nodes.name: Finite fields
nodes.intuition: Finite fields are arithmetic systems in which every nonzero number can be divided by. Their sizes are prime powers, and their nonzero elements cycle through powers of one generator.
nodes.conditions: p is prime and m≥1. For each p^m a field exists uniquely up to isomorphism; every finite field has such a size. Cq−1 denotes a cyclic group of order q−1.
nodes.example: F₄ can be built as F₂[t]/(t²+t+1), and its three nonzero elements form a cycle.

patterns.why: Field axioms tightly constrain possible finite arithmetic systems.
Repeated powers organize the nonzero elements into a cycle.

nodes.name: Frobenius homomorphism
nodes.intuition: In prime characteristic the intermediate binomial terms disappear. Raising to the pth power unexpectedly becomes a structure-preserving operation.
nodes.conditions: The identities hold in a commutative ring of prime characteristic p. Frobenius is injective on fields, and is an automorphism on finite fields; it need not be surjective on every infinite field.
nodes.example: In characteristic 2, (a+b)²=a²+b² because 2ab=0.

patterns.why: Powering preserves addition and multiplication under the characteristic-p hypothesis.
On a finite field Frobenius is an automorphism of its arithmetic.

nodes.name: Fundamental theorem of Galois theory
nodes.intuition: Adding more numbers to the fixed field leaves fewer allowed symmetries. This reverses inclusion and turns questions about polynomial roots into questions about subgroups.
nodes.conditions: L/F is a finite Galois extension (finite, normal and separable). K ranges over intermediate fields and H over subgroups of Gal(L/F); Lᴴ is the fixed field. The maps are inverse and inclusion-reversing. K/F is Galois iff Gal(L/K) is normal, then Gal(K/F)≅Gal(L/F)/Gal(L/K).
nodes.example: For Q(√2)/Q, the two automorphisms send √2 to ±√2; fixing √2 leaves only the identity.

patterns.why: Larger subfields correspond to smaller symmetry subgroups.
Fixed elements identify fields through their automorphisms.

nodes.name: Matrix commutator and Lie bracket
nodes.intuition: The commutator measures how much the order of two linear actions matters. For infinitesimal symmetries, it produces the new direction generated by doing the actions in opposite orders.
nodes.conditions: A and B are same-size square matrices over a field; the commutator is bilinear and satisfies [A,A]=0 and the Jacobi identity. Interpretation as infinitesimal flows uses real or complex matrix Lie groups.

patterns.why: The difference compares the two composition orders.
Associative multiplication induces a Lie-algebra operation.

nodes.name: Jacobi identity
nodes.intuition: Failures of pairwise commutation cannot vary independently. The three nested commutators balance in a cyclic relation.
nodes.conditions: A,B,C lie in an associative algebra with the commutator bracket, or in any Lie algebra where Jacobi is an axiom. For vector fields the bracket is the commutator acting on smooth functions.
nodes.example: For matrix commutators, expanding the six positive and six negative triple products cancels them pairwise.

patterns.why: The identity is a defining compatibility law of Lie algebras.
Cyclic permutation preserves the sum of nested brackets.

nodes.name: Permutations and falling factorials
nodes.intuition: Choose an ordered list without replacement: every previous choice removes one option from the next step. Multiplication accounts for all successive choices.
nodes.conditions: n,k are integers with 0≤k≤n; P(n,0)=1 counts the empty list. Objects are distinct and order matters.
nodes.example: There are 5·4·3=60 ordered lists of three distinct objects from five.

patterns.why: Independent successive choice counts multiply.
Each selection reduces the remaining choices by one.

nodes.name: Binomial coefficient
nodes.intuition: A binomial coefficient counts ways to choose a subset of a fixed size. Division removes the many orders that describe the same subset.
nodes.conditions: n is a nonnegative integer and 0≤k≤n; conventionally the coefficient is zero for integer k outside this range.
nodes.example: Choosing three people from seven gives C(7,3)=35 groups.

patterns.why: The formula counts k-element subsets.
Choosing a subset or its complement gives C(n,k)=C(n,n−k).

nodes.name: Pascal’s rule
nodes.intuition: A chosen subset either contains a distinguished element or it does not. These two disjoint cases cover every possibility.
nodes.conditions: n≥1 is an integer and k is any integer; coefficients outside 0≤k≤n are interpreted as zero.

patterns.why: A size-n counting problem reduces to two size-(n−1) problems.
Contain-or-omit gives disjoint exhaustive cases.

nodes.name: Vandermonde’s identity
nodes.intuition: Choose r objects from two populations, either all at once or by tracking how many come from each population. The two descriptions must count the same subsets.
nodes.conditions: m,n,r are nonnegative integers; binomial coefficients outside their usual range are zero.
nodes.example: Selecting two objects from groups of sizes 2 and 3 gives 3+6+1=10 choices.

patterns.why: Both sides count the same subset family.
The summation separates cases by contribution from the first group.

nodes.name: Multinomial coefficient
nodes.intuition: When objects are assigned to several labeled groups, permutations within each group do not make a new assignment. Divide the full ordering count by each internal redundancy.
nodes.conditions: n₁,…,nᵣ are nonnegative integers summing to n; the groups are labeled.
nodes.example: The word BANANA has 6!/(3!2!1!)=60 distinct letter arrangements.

patterns.why: The formula counts allocations to labeled categories.
Permutations within one category are identified.

nodes.name: Stars and bars
nodes.intuition: Place separators between identical items to divide them among labeled bins. Empty bins correspond to adjacent separators or separators at the ends.
nodes.conditions: n≥0 and k≥1 are integers; the items are indistinguishable, bins are distinguishable, and empty bins are allowed.
nodes.example: Distributing five identical tokens among three people gives C(7,2)=21 possibilities.

patterns.why: Allocations are put in bijection with separator choices.
A total is split into nonnegative parts.

nodes.name: Inclusion–exclusion principle
nodes.intuition: First add individual counts, then remove double counts, restore triple counts, and continue. Each element’s total coefficient becomes exactly one.
nodes.conditions: A₁,…,Aₙ are finite sets and n≥1. The identity extends to finite families of measurable sets with a finite measure in place of cardinality.
nodes.example: For three sets, add their sizes, subtract the three pairwise intersections, then add the triple intersection.

patterns.why: Alternating overlap corrections count each included element once.
Membership is separated according to all intersection patterns.

nodes.name: Pigeonhole principle
nodes.intuition: At least one bin is no smaller than the average occupancy. Integrality rounds this simple average bound up to a guaranteed count.
nodes.conditions: N≥0 objects are assigned to k≥1 bins; nᵢ are their nonnegative integer occupancies.
nodes.example: Among 13 people, at least two share a birth month.

patterns.why: The maximum cannot be below the arithmetic mean.
Integer occupancy strengthens the average bound.

nodes.name: Derangement count
nodes.intuition: A derangement permutes objects so none returns to its original place. Alternating corrections remove permutations with one or more fixed positions.
nodes.conditions: n≥0 is an integer, and D₀=1. The displayed sum is finite and exact.

patterns.why: The formula counts permutations avoiding every fixed position.
Inclusion–exclusion organizes forbidden fixed-position subsets.

nodes.name: Catalan numbers
nodes.intuition: Many nested objects split at their first outer pair into a left part and a right part. The same recursive shape appears in balanced parentheses, triangulations and rooted binary trees.
nodes.conditions: n≥0 is an integer. Cₙ counts balanced parenthesis strings of n pairs, or full ordered binary trees with n internal vertices.
nodes.example: C₃=5 gives the five balanced strings of three pairs of parentheses.

patterns.why: The outermost structural split leaves two smaller objects.
The closed formula counts several families with the same recursive construction.

nodes.name: Stirling numbers of the second kind
nodes.intuition: When adding the last object to a set partition, either place it in one of k existing blocks or give it a new singleton block. These are the only possibilities.
nodes.conditions: S(n,k) counts partitions of an n-element labeled set into k nonempty unlabeled blocks; recurrence for n,k≥1. Boundary values: S(0,0)=1; S(n,0)=0 for n>0; S(0,k)=0 for k>0.

patterns.why: Adding the final labeled object relates adjacent partition counts.
Existing-block and new-block cases are disjoint.

nodes.name: Bell numbers
nodes.intuition: Bell numbers count every way of chunking a labeled set into nonempty groups. To build the next partition, choose which old objects stay outside the block of the new object.
nodes.conditions: n≥0, B₀=1; S(n,k) is a Stirling number of the second kind. The partitions have unlabeled nonempty blocks.
nodes.example: A three-element set has B₃=5 partitions.

patterns.why: All possible groupings of a labeled set are counted.
The block containing a distinguished object leaves a smaller partition problem.

nodes.name: Ordinary generating function
nodes.intuition: A generating function stores an entire sequence as coefficients of one object. Manipulating that object turns recurrences and counting constructions into algebra.
nodes.conditions: The primary interpretation is a formal power series over a specified coefficient ring, so analytic convergence is unnecessary. To evaluate it numerically, restrict z to a region where the series converges.
nodes.example: The constant sequence aₙ=1 has generating function 1/(1−z).

patterns.why: One algebraic object encodes all sequence entries.
Coefficient extraction recovers each indexed contribution.

nodes.name: Product rule for ordinary generating functions
nodes.intuition: To build a combined object of total size n, choose how much size each component receives. Every possible split contributes a product of counts.
nodes.conditions: A and B are formal power series over a commutative ring; each coefficient sum is finite. For numerical power series the identity holds inside both radii of convergence.
nodes.example: If aₙ=bₙ=1, the product has coefficient n+1, counting splits n=k+(n−k).

patterns.why: Multiplication encodes combination of components.
All allowable size splits contribute to one coefficient.

nodes.name: Exponential generating function
nodes.intuition: Dividing by factorials makes multiplication automatically choose which labels belong to each component. This is natural for combinatorial structures on labeled objects.
nodes.conditions: A and B are formal series over a field of characteristic zero, with bₙ defined using the same n! normalization. Analytic evaluation requires convergence.
nodes.example: For labeled sets with one structure on each size, A(z)=eᶻ; pairing two such structures gives coefficients 2ⁿ.

patterns.why: The factorial normalization packages labeled combinatorial counts.
The product includes the binomial choice of which labels go to each component.

nodes.name: Fibonacci recurrence
nodes.intuition: The next state depends on the two previous states. The same rule counts constructions whose first choice leaves one of two possible smaller sizes.
nodes.conditions: n≥0 is an integer; the initial conditions are part of the definition and distinguish this sequence from other solutions to the recurrence.
nodes.example: F₂=1,F₃=2,F₄=3,F₅=5.

patterns.why: Two earlier values determine the next one.
Tiling a strip with unit and double tiles separates according to the first tile.

nodes.name: Binet’s formula
nodes.intuition: A coupled recurrence becomes a difference of two independent exponential modes. Irrational pieces cancel to produce exact integers.
nodes.conditions: n≥0 is an integer and F₀=0,F₁=1 with the Fibonacci recurrence. The displayed formula is exact; replacing it by φⁿ/√5 is an approximation.
nodes.example: At n=3, the expression equals 2 exactly.

patterns.why: The solution separates into two characteristic modes.
Each mode changes by a fixed multiplicative factor per step.

nodes.name: Characteristic-root solution of a linear recurrence
nodes.intuition: A constant linear recurrence has exponential modes, just as a constant linear differential equation does. Initial values determine how much of each mode is present.
nodes.conditions: d≥1; coefficients and initial values are complex; c₀≠0; rᵢ are the d distinct roots of rᵈ−Σⱼ₌₀ᵈ⁻¹cⱼrʲ. The simple displayed solution requires distinct roots; repeated roots need polynomial factors in n.
nodes.example: For aₙ₊₂=3aₙ₊₁−2aₙ, every solution has the form α+β2ⁿ.

patterns.why: The rule ties each value to finitely many predecessors.
Distinct characteristic roots produce independent exponential solutions.

nodes.name: Integer partition generating function
nodes.intuition: For each allowed part size, choose how many copies to include. Multiplication combines these independent choices while the exponent records their total size.
nodes.conditions: p(n) counts unordered partitions of the nonnegative integer n into positive integers and p(0)=1. The identity is formal: each coefficient depends on only finitely many factors; it also converges for |z|<1.
nodes.example: The five partitions of 4 are 4,3+1,2+2,2+1+1 and 1+1+1+1.

patterns.why: An infinite product encodes choices of multiplicities.
A partition separates into independent counts of each part size.

nodes.name: Handshake lemma
nodes.intuition: Every edge contributes one endpoint at each end. Counting edge endpoints by vertices or by edges gives the same total.
nodes.conditions: G=(V,E) is a finite undirected graph. If loops are allowed, each loop contributes two to its vertex degree.
nodes.example: A triangle has three vertices of degree 2, giving total degree 6=2·3.

patterns.why: Edge incidences are counted in two different ways.
Every edge contributes exactly two incidences.

nodes.name: Adjacency powers count walks
nodes.intuition: Matrix multiplication sums over intermediate vertices, so repeated multiplication follows every possible step sequence. The power records routes with repeated vertices allowed.
nodes.conditions: A is the adjacency matrix of a finite graph, with Aᵢⱼ counting directed edges from i to j; k≥0 and A⁰=I. For weighted entries, powers sum products of edge weights instead of unweighted counts.
nodes.example: In a triangle, (A²)₁₁=2 because two length-two walks return to vertex 1.

patterns.why: Each matrix-power term encodes a possible walk.
Joining a first segment to a second segment matches matrix multiplication.

nodes.name: Graph Laplacian
nodes.intuition: The Laplacian compares each vertex value with its neighbors. Constant signals create no disagreement, so they lie in its kernel.
nodes.conditions: G is a finite undirected graph with symmetric nonnegative edge weights and no self-loops; A is the weighted adjacency matrix and Dᵢᵢ=ΣⱼAᵢⱼ. Zero-weight edges may be omitted.
nodes.example: For a single edge of weight w, L=[[w,−w],[−w,w]].

patterns.why: The operator combines neighboring values by a linear rule.
Row sums vanish, so constant values generate no net change.

nodes.name: Graph Dirichlet energy
nodes.intuition: A signal’s graph energy is the total disagreement across edges. Minimizing it favors similar values at strongly connected vertices.
nodes.conditions: x is real and L is the Laplacian of a finite undirected graph with symmetric nonnegative weights; the factor 1/2 compensates for summing both edge orientations.
nodes.example: For one edge of weight 3 joining values 2 and 5, the energy is 3·(2−5)²=27.

patterns.why: The matrix expression is a sum of nonnegative squared differences.
Low energy means the signal varies gently across weighted edges.

nodes.name: Matrix–tree theorem
nodes.intuition: A determinant of local edge interactions counts global spanning trees. Deleting one row and column removes the constant direction that makes the full Laplacian singular.
nodes.conditions: G is a finite undirected graph with n≥2 vertices and nonnegative weights; L⁽ⁱ⁾ deletes row and column i. τ is the sum over spanning trees of the product of their edge weights; it is zero if the graph is disconnected.
nodes.example: For a triangle, a Laplacian cofactor [[2,−1],[−1,2]] has determinant 3, matching its three spanning trees.

patterns.why: A determinant evaluates a global combinatorial count.
Removing one reference vertex eliminates the constant-potential freedom.

nodes.name: Cayley’s formula for labeled trees
nodes.intuition: Every labeled tree can be encoded by a sequence of n−2 labels. The independent choices in that sequence explain the simple power.
nodes.conditions: n≥2 is an integer; trees are undirected simple connected acyclic graphs on the fixed labeled vertex set.
nodes.example: There are 4²=16 trees on four labeled vertices.

patterns.why: Prüfer sequences give a bijection with all length-(n−2) label lists.
Repeatedly removing leaves yields an encoding of the whole tree.

nodes.name: Euler’s formula for connected planar graphs
nodes.intuition: Drawing a connected graph on a sphere balances vertices, edges and regions. Refining the drawing adds pieces in ways that preserve the alternating total.
nodes.conditions: G is a finite connected graph embedded in the plane without crossings; F counts all complementary faces including the unbounded face. A disconnected graph with c components satisfies V−E+F=1+c.
nodes.example: A cube graph has 8 vertices, 12 edges and 6 faces: 8−12+6=2.

patterns.why: Edges separate faces while vertices join edges.
The alternating count survives changes of the planar embedding.

nodes.name: Edges in a finite tree
nodes.intuition: A tree spends exactly one edge to attach each vertex after the first. Any additional edge would create a cycle.
nodes.conditions: A finite tree is a nonempty connected undirected graph with no cycles. More generally a forest with c components has |E|=|V|−c.
nodes.example: A tree joining eight vertices has seven edges.

patterns.why: Each new vertex requires exactly one connecting edge.
Removing a leaf reduces both vertex and edge counts by one.

nodes.name: Hall’s marriage theorem
nodes.intuition: Every group of requesters must collectively have enough distinct options. Remarkably, checking this shortage condition for all groups is also sufficient for a complete assignment.
nodes.conditions: G=(U,V,E) is a finite bipartite graph; N(S) is the set of neighbors of S, and a matching uses no vertex twice. Saturating U matches every vertex in U, without requiring all of V to be matched.
nodes.example: Three tasks can be assigned distinct workers only if every subset of tasks has at least as many qualified workers.

patterns.why: Each subset needs at least one distinct destination per member.
The condition characterizes whether a maximum matching reaches size |U|.

nodes.name: Max-flow min-cut theorem
nodes.intuition: Every route from source to sink must cross a separating cut. The tightest total cut capacity is exactly the largest feasible flow.
nodes.conditions: The network is a finite directed graph with distinct s,t and finite nonnegative capacities. A feasible flow obeys 0≤f(u,v)≤c(u,v) and flow conservation at every other vertex; |f| is net flow out of s.
nodes.example: If two edge-disjoint source-to-sink routes have capacities 2 and 3, and no smaller cut intervenes, maximum flow is 5.

patterns.why: Optimizing a flow and optimizing a separating cut have equal values.
Internal vertices transmit exactly the amount of flow they receive.

nodes.name: Chromatic polynomial deletion–contraction
nodes.intuition: Colorings of the graph with an edge removed split into those whose endpoints differ and those whose endpoints agree. Contracting the edge counts the agreement case.
nodes.conditions: G is a finite simple graph and e is an edge between distinct vertices; P_G(q) counts proper vertex colorings with q colors for integers q≥0. In G/e merge parallel edges. The polynomial identity holds for all q.
nodes.example: For a triangle, deleting an edge gives a path and contracting it gives an edge, so q(q−1)²−q(q−1)=q(q−1)(q−2).

patterns.why: Smaller graphs determine the coloring polynomial.
Endpoint agreement and disagreement partition the relaxed colorings.

nodes.name: Cycle rank of a finite graph
nodes.intuition: After a spanning forest connects each component, every remaining edge creates one independent cycle. Cycles are the edge flows that have no net source at any vertex.
nodes.conditions: G is a finite undirected graph with c connected components; orient edges arbitrarily and let B be its vertex-edge incidence matrix over R. Loops can be handled as zero columns.
nodes.example: A connected triangle has cycle dimension 3−3+1=1.

patterns.why: Kernel vectors represent circulations with zero net vertex imbalance.
Excess edges over a spanning forest count independent cycles.

nodes.name: Euclidean division of integers
nodes.intuition: Every integer has a unique whole-number quotient and a small leftover after division by a positive integer. The remainder is a canonical representative of its modular class.
nodes.conditions: a is an integer and b is a positive integer; unique integers q,r satisfy the formula, including when a is negative.
nodes.example: −17=5·(−4)+3, so the nonnegative remainder is 3.

patterns.why: The number splits into a multiple and a bounded remainder.
A smaller remainder enables repeated division algorithms.

nodes.name: Euclidean algorithm
nodes.intuition: Removing whole multiples does not change which integers divide both numbers. Repeating the operation makes the numbers smaller until the common divisor is exposed.
nodes.conditions: a,b are nonnegative integers with b>0; iterate until the second argument is zero, using gcd(a,0)=a. At least one initial integer is nonzero.

patterns.why: Each step replaces the pair with a smaller remainder pair.
The set of common divisors survives subtracting a multiple.

nodes.name: Bézout’s identity
nodes.intuition: The smallest positive integer combination of two integers is their greatest common divisor. Repeated addition and subtraction reach exactly the multiples of that gcd.
nodes.conditions: a,b are integers not both zero; gcd(a,b)>0. The coefficients x,y exist but are generally not unique.

patterns.why: Integer linear combinations characterize the reachable values.
The ideal generated by a and b is generated by their gcd.

nodes.name: GCD–LCM product formula
nodes.intuition: For each prime, the shared part uses the smaller exponent and the combined coverage uses the larger. Together they use the same total exponent as the original two numbers.
nodes.conditions: a,b are positive integers; gcd and lcm are taken positive.
nodes.example: For 12 and 18, gcd=6 and lcm=36, so 6·36=12·18.

patterns.why: Minimum and maximum prime exponents split the original pair of exponent counts.
Greatest common divisor and least common multiple reverse shared-versus-covering roles.

nodes.name: Fundamental theorem of arithmetic
nodes.intuition: Every positive integer is assembled from prime building blocks in a unique way. The multiplicities turn divisibility questions into coordinatewise comparisons.
nodes.conditions: n>1 is an integer; pᵢ are distinct primes and aᵢ≥1 integers. The factorization is unique up to ordering; n=1 is the empty product.

patterns.why: Primes provide unique multiplicative building blocks.
Divisibility is encoded by inequalities between prime exponents.

nodes.name: Congruence modulo an integer
nodes.intuition: Two numbers are equivalent when they differ by a whole number of complete cycles. Congruence forgets position along the infinite line while retaining position around the cycle.
nodes.conditions: a,b are integers and m≥1 is an integer; congruence is an equivalence relation compatible with addition and multiplication.
nodes.example: 17≡5 mod 12 because their difference is 12.

patterns.why: Adding a multiple of m leaves the residue unchanged.
Arithmetic descends consistently to residue classes.

nodes.name: Modular inverse criterion
nodes.intuition: Division modulo m works exactly when a shares no prime obstruction with the modulus. Bézout coefficients construct the inverse explicitly.
nodes.conditions: a is an integer and m≥2; when an inverse exists, its residue class modulo m is unique.
nodes.example: 3⁻¹≡5 mod 7 because 3·5=15≡1.

patterns.why: Invertible residue classes form the unit group.
Multiplication by a and multiplication by its inverse undo one another.

nodes.name: Linear Diophantine equations
nodes.latex: ax+by=c\text{ has integer solutions}\iff d\mid c,\qquad d=\gcd(a,b)
nodes.intuition: Integer linear equations live on a grid, so ordinary real solvability is not enough. The gcd is the spacing between attainable values.
nodes.conditions: a,b,c are integers, a,b not both zero, and d>0. If (x₀,y₀) is one solution, all are x=x₀+(b/d)t, y=y₀−(a/d)t with t∈Z.
nodes.example: 6x+9y=12 is solvable since 3 divides 12; all solutions include x=2+3t,y=−2t.

patterns.why: Integer coefficients restrict values to the ideal dZ.
Solutions form a lattice of points on a line.

nodes.name: Chinese remainder theorem
nodes.latex: \mathbb Z/M\mathbb Z\cong\prod_{i=1}^{r}\mathbb Z/m_i\mathbb Z,\qquad x\equiv\sum_i a_i M_i y_i\pmod M
nodes.intuition: Independent modular views can be recombined without losing information. Each term in the construction is tuned to affect exactly one modulus.
nodes.conditions: mᵢ≥2 are pairwise coprime integers, M=∏ᵢmᵢ, Mᵢ=M/mᵢ and Mᵢyᵢ≡1 mod mᵢ. For any residues aᵢ, there is a unique solution modulo M to x≡aᵢ mod mᵢ; the first map is a ring isomorphism.
nodes.example: x≡2 mod 3 and x≡3 mod 5 combine to x≡8 mod 15.

patterns.why: One arithmetic system splits into independent coprime components.
Componentwise residues can be assembled into one global class.

nodes.name: Fermat’s little theorem
nodes.latex: a^p\equiv a\pmod p,\qquad p\nmid a\Longrightarrow a^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod p
nodes.intuition: Modulo a prime, multiplication by a nonzero residue permutes all nonzero residues. Their product reveals the periodicity of powers.
nodes.conditions: p is prime and a is any integer; the second form additionally requires p not dividing a. Composite moduli can satisfy some Fermat congruences, so the converse is false.

patterns.why: Multiplication permutes the nonzero residue classes.
Powers repeat modulo a fixed prime.

nodes.name: Euler’s totient function
nodes.intuition: Count the integers up to n that avoid every prime divisor of n. Each distinct prime removes its share of forbidden residues.
nodes.conditions: n≥1 is an integer and the product runs over distinct prime divisors; φ(1)=1 via the empty product. Equivalently φ(n)=#{1≤k≤n:gcd(k,n)=1}.

patterns.why: The function counts invertible residue classes.
Distinct prime obstructions factor into separate corrections.

nodes.name: Euler’s theorem on powers modulo n
nodes.intuition: The invertible residues form a finite group, so repeatedly multiplying by one residue must cycle within that group. The group size is a universal exponent that returns every element to one.
nodes.conditions: n≥2 is an integer and gcd(a,n)=1. φ(n) counts the units modulo n; it need not be the smallest exponent that works.
nodes.example: For n=10, φ(n)=4 and 3⁴=81≡1 mod 10.

patterns.why: Units modulo n form a finite multiplicative group.
A fixed power returns every unit to the identity.

nodes.name: Wilson’s theorem
nodes.intuition: For a prime modulus, every nonzero residue pairs with a distinct inverse except 1 and −1. Those two leftovers determine the factorial product.
nodes.conditions: p is an integer greater than 1. The equivalence is exact, though it is generally inefficient as a computational primality test.

patterns.why: Inverse pairing cancels most residue factors.
The surviving self-inverse units determine the product.

nodes.name: Legendre symbol
nodes.latex: \left(\frac ap\right)=\begin{cases}0&p\mid a\\1&a\not\equiv0\text{ is a square mod }p\\-1&a\text{ is not a square mod }p\end{cases}
nodes.intuition: The Legendre symbol compresses a square-root existence question into a sign. Multiplying signs corresponds to multiplying residue classes.
nodes.conditions: p is an odd prime and a is an integer. On nonzero residues it is a multiplicative map to {1,−1}.
nodes.example: Modulo 7, 2 is a square because 3²≡2, so (2/7)=1; 3 is not a square, so (3/7)=−1.

patterns.why: The nonzero symbol is a multiplicative character.
Residues separate into zero, squares and nonsquares.

nodes.name: Euler’s criterion
nodes.intuition: Half the universal group exponent separates squares from nonsquares. The result is one for squares and minus one for nonsquares.
nodes.conditions: p is an odd prime and a is any integer, including multiples of p for which both sides are zero modulo p.
nodes.example: For a=3,p=7, 3³=27≡−1, so 3 is a nonsquare modulo 7.

patterns.why: A group power realizes the quadratic character.
The value depends only on the residue class.

nodes.name: Quadratic reciprocity
nodes.intuition: Whether one prime is a square modulo another is almost a symmetric question. A sign flip occurs exactly when both primes are 3 modulo 4.
nodes.conditions: p and q are distinct odd primes. The Legendre symbols use the lower prime as modulus. The supplementary laws for −1 and 2 are separate statements.

patterns.why: The formula exchanges the roles of numerator prime and modulus prime.
The reciprocity defect is controlled by the two parity classes.

nodes.name: Number of positive divisors
nodes.intuition: A divisor independently chooses how many copies of each prime to keep. Multiply the number of choices across primes.
nodes.conditions: n≥1 is an integer; the prime factorization uses distinct primes with positive exponents. For n=1 the empty product gives τ(1)=1.
nodes.example: 72=2³3² has (3+1)(2+1)=12 positive divisors.

patterns.why: Each prime contributes a finite list of exponent choices.
Prime exponents make divisor selection independent.

nodes.name: Sum of positive divisors
nodes.intuition: The contribution from each prime is a short geometric series. Multiplying these series produces every divisor exactly once.
nodes.conditions: n≥1 and n=∏ᵢpᵢᵃⁱ is its prime factorization; the empty product gives σ(1)=1. Every sum and product here is finite.

patterns.why: All divisor values are added.
Independent prime-power choices factor the sum.

nodes.name: Möbius function
nodes.latex: \mu(n)=\begin{cases}1&n=1\\(-1)^r&n\text{ is a product of }r\text{ distinct primes}\\0&\text{some prime square divides }n\end{cases}
nodes.intuition: The Möbius function assigns alternating signs to square-free prime selections. These signs undo the overcounting created by summing over divisors.
nodes.conditions: n is a positive integer; the r=0 case corresponds to n=1. Square-free means no squared prime divides n.
nodes.example: μ(30)=−1 because 30 has three distinct prime factors, while μ(12)=0.

patterns.why: Only distinct prime selections contribute.
The value depends on the number of prime factors, not their order.

nodes.name: Möbius inversion over divisors
nodes.intuition: A divisor sum blends contributions from all factors of a number. Möbius weights cancel the inherited contributions and recover the original one.
nodes.conditions: f,F are arithmetic functions from positive integers to a commutative ring; all divisor sums are finite and μ is interpreted as an integer coefficient.
nodes.example: Because Σd|n φ(d)=n, inversion gives φ(n)=Σd|n μ(d)n/d.

patterns.why: The formula separates a direct contribution from those inherited from proper divisors.
Divisor summation and Möbius-weighted summation are inverse operations.

nodes.name: Dirichlet convolution
nodes.intuition: Convolution can split an index multiplicatively instead of additively. Every factorization n=d·(n/d) contributes one pair of function values.
nodes.conditions: f,g map positive integers into a commutative ring. Here 1(n)=1, ε(1)=1 and ε(n)=0 for n>1; μ is the Möbius function. All sums are finite.
nodes.example: For f=g=1, (1*1)(n)=τ(n), the divisor count.

patterns.why: All multiplicative decompositions of the index combine the two functions.
Arithmetic functions form a commutative convolution algebra with identity ε.

nodes.name: Prime exponent in a factorial
nodes.intuition: Count one factor of p from every multiple of p, another from every multiple of p², and so on. Higher prime powers contribute repeatedly because they contain several copies.
nodes.conditions: n≥0 is an integer and p is prime; vₚ is the exponent of p in the factorization. The displayed sum has only finitely many nonzero terms.

patterns.why: Multiples of successive prime powers count repeated prime factors.
Each level adds one more layer of p-divisibility.

nodes.name: p-adic absolute value and ultrametric
nodes.intuition: Two rational numbers are close when their difference is divisible by a high power of p. This replaces ordinary magnitude with agreement in prime-power arithmetic.
nodes.conditions: p is prime. For nonzero rational x=pᵏa/b with p dividing neither a nor b, vₚ(x)=k; set |0|ₚ=0. The inequality holds on Q and its completion Qₚ.
nodes.example: In 2-adic distance, 9 and 1 are only |8|₂=1/8 apart.

patterns.why: Prime divisibility becomes a non-Euclidean notion of distance.
Completing this distance produces the p-adic field.

nodes.name: Continued-fraction convergent recurrence
nodes.intuition: A continued fraction builds rational approximations by repeatedly inverting the leftover part. The determinant identity ensures consecutive approximations stay arithmetically adjacent.
nodes.conditions: For a simple continued fraction [a₀;a₁,…], a₀∈Z and aₙ≥1 for n≥1. Set p₋₂=0,p₋₁=1,q₋₂=1,q₋₁=0; n≥0 in the recurrences, and n≥1 in the determinant identity. pₙ/qₙ is the nth convergent.
nodes.example: For √2=[1;2,2,…], the convergents begin 1,3/2,7/5,17/12.

patterns.why: Each numerator and denominator uses its two predecessors.
Convergents provide unusually efficient rational approximations, with precise best-approximation theorems requiring a chosen error criterion.

nodes.name: Cross product in three dimensions
nodes.intuition: The cross product packages oriented area into a perpendicular vector. Its magnitude measures how much two directions spread out instead of overlapping.
nodes.conditions: a,b lie in oriented Euclidean R³ with the standard right-handed coordinate basis; the norm is Euclidean.
nodes.example: (1,0,0)×(0,2,0)=(0,0,2), an area vector of magnitude 2.

patterns.why: The result is perpendicular to both input vectors.
Its norm is the spanned parallelogram area.

nodes.name: Curvature of a regular space curve
nodes.intuition: Curvature measures how quickly the tangent direction turns per unit distance traveled. Dividing by arc length separates bending from the speed used to trace the curve.
nodes.conditions: r is a C² regular curve in R³, so r′(t)≠0; s is arc length and T=r′/‖r′‖. A planar curve can be embedded in R³. This is nonnegative curvature.
nodes.example: A circle of radius R>0 has constant curvature 1/R.

patterns.why: The changing tangent quantifies how the curve departs from its local straight-line direction.
Uniformly enlarging a curve by R divides curvature by R.

nodes.name: Torsion of a space curve
nodes.intuition: Torsion measures how the osculating plane twists as you follow a curve. A curve may bend without twisting if it stays in one plane.
nodes.conditions: r is C³ and regular in oriented R³, with r′×r″≠0 on the interval. The sign convention agrees with B=T×N and dB/ds=−τN.
nodes.example: The circular helix r(t)=(a cos t,a sin t,bt), a>0, has τ=b/(a²+b²).

patterns.why: Twisting is measured relative to the moving tangent-normal plane.
A moving frame exposes the curve’s local three-dimensional geometry.

nodes.name: Frenet–Serret equations
nodes.intuition: A curve carries its own moving orthonormal frame. Two scalar functions, curvature and torsion, describe all infinitesimal changes of that frame.
nodes.conditions: The curve is C³, parametrized by arc length, and has κ>0. T=r′, N=T′/κ and B=T×N; derivatives are with respect to s. The formula treats T,N,B as a column of vector entries.
nodes.example: For a plane circle, τ=0 and the tangent and normal rotate while the binormal stays fixed.

patterns.why: The frame moves with the curve instead of using fixed axes.
The skew-symmetric coefficient matrix preserves frame inner products.

nodes.name: First fundamental form of a surface
nodes.latex: ds^2=E\,du^2+2F\,du\,dv+G\,dv^2,\quad E=r_u\cdot r_u,\ F=r_u\cdot r_v,\ G=r_v\cdot r_v
nodes.intuition: Surface coordinates may stretch and tilt a flat grid. The first fundamental form records the actual lengths and angles represented by coordinate changes.
nodes.conditions: r(u,v) is a C¹ regular parametrized surface in R³, so rᵤ and rᵥ are linearly independent. The 2×2 coefficient matrix is positive definite.
nodes.example: For a cylinder r(u,v)=(R cos u,R sin u,v), ds²=R²du²+dv².

patterns.why: The formula measures lengths of tangent displacements.
Metric coefficients translate coordinate changes into actual geometric size.

nodes.name: Area of a parametrized surface
nodes.intuition: A tiny coordinate rectangle becomes a tangent parallelogram on the surface. Adding its local area multiplier gives the total area.
nodes.conditions: r:D→R³ is a regular C¹ patch, one-to-one except on a set of area measure zero, and the area density is integrable. Without the one-to-one qualification, the parameter integral counts multiplicity.
nodes.example: For a graph z=f(x,y), the density is √(1+fₓ²+fᵧ²).

patterns.why: Total area adds local area contributions.
The derivative replaces a tiny patch by its tangent parallelogram.

nodes.name: Shape operator and second fundamental form
nodes.intuition: The surface bends when its unit normal changes from point to point. The shape operator converts a tangent direction into that change, and the second fundamental form reads its normal bending.
nodes.conditions: The surface is an oriented C² immersed surface in R³ with unit normal N. Identify the tangent plane of S² at N(p) with the tangent plane of the surface; S is self-adjoint for the induced metric. Our convention is S=−dN.
nodes.example: For a sphere of radius R with outward normal, S=−I/R and both principal curvatures are −1/R.

patterns.why: Differentiating the normal captures local bending.
II(u,u) measures normal bending quadratically in a tangent vector.

nodes.name: Gaussian curvature of a surface
nodes.intuition: Gaussian curvature combines bending in the two principal directions. Same-sign bending is dome-like, opposite-sign bending is saddle-like, and its value is intrinsic to the surface metric.
nodes.conditions: The oriented surface is C² and regular in R³; S=−dN. E,F,G are first-form coefficients and e=rᵤᵤ·N, f=rᵤᵥ·N, g=rᵥᵥ·N are second-form coefficients. Smoothness can be increased for differential curvature identities.
nodes.example: A sphere of radius R has K=1/R²; a circular cylinder has K=0.

patterns.why: The two principal bendings combine multiplicatively.
K is unchanged by reversing the normal and is determined by the intrinsic metric.

nodes.name: Mean curvature of a surface
nodes.intuition: Mean curvature is the average of the two principal bendings. It also equals the angular average of normal curvature across all unit tangent directions.
nodes.conditions: The surface is an oriented C² immersed surface in R³, with S=−dN and real principal curvatures k₁,k₂. Reversing the normal reverses H; some texts use the unnormalized trace instead.
nodes.example: An outward-oriented sphere of radius R has H=−1/R in this convention; a saddle with k₁=−k₂ has H=0.

patterns.why: The principal curvatures enter with equal weights.
Smooth minimal surfaces have H=0 as the local stationarity condition for area.

nodes.name: Euler’s formula for normal curvature
nodes.intuition: Bending in an arbitrary tangent direction mixes the two principal bendings. Squared direction components supply the weights.
nodes.conditions: The surface is oriented and C²; e₁,e₂ are orthonormal principal directions of S=−dN, and the unit tangent direction is cosθ e₁+sinθ e₂. Normal curvature is II(v,v).
nodes.example: If k₁=1 and k₂=3, a direction at 45° has normal curvature 2.

patterns.why: Nonnegative squared trigonometric weights sum to one.
The directional curvature is a Rayleigh quotient of the shape operator.

nodes.name: Riemannian metric
nodes.intuition: A Riemannian metric assigns an inner product to every tangent space, varying smoothly from point to point. It tells a traveler how to measure distances and angles locally.
nodes.conditions: M is a smooth manifold; gᵢⱼ=gⱼᵢ is a smooth positive definite matrix in each coordinate chart. Repeated indices are summed from 1 to the manifold dimension; v is a real tangent vector.
nodes.example: Euclidean polar coordinates have ds²=dr²+r²dθ² away from r=0.

patterns.why: The metric defines local lengths and angles.
Squared tangent length is a positive definite quadratic form.

nodes.name: Riemannian length and distance
nodes.intuition: Add the local lengths along a path, then choose the least possible path length between endpoints. The metric turns an infinitesimal ruler into a global distance.
nodes.conditions: (M,g) is a connected Riemannian manifold; γ is piecewise C¹ on a compact interval. The infimum ranges over such joining paths. A minimizing path need not exist unless further hypotheses, such as completeness, hold.
nodes.example: On a circle of radius R, the distance is R times the smaller angular separation.

patterns.why: Path length adds infinitesimal metric lengths.
Distance is an infimum over all connecting paths.

nodes.name: Riemannian volume element
nodes.intuition: The determinant measures how a coordinate box changes volume under the local metric. Its square root converts squared inner-product information into volume.
nodes.conditions: g is a smooth positive definite metric in a coordinate chart. The expression defines a volume density on any Riemannian manifold; on an oriented manifold use the oriented form √det(g) dx¹∧…∧dxⁿ.
nodes.example: In Euclidean spherical coordinates, the density is r² sinθ dr dθ dφ on the usual coordinate range.

patterns.why: The metric determinant supplies the volume of a coordinate parallelepiped.
The density transformation compensates for changing charts.

nodes.name: Christoffel symbols of the Levi-Civita connection
nodes.intuition: The metric determines how to compare tangent directions at nearby points while preserving lengths and having no torsion. Christoffel symbols record this comparison in a chosen coordinate system.
nodes.conditions: g is a smooth Riemannian metric, (gⁱʲ) is its inverse matrix, and repeated indices are summed. These coefficients belong to the unique torsion-free metric-compatible connection; they are not tensor components under general coordinate changes.
nodes.example: For ds²=dr²+r²dθ², Γʳθθ=−r and Γθrθ=Γθθr=1/r for r>0.

patterns.why: First derivatives of the metric determine local connection coefficients.
The coefficients correct for a coordinate frame that varies with position.

nodes.name: Covariant derivative in coordinates
nodes.intuition: Differentiating vector components alone confuses actual change with movement of the coordinate frame. The connection correction separates those two effects.
nodes.conditions: V is a smooth tangent vector field, Γ are the coefficients of a specified affine connection, and repeated j is summed. For Riemannian geometry we use the Levi-Civita connection.
nodes.example: A constant Cartesian vector has nonconstant polar components, but its Euclidean covariant derivative is still zero.

patterns.why: The correction makes vector differentiation independent of chart choices.
It measures first-order change relative to the chosen connection.

nodes.name: Geodesic equation
nodes.intuition: A geodesic moves without turning relative to the surface’s own connection. Its coordinates may accelerate even while its intrinsic acceleration is zero.
nodes.conditions: x(t) is a C² curve on a smooth Riemannian manifold with Levi-Civita symbols; t is an affine parameter and repeated indices are summed. Geodesics locally minimize length over sufficiently short segments, not necessarily over their whole length.
nodes.example: Great circles are geodesics on a round sphere; a sufficiently long great-circle arc is not the shortest route between its endpoints.

patterns.why: The covariant acceleration is zero at each point.
Affinely parametrized geodesics are stationary paths of the energy functional.

nodes.name: Parallel transport along a curve
nodes.intuition: Parallel transport gives a rule for carrying a direction along a path without intrinsic turning. After a loop, the direction may return rotated because the space is curved.
nodes.conditions: γ is a smooth or piecewise smooth curve and Γ belong to a smooth connection; an initial tangent vector determines a unique transported field on the compact parameter interval. For Levi-Civita transport, inner products are preserved.
nodes.example: Transport around a triangle on a sphere generally rotates a vector by an angle related to the enclosed curvature.

patterns.why: Levi-Civita parallel transport preserves lengths and angles.
Transport along concatenated paths composes the transport maps.

nodes.name: Riemann curvature tensor
nodes.intuition: Curvature measures the failure of two directional comparisons to commute after correcting for noncommuting vector fields. It detects geometry that no coordinate change can remove.
nodes.conditions: M has a smooth connection; for geometric curvature here use the Levi-Civita connection of g, and smooth vector fields X,Y,Z. This sign convention makes a round sphere have positive sectional curvature when K(u,v)=g(R(u,v)v,u)/area².
nodes.example: Euclidean space has R=0 even in curvilinear coordinates with nonzero Christoffel symbols.

patterns.why: The two second-derivative orders are compared.
The bracket correction makes the result a tensor independent of coordinates.

nodes.name: Sectional curvature
nodes.intuition: Each two-dimensional tangent plane has its own curvature measurement. Dividing by the plane’s squared area removes dependence on how its two basis vectors were chosen.
nodes.conditions: u,v are linearly independent real tangent vectors at one point of a Riemannian manifold. R uses ∇X∇Y−∇Y∇X−∇[X,Y]; the denominator is strictly positive.
nodes.example: Every tangent plane of a round sphere of radius R has sectional curvature 1/R².

patterns.why: The denominator is the squared area of the chosen tangent parallelogram.
The quotient depends on the plane, not its chosen basis.

nodes.name: Ricci and scalar curvature as traces
nodes.intuition: Ricci curvature summarizes how a chosen direction bends against all perpendicular directions. Scalar curvature adds the directional summaries into one number.
nodes.conditions: e₁,…,eₙ is any orthonormal basis at a point of a smooth Riemannian manifold. R uses the stated sphere-positive convention; both contractions are basis-independent. These are sums, not normalized averages.
nodes.example: An n-dimensional manifold of constant sectional curvature c has Ric=(n−1)cg and Scal=n(n−1)c.

patterns.why: Sectional contributions are summed into progressively coarser curvature measures.
Taking tensor traces removes basis dependence.

nodes.name: Laplace–Beltrami operator
nodes.intuition: Diffusion on a curved space must account for both directional lengths and local volume. The Laplace–Beltrami operator is divergence of the metric gradient.
nodes.conditions: f is C² and g is a smooth Riemannian metric in a chart; repeated indices are summed. This convention is Δg=divg gradg, giving Σ∂ᵢ² in Euclidean coordinates; some texts use its negative.
nodes.example: On the Euclidean plane in polar coordinates, Δf=frr+(1/r)fr+(1/r²)fθθ for r>0.

patterns.why: The inverse metric and volume density adapt derivatives to geometry.
The operator compares second-order local variation.

nodes.name: Gauss–Bonnet theorem for closed surfaces
nodes.intuition: Local bending accumulates into a global topological invariant. Stretching and reshaping a closed surface can redistribute curvature but cannot change its total unless its topology changes.
nodes.conditions: M is a compact oriented smooth Riemannian two-manifold without boundary, K its Gaussian curvature and χ its Euler characteristic. Boundary and corner versions require extra terms, omitted here.
nodes.example: A sphere has total curvature 4π and χ=2; a torus has total curvature 0 and χ=0.

patterns.why: Integrating all local curvature produces a single global quantity.
The integral is unchanged by smooth changes of the metric.
Topology constrains how local geometric bending can assemble globally.

nodes.name: Exterior derivative
nodes.intuition: One derivative operation unifies differential, curl and divergence by acting on oriented measurement objects of successive dimensions. Differentiating twice cancels because mixed derivatives are symmetric while orientation is antisymmetric.
nodes.conditions: ω is a smooth k-form in a coordinate chart, dxᴵ=dxⁱ¹∧…∧dxⁱᵏ with increasing multi-indices, and dω is a (k+1)-form. The identity d²=0 holds globally on smooth manifolds.
nodes.example: For ω=x dy in R², dω=dx∧dy.

patterns.why: The derivative is paired with geometric boundary by Stokes’ theorem.
The square-zero rule creates a cochain complex.

nodes.name: Wedge product and graded commutativity
nodes.intuition: The wedge product combines oriented measurements in different directions. Repeating a direction gives zero because it cannot create new oriented volume.
nodes.conditions: α is a k-form and β an ℓ-form over R on the same manifold, or alternating covariant tensors on one real vector space. The wedge product is bilinear and associative.
nodes.example: dx∧dy measures oriented coordinate area, and swapping the axes gives dy∧dx=−dx∧dy.

patterns.why: Alternating multilinearity creates a graded algebra.
Swapping blocks of directions produces the sign determined by their degrees.

nodes.name: Pullback of a differential form
nodes.intuition: A form on the destination becomes a measurement on the starting space by first pushing its input directions forward. Differentiation respects this transfer.
nodes.conditions: F:M→N is smooth and ω is a smooth k-form on N; F*ω is a k-form on M. No invertibility of F is required.
nodes.example: If F(u,v)=(2u,3v), then F*(dx∧dy)=6 du∧dv.

patterns.why: Tangent directions move forward while measurements pull backward.
Pullback reverses composition: (G∘F)*=F*G*.

nodes.name: Cartan’s formula for the Lie derivative
nodes.intuition: The change of a form under a flow splits into two simpler operations: insert the flow direction and differentiate, or differentiate and then insert. This connects motion with the algebra of forms.
nodes.conditions: X is a smooth vector field and ω a smooth differential form; ιX is contraction with X and LX is the Lie derivative defined through the local flow. For zero-forms take contraction to be zero.
nodes.example: For a function f, the formula gives LXf=ιXdf=X(f).

patterns.why: Flow-induced change splits into two complementary derivative-contraction terms.
The identity combines degree-raising and degree-lowering operations.

nodes.name: Topology by open sets
nodes.intuition: Topology specifies which regions count as open without committing to numerical distances. Arbitrary unions and finite intersections preserve the notion of being locally inside a region.
nodes.conditions: T is a collection of subsets of X; every Uα and Uⱼ lies in T, A is any index set, and m is finite. Infinite intersections are not required to be open.
nodes.example: The intervals (a,b) generate the usual topology of the real line.

patterns.why: Closure rules organize a collection of subsets.
Open regions formalize what it means for a point to lie locally inside a set.

nodes.name: Continuity by inverse images
nodes.latex: f:X\to Y\text{ continuous}\iff f^{-1}(U)\text{ is open in }X\ \text{for every open }U\subseteq Y
nodes.intuition: A destination neighborhood pulls back to a neighborhood condition on inputs. This captures continuity even when distance and coordinates are unavailable.
nodes.conditions: X,Y are topological spaces and f is any map; f⁻¹(U) denotes a set inverse image and does not require f to be invertible.
nodes.example: Every map from a discrete topological space is continuous because every input subset is open.

patterns.why: A forward point map pulls open-set information backward.
Inverse images preserve unions and intersections and reverse function composition.

nodes.name: Homeomorphism
nodes.latex: f:X\to Y,\quad g:Y\to X,\quad g\circ f=\operatorname{id}_X,\quad f\circ g=\operatorname{id}_Y
nodes.intuition: Two spaces have the same topological shape when a continuous relabeling can be continuously reversed. Length and curvature may change while neighborhood structure is preserved.
nodes.conditions: Both f and g are continuous maps; the equations make them inverse bijections. A continuous bijection alone need not be a homeomorphism.
nodes.example: An open interval is homeomorphic to the real line, even though its ordinary length is finite.

patterns.why: Topological invariants survive continuous reversible relabeling.
The two inverse maps recover each other’s spaces.

nodes.name: Homotopy of maps
nodes.intuition: A homotopy is a continuous movie deforming one map into another. It formalizes changing shape without jumping or tearing the map.
nodes.conditions: F is continuous for the product topology; f₀,f₁:X→Y are its endpoint maps. For based homotopies, the chosen basepoint is held fixed throughout.
nodes.example: The maps f₀(x)=0 and f₁(x)=x from R to R are homotopic through F(x,t)=tx.

patterns.why: Homotopies can be concatenated in time and composed with continuous maps.
Homotopy-invariant constructions ignore these continuous deformations.

nodes.name: Fundamental group
nodes.intuition: The fundamental group records loops that cannot be deformed into one another while their starting point stays fixed. Its multiplication is following one loop and then another.
nodes.conditions: X is a topological space with basepoint x₀; all loops are continuous and the equivalence is homotopy fixing endpoints. Concatenation gives a group only after passing to homotopy classes.
nodes.example: A disk has trivial fundamental group, while a torus has fundamental group Z².

patterns.why: Loop concatenation becomes an associative group operation on classes.
Continuous endpoint-fixing deformation preserves the loop class.

nodes.name: Fundamental group of the circle
nodes.intuition: A loop around a circle remembers its net number of turns. Continuous deformation can remove detours but cannot change that integer winding count.
nodes.conditions: γ is a continuous loop based at 1 in S¹⊂C; γ̃ is a continuous real lift with e^(iγ̃(t))=γ(t) and γ̃(0)=0. The endpoint difference is an integer multiple of 2π.
nodes.example: The loop γ(t)=e^(6πit) represents the integer 3.

patterns.why: The invariant counts oriented net turns.
Winding number remains fixed under based homotopy.

nodes.name: Seifert–van Kampen theorem
nodes.intuition: Global loops can be built from loops in overlapping regions. The overlap supplies exactly the relations needed to identify local descriptions of the same loop.
nodes.conditions: X=U∪V where U,V and U∩V are nonempty path-connected open subsets; choose one basepoint in U∩V. The amalgamated product means the quotient of the free product identifying images of every overlap loop under the inclusion maps; those maps need not be injective.
nodes.example: A figure-eight space has fundamental group the free group on two generators, using suitable overlapping neighborhoods.

patterns.why: The whole space is reconstructed from overlapping pieces.
Gluing spaces becomes a pushout of groups.

nodes.name: Number of sheets and subgroup index
nodes.intuition: Lifting loops moves among the sheets above a point. Loops that return to the chosen starting sheet form a subgroup, and its cosets label all sheets.
nodes.conditions: p:X̃→X is a covering map, X and X̃ are path-connected and locally path-connected, and p(x̃₀)=x₀. The formula is a cardinal equality, allowing infinitely many sheets; p* is injective.
nodes.example: The covering S¹→S¹, z↦zᵐ for m≥1, has m sheets and corresponds to mZ⊂Z.

patterns.why: Cosets count the distinct endpoints of lifted loops.
A geometric covering is related to algebraic subgroup data.

nodes.name: Oriented simplex boundary
nodes.intuition: A simplex’s boundary is the sum of its faces with compatible orientations. Alternating signs arrange for shared boundaries to cancel when pieces are glued.
nodes.conditions: k≥1 and the ordered vertices form a simplex in a simplicial complex; the hat means omit that vertex. Extend the map linearly to chains over Z or a stated coefficient ring; set ∂=0 on zero-dimensional chains for unreduced homology.
nodes.example: The oriented triangle boundary is [v₁,v₂]−[v₀,v₂]+[v₀,v₁].

patterns.why: The operator turns a region into its oriented boundary pieces.
Boundaries add across chains, enabling shared-face cancellation.

nodes.name: The boundary of a boundary is zero
nodes.intuition: An oriented boundary already closes up. Taking its boundary again leaves pairs of equal pieces with opposite signs and therefore nothing.
nodes.conditions: ∂ are the standard boundary maps in a simplicial or singular chain complex, with coefficients in Z or any chosen commutative ring. More abstractly this is the defining condition of a chain complex.
nodes.example: The endpoints of the three oriented edges around a triangle cancel at every vertex.

patterns.why: Closing a boundary eliminates any further boundary.
All lower-dimensional contributions cancel in pairs.

nodes.name: Homology as cycles modulo boundaries
nodes.intuition: Homology records closed chains that cannot be filled by higher-dimensional chains. It ignores the cycles that are merely boundaries of material already present.
nodes.conditions: Use a singular chain complex of X over a commutative coefficient ring R, or a simplicial/cellular complex computing the same homology when applicable. The inclusion im ∂k+1⊆ker ∂k follows from ∂²=0.
nodes.example: For a circle, H₀(S¹;Z)=Z and H₁(S¹;Z)=Z, with higher groups zero.

patterns.why: Unfillable cycles record global obstructions.
A quotient removes boundary cycles from all cycles.

nodes.name: Euler characteristic
nodes.intuition: Euler characteristic balances pieces of alternating dimension. Refining a shape changes the individual cell counts but preserves the total.
nodes.conditions: X is a finite CW complex (including a finite simplicial complex); cₖ is its number of k-cells. The alternating sum is independent of the finite cell decomposition and invariant under homotopy equivalence.
nodes.example: A torus with one vertex, two edges and one face has χ=1−2+1=0.

patterns.why: Cells of successive dimensions enter with alternating signs.
The total survives subdivision and homotopy equivalence.

nodes.name: Euler–Poincaré formula
nodes.intuition: Local chain pieces that cancel as boundaries disappear from the alternating total. What survives is a balance of global homological features.
nodes.conditions: X is a finite CW complex, F any field, and bₖ are finite Betti numbers. The equality follows from its finite-dimensional cellular chain complex.
nodes.example: For a torus, b₀=1,b₁=2,b₂=1, so χ=0.

patterns.why: Chain spaces split into cycles and noncycles, and cycles into boundaries and homology.
Alternating cancellation preserves the same total from cells to homology.

nodes.name: Exactness of consecutive maps
nodes.intuition: Exactness says that every obstruction killed by the next map is explained by the preceding map. There is no unexplained information left in the middle.
nodes.conditions: f,g are homomorphisms of abelian groups or linear maps (or module maps); the equality is in B. A sequence is exact when this holds at every indicated position.
nodes.example: For a linear map T, 0→ker T→V→im T→0 is exact.

patterns.why: The kernel of one map is completely accounted for by the previous image.
Exactness expresses compatibility among several homomorphisms.

nodes.name: Mayer–Vietoris exact sequence
nodes.latex: \cdots\to H_k(U\cap V)\to H_k(U)\oplus H_k(V)\to H_k(X)\to H_{k-1}(U\cap V)\to\cdots
nodes.intuition: To understand cycles in a union, track cycles inside each piece and the ways those pieces overlap. The connecting map records cycles that only close after the two sides are combined.
nodes.conditions: X=U∪V with U,V open; use singular homology with a fixed abelian coefficient group. The first map is induced by (inclusion, minus inclusion), the next by addition of inclusion maps; the sequence is exact. No connectedness assumption is needed.
nodes.example: Cover a circle by two overlapping arcs whose intersection has two components; the sequence detects one independent loop.

patterns.why: Global homology is related to homology of two pieces and their overlap.
The connecting homomorphism records the boundary left on the overlap.

nodes.name: Künneth formula over a field
nodes.intuition: A cycle in a product can combine a p-dimensional cycle from one factor with a q-dimensional cycle from the other. Their dimensions add while their independent choices form tensor products.
nodes.conditions: X,Y are topological spaces and F is a field; use singular homology. The cross-product map gives the natural isomorphism. Integral coefficients generally require additional Tor terms.
nodes.example: For S¹×S¹, the two circle factors give b₁=2, and their product gives b₂=1.

patterns.why: Product-space homology splits by dimension contributed from each factor.
Independent cycles combine by the homological cross product.

nodes.name: Poincaré duality
nodes.intuition: On a closed oriented manifold, k-dimensional measurements correspond to complementary-dimensional cycles. The ambient dimension creates a global pairing between apparently different degrees.
nodes.conditions: M is a closed (compact without boundary) oriented n-dimensional manifold and F a field; [M] is the fundamental class with those coefficients. Nonorientable manifolds require suitable coefficients or local systems; manifolds with boundary need a relative version.
nodes.example: For a closed oriented surface, b₀=b₂=1 on each connected component, while b₁ records the remaining independent loops.

patterns.why: Cohomology in degree k corresponds to homology in degree n−k.
Betti numbers satisfy bₖ=bₙ₋ₖ under these hypotheses.

nodes.name: Degree of a map
nodes.intuition: Degree counts how many times one oriented closed manifold wraps over another, with orientation signs. Composition multiplies wrapping counts.
nodes.conditions: f:M→N is continuous between connected closed oriented manifolds of the same dimension; fundamental classes use integral homology. The composition formula assumes a third connected closed oriented manifold of that dimension.
nodes.example: The circle map z↦zᵐ has degree m, and a reflection of the circle has degree −1.

patterns.why: Signed covering of the target produces an integer invariant.
Wrapping counts multiply under composition.

nodes.name: Brouwer fixed-point theorem
nodes.intuition: Any continuous self-map of a closed ball leaves some point fixed. The ball’s topology prevents every point from being shifted away from itself at once.
nodes.conditions: Bⁿ is the closed unit ball in finite-dimensional Euclidean space and n≥1; f maps the entire ball into itself. The theorem guarantees existence, not uniqueness or convergence of iteration.
nodes.example: On [0,1], the map f(x)=1−x has the fixed point x=1/2.

patterns.why: Topology forces an unchanged point of a self-map.
Compact ball geometry supplies the required global setting.

nodes.name: Lefschetz fixed-point theorem
nodes.intuition: Add the action of a map on homology with alternating signs. A nonzero total is an algebraic certificate that the map cannot avoid all fixed points.
nodes.conditions: X is a finite simplicial complex and f:X→X continuous; the rational homology groups are finite-dimensional and vanish in high degrees, so the sum is finite. The converse is false: L(f)=0 does not rule out fixed points.
nodes.example: For a circle map of degree d, L(f)=1−d; therefore d≠1 forces a fixed point.

patterns.why: A homological invariant detects existence of a fixed point.
Alternating traces combine information from all homological degrees.

nodes.name: De Rham’s theorem
nodes.intuition: Closed differential forms detect the same real topological information as singular cohomology. Integration is the bridge: a form measures a cycle, while exact forms integrate to zero on cycles.
nodes.conditions: M is a smooth Hausdorff second-countable manifold; take real smooth forms and real singular cohomology. The isomorphism is induced by integration over smooth singular chains and extends through their equivalence with ordinary singular theory. Integral torsion is invisible to real coefficients. Here k≥0 and Ω⁻¹ is zero.
nodes.example: The circle has one independent degree-one de Rham class, detected by integrating once around it.

patterns.why: Forms pair with geometric cycles by integration.
Exact forms vanish on cycles through Stokes’ theorem.
Two different cochain complexes have isomorphic cohomology.

nodes.name: De Morgan’s laws
nodes.latex:
eg(P\land Q)\iff(
eg P\lor
eg Q),\qquad
eg(P\lor Q)\iff(
eg P\land
eg Q)
nodes.intuition: Negating a combined condition reverses whether all parts or at least one part are required. A failed conjunction needs one failure; a failed disjunction needs both failures.
nodes.conditions: P,Q are propositions in classical two-valued logic. The analogous set identities use complements relative to a fixed universal set.
nodes.example: “Not both numbers are positive” means at least one is not positive.

patterns.why: Negation exchanges conjunction and disjunction.
The laws are the complement rules of Boolean algebra.

nodes.name: Negating quantifiers
nodes.latex:
eg( orall x\,P(x))\iff\exists x\,
eg P(x),\qquad
eg(\exists x\,P(x))\iff orall x\,
eg P(x)
nodes.intuition: To refute a universal statement, produce one counterexample. To refute an existence statement, rule out every candidate.
nodes.conditions: Classical first-order logic with a specified domain and predicate P; quantifiers bind the same variable over the same domain on both sides.
nodes.example: Negating “every real number has a positive square” produces “some real number has a square that is not positive,” witnessed by zero.

patterns.why: Universal and existential claims exchange under negation.
A global statement is analyzed through its individual instances.

nodes.name: Implication and contrapositive
nodes.intuition: An implication forbids only one situation: the premise holds and the conclusion fails. The contrapositive forbids exactly that same situation from the opposite direction.
nodes.conditions: P,Q are propositions in classical two-valued logic. The converse Q⇒P is generally a different claim.
nodes.example: “If an integer is divisible by 4, it is even” is equivalent to “if it is odd, it is not divisible by 4.”

patterns.why: Premise and conclusion exchange roles after negation.
The same truth condition has implication and disjunction forms.

nodes.name: Cantor’s power-set theorem
nodes.intuition: A list indexed by X can never contain every subset of X. Construct the subset that disagrees with the proposed list at its own index, and it must be missing.
nodes.conditions: X is any set. For every proposed function f:X→P(X), the diagonal subset D is not in its image; an injection X→P(X) exists via singleton sets. No finiteness assumption is needed.
nodes.example: For a finite set with n elements, its power set has 2ⁿ elements; the theorem also distinguishes infinite sizes.

patterns.why: Subsets encode independent yes-or-no membership decisions.
The theorem compares cardinal sizes and proves that power sets always have strictly more elements.

nodes.name: Soundness and completeness of first-order logic
nodes.intuition: Formal derivation and truth in every model agree for classical first-order consequence. The result connects symbol manipulation with semantic meaning.
nodes.conditions: Γ is a set of first-order sentences and φ a first-order sentence in one language, with a standard sound and complete proof calculus. Γ⊨φ means every structure satisfying Γ satisfies φ. This is logical completeness, not the claim that a fixed arithmetic theory proves every true arithmetic sentence.
nodes.example: If Γ contains ∀x(P(x)⇒Q(x)) and P(c), then it both formally proves and semantically entails Q(c).

patterns.why: Syntactic provability corresponds to semantic consequence.
A rule-based proof system matches a precise class of structures.

nodes.name: Compactness theorem for first-order logic
nodes.latex: \Gamma\text{ has a model}\iff\text{every finite }\Gamma_0\subseteq\Gamma\text{ has a model}
nodes.intuition: An infinite first-order specification is consistent with some structure if every finite part can be satisfied. A contradiction cannot require genuinely infinitely many premises.
nodes.conditions: Γ is a set of sentences in classical first-order logic and models use the usual nonempty-domain semantics. The property need not hold for stronger logics such as full second-order logic.
nodes.example: Adding a constant c and requirements c>1,c>2,… to the theory of ordered fields is finitely satisfiable, so it has a model containing an element larger than every standard integer.

patterns.why: Finite satisfiability guarantees a global model, although this is not a numerical limit theorem.
The consistency of all finite fragments controls the whole specification.

nodes.name: Euler gamma integral
nodes.intuition: A weighted exponential integral extends factorials to a continuous argument.
nodes.conditions: The integral converges absolutely for complex z with Re z>0; t^{z−1}=exp((z−1)log t) for real t>0.

patterns.why: An integral combines all positive scales.
Exponential decay controls the tail.

nodes.name: Gamma recurrence and factorial values
nodes.intuition: One integration by parts shifts the argument and extracts its current value.
nodes.conditions: First identity holds for Re z>0 directly, and meromorphically elsewhere; finite values exclude poles. n is a nonnegative integer.

patterns.why: One argument step multiplies by the previous argument.
Vanishing endpoint terms leave a shifted integral.

nodes.name: Euler reflection formula
nodes.intuition: Gamma values on opposite sides of one-half pair into an elementary trigonometric expression.
nodes.conditions: z is complex and not an integer; both sides are interpreted by meromorphic continuation.
nodes.example: At z=1/2 the identity yields Γ(1/2)²=π.

patterns.why: The paired arguments sum to one.
Complementary arguments trade one gamma value for the other.

nodes.name: Legendre duplication formula
nodes.intuition: Two half-step gamma factors combine into one factor at doubled scale.
nodes.conditions: Re z>0 is sufficient for the displayed finite identity; it extends meromorphically.

patterns.why: The argument doubles while a power of two compensates.
Integer and half-integer contributions combine.

nodes.name: Stirling asymptotic formula for gamma
nodes.intuition: The gamma integral is concentrated near its peak; its local quadratic shape determines the leading factor.
nodes.conditions: x is positive real tending to infinity; ∼ means the ratio tends to one, not exact equality.

patterns.why: A quadratic expansion near the dominant point controls the integral.
The relative error vanishes asymptotically.

nodes.name: Digamma logarithmic derivative
