nodes.intuition: The digamma function measures relative change of gamma and turns its multiplicative recurrence into addition.
nodes.conditions: z avoids 0,−1,−2,… for finite values; the recurrence is used where both sides are defined.
nodes.example: ψ(n)=H_{n−1}−γ for positive integer n.

patterns.why: A logarithmic derivative measures relative growth.
Shifting the argument adds a reciprocal.

nodes.name: Polygamma reciprocal-power series
nodes.intuition: Higher relative-growth derivatives of gamma are encoded by a convergent lattice sum.
nodes.conditions: m≥1 is an integer and Re z>0; the series converges absolutely and locally uniformly.

patterns.why: The derivative sums contributions at shifted arguments.
Power decay gives convergent infinite sums.

nodes.name: Euler beta integral
nodes.intuition: Beta balances two endpoint powers and separates total size from the share assigned to each coordinate.
nodes.conditions: Re a>0 and Re b>0 for the integral; powers use the real logarithm on (0,1).

patterns.why: Two gamma variables become a sum and a proportion.
Replacing t by 1−t exchanges a and b.

nodes.name: Incomplete gamma decomposition
nodes.intuition: Split the gamma mass at a threshold into accumulated and remaining portions.
nodes.conditions: a>0 and x≥0 are real; these hypotheses ensure convergence and the stated decomposition.

patterns.why: A threshold partitions one integral into two.
Moving the threshold accumulates density.

nodes.name: Error function and Gaussian mass
nodes.intuition: The error function records accumulated Gaussian mass on a convenient scale.
nodes.conditions: x is real; Φ is the standard normal CDF. The integral definition extends to an entire complex function.
nodes.example: erf(0)=0 and erf(x)→1 as x→+∞.

patterns.why: Integrating the Gaussian gives cumulative mass.
The √2 coordinate rescaling matches standard-normal variance.

nodes.name: Gaussian tail asymptotic expansion
nodes.intuition: Repeated integration by parts peels off successively smaller corrections to a Gaussian tail.
nodes.conditions: x→+∞ on the real axis; (−1)!!=1. The infinite expression is asymptotic and generally divergent; truncate at finite order.
nodes.example: Leading order is erfc(x)≈e^(−x²)/(√π x).

patterns.why: Finite truncations have controlled asymptotic order.
Integration by parts generates successive coefficients.

nodes.name: Dawson integral and its differential equation
nodes.intuition: An exponential integrating factor balances a rapidly growing integral to produce a bounded-scale response.
nodes.conditions: x is real; the definition extends to an entire function; F(0)=0 selects the solution.
nodes.example: F′(0)=1 and F is odd.

patterns.why: Opposite exponential factors balance.
An even integrand gives an odd solution.

nodes.name: Fresnel sine and cosine integrals
nodes.intuition: Quadratic phase makes the oscillations speed up, causing cancellation without absolute integrability.
nodes.conditions: x is real; as x→+∞, C(x) and S(x) converge conditionally to 1/2.
nodes.example: The curve (C(x),S(x)) is a Cornu spiral.

patterns.why: Oscillating increments build a limiting total.
The two integrals are real and imaginary parts of a chirp integral.

nodes.name: Exponential integral E1
nodes.intuition: An inverse-scale weight modifies exponential accumulation into a logarithmic singularity near zero.
nodes.conditions: x>0 real; the displayed derivative follows on that interval. Complex continuation requires a branch choice.
nodes.example: E1(x)=Γ(0,x), using the convergent upper incomplete gamma integral for x>0.

patterns.why: All scales above x contribute.
The origin has logarithmic rather than power-law divergence.

nodes.name: Sine and cosine integrals
nodes.intuition: Inverse-distance weighting accumulates oscillations; cancellation makes the infinite cosine tail converge.
nodes.conditions: x>0 is real; sin(t)/t has continuous value 1 at t=0; the cosine tail is conditionally convergent.
nodes.example: Si(x)→π/2 as x→+∞.

patterns.why: Oscillating contributions accumulate over scale.
Conditional convergence comes from cancellation.

nodes.name: Bessel function of the first kind
nodes.intuition: A factorial-weighted power series provides oscillating functions adapted to radial coordinates.
nodes.conditions: For the stated real-valued convention take x>0 and real ν; reciprocal gamma handles vanishing coefficients at its zeros. The series converges for every such x.

patterns.why: The series packages coefficients fixed by a radial ODE.
The powers depend on x/2.

nodes.name: Bessel differential equation
nodes.intuition: Radial curvature adds a first derivative and an inverse-square angular contribution to an oscillator equation.
nodes.conditions: x>0; ν is real. Jν is one solution; a second independent solution can be taken as Yν.
nodes.example: For ν=0, a regular-at-zero solution is J0(x).

patterns.why: Polar separation produces the radial operator.
Angular Fourier modes fix the parameter ν.

nodes.name: Bessel order recurrence
nodes.intuition: Neighboring angular orders are coupled by a short algebraic recurrence.
nodes.conditions: x>0 and ν real; standard Bessel first-kind functions are used.

patterns.why: Two adjacent orders determine another.
Order shifts satisfy a closed linear relation.

nodes.name: Bessel derivative as neighboring orders
nodes.intuition: Differentiating in radius can be traded for subtracting adjacent orders.
nodes.conditions: x>0, real ν; derivatives use the same first-kind Bessel convention.

patterns.why: A continuous derivative is encoded by discrete shifts in order.
Neighboring functions recover derivatives.

nodes.name: Bessel modes orthogonal with radial weight
nodes.intuition: Radial eigenmodes are perpendicular when the area-element weight r is included.
nodes.conditions: ν≥0, m,n≥1 integers; jν,n are distinct positive zeros of Jν. The regular radial solution is selected at zero.
nodes.example: For ν=0 these modes represent radially symmetric Dirichlet data on a disk.

patterns.why: Distinct eigenvalues cancel in the weighted inner product.
Zero boundary values remove the boundary term.

nodes.name: Large-argument Bessel oscillation
nodes.intuition: Far from the origin, radial oscillations resemble cosine waves with an amplitude that decays as a square root.
nodes.conditions: x→+∞ and ν is fixed real; the remainder inside brackets is additive, not relative near cosine zeros.
nodes.example: J0(x) oscillates with phase x−π/4 and amplitude √(2/(πx)).

patterns.why: The envelope follows x^(−1/2).
The elementary oscillation describes the large-x limit.

nodes.name: Modified Bessel first-kind function
nodes.intuition: Removing the alternating signs turns radial oscillation into exponential-type behavior.
nodes.conditions: x>0 and real ν; the convergent series solves the displayed modified Bessel equation.

patterns.why: The modified equation supports exponential growth or decay.
Its coefficients differ from Jν by alternating signs.

nodes.name: Modified Bessel decaying solution
nodes.intuition: A continuum of exponentially damped contributions selects the decaying modified radial solution.
nodes.conditions: x>0, real ν. This representation converges and gives Kν=K−ν.

patterns.why: Changing the sign of ν leaves the integral unchanged.
Damping selects the solution that decays at infinity.

nodes.name: Hankel combinations of Bessel solutions
nodes.intuition: Complex combinations separate the two radial oscillatory phases.
nodes.conditions: x>0, real ν; Jν,Yν use the standard real Bessel normalization. Incoming/outgoing labels depend on the time convention.
nodes.example: For time dependence e^(−iωt), Hν^(1)(kr) has outgoing large-r phase.

patterns.why: Two real solutions become two complex phase modes.
Cosine and sine combine into exponential phases.

nodes.name: Spherical Bessel functions
nodes.intuition: A half-order shift and a radial scale factor adapt cylindrical functions to three dimensions.
nodes.conditions: n≥0 is an integer and x>0; j0 extends continuously to value 1 at zero.
nodes.example: j1(x)=sin(x)/x²−cos(x)/x.

patterns.why: The three-dimensional radial operator changes the effective order.
The x^(−1/2) factor changes radial decay.

nodes.name: Airy equation and normalized solutions
nodes.intuition: Airy functions describe the transition between oscillation and exponential behavior when a linear coefficient changes sign.
nodes.conditions: x is real or complex; the displayed initial values uniquely specify the entire solution Ai. Bi denotes the conventional independent solution.
nodes.example: Ai(x) decays for large positive x and oscillates for negative x.

patterns.why: A coefficient with a simple zero is locally linear.
Two independent solutions span the second-order solution space.

nodes.name: Airy positive-axis decay
nodes.intuition: Integrating the local decay rate √x produces the characteristic x^(3/2) exponent.
nodes.conditions: x tends to positive infinity; ∼ denotes ratio convergence for the decaying Ai solution.
nodes.example: The exponent equals −∫₀ˣ√t dt.

patterns.why: The exponent accumulates a position-dependent decay rate.
Power-law amplitude accompanies a stretched exponential.

nodes.name: Legendre polynomials by Rodrigues formula
nodes.intuition: Repeated differentiation generates polynomials whose lower-degree moments cancel.
nodes.conditions: n≥0 integer; x real or complex. The normalization is Pn(1)=1.

patterns.why: Endpoint zeros allow repeated integration-by-parts cancellation.
Derivative order tracks polynomial degree.

nodes.name: Legendre orthogonality and normalization
nodes.intuition: Legendre modes separate polynomial information into independent directions on a finite interval.
nodes.conditions: m,n are nonnegative integers; Pn(1)=1.
nodes.example: ∫₋₁¹x²dx=2/3 agrees with P1=x.

patterns.why: Distinct degrees have zero inner product.
Coefficients isolate independent polynomial components.

nodes.name: Legendre polynomial eigenvalue equation
nodes.intuition: One differential operator organizes every polynomial degree into its own eigenvalue.
nodes.conditions: n≥0 integer; the polynomial identity holds for all x; the Sturm–Liouville interpretation uses −1<x<1 and regular endpoint behavior.
nodes.example: P1=x has eigenvalue 2.

patterns.why: Self-adjoint structure explains separation of eigenmodes.
One operator diagonalizes on the whole polynomial family.

nodes.name: Generating function for Legendre polynomials
nodes.intuition: A single inverse-square-root kernel stores every Legendre polynomial as a coefficient.
nodes.conditions: For real |x|≤1 and complex |t|<1; the square root is the branch equal to 1 at t=0.
nodes.example: At x=1 the expression reduces to 1/(1−t).

patterns.why: Degree becomes a power-series index.
The kernel treats angular geometry through x.

nodes.name: Relative rounding model
nodes.intuition: Rounding behaves like a small relative perturbation to one exact arithmetic operation.
nodes.conditions: Round to nearest in binary precision p; u=2^(−p); ∘ is +,−,× or ÷ with a finite normal exact result and nonzero divisor. Underflow and overflow are excluded.
nodes.example: Binary64 has unit roundoff 2^(−53).

patterns.why: Relative error is scale-sensitive only near exponent limits.
Small arithmetic perturbations can be propagated linearly.

nodes.name: Relative condition number of a scalar function
nodes.intuition: Conditioning measures how much a small relative input error is magnified by the mathematical problem itself.
nodes.conditions: f is differentiable near real x≠0 and f(x)≠0; this is a first-order local measure.
nodes.example: For f(x)=x^a on x>0, κf=|a|.

patterns.why: Derivative controls small input perturbations.
Both input and output changes are relative.

nodes.name: Linear-system condition number
nodes.intuition: An invertible map is sensitive when it stretches some directions far more than others.
nodes.conditions: A is an invertible square real or complex matrix; the first norm is an induced operator norm, the second is Euclidean.

patterns.why: Directional stretching controls sensitivity.
A scalar rescaling does not change κ.

nodes.name: Residual-to-solution error bound
nodes.intuition: A small equation defect certifies accuracy only after accounting for conditioning.
nodes.conditions: A invertible, Ax=b≠0, compatible vector and induced matrix norms.
nodes.example: A residual of 10^(−10) with κ=10^8 may certify only a 10^(−2) relative error.

patterns.why: The inverse maps equation defects to errors.
Operator norms bound error amplification.

nodes.name: Normwise backward error of a linear solve
nodes.intuition: Ask how much the input equations must change to make the computed answer exact.
nodes.conditions: Euclidean vector and induced matrix norm; A,b not both zero and denominator positive. This equals the minimal common relative normwise perturbation bound for A and b.
nodes.example: An exact solution has η=0 even if its problem is ill-conditioned.

patterns.why: Input perturbation is separated from solution error.
The residual is normalized by input scales.

nodes.name: Horner nested polynomial evaluation
nodes.intuition: Reuse each partial polynomial instead of computing powers separately.
nodes.conditions: p(x)=∑k=0^n akx^k over real or complex arithmetic; the identity is exact before rounding.
nodes.example: 1+2x+3x² becomes 1+x(2+3x).

patterns.why: One multiply-add incorporates each coefficient.
A polynomial is nested by degree.

nodes.name: Bisection root bracketing
nodes.intuition: Keep a sign-changing bracket and halve its uncertainty at every step.
nodes.conditions: f continuous on [a0,b0], f(a0)f(b0)<0; [an,bn] is the bracket after n halvings and r is a root inside it.
nodes.example: Ten halvings reduce a unit bracket to width 1/1024.

patterns.why: The midpoint halves an interval.
The error bound decreases geometrically.

nodes.name: Secant root iteration
nodes.intuition: Estimate the derivative from two recent values and follow the resulting line to zero.
nodes.conditions: Denominator nonzero; local convergence of order (1+√5)/2 holds near a simple root for sufficiently smooth f and sufficiently close suitable starting points. Global convergence is not guaranteed.
nodes.example: Applied to x²−2, no derivative evaluation is needed.

patterns.why: A secant replaces the tangent.
Two iterates determine the next.

nodes.name: Newton iteration for nonlinear systems
nodes.intuition: Solve the local linearized equations, then correct the current point.
nodes.conditions: F:Rⁿ→Rⁿ is C² near a root with nonsingular Jacobian; sufficiently close starts give local quadratic convergence. Each step requires an invertible current Jacobian.
nodes.example: Two intersecting nonlinear curves can be solved by a 2×2 Jacobian system.

patterns.why: The Jacobian replaces a nonlinear map locally.
Linear corrections are repeated.

nodes.name: Broyden rank-one Jacobian update
nodes.intuition: Repair a Jacobian approximation just enough to match the newest observed displacement.
nodes.conditions: Real nonzero step sk=xk+1−xk; this is the good Broyden Jacobian update for rootfinding. Convergence needs additional local regularity and suitable initialization.
nodes.example: The update satisfies Bk+1 sk=yk exactly.

patterns.why: Recent function changes calibrate a linear model.
The update minimizes Frobenius change under the secant constraint.

nodes.name: Polynomial interpolation remainder
nodes.intuition: Interpolation error combines an unknown high derivative with an explicit node-placement factor.
nodes.conditions: Distinct real nodes xj and x lie in an interval where f∈C^(n+1); ξ lies in their convex hull, and pn interpolates f at the nodes.
nodes.example: For linear interpolation the error involves (x−x0)(x−x1)f″(ξ)/2.

patterns.why: Higher derivatives control approximation error.
Distances to all nodes multiply.

nodes.name: Newton divided-difference interpolation
nodes.intuition: Add one node at a time while preserving every previously fitted value.
nodes.conditions: Nodes are distinct; f[xi]=f(xi); the empty product is 1.
nodes.example: Appending a node adds only one new highest-degree basis term.

patterns.why: Divided differences reuse neighboring tables.
Each new term vanishes at all older nodes.

nodes.name: Barycentric polynomial evaluation
nodes.latex: p(x)=\frac{\sum_{j=0}^n w_j f_j/(x-x_j)}{\sum_{j=0}^n w_j/(x-x_j)},\qquad w_j=\prod_{k\ne j}(x_j-x_k)^{-1}
nodes.intuition: Common factors cancel from the Lagrange formula, yielding efficient repeated evaluation.
nodes.conditions: Distinct nodes; x≠xj in the formula and p(xj)=fj by continuity. Exact weights are assumed for the polynomial identity.
nodes.example: Multiplying every weight by the same nonzero constant leaves p unchanged.

patterns.why: A common weight scale cancels.
Node contributions are combined as a ratio.

nodes.name: Lebesgue constant interpolation bound
nodes.intuition: Approximation quality depends on both the best available polynomial and amplification caused by node placement.
nodes.conditions: Distinct nodes in a compact real interval; f continuous; ℓj are Lagrange cardinal polynomials on that interval.
nodes.example: Large Λn warns that tiny data errors may become large interpolation errors.

patterns.why: The bound compares actual and best errors.
Cardinal basis magnitudes measure amplification.

nodes.name: Chebyshev root nodes
nodes.intuition: Cluster nodes near interval endpoints to reduce the largest nodal product.
nodes.conditions: j=0,…,n and n≥0; on [−1,1] the monic polynomial 2^(−n)Tn+1 minimizes the uniform norm among monic degree n+1 polynomials.
nodes.example: For n=1 the nodes are ±1/√2.

patterns.why: Equioscillation minimizes the nodal product norm.
Equally spaced angles become clustered real nodes.

nodes.name: Natural cubic spline interpolation
nodes.intuition: Join local cubic pieces smoothly rather than forcing one high-degree polynomial across all data.
nodes.conditions: Strictly increasing real knots and real data; these conditions determine a unique natural cubic spline.
nodes.example: For two knots the natural spline is the straight line between them.

patterns.why: Local polynomial pieces approximate different regions.
Endpoint curvature conditions close the interior matching equations.

nodes.name: Second-order centered derivative formula
nodes.intuition: Symmetric samples cancel the leading one-sided bias.
nodes.conditions: f is C³ near x; h→0 with both sample points in the domain. The claim concerns truncation error before rounding.
nodes.example: The formula differentiates every quadratic exactly.

patterns.why: Odd and even Taylor terms separate.
Small displacements estimate slope.

nodes.name: Centered second-derivative stencil
nodes.intuition: Compare the center with its neighbors to detect curvature.
nodes.conditions: f∈C⁴ near x, h→0; all three sample points lie in the domain.
nodes.example: For f=x² the stencil gives 2 exactly.

patterns.why: Curvature is detected by a second difference.
Symmetric neighbors cancel odd Taylor terms.

nodes.name: Truncation–roundoff balance for a derivative
nodes.intuition: Smaller steps reduce Taylor error but amplify errors in nearly equal sampled values.
nodes.conditions: Centered first differences with smooth f, function-evaluation errors of magnitude O(u), and problem-dependent bounded constants; the scaling is not a universal step prescription.
nodes.example: Making h arbitrarily tiny can worsen a numerical derivative.

patterns.why: Two opposing errors set a useful scale.
Cubic balancing gives the u^(1/3) step scale.

nodes.name: Richardson extrapolation
nodes.intuition: Combine two resolutions to cancel their shared leading error term.
nodes.conditions: A(h)=A+ch^p+O(h^(p+q)) as h→0, with p,q>0 fixed and the same coefficient c for both scales.

patterns.why: Subtracting resolutions eliminates one error component.
The known power p determines cancellation weights.

nodes.name: Composite midpoint quadrature
nodes.intuition: Use each cell’s central value so the first-order local variation cancels.
nodes.conditions: h=(b−a)/n, n≥1, a<b, f∈C²[a,b].
nodes.example: On [0,1], one midpoint sample of x² gives 1/4 instead of 1/3.

patterns.why: Cell centers represent local averages.
Odd local terms integrate to zero.

nodes.name: Gaussian quadrature exactness
nodes.intuition: Choose both sample locations and weights to match twice as many polynomial moments.
nodes.conditions: Positive integrable weight w on a finite interval, finite moments and support containing at least n+1 points; xj are zeros of its degree-n orthogonal polynomial.
nodes.example: Two-point Gauss–Legendre integrates every cubic exactly.

patterns.why: The nodal polynomial annihilates lower-degree factors.
Movable nodes increase polynomial exactness.

nodes.name: Gauss–Legendre nodes and weights
nodes.intuition: Legendre roots and their slopes determine optimal polynomial integration samples on a symmetric interval.
nodes.conditions: j=1,…,n are the distinct roots in (−1,1); Pn(1)=1; the integration interval is [−1,1].
nodes.example: For n=2, nodes are ±1/√3 and both weights equal 1.

patterns.why: Legendre polynomials fix the nodes.
Nodes and weights occur in reflected pairs.

nodes.name: Romberg extrapolation table
nodes.intuition: Repeatedly remove even-power errors from nested trapezoidal estimates.
nodes.conditions: 0≤j≤k; T is composite trapezoidal quadrature. Smoothness sufficient for the required Euler–Maclaurin error expansion is needed for predicted orders.
nodes.example: R1,1 is the first Richardson-improved estimate.

patterns.why: A triangular table reuses previous resolutions.
Each refinement halves the step.

nodes.name: Clenshaw–Curtis interpolatory quadrature
nodes.intuition: Interpolate on an endpoint-clustered cosine grid and integrate the resulting polynomial.
nodes.conditions: n≥1, j=0,…,n; In is the degree≤n polynomial interpolant. Exactness holds for all polynomials of degree≤n. Faster convergence needs regularity.
nodes.example: At n=2 the nodes are −1,0,1 and the rule is Simpson’s rule.

patterns.why: A uniform angle grid clusters real nodes.
Polynomial coefficients can be integrated separately.

nodes.name: Householder elimination step for QR
nodes.intuition: Reflect an entire column tail onto one coordinate axis in one norm-preserving operation.
nodes.conditions: Real nonzero x; use sign(0)=1. Embedded reflectors successively zero entries below the diagonal.
nodes.example: A sequence of reflectors produces QᵀA=R.

patterns.why: Reflection preserves Euclidean lengths.
Column tails are removed step by step.

nodes.name: Gaussian elimination and pivoted LU
nodes.intuition: Eliminate one column at a time while storing the multipliers for later solves.
nodes.conditions: A is nonsingular square; row pivoting selects a nonzero pivot. L is unit lower triangular, U upper triangular, P records row swaps; the update uses the current pivoted matrix.
nodes.example: Solving Ax=b becomes Ly=Pb then Ux=y.

patterns.why: One matrix becomes permutation and triangular factors.
Each pivot reduces the remaining system.

nodes.name: Dominant-eigenvector power iteration
nodes.intuition: Repeated multiplication suppresses directions whose eigenvalues have smaller magnitude.
nodes.conditions: A is diagonalizable with one simple eigenvalue λ1 satisfying |λ1|>|λj| for j>1; x0 has nonzero component along its eigenvector in the eigenbasis. Direction converges up to sign or complex phase.
nodes.example: For diag(3,1), the second-to-first coordinate ratio shrinks by 1/3 per step.

patterns.why: Repeated multiplication amplifies the dominant mode.
Eigenbasis components evolve independently.

nodes.name: Shifted inverse eigenvector iteration
nodes.intuition: Invert a shifted operator to make an eigenvalue near the shift become dominant.
nodes.conditions: μ is not an eigenvalue; for convergence assume diagonalizable A, a unique eigenvalue closest to μ, and a nonzero initial component in its eigendirection.
nodes.example: A shift near an interior eigenvalue targets it instead of the largest-magnitude one.

patterns.why: The same eigenvectors acquire reciprocal shifted eigenvalues.
Repeated solves select a mode.

nodes.name: Hermite polynomials in Gaussian weight
nodes.intuition: Gaussian derivatives reproduce the same envelope multiplied by polynomials.
nodes.conditions: n≥0 integer; this is the physicists’ normalization, with weight e^(−x²).

patterns.why: Differentiation increases degree.
The Gaussian envelope is preserved.

nodes.name: Hermite orthogonality
nodes.intuition: The Gaussian-weighted inner product separates polynomial degrees.
nodes.conditions: m,n≥0 integers; Hn is the physicists’ Hermite polynomial.
nodes.example: ∫e^(−x²)(2x)²dx=2√π.

patterns.why: Distinct degrees cancel.
The Gaussian weight is an exponential quadratic.

nodes.name: Hermite exponential generating function
nodes.intuition: A shifted Gaussian packages all Gaussian derivative polynomials.
nodes.conditions: x,t complex; the series converges for every finite t. Physicists’ normalization is used.
nodes.example: The coefficient of t² is 2x²−1=H2(x)/2.

patterns.why: One exponential stores all degrees.
Translation of a Gaussian generates derivatives.

nodes.name: Generalized Laguerre polynomials
nodes.intuition: Differentiation generates polynomials adapted to a power-weighted exponential on a half-line.
nodes.conditions: n≥0 integer, α>−1, x>0; the expression extends as a polynomial to all x.

patterns.why: The weight matches a gamma-shaped density.
Repeated derivatives organize polynomial degree.

nodes.name: Laguerre weighted orthogonality
nodes.intuition: Gamma-weighted polynomial modes separate behavior on an unbounded positive interval.
nodes.conditions: α>−1 and m,n are nonnegative integers.
nodes.example: With α=0 every Ln has squared norm 1.

patterns.why: Different degrees have zero weighted inner product.
The gamma factor gives the exact norm.

nodes.name: Jacobi polynomial Rodrigues formula
nodes.intuition: Independent endpoint exponents tailor a polynomial family to unequal endpoint behavior.
nodes.conditions: n≥0 integer, α,β>−1 and −1<x<1; the result extends polynomially to all x.
nodes.example: α=β=0 recovers Legendre polynomials.

patterns.why: Endpoint powers determine the weighted moments.
Repeated integration annihilates lower-degree polynomials.

nodes.name: Chebyshev polynomials as multiple-angle cosines
nodes.intuition: A cosine coordinate turns oscillation frequency into polynomial degree.
nodes.conditions: n≥0 integer and θ real; the identity uniquely determines a real polynomial.

patterns.why: A cosine substitution polynomializes harmonics.
Even and odd degrees inherit reflection parity.

nodes.name: Chebyshev three-term recurrence
nodes.intuition: Two neighboring polynomials generate the next without expanding large powers.
nodes.conditions: n≥1 integer; x real or complex.

patterns.why: Two previous degrees suffice.
Multiplication by x has a sparse basis representation.

nodes.name: Chebyshev weighted orthogonality
nodes.intuition: The endpoint weight exactly compensates for stretching in the cosine coordinate.
nodes.conditions: m,n≥0 integers; integrals are improper but convergent.
nodes.example: T0 and T1 are orthogonal because the weighted integrand is odd.

patterns.why: Cosine modes are perpendicular.
The Jacobian supplies the endpoint weight.

nodes.name: Gegenbauer generating function
nodes.intuition: Changing one kernel exponent generates a family that includes Legendre polynomials.
nodes.conditions: λ>0, real |x|≤1, complex |t|<1; the analytic branch equals 1 at t=0.
nodes.example: λ=1/2 gives Cn^(1/2)=Pn.

patterns.why: The kernel stores every degree.
An exponent parameter changes the polynomial family.

nodes.name: Christoffel–Darboux kernel identity
nodes.intuition: A long orthogonal-polynomial sum telescopes to its last two modes.
nodes.conditions: pj are orthogonal real polynomials for a positive measure with finite moments, hj=∫pj²dμ>0, kj their leading coefficients; x≠y. The diagonal is the continuous limit.
nodes.example: The kernel reproduces polynomials of degree at most n.

patterns.why: Many basis terms collapse to two endpoint degrees.
The kernel reproduces the orthogonal projection.

nodes.name: Gauss hypergeometric series
nodes.intuition: A rational ratio between neighboring coefficients unifies many familiar special functions.
nodes.example: 2F1(a,b;b;z)=(1−z)^(−a) on its analytic branch.

patterns.why: A coefficient rule packages a family.
Consecutive coefficients have a rational ratio.

nodes.name: Gauss hypergeometric differential equation
nodes.intuition: Three regular singular points organize a large family of second-order equations.
nodes.conditions: a,b,c complex; c avoids nonpositive integers for the standard series solution near z=0.
nodes.example: Legendre’s equation follows from a=−n,b=n+1,c=1,z=(1−x)/2.

patterns.why: Affine substitutions identify familiar equations.
Local series track behavior at singular points.

nodes.name: Euler integral for the hypergeometric function
nodes.intuition: Hypergeometric evaluation becomes an average of a power function under a beta-shaped weight.
nodes.conditions: Re c>Re b>0 and z lies off [1,∞); use the principal branch for (1−zt)^(−a).
nodes.example: At z=0 the beta normalization makes the result 1.

patterns.why: A normalized beta weight averages the power kernel.
Parameters become endpoint exponents.

nodes.name: Gauss hypergeometric summation at one
nodes.intuition: At the boundary argument one, the power kernel merges with a beta endpoint weight.
nodes.conditions: c avoids nonpositive integers and Re(c−a−b)>0; reciprocal gamma interprets zeros where denominator factors have poles.
nodes.example: For a=b=1,c=3 the value is 2.

patterns.why: A boundary series value is controlled by an endpoint exponent.
An infinite series collapses to gamma ratios.

nodes.name: Confluent hypergeometric Kummer function
nodes.intuition: Coalescing singularities leaves an entire power-series solution of a simpler hypergeometric equation.
nodes.conditions: a,b complex, b not a nonpositive integer; the series converges for all complex z.
nodes.example: 1F1(a;a;z)=e^z when a avoids forbidden denominator values.

patterns.why: A rational coefficient rule defines the solution.
Confluence is a scaled parameter limit of 2F1.

nodes.name: Generalized hypergeometric pFq series
nodes.intuition: Products of rising factors encode many coefficient recurrences in one notation.
nodes.conditions: No bj is a nonpositive integer. For nonterminating series: entire if p≤q; radius 1 if p=q+1; radius 0 if p>q+1. Boundary cases need further conditions.
nodes.example: 0F0(z)=e^z and 0F1 relates to Bessel functions.

patterns.why: Parameters encode a coefficient sequence.
Successive coefficients have a rational ratio.

nodes.name: Complete elliptic integral of the first kind
nodes.intuition: A trigonometric integral gains a scale factor that becomes singular as the modulus approaches one.
nodes.conditions: 0≤k<1 real; k is the modulus, not the parameter m=k².
nodes.example: K(0)=π/2 and K(k)→∞ as k→1−.

patterns.why: A varying local factor accumulates over a quarter-cycle.
The endpoint becomes singular at unit modulus.

nodes.name: Complete elliptic integral of the second kind
nodes.intuition: The elliptic second-kind integral adds weighted local lengths along an ellipse.
nodes.conditions: 0≤k≤1 real; modulus convention k is used.
nodes.example: An ellipse with semiaxes a≥b>0 has perimeter 4aE(√(1−b²/a²)).

patterns.why: The integrand measures arc-length density.
Local lengths sum to a perimeter.

nodes.name: Arithmetic–geometric mean evaluation of K
nodes.intuition: Alternating arithmetic and geometric averaging preserves an elliptic quantity while the two values merge rapidly.
nodes.conditions: 0≤k<1; a0=1,b0=√(1−k²)>0; AGM is their common limit.
nodes.example: For k=0 the iteration stays at 1 and K=π/2.

patterns.why: Two means converge to one shared scale.
A transformed elliptic integral is invariant under the update.

nodes.name: Jacobi elliptic sine through inversion
nodes.intuition: Invert elliptic arc accumulation to obtain nonlinear periodic analogues of sine and cosine.
nodes.conditions: 0≤k<1, real u; φ is the continuously chosen real amplitude. Set dn(u,k)=√(1−k²sn²(u,k)).
nodes.example: At k=0, sn(u,0)=sin u and cn(u,0)=cos u.

patterns.why: An accumulated coordinate is inverted.
Amplitude separates nonlinear timing from trigonometric position.

nodes.name: Lambert W inverse relation
nodes.intuition: W undoes a variable multiplied by its own exponential.
nodes.conditions: The derivative formula is on any analytic branch away from z=0 and W=−1; W0′(0)=1 by continuation. Real W0 exists for z≥−1/e; W−1 is real on [−1/e,0).

patterns.why: An implicit nonlinear product is inverted.
The variable appears both outside and inside an exponential.

nodes.name: Riemann zeta Dirichlet series
nodes.intuition: Zeta gathers reciprocal powers of every positive integer into one complex function.
nodes.conditions: Re s>1 gives absolute convergence; analytic continuation elsewhere is a different representation and has a pole at s=1.

patterns.why: Every positive integer contributes one scale.
n^(−s)=exp(−s log n) converts scales into exponentials.

nodes.name: Completed zeta reflection symmetry
nodes.intuition: Gamma and pi factors reveal a reflection symmetry hidden in the original integer sum.
nodes.conditions: The equality holds meromorphically; Λ has simple poles at s=0 and s=1. It is not a claim that the defining Dirichlet series converges everywhere.
nodes.example: Values on the right half-plane determine continued values on the left.

patterns.why: Completion makes reflection s↦1−s explicit.
Gamma factors balance scale transforms.

nodes.name: Zeta values at positive even integers
nodes.intuition: Even reciprocal-power sums are rational multiples of corresponding powers of pi.
nodes.conditions: n≥1 integer; Bernoulli numbers use t/(e^t−1)=∑Bm t^m/m! near zero.

patterns.why: Bernoulli coefficients control exact sums.
Fourier expansions connect integer modes with powers of pi.

nodes.name: Hurwitz shifted zeta function
nodes.intuition: Shift the integer lattice before accumulating reciprocal powers.
nodes.conditions: a>0 real and Re s>1 for the series; the shift identity continues meromorphically in s.

patterns.why: A unit shift removes one term.
The offset changes the smallest contributing scale.

nodes.name: Polylogarithm power series
nodes.intuition: Polynomially damped geometric coefficients connect logarithms with zeta values.
nodes.conditions: |z|<1 and s complex; the derivative holds there, including its continuous interpretation at zero. Other arguments need continuation and branches.
nodes.example: Li1(z)=−log(1−z).

patterns.why: The power series weights each integer scale.
Differentiation lowers the order.

nodes.name: Jacobi theta Gaussian lattice sum
nodes.intuition: A Gaussian sampled across an integer lattice packages discrete and continuous scales together.
nodes.conditions: t is positive real; the sum converges absolutely and locally uniformly. It equals θ3(0,e^(−πt)).

patterns.why: The lattice sums identical translated modes.
Squared lattice distance controls Gaussian damping.

nodes.name: Jacobi theta scale inversion
nodes.intuition: A narrow Gaussian sampled densely has the same information as its reciprocal-scale Fourier lattice.
nodes.conditions: t>0 real; ϑ(t)=∑n∈Z exp(−πn²t).
nodes.example: At small t, ϑ(t)∼t^(−1/2).

patterns.why: Reciprocal scales exchange a lattice with its Fourier counterpart.
The prefactor compensates for Gaussian width.

nodes.name: Mellin transform
nodes.intuition: Mellin analysis turns multiplicative scaling into an additive frequency coordinate.
nodes.conditions: Use complex s in a strip where ∫₀∞x^(Re s−1)|f(x)|dx<∞. Outside it, continuation requires separate justification.
nodes.example: The Mellin transform of e^(−x) is Γ(s) for Re s>0.

patterns.why: Powers are the natural probes of dilation.
x=e^u converts multiplicative scales into additive coordinates.

nodes.name: Regularized incomplete beta function
nodes.intuition: Normalize a partial beta integral to measure a fraction of total endpoint-weighted mass.
nodes.conditions: a,b>0 and 0≤x≤1 real.

patterns.why: Normalization converts mass into a fraction.
The threshold x determines accumulated weight.

nodes.name: Krylov subspace for a matrix action
nodes.intuition: Repeated matrix action builds a small space containing progressively richer polynomial responses.
nodes.conditions: A square real or complex, b nonzero, m≥1; the space may stop growing before dimension m.
nodes.example: If b is an eigenvector, every Krylov space has dimension one.

patterns.why: Each new vector is another matrix action.
Polynomial responses live in a low-dimensional span.

nodes.name: Arnoldi orthogonal reduction
nodes.intuition: Orthogonalize each new matrix action to represent the large operator by a small Hessenberg matrix.
nodes.conditions: Columns of Qm span a Krylov space; exact arithmetic and no breakdown through step m; Hbar is (m+1)×m upper Hessenberg. At a breakdown the already-built subspace is invariant and a shorter relation applies.
nodes.example: A zero new residual indicates an invariant Krylov subspace.

patterns.why: New directions are orthogonalized.
A large operator is represented on a small subspace.

nodes.name: Lanczos three-term recurrence
nodes.intuition: Hermitian symmetry reduces orthogonal Krylov construction to three neighboring vectors.
nodes.conditions: A Hermitian, normalized start, exact arithmetic, and no breakdown; αj real and βj≥0. Finite precision can destroy orthogonality.
nodes.example: The projected matrix Qm*AQm is tridiagonal.

patterns.why: Hermitian symmetry eliminates distant recurrence coefficients.
Three neighboring basis vectors suffice.

nodes.name: GMRES minimum-residual iterate
nodes.intuition: Choose the combination of explored directions that best satisfies the equations.
nodes.conditions: A nonsingular square matrix, r0 nonzero until termination, and exact arithmetic; the minimizer is unique over the affine Krylov space. Restarting changes the global minimization property.
nodes.example: Unrestarted GMRES solves the system in at most n steps in exact arithmetic; an earlier Arnoldi breakdown is a successful termination for nonsingular A.

patterns.why: The residual norm is minimized in a growing subspace.
Residual is perpendicular to A times the search space.

nodes.name: Conjugate-gradient recurrence for SPD systems
nodes.intuition: Use mutually A-orthogonal search directions so new corrections preserve earlier progress.
nodes.conditions: A real symmetric positive definite; r0=b−Ax0,p0=r0; stop when residual is zero. Exact arithmetic gives termination in at most n steps.
nodes.example: For A=I the first correction solves the system.

patterns.why: Search directions are conjugate in the A-inner product.
The energy error is a positive quadratic.

nodes.name: Preconditioned linear system
nodes.intuition: Change the shape of the equations using an easier approximate inverse.
nodes.conditions: M is nonsingular and its action can be solved efficiently; the equation has the same solution as Ax=b. Convergence depends on more than condition number for general nonsymmetric A.
nodes.example: A diagonal M rescales equations before iteration.

patterns.why: Equivalent equations expose different numerical geometry.
Spectral clustering can improve iterative behavior.

nodes.name: Bauer–Fike eigenvalue perturbation bound
nodes.intuition: A poorly conditioned eigenvector basis can amplify small matrix perturbations into large eigenvalue shifts.
nodes.conditions: A complex diagonalizable square matrix, E arbitrary of the same size, μ any perturbed eigenvalue.
nodes.example: For normal A choose unitary V, giving a bound of ‖E‖2.

patterns.why: Eigenbasis conditioning controls perturbations.
Disks around old eigenvalues bound new ones.

nodes.name: QR iteration for eigenvalues
nodes.intuition: Repeated orthogonal similarities expose eigenvalues while preserving the underlying spectrum.
nodes.conditions: Qk unitary, Rk upper triangular; shifts μk are specified. The similarity identity is exact; convergence needs suitable shifts and assumptions.
nodes.example: For symmetric matrices, practical shifted iterations approach diagonal form.

patterns.why: Every step preserves eigenvalues.
Factorization and reversal are repeated.

nodes.name: Iterative refinement of a linear solve
nodes.intuition: Recompute the remaining defect and solve for a correction using the existing factorization.
nodes.conditions: A nonsingular; approximate correction solves are used computationally. Improvement requires sufficiently accurate residuals and controlled solve error relative to conditioning.
nodes.example: In exact arithmetic one exact correction solve recovers the exact solution.

patterns.why: Each pass corrects the remaining defect.
For a linear problem the defect-to-error relation is exact.

nodes.name: Jacobi stationary linear iteration
nodes.intuition: Update every coordinate from the old iterate using only its own diagonal solve.
nodes.conditions: D has nonzero diagonal; convergence for every start is equivalent to spectral radius ρ(−D⁻¹(L+U))<1. Strict row diagonal dominance is sufficient.
nodes.example: All coordinates can be updated in parallel.

patterns.why: The linear solve is rewritten as a fixed point.
Diagonal and off-diagonal effects are separated.

nodes.name: Gauss–Seidel linear iteration
nodes.intuition: Use each freshly updated coordinate immediately in subsequent equations.
nodes.conditions: D+L nonsingular; convergence holds for symmetric positive definite A or strictly row diagonally dominant A. It is not guaranteed for every invertible A.
nodes.example: One sweep solves a lower-triangular system with the previous upper-triangular contribution.

patterns.why: New values are reused within a sweep.
Triangular splitting organizes dependencies.

nodes.name: Backward Euler time step
nodes.intuition: Use the slope at the unknown endpoint, trading an implicit solve for stronger damping.
nodes.conditions: ODE y′=f(t,y), h>0. Under standard smoothness/Lipschitz conditions and well-solved implicit steps, the global order is one.
nodes.example: For y′=λy, amplification is 1/(1−hλ).

patterns.why: The endpoint must solve an implicit equation.
The slope estimates change across one step.

nodes.name: Implicit trapezoidal ODE step
nodes.intuition: Average initial and final slopes to obtain a second-order implicit step.
nodes.conditions: Smooth Lipschitz f and sufficiently small h for the chosen implicit solve; global order two.
nodes.example: For y′=λy, amplification is (1+hλ/2)/(1−hλ/2).

patterns.why: Two endpoint slopes are averaged.
A trapezoid approximates the time integral.

nodes.name: Explicit midpoint Runge–Kutta step
nodes.intuition: Predict the midpoint, then use its slope for the whole interval.
nodes.conditions: Smooth Lipschitz f; fixed step h; global order two under standard bounded-derivative hypotheses.
nodes.example: For y′=λy, amplification is 1+hλ+(hλ)²/2.

patterns.why: A half-step prediction samples the interior slope.
Two slope evaluations form one update.

nodes.name: Two-step Adams–Bashforth method
nodes.intuition: Extrapolate the recent slope history instead of evaluating new intermediate stages.
nodes.conditions: Uniform h, fn=f(tn,yn); a second-order accurate starting value and smooth Lipschitz f give global order two.
nodes.example: The negative old-slope weight extrapolates a rising slope trend.

patterns.why: Two stored slopes determine the update.
A slope interpolant is integrated over the next interval.

nodes.name: Second-order backward differentiation formula
nodes.intuition: Differentiate a quadratic through recent states at its newest endpoint.
nodes.conditions: Uniform step h; sufficiently smooth Lipschitz problem, accurate start, and solvable implicit equations; global order two.
nodes.example: For a constant solution both sides vanish when f=0.

patterns.why: Two previous states support an implicit update.
Polynomial differentiation approximates the endpoint derivative.

nodes.name: General Runge–Kutta stage formula
nodes.latex: k_i=f(t_n+c_i h,y_n+h\sum_{j=1}^s a_{ij}k_j),\qquad y_{n+1}=y_n+h\sum_{i=1}^s b_i k_i
nodes.intuition: A table of coefficients specifies how trial slopes inform one another and the final update.
nodes.conditions: Finite s and specified real coefficients; ai,j=0 for j≥i makes the method explicit. Consistency and higher order require coefficient conditions.
nodes.example: Classical RK4 is one four-stage explicit tableau.

patterns.why: Stage equations combine multiple evaluations.
A weighted slope sum approximates time-integrated change.

nodes.name: Embedded Runge–Kutta error estimate
nodes.intuition: Reuse the same stages in two accuracy formulas and let their disagreement suggest a step size.
nodes.conditions: The pair’s difference is assumed O(h^(p+1)); η∈(0,1) is a safety factor; use scaled error norms and practical bounds. The estimate is not a universal rigorous error certificate.
nodes.example: A large estimated error reduces the proposed step.

patterns.why: Error estimates control later resolution.
The expected error order determines the step exponent.

nodes.name: Absolute stability region of a time integrator
nodes.intuition: A numerical method must avoid amplifying modes that the differential equation damps.
nodes.conditions: Apply a one-step method to y′=λy; R is its amplification function where defined. This linear test does not settle all nonlinear stability.
nodes.example: Forward Euler has R(z)=1+z and stability disk |1+z|≤1.

patterns.why: Only the product hλ enters the test.
Numerical amplification approximates e^(hλ).

nodes.name: A-stability of one-step methods
nodes.intuition: All linearly decaying modes remain nonamplifying regardless of step size.
nodes.conditions: S is the absolute stability region; boundary points are interpreted where the amplification function is defined. A-stability does not guarantee accuracy for large steps.
nodes.example: Backward Euler and implicit trapezoidal are A-stable.

patterns.why: Nonamplification respects decay in the linear test.
Stability is distinct from approximation accuracy.

nodes.name: Zero-stability root condition
nodes.intuition: Parasitic recurrence modes must not grow as the step size goes to zero.
nodes.conditions: For a fixed-step linear multistep method ∑αjyn+j=h∑βjfn+j with αk≠0, zero-stability is equivalent to the displayed condition on every root of ρ.
nodes.example: A repeated root at ζ=1 causes polynomial growth in the homogeneous recurrence.

patterns.why: Step-to-step errors satisfy a recurrence.
Uniform control as h→0 is essential.

nodes.name: Consistency plus zero-stability gives convergence
nodes.intuition: Small local defects accumulate safely only if the recurrence does not amplify them uncontrollably.
nodes.conditions: Fixed-step linear multistep methods for sufficiently smooth well-posed Lipschitz ODE initial-value problems, with convergent starting values.
nodes.example: A locally accurate but zero-unstable scheme may diverge as h→0.

patterns.why: Local approximation and propagation jointly determine convergence.
Stability controls repeated error accumulation.

nodes.name: Explicit centered heat-equation scheme
nodes.intuition: Diffusion updates each grid value by averaging it with its neighbors.
nodes.conditions: Uniform one-dimensional grid, κ>0, standard periodic or homogeneous Dirichlet setting; r≤1/2 ensures the usual explicit stability and nonnegative weights.
nodes.example: At r=1/2 the next value is the mean of its two neighbors.

patterns.why: Stable steps form a convex local average.
Time step scales quadratically with mesh size.

nodes.name: Crank–Nicolson diffusion discretization
nodes.intuition: Average diffusion at the beginning and end of a step to gain second-order time accuracy.
nodes.conditions: Lh is the semidiscrete diffusion matrix with nonpositive real eigenvalues in a stable symmetric spatial discretization. The method is linearly unconditionally stable but may have sign oscillations for stiff modes.
nodes.example: A Fourier mode with eigenvalue λ≤0 is multiplied by (1+Δtλ/2)/(1−Δtλ/2).

patterns.why: Endpoint diffusion rates are averaged.
Eigenmodes reduce stability to scalar factors.

nodes.name: First-order upwind advection scheme
nodes.intuition: A positive-speed signal is sampled from the side where information arrives.
nodes.conditions: c>0; uniform grid; 0≤ν≤1 for the convex-combination stability property. For negative speed reverse the spatial direction.
nodes.example: At ν=1 the data shift exactly one cell per step.

patterns.why: Stable steps mix the present and upstream values.
On a periodic grid the total discrete sum is preserved.

nodes.name: CFL numerical-domain condition
nodes.intuition: A numerical stencil must reach every point that can influence the exact solution.
nodes.conditions: This bound is necessary for convergence of explicit nearest-neighbor schemes for constant-speed advection; wider or implicit stencils have different conditions. It is not sufficient for stability by itself.
nodes.example: A physical characteristic cannot cross more than one cell in one such explicit step.

patterns.why: Signal travel must fit within stencil reach.
The dimensionless Courant number compares two speeds.

nodes.name: Method of lines semidiscretization
nodes.intuition: Discretize space first and leave time to an ODE solver.
nodes.conditions: A spatial grid and boundary treatment define Dxx; consistency and stability of both discretizations are needed for convergence.
nodes.example: The largest diffusion eigenvalues scale like −1/(Δx)², making fine grids stiff.

patterns.why: Space and time approximation are separated.
A spatial derivative becomes a matrix action.

nodes.name: Galerkin stiffness system for Poisson
nodes.intuition: Require the residual to vanish against a finite collection of test functions.
nodes.conditions: Linearly independent basis functions φj in H0¹(Ω), bounded Lipschitz Ω, f∈L²; K is positive definite for the Dirichlet Poisson problem.
nodes.example: Piecewise-linear basis functions give sparse couplings between neighboring mesh vertices.

patterns.why: The weak equation is enforced on a finite test space.
The stiffness matrix represents Dirichlet energy.

nodes.name: Céa quasi-optimal Galerkin error
nodes.intuition: A stable Galerkin solution is nearly as accurate as the best approximation in its chosen space.
nodes.conditions: Real Hilbert V; bilinear a bounded by M and coercive with α>0; Vh a finite-dimensional subspace; exact and Galerkin solutions have the same continuous linear right-hand functional.
nodes.example: For the energy norm of a symmetric coercive form the factor can be 1.

patterns.why: Galerkin orthogonality controls the error.
Actual error is compared with best-space distance.

nodes.name: Shooting method for a two-point boundary problem
nodes.intuition: Guess a missing initial slope, integrate forward, and adjust until the far boundary is met.
nodes.conditions: A second-order ODE with a well-defined initial-value solution reaching b for candidate slopes; solutions and their sensitivities may be ill-conditioned.
nodes.example: A scalar root solve adjusts s to enforce y(b)=β.

patterns.why: An ODE solve becomes the function in a rootfinding problem.
Two endpoint requirements are joined by an interior trajectory.

nodes.name: Differentiation matrix on interpolation nodes
nodes.intuition: Differentiate each cardinal basis function once, then reuse the resulting matrix on any data vector.
nodes.conditions: n+1 distinct nodes; pj=p(xj), and ℓj are their degree-n Lagrange basis polynomials. Exactness is polynomial, not arbitrary-data accuracy.
nodes.example: D times the constant vector is zero.

patterns.why: Differentiation is represented by a matrix.
Cardinal basis derivatives determine all entries.

nodes.name: Adaptive Simpson local error estimate
nodes.latex: E\approx\frac{S_{\rm fine}-S_{\rm coarse}}{15},\qquad I\approx S_{\rm fine}+\frac{S_{\rm fine}-S_{\rm coarse}}{15}
nodes.intuition: Compare one Simpson panel with two half-panels and spend more samples where they disagree.
nodes.conditions: Smooth integrand in an asymptotic error regime; Sfine uses two half-panels on the same interval. The estimate can miss narrow unsampled features and is not a universal certificate.
nodes.example: A small estimated local error lets a panel remain coarse.

patterns.why: Intervals are subdivided only where needed.
Halving reduces the leading composite Simpson error by 16.

nodes.name: Gaussian quadrature remainder
nodes.intuition: The first missed derivative is multiplied by the squared nodal polynomial’s weighted size.
nodes.conditions: f∈C^(2n)[a,b], positive integrable weight w with finite moments, πn monic orthogonal degree n, and Gaussian Qn; ξ∈(a,b).
nodes.example: For a function with f^(2n)≥0, Gaussian quadrature underestimates its weighted integral.

patterns.why: The nodal polynomial appears squared.
The first unmatched derivative controls the error.

nodes.name: Clenshaw evaluation of a Chebyshev series
nodes.intuition: Evaluate a whole polynomial expansion backward using its basis recurrence.
nodes.conditions: The backward recurrence runs k=n,…,1; finite coefficients and real or complex x. Formula is exact before rounding.
nodes.example: This avoids expanding Chebyshev polynomials into monomials.

patterns.why: Backward accumulation uses two stored values.
Basis coefficients are evaluated without basis conversion.

nodes.name: Givens plane rotation for elimination
nodes.intuition: Rotate two coordinates to remove one entry while preserving their length.
nodes.conditions: a,b real and not both zero; use a scaled hypot evaluation numerically to avoid unnecessary overflow.
nodes.example: The pair (3,4) rotates to (5,0).

patterns.why: The rotation preserves Euclidean norm.
Only two coordinates change in each elimination.

nodes.name: Differentiation under an integral
nodes.intuition: Differentiate a continuously changing accumulation when one integrable bound controls its local rate.
nodes.conditions: Near t0, f(t,x) is differentiable in t almost everywhere, |∂tf|≤g∈L¹, and f(t0,·)∈L¹. Then the identity holds at t0 if the pointwise derivatives exist there.
nodes.example: Differentiating a gamma integral introduces a factor log x.

patterns.why: A derivative passes through an accumulation operator.
Domination controls difference quotients.

nodes.name: Leibniz rule with moving integration limits
nodes.intuition: Accumulation changes because the integrand changes and because its boundaries move.
nodes.conditions: a,b are C¹ and f,∂tf continuous on a neighborhood of the region swept by the limits.
nodes.example: For ∫₀ᵗx²dx, the derivative is t².

patterns.why: Boundary motion adds endpoint terms.
Interior change is integrated.

nodes.name: Faà di Bruno higher chain rule
nodes.intuition: Higher derivatives distribute repeated differentiations among inner-function factors in every possible grouping.
nodes.conditions: n≥1 integer; f and g are C^n on appropriate neighborhoods; each mj is a nonnegative integer.

patterns.why: Derivatives of nested functions combine.
Partitions of differentiations determine coefficients.

nodes.name: Euler identity for homogeneous functions
nodes.intuition: A scaling law determines the directional derivative along rays.
nodes.conditions: f is C¹ on an open cone in Rⁿ; homogeneity holds for positive t; k is real.
nodes.example: For a quadratic form, x·∇Q=2Q.

patterns.why: The degree is the radial growth rate.
Differentiating scale gives a local identity.

nodes.name: Hessian chain rule for a scalar composite
nodes.intuition: Curvature comes both from the outer function and from bending of the inner coordinates.
nodes.conditions: g:Rⁿ→Rᵐ and f:Rᵐ→R are C² on compatible open domains; all terms are evaluated at x unless indicated.
nodes.example: For affine g the second sum vanishes.

patterns.why: Two distinct curvature sources combine.
Hessians transform through Jacobian quadratic forms.

nodes.name: Integral mean-value formula for vector maps
nodes.intuition: The finite change of a map is the accumulated directional derivative along a straight segment.
nodes.conditions: F:C¹(U,Rᵐ), U⊂Rⁿ open, and the entire segment [x,y] lies in U.
nodes.example: A uniform bound ‖DF‖≤L on the segment gives ‖F(y)−F(x)‖≤L‖y−x‖.

patterns.why: Local changes integrate to total displacement.
Jacobians describe each small segment step.

nodes.name: Hadamard factorization near a vanishing point
nodes.intuition: A smooth function vanishing at the origin contains one coordinate factor in every term.
nodes.conditions: f is C∞ on a star-shaped open neighborhood of 0 in Rⁿ; each gj is smooth there. C^k versions lose at most one derivative.
nodes.example: In one variable, f(x)−f(0)=xg(x).

patterns.why: A vanishing function splits into coordinate-weighted pieces.
Coefficients average derivatives along a ray.

nodes.name: Total variation of a real function
nodes.intuition: Count all upward and downward movement, including changes that cancel in the net displacement.
nodes.conditions: f:[a,b]→R; bounded variation means the supremum over finite partitions is finite.
nodes.example: For monotone f, Var f=|f(b)−f(a)|.

patterns.why: Absolute increments add every movement.
Variation measures the length traveled by function values.

nodes.name: Jordan decomposition of a BV function
nodes.intuition: Separate total motion into accumulated upward and downward movement.
nodes.conditions: A real function on [a,b] has bounded variation iff it is a difference of two bounded increasing functions. One choice uses V(x)=Var[a,x]f and g=(V+f)/2,h=(V−f)/2.
nodes.example: A smooth oscillating function splits according to the positive and negative parts of its derivative.

patterns.why: Two monotone parts encode all variation.
Each part records only one direction of change.

nodes.name: Absolute continuity and integral recovery
nodes.latex: f(x)=f(a)+\int_a^x g(t)dt,\quad g\in L^1[a,b]\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f\in AC[a,b]
nodes.intuition: Absolute continuity means every change is accounted for by an integrable rate, with no hidden singular movement.
nodes.conditions: Real f on a compact interval; in this representation f′=g almost everywhere. Equivalent interval definition requires small total interval length to force small total increments.
nodes.example: The Cantor function is continuous and BV but is not absolutely continuous.

patterns.why: An integrable derivative accounts for all change.
Almost-everywhere differentiation supports integral recovery.

nodes.name: Riemann–Stieltjes integral
nodes.intuition: Accumulate f according to increments of another function rather than uniform coordinate increments.
nodes.conditions: A sufficient setting is f continuous and α of bounded variation on [a,b], with arbitrary tagged partitions.
nodes.example: If α is C¹, ∫f dα=∫fα′dx.

patterns.why: Integrator increments determine accumulated weights.
Smooth integrators contribute a derivative density.

nodes.name: Stieltjes integration by parts
nodes.intuition: Exchange which factor supplies increments while keeping the boundary product.
nodes.conditions: A sufficient setting is real continuous f,g of bounded variation on [a,b]. If both may jump, extra conventions or jump corrections are needed.
nodes.example: With g(x)=x the formula recovers ∫f dx+∫x df=[xf].

patterns.why: Either factor can supply the integrator.
Interior increments reduce to endpoint products.

nodes.name: Hölder continuity seminorm
nodes.intuition: A power law bounds how quickly values can separate across short distances.
nodes.conditions: 0<α≤1 on a metric subset of Euclidean space; α=1 is Lipschitz continuity.
nodes.example: √x is Hölder-1/2 on [0,1] but not Lipschitz there.

patterns.why: Distance enters with a regularity exponent.
The bound compares distances in domain and range.

nodes.name: Almost-everywhere differentiability of Lipschitz maps
nodes.latex: f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\text{ Lipschitz}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad Df(x)\text{ exists a.e.}
nodes.intuition: A global slope bound forces a genuine linear approximation at almost every point.
nodes.conditions: Lebesgue almost everywhere; local Lipschitz continuity gives the local version. Differentiability means total Fréchet differentiability, not merely coordinate derivatives.
nodes.example: The function |x| fails to differentiate at 0 but differentiates elsewhere.

patterns.why: Lipschitz maps have tangent linear maps almost everywhere.
A distance bound enforces regularity.

nodes.name: Egorov almost-uniform convergence
nodes.latex: f_n\to f\ \text{a.e.}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists E:\ \mu(E)<\varepsilon,\ f_n\to f\text{ uniformly on }X\setminus E
nodes.intuition: Remove a small exceptional region and pointwise convergence becomes uniform.
nodes.conditions: Measurable finite-valued functions on a finite measure space; convergence almost everywhere. The removed set depends on ε.
nodes.example: On [0,1], xn converges uniformly away from a small neighborhood of 1.

patterns.why: Weak pointwise control upgrades outside an exceptional set.
Space splits into controlled and exceptional regions.

nodes.name: Lusin approximation by continuous restrictions
nodes.latex: \forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists K\subset E\text{ compact}:\ |E\setminus K|<\varepsilon,\quad f|_K\text{ continuous}
nodes.intuition: A measurable function looks continuous after removing a set of arbitrarily small measure.
nodes.conditions: E⊂Rⁿ measurable with finite Lebesgue measure; f:E→R measurable and finite almost everywhere, adjusted on a null set if needed.
nodes.example: Even a discontinuous measurable function has continuous restrictions on nearly all of a bounded interval.

patterns.why: Small exceptional sets isolate irregular behavior.
Approximation is in measure, not uniform over all E.

nodes.name: Convergence in measure
nodes.intuition: Large errors are allowed, but the region where they occur must shrink in measure.
nodes.conditions: Measurable functions on a fixed measure space; finite-measure assumptions are needed for some relations with almost-everywhere convergence.
nodes.example: The spikes n·1[0,1/n] converge in measure to zero but not in L¹.

patterns.why: Error is measured by exceptional-set size.
A threshold converts function differences to measurable sets.

nodes.name: Uniform integrability by tail control
nodes.intuition: No member of the family can hide a fixed amount of integral mass in arbitrarily tall spikes.
nodes.conditions: A family of integrable functions on a finite measure space; this tail condition also yields a uniform L¹ bound.
nodes.example: A common L¹ dominating function implies uniform integrability.

patterns.why: Integral mass in extreme tails must disappear uniformly.
One tail bound controls the entire family.

nodes.name: Vitali convergence theorem
nodes.intuition: Small bad sets cannot obstruct convergence if they also cannot carry substantial mass.
nodes.conditions: Finite measure space; fn integrable, f finite almost everywhere and measurable. The hypotheses imply f∈L¹.
nodes.example: The spike family n·1[0,1/n] fails uniform integrability, explaining its missing L¹ limit.

patterns.why: Bounded values and exceptional tails are controlled separately.
Measure convergence upgrades to norm convergence.

nodes.name: Jordan decomposition of a finite signed measure
nodes.intuition: Separate positive and negative mass on disjoint measurable supports.
nodes.conditions: ν is a finite signed measure; ν± are unique finite positive mutually singular measures.
nodes.example: For density g, ν± have densities max(±g,0).

patterns.why: Positive and negative mass are separated.
Total variation counts both signs positively.

nodes.name: Total variation measure and integral bound
nodes.intuition: Partition mass finely enough that opposite signs cannot cancel each other.
nodes.conditions: ν finite real or complex measure; supremum over finite measurable partitions of E; f integrable with respect to |ν|.
nodes.example: For ν=gμ, |ν|=|g|μ.

patterns.why: Partitions reveal hidden cancellation.
Absolute mass bounds the integral magnitude.

nodes.name: Lebesgue decomposition of measures
nodes.intuition: Separate a measure into a density visible to the reference measure and mass on a reference-null set.
nodes.conditions: μ,ν are σ-finite positive measures; f≥0 measurable and νs positive are unique up to μ-null changes of f.
nodes.example: Lebesgue measure plus a point mass splits into continuous density 1 and a singular atom.

patterns.why: Density and singular components are separated.
The reference measure determines what counts as a density.

nodes.name: Carathéodory measurable-set criterion
nodes.intuition: A measurable set cuts every test set without creating or losing outer mass.
nodes.conditions: μ* is an outer measure on all subsets of X. Sets E satisfying this criterion form a σ-algebra, and μ* restricted to it is a complete measure.
nodes.example: Intervals satisfy the criterion for Lebesgue outer measure.

patterns.why: A set and its complement partition outer mass.
The criterion constructs a σ-algebra.

nodes.name: Completeness of Lp spaces
nodes.intuition: Approximations that become mutually close have a limit inside the same normed function space.
nodes.conditions: Any measure space; functions are identified almost everywhere; the Cauchy condition is as m,n→∞.
nodes.example: An absolutely summable series of Lp norms yields convergence of the function series in Lp.

patterns.why: No norm-Cauchy sequence escapes the space.
Closeness is measured in an integral norm.

nodes.name: Dual representation of Lp functionals
nodes.intuition: Every continuous linear measurement of an Lp function is integration against a conjugate-exponent weight.
nodes.conditions: Real Lp spaces on a σ-finite measure space, 1≤p<∞, 1/p+1/q=1. Complex conventions may insert conjugation. The statement excludes the full dual of L∞.
nodes.example: At p=2 this is Hilbert-space Riesz representation.

patterns.why: Conjugate exponents pair function spaces.
A functional accumulates weighted function values.

nodes.name: Interpolation inequality for Lp norms
nodes.intuition: Control at two integrability exponents supplies control between them.

patterns.why: Log norms interpolate along reciprocal exponents.
Exponents preserve homogeneity in f.

nodes.name: Baire category theorem
nodes.intuition: A complete space cannot be assembled from countably many closed pieces that are all locally thin.
nodes.conditions: X is a nonempty complete metric space; interiors are relative to X. Equivalently, countable intersections of dense open sets are dense.
nodes.example: R cannot be a countable union of closed sets with empty interior.

patterns.why: Countably many thin pieces cannot cover a complete space.
Completeness supports nested-ball constructions.

nodes.name: Uniform boundedness principle
nodes.intuition: Pointwise bounded responses force a common operator bound when the input space is complete.
nodes.conditions: X Banach, Y normed, and each Tα:X→Y bounded linear; arbitrary indexed families are allowed.
nodes.example: A weakly convergent sequence in a Banach space is norm bounded.

patterns.why: Linearity propagates local bounds across the space.
Completeness converts pointwise control to uniform norm control.

nodes.name: Banach open mapping theorem
nodes.latex: T:X\twoheadrightarrow Y\text{ bounded linear}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad T(U)\text{ open for every open }U
nodes.intuition: A surjective continuous linear map between complete spaces cannot flatten every neighborhood arbitrarily.
nodes.conditions: X,Y Banach over R or C; surjectivity is essential.
nodes.example: A bijective bounded linear map between Banach spaces has continuous inverse.

patterns.why: Images of neighborhoods contain neighborhoods.
Scaling extends a local ball estimate globally.

nodes.name: Bounded inverse theorem
nodes.intuition: An algebraically reversible bounded map between Banach spaces has a stable continuous inverse.
nodes.conditions: X and Y are Banach spaces; both completeness assumptions matter.
nodes.example: A bijective bounded operator has ‖Tx‖≥c‖x‖ for some c>0.

patterns.why: Forward and inverse operators compose to the identity.
Inverse continuity gives a uniform lower bound on forward stretching.

nodes.name: Closed graph theorem
nodes.latex: x_n\to x,\ Tx_n\to y\Longrightarrow y=Tx\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad T\text{ bounded}
nodes.intuition: A linear operator defined everywhere is continuous if its graph admits no missing limit points.
nodes.conditions: T:X→Y linear, defined on all of Banach X, with Y Banach. Closed unbounded operators can exist on proper domains.
nodes.example: Differentiation is not bounded on C[0,1] with the sup norm and cannot be an everywhere-defined closed derivative there.

patterns.why: Graph closure controls simultaneous limits.
Linearity upgrades closure to continuity.

nodes.name: Weak convergence in a Banach space
nodes.intuition: Every fixed continuous linear measurement settles down, even if norm distance does not.
nodes.conditions: X is a Banach space; X* consists of bounded scalar-valued linear functionals.
nodes.example: An orthonormal sequence in an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space converges weakly to zero but has norm one.

patterns.why: Convergence is tested by dual measurements.
Weak convergence asks less than norm convergence.

nodes.name: Weak-star convergence of dual functionals
nodes.intuition: Compare functionals only through their evaluations on original-space vectors.
nodes.conditions: ℓn,ℓ∈X*, X normed; weak-star topology is σ(X*,X). It can differ from weak topology on X*.
nodes.example: Bounded linear functionals may converge on every input without converging in operator norm.

patterns.why: Original vectors test elements of the dual.
Pointwise evaluation defines a weaker topology.

nodes.name: Banach–Alaoglu compactness
nodes.intuition: A bounded family of linear measurements is compact when observed one input at a time.
nodes.conditions: X normed. Weak-star compactness does not automatically mean sequential compactness; if X is separable, the dual ball is weak-star metrizable and sequentially compact.
nodes.example: Bounded L∞ functions admit weak-star convergent subnets when viewed as the dual of L¹ in the standard σ-finite setting.

patterns.why: The compact topology is defined by primal evaluations.
Weaker topology restores compactness lost in norm.

nodes.name: Canonical embedding and reflexivity
nodes.latex: J:X\to X^{**},\quad Jx(\ell)=\ell(x),\qquad X\text{ reflexive}\iff J(X)=X^{**}
nodes.intuition: A space is reflexive when measuring its measurements introduces no genuinely new vectors.
nodes.conditions: X is Banach; J is an isometric embedding. For 1<p<∞, Lp is reflexive on standard measure spaces; infinite-dimensional L¹ and L∞ need not be.
nodes.example: Every Hilbert space is reflexive.

patterns.why: Taking the continuous dual twice returns the original space.
The canonical embedding preserves norm.

nodes.name: Norm is weakly lower semicontinuous
nodes.intuition: Weak limits can lose visible norm but cannot acquire more than the limiting lower bound.
nodes.conditions: X normed and weak convergence defined through its continuous dual; sequence formulation shown.
nodes.example: An orthonormal sequence weakly tends to zero, so its norm can drop from one to zero.

patterns.why: Norm sublevel balls are weakly closed.
Weak limits preserve a one-sided norm bound.

nodes.name: Adjoint operator between continuous duals
nodes.intuition: Pull an output measurement backward to become a measurement on the input.
nodes.conditions: T:X→Y bounded linear between normed spaces; duals contain bounded linear functionals.
nodes.example: For matrices, dual-coordinate representation is transpose, with complex conjugation under Hermitian identifications.

patterns.why: Measurements move opposite to vectors.
The adjoint is precomposition by T.

nodes.name: Compact linear operator
nodes.intuition: A compact operator turns bounded input families into outputs with convergent subsequences.
nodes.conditions: T:X→Y bounded linear, X,Y Banach; BX is the closed unit ball. In metric spaces this is equivalent to every bounded sequence having an image-convergent subsequence.
nodes.example: An integral operator with continuous kernel on a compact interval is compact on C[a,b].

patterns.why: Bounded sequences gain convergent images.
Finite-rank operators are basic compact examples.

nodes.name: Spectral expansion of a compact self-adjoint operator
nodes.latex: Tx=\sum_j\lambda_j\langle e_j,x\rangle e_j,\qquad \lambda_j\to0\text{ if infinitely many nonzero eigenvalues}
nodes.intuition: An infinite-dimensional symmetric compact operator decomposes into orthogonal modes whose strengths fade away.
nodes.conditions: T compact self-adjoint on a Hilbert space; ej form an orthonormal basis of the closure of ran T for nonzero eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity; the sum converges in norm. The inner product is conjugate-linear in the first slot and linear in the second.
nodes.example: A compact symmetric integral kernel has such an eigenfunction expansion.

patterns.why: Self-adjoint eigenmodes are perpendicular.
Compactness forces nonzero eigenvalues toward zero.

nodes.name: Fredholm alternative for compact perturbations
nodes.intuition: A compact perturbation of identity fails to invert only through finite-dimensional compatibility obstructions.
nodes.conditions: K compact on a Hilbert space; range is closed. If I−K is not invertible, its kernel is nonzero and finite-dimensional.
nodes.example: Solvability of (I−K)u=f requires f to be orthogonal to adjoint null vectors.

patterns.why: Adjoint null vectors detect solvability obstructions.
Range and adjoint kernel separate compatible data.

nodes.name: Resolvent and spectrum of a bounded operator
nodes.intuition: Probe an operator by asking which shifts can be stably inverted.
nodes.conditions: T bounded linear on a nonzero complex Banach space. In infinite dimensions, spectrum can contain values with no eigenvector.
nodes.example: The unilateral shift has spectral points that are not all eigenvalues.

patterns.why: Invertibility is tested in the algebra of bounded operators.
The spectrum records unstable or impossible inverse shifts.

nodes.name: Resolvent identity
nodes.intuition: Changing the spectral parameter factors into two inverse responses and one scalar difference.
nodes.conditions: z,w in the resolvent set of the same bounded operator T.
nodes.example: Taking w→z gives R′(z;T)=−R(z;T)².

patterns.why: Inverse differences factor despite operator notation.
The identity controls the derivative of the inverse family.

nodes.name: Gelfand spectral radius formula
nodes.intuition: Long-run root growth of operator powers reveals the outer radius of the spectrum.
nodes.conditions: T bounded on a nonzero complex Banach space; any operator norm induced by the fixed Banach norm may be used.
nodes.example: A nilpotent operator has spectral radius zero even if its norm is large.

patterns.why: Asymptotic power growth determines spectral size.
Repeated operator action exposes the dominant scale.

nodes.name: Real Stone–Weierstrass theorem
nodes.intuition: An algebra of simple functions approximates every continuous function if it distinguishes points and includes constants.
nodes.conditions: K compact Hausdorff; A a real subalgebra of C(K,R), containing constants and separating every pair of distinct points. Complex versions also require closure under conjugation.
nodes.example: Real polynomials are dense in continuous functions on a compact interval.

patterns.why: An algebra closed under products builds approximations.
Density is in the uniform norm.

nodes.name: Dini monotone convergence theorem
nodes.intuition: On a compact space, monotone continuous approximation to a continuous limit cannot hide a persistent moving error.
nodes.conditions: K compact; pointwise monotone convergence, either decreasing or increasing; all functions and the limit are real-valued continuous.
nodes.example: Continuous monotone approximations to a continuous target on [0,1] converge uniformly.

patterns.why: Compactness strengthens pointwise convergence to uniform convergence.
Nested error sets must eventually become empty.

nodes.name: Hilbert operator norm-square identity
nodes.intuition: The squared size of an operator is encoded by its positive self-adjoint energy operator.
nodes.conditions: T bounded between Hilbert spaces; adjoints use the Hilbert inner product and norms are operator norms.
nodes.example: For a matrix, the largest eigenvalue of A*A is σmax(A)².

patterns.why: ‖Tx‖² is the quadratic form of T*T.
The adjoint returns output measurements to inputs.

nodes.name: Dirac point-evaluation distribution
nodes.intuition: A point mass is described by what it does to test functions instead of by a finite density.
nodes.conditions: a∈Rⁿ; φ∈Cc∞(Rⁿ). δa is both a positive measure and a distribution; it is not an ordinary integrable function.
nodes.example: Convolution with δ0 leaves a function unchanged.

patterns.why: Test-function response defines the object.
All mass is concentrated at one point.

nodes.name: Cauchy principal-value distribution 1/x
nodes.intuition: Symmetric cancellation extracts a finite response from a nonintegrable singular kernel.
nodes.conditions: φ∈Cc∞(R); the limit is symmetric around zero. It is not an absolutely convergent Lebesgue integral near zero.
nodes.example: The odd singularity cancels against the constant term φ(0).

patterns.why: Symmetric deletion pairs opposite singular contributions.
A prescribed limiting process defines the object.

nodes.name: Derivative of a jump is a delta
nodes.intuition: A sudden unit jump contributes a point impulse to the generalized derivative.
nodes.conditions: Equality is in distributions on R; changing H(0) has no effect.
nodes.example: A piecewise smooth function with jump J at a gains Jδa in its distributional derivative.

patterns.why: A jump appears as an internal boundary term.
The delta records the total jump size.

nodes.name: Delta under a smooth scalar map
nodes.intuition: Each simple zero contributes point mass weighted by the reciprocal local stretching.
nodes.conditions: g:R→R smooth; zeros are simple and locally finite on the test-function support. The pullback distribution is defined under this transversality condition.

patterns.why: Local inverse Jacobians weight point masses.
Only the slope at each simple zero enters.

nodes.name: Convolution of a distribution with a test function
nodes.intuition: Slide a smooth probe across a generalized function to obtain an ordinary smooth response.
nodes.conditions: T∈D′(Rⁿ), φ∈Cc∞(Rⁿ); the result is C∞. More general distribution pairs require support or growth conditions.
nodes.example: δa*φ=φ(·−a).

patterns.why: A moving probe converts a generalized object into a smooth function.
Differentiation can act on the probe.

nodes.name: Schwartz rapidly decreasing functions
nodes.intuition: A Schwartz function and every derivative decay faster than any inverse polynomial.
nodes.conditions: α,β range over all nonnegative multi-indices. The displayed seminorms define the Schwartz topology.
nodes.example: The Gaussian e^(−|x|²) is Schwartz.

patterns.why: Every polynomially weighted derivative stays bounded.
