Rapid decay controls transforms and integrations by parts.

nodes.name: Tempered distributions
nodes.latex: \mathcal S^\prime(\mathbb R^n)=\{\text{continuous linear functionals on }\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)\}
nodes.intuition: Polynomial-growth generalized functions act on rapidly decaying probes.
nodes.conditions: Continuity is with respect to the Schwartz seminorm topology. Every polynomially bounded locally integrable function defines one; arbitrary distributions need not be tempered.
nodes.example: Dirac masses and polynomials are tempered distributions.

patterns.why: Schwartz probes define a continuous dual.
Polynomial growth is compatible with rapid decay.

nodes.name: Fourier transform on Schwartz space and its dual
nodes.latex: \widehat f(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)e^{-ix\cdot\xi}dx,\quad\mathcal F:\mathcal S\to\mathcal S,\quad\langle\widehat T,\varphi\rangle=\langle T,\widehat\varphi\rangle
nodes.intuition: Rapid decay and smoothness exchange roles under Fourier transformation, and duality extends the transform beyond functions.
nodes.conditions: The displayed unnormalized negative-phase transform is a continuous automorphism of S; inverse has factor (2π)^(−n). The dual definition uses the bilinear distribution pairing.
nodes.example: With this convention, the Fourier transform of δ0 is the constant distribution 1.

patterns.why: The transform extends by transposing its action on test functions.
Spatial decay and frequency smoothness are exchanged.

nodes.name: Poisson summation formula
nodes.intuition: Sampling in space becomes periodic frequency sampling on the reciprocal lattice.
nodes.conditions: f∈S(Rⁿ); Fourier convention is fhat(ξ)=∫f(x)e^(−ix·ξ)dx. Both sums converge absolutely.
nodes.example: Applying the identity to exp(−πt|x|²) gives theta scale inversion.

patterns.why: Integer and reciprocal lattices exchange through Fourier transformation.
Periodization converts translation symmetry into discrete frequencies.

nodes.name: Sobolev inequality on Euclidean space
nodes.intuition: An integrable gradient forces stronger integrability of the function.
nodes.conditions: n≥2, 1≤p<n, initially u∈Cc∞(Rⁿ); extension holds in the corresponding homogeneous completion or W0¹,p setting.
nodes.example: In dimension 3, an L² gradient controls the L6 norm.

patterns.why: The exponent p* is fixed by dilation balance.
Gradient control bounds function size.

nodes.name: Morrey Hölder estimate
nodes.intuition: A sufficiently integrable gradient prevents sharp small-scale jumps and creates a continuous representative.
nodes.conditions: p>n, initially u∈Cc∞(Rⁿ); W¹,p functions have a Hölder representative with exponent 1−n/p.
nodes.example: In one dimension p=2 gives a 1/2-Hölder bound.

patterns.why: The Hölder exponent balances dimension and integrability.
Gradient bounds control finite changes.

nodes.name: Compact Sobolev embedding
nodes.intuition: Derivative control prevents bounded function sequences from shifting or oscillating too freely inside a bounded region.
nodes.conditions: Ω bounded open in Rⁿ, 1≤p<n, p*=np/(n−p). The strict inequality q<p* is essential in general; zero-boundary space is used.
nodes.example: A bounded H0¹ sequence in a bounded three-dimensional domain has an L²-convergent subsequence.

patterns.why: Weak derivative bounds yield strong subsequential convergence.
Compactness fails at the scale-invariant critical exponent.

nodes.name: Boundary trace of a Sobolev function
nodes.intuition: A function without pointwise values everywhere can still have a well-defined boundary restriction.
nodes.conditions: Ω bounded with C¹ boundary, 1≤p<∞; trace is the bounded extension of ordinary restriction for smooth functions, with surface measure on ∂Ω.
nodes.example: H0¹ functions have zero trace.

patterns.why: Interior derivative control determines a boundary object.
Trace is defined through continuous extension.

nodes.name: Hardy inverse-distance inequality
nodes.intuition: Gradient control limits how much mass a function can place near an inverse-distance singularity.
nodes.conditions: 1<p<n and u∈Cc∞(Rⁿ); the singular point is the origin.
nodes.example: In dimension 3 with p=2, ∫|u|²/|x|²≤4∫|∇u|².

patterns.why: Both sides have the same dilation degree.
Distance from a singular point supplies the weight.

nodes.name: Sobolev chain rule
nodes.intuition: A smooth scalar change of a weakly differentiable function obeys the expected local derivative law.
nodes.conditions: u∈W¹,p(Ω), 1≤p<∞; F∈C¹(R), F′ bounded and F(0)=0. Then F(u)∈W¹,p even when Ω has infinite measure.
nodes.example: F(s)=tanh s preserves W¹,p and has bounded derivative.

patterns.why: Weak differentiation respects a controlled composite.
Smooth approximation transfers the classical chain rule.

nodes.name: Sobolev product rule
nodes.intuition: Multiplication remains compatible with weak derivatives when bounded factors keep all products integrable.
nodes.conditions: u,v∈W¹,p(Ω)∩L∞(Ω), 1≤p<∞; then uv∈W¹,p(Ω). More general exponent versions need separate Hölder conditions.
nodes.example: Products of bounded H¹ functions remain H¹.

patterns.why: The derivative splits across the two factors.
Bounded multiplication preserves the Sobolev space.

nodes.name: Hardy–Littlewood maximal weak bound
nodes.intuition: Test every local averaging scale and control how much space can have a large average.
nodes.conditions: f∈L¹(Rⁿ), λ>0; centered Euclidean balls and Lebesgue measure are used.
nodes.example: A narrow spike may raise nearby averages, but the large-average region has controlled measure.

patterns.why: All radii compete in the local supremum.
Covering balls control exceptional-set size.

nodes.name: Marcinkiewicz weak-to-strong interpolation
nodes.intuition: Control of rare large outputs at two exponents yields full norm control between them.
nodes.conditions: T sublinear with weak-type bounds on compatible measure spaces; 1≤p0<p<p1<∞. Lp,∞ denotes the weak norm supλ>0 λ μ(|g|>λ)^(1/p).
nodes.example: The result is a central step in upgrading maximal-operator bounds.

patterns.why: Split input into large and small values.
Intermediate reciprocal exponents inherit estimates.

nodes.name: Hilbert transform and its Fourier multiplier
nodes.intuition: An odd singular kernel rotates the phases of positive and negative frequencies in opposite directions.
nodes.conditions: Initially f Schwartz; Fourier convention exp(−ixξ); the transform extends boundedly on Lp(R) for 1<p<∞, not strongly on L¹ or L∞.
nodes.example: On nonzero Fourier modes, applying H twice gives minus the original mode.

patterns.why: A singular spatial kernel becomes a simple frequency multiplier.
Odd kernel symmetry determines opposite phase signs.

nodes.name: Morera integral criterion
nodes.latex: f\in C(\Omega),\quad\oint_{\partial T}f(z)\,dz=0\ \forall T\Subset\Omega\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f\text{ holomorphic}
nodes.intuition: Vanishing circulation around every small triangle forces complex differentiability.
nodes.conditions: Ω open in C; T denotes every filled triangle contained in Ω with positive boundary orientation.
nodes.example: Uniform limits of holomorphic functions on compact sets satisfy the integral criterion.

patterns.why: Small boundary integrals determine interior analyticity.
Contour tests are linear in f.

nodes.name: Riemann removable-singularity theorem
nodes.latex: f\text{ holomorphic on }0<|z-a|<r,\quad |f|\le M\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f\text{ extends holomorphically to }a
nodes.intuition: A bounded isolated hole contains no genuine analytic obstruction.
nodes.conditions: Boundedness is needed in some punctured neighborhood of a; the extension is unique.
nodes.example: sin z/z extends at 0 with value 1.

patterns.why: The missing value is recovered by an analytic limit.
No negative Laurent powers survive boundedness.

nodes.name: Local factorization at a holomorphic zero
nodes.intuition: Near a zero, a holomorphic function is a pure integer power times a nonvanishing factor.
nodes.conditions: f holomorphic near a and not identically zero there; m≥0 is the first derivative order with f^(m)(a)≠0.
nodes.example: z³e^z has a zero of order three at zero.

patterns.why: Multiplicity is separated from a nonzero analytic factor.
The first nonzero Taylor term fixes local behavior.

nodes.name: Pole order and reciprocal zeros
nodes.latex: f(z)=(z-a)^{-m}g(z),\quad g(a)\ne0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 1/f\text{ has a zero of order }m
nodes.intuition: A pole is a finite-order zero viewed through reciprocation.
nodes.conditions: m≥1 integer; f holomorphic on a punctured neighborhood, g holomorphic and nonzero at a.
nodes.example: 1/z² has a pole of order two.

patterns.why: Zeros and poles exchange under reciprocation.
A singular power is separated from a regular factor.

nodes.name: Casorati–Weierstrass density near an essential singularity
nodes.intuition: Near an essential singularity, the values come arbitrarily close to every complex target.
nodes.conditions: f holomorphic on a punctured neighborhood and a an essential singularity; every sufficiently small r>0 is allowed.
nodes.example: e^(1/z) has dense image in every punctured disk around zero.

patterns.why: Approach to a singularity creates arbitrarily varied limiting values.
Every target value is approximated.

nodes.name: Little Picard theorem
nodes.latex: f:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C\text{ entire nonconstant}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad|\mathbb C\setminus f(\mathbb C)|\le1
nodes.intuition: A nonconstant entire map cannot avoid two complex values.
nodes.conditions: No growth assumption is required; the conclusion is about omitted finite values.
nodes.example: e^z omits zero and shows that one exception is possible.

patterns.why: Global analytic maps have strongly constrained ranges.
Affine output changes preserve the omitted-value count.

nodes.name: Great Picard theorem at an isolated essential singularity
nodes.latex: f\text{ essential at }a\Longrightarrow f\text{ assumes every value, with at most one exception, infinitely often near }a
nodes.intuition: An essential singularity produces repeated coverage of almost the entire complex plane at every small scale.
nodes.conditions: f holomorphic on a punctured disk about a; every smaller punctured disk has the stated property. The meromorphic version has a different omitted-value count on the sphere.
nodes.example: e^(1/z) repeatedly takes every nonzero value near zero.

patterns.why: Infinitely many preimages accumulate at the singularity.
Range coverage is stronger than density.

nodes.name: Open mapping theorem for holomorphic functions
nodes.latex: f:\Omega\to\mathbb C\text{ holomorphic nonconstant}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(U)\text{ open for every open }U\subseteq\Omega
nodes.intuition: A nonconstant analytic map sends local regions to regions rather than collapsing them into curves.
nodes.conditions: Ω is a connected open subset of C; nonconstancy is essential.
nodes.example: z↦z² maps a small disk around zero to another disk, despite derivative zero at the center.

patterns.why: Local neighborhoods have neighborhood images.
Local power structure controls mapping near critical points.

nodes.name: Holomorphic local inverse theorem
nodes.intuition: A nonzero complex derivative gives a locally reversible rotation and scaling.
nodes.conditions: f holomorphic near a; inverse exists between sufficiently small neighborhoods and is holomorphic. The statement is local, not global injectivity.
nodes.example: e^z has local logarithmic inverses but no global inverse on C.

patterns.why: Nonzero derivative prevents local collapse.
Inverse derivatives undo forward derivatives.

nodes.name: Analytic logarithm criterion
nodes.intuition: A global logarithm exists exactly when multiplicative winding disappears around every loop.
nodes.conditions: f is nonvanishing holomorphic on a domain Ω; loops are piecewise C1. The logarithm g is holomorphic; any two choices differ by 2πik for one integer k, and fixing its value at one point makes it unique.
nodes.example: Every nonvanishing holomorphic function on a simply connected domain has a holomorphic logarithm.

patterns.why: Loop integrals detect a global obstruction.
A primitive of f′/f recovers logarithmic coordinates.

nodes.name: Holomorphic nth root on a simply connected domain
nodes.intuition: Divide a continuous logarithmic coordinate to construct a consistent root branch.
nodes.conditions: n≥1 integer, Ω simply connected domain, f holomorphic and nowhere zero. Different choices multiply h by an nth root of unity.
nodes.example: A nowhere-zero analytic function on a disk admits an analytic square root.

patterns.why: Logarithms turn roots into division.
Exponential and logarithm construct the branch.

nodes.name: Primitive criterion for a holomorphic function
nodes.intuition: A function can be integrated globally without path ambiguity precisely when all loop totals vanish.
nodes.conditions: f holomorphic on a domain Ω; loops piecewise C¹. A primitive is unique up to a constant.
nodes.example: 1/z has no primitive on C\{0}.

patterns.why: Loop accumulation vanishes for exact derivatives.
Endpoint differences replace interior path integrals.

nodes.name: Contour winding number
nodes.intuition: Count the net number of turns a closed path makes around a point.
nodes.conditions: γ closed piecewise C¹, a not on its image; self-intersections are allowed and orientation affects the sign.
nodes.example: A counterclockwise circle around a has winding number 1.

patterns.why: Homotopies avoiding a preserve the integer.
The integral accumulates angular change.

nodes.name: Residue at a pole of arbitrary order
nodes.intuition: Remove the singular power and extract the Taylor coefficient that becomes a simple-pole term.
nodes.conditions: f has a pole of order at most m≥1 at a; the bracketed product extends holomorphically.
nodes.example: Res₀(e^z/z³)=1/2.

patterns.why: A Laurent coefficient becomes a Taylor coefficient.
One finite derivative extracts the residue.

nodes.name: Residue at infinity and global residue balance
nodes.intuition: The point at infinity supplies the final residue needed to balance every finite singularity.
nodes.conditions: For the sum, f is rational, equivalently meromorphic on the Riemann sphere. The definition applies when infinity is an isolated singularity.
nodes.example: For f(z)=1/z the finite residue is 1 and the infinity residue is −1.

patterns.why: w=1/z turns infinity into a local point.
Residues sum to zero on the sphere.

nodes.name: Jensen formula for zeros in a disk
nodes.intuition: Boundary-average logarithmic size records how many zeros lie inside and how close they are to the center.
nodes.conditions: f holomorphic near the closed disk, f(0)≠0, and no zeros on its boundary; zeros aj are counted with multiplicity.
nodes.example: With no zeros inside, log|f| satisfies the harmonic mean-value equality.

patterns.why: A boundary average detects interior zeros.
Zero positions determine the gap from the central value.

nodes.name: Hurwitz preservation of zero counts
nodes.latex: f_n\to f\text{ locally uniformly},\ f\not\equiv0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad N_D(f_n)=N_D(f)\text{ eventually}
nodes.intuition: Stable analytic approximation preserves zeros inside a boundary where the limit does not vanish.
nodes.conditions: Holomorphic fn on a common open Ω, converging locally uniformly to f; the closure of the Jordan domain D is compactly contained in Ω, with piecewise smooth boundary and no boundary zeros of f. Counts include multiplicity.
nodes.example: A locally uniform limit of nowhere-zero holomorphic functions is zero-free or identically zero.

patterns.why: Uniform boundary closeness preserves discrete data.
Zero count is unchanged by sufficiently small analytic perturbation.

nodes.name: Montel normal-family theorem
nodes.intuition: Local value bounds give enough derivative control to extract convergent analytic subsequences.
nodes.conditions: F a family of holomorphic functions on a domain Ω; normal here means every sequence has a subsequence converging uniformly on compact subsets to a holomorphic function.
nodes.example: Holomorphic self-maps of the unit disk form a normal family.

patterns.why: Local boundedness gives compactness in the analytic topology.
Cauchy estimates control derivatives on smaller sets.

nodes.name: Locally uniform limit theorem for holomorphic functions
nodes.latex: f_n\to f\text{ uniformly on compacta}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f\text{ holomorphic},\quad f_n^{(k)}\to f^{(k)}\text{ locally uniformly}
nodes.intuition: Uniform control on every compact region preserves analyticity and all its derivatives.
nodes.conditions: fn holomorphic on a common open set; k≥0 fixed integer. Pointwise convergence alone is insufficient.
nodes.example: Taylor polynomials converge with all derivatives on smaller disks inside the convergence radius.

patterns.why: One convergence mode controls all derivative orders.
Contour formulas recover derivatives from nearby values.

nodes.name: Riemann mapping theorem
nodes.latex: \Omega\subsetneq\mathbb C\text{ simply connected domain}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\exists f:\Omega\overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow}\mathbb D\text{ biholomorphic}
nodes.intuition: Every proper simply connected planar domain has the same internal complex geometry as a disk.
nodes.conditions: Ω nonempty, open, connected and simply connected; Ω≠C. Prescribing f(a)=0 and f′(a)>0 determines the map uniquely.
nodes.example: The upper half-plane is mapped to the disk by a Möbius transformation.

patterns.why: An analytic bijection changes the domain’s shape.
Normalization removes disk-automorphism freedom.

nodes.name: Schwarz–Pick contraction
nodes.intuition: Holomorphic disk maps contract the disk’s natural non-Euclidean distance scale.
nodes.conditions: f holomorphic from the open unit disk to itself; z,w in the disk. Equality at distinct points, or derivative equality at one point, forces a disk automorphism.
nodes.example: At w=0 and f(0)=0 the first inequality is Schwarz’s lemma.

patterns.why: The disk metric contracts.
Automorphisms move comparison points to the origin.

nodes.name: All conformal automorphisms of the disk
nodes.intuition: Every reversible analytic disk map combines moving one point to the center with a rotation.
nodes.conditions: These and only these maps are biholomorphic self-maps of the open unit disk.
nodes.example: a=0 gives a pure rotation.

patterns.why: The family preserves the disk and its hyperbolic metric.
Point relocation and rotation generate the automorphism.

nodes.name: Harmonic conjugate construction
nodes.intuition: Rotate the gradient of a harmonic function by a quarter turn to obtain the gradient of its conjugate.
nodes.conditions: u∈C² harmonic on a simply connected planar domain. The conjugate exists globally and is unique up to a real constant.
nodes.example: For u=x²−y² one conjugate is v=2xy.

patterns.why: Real and imaginary parts exchange through a rotated gradient.
Harmonicity gives the integrability condition.

nodes.name: Harnack inequality on a disk
nodes.intuition: Positivity prevents a harmonic function from spiking sharply in the interior relative to its central value.
nodes.conditions: u nonnegative harmonic in a neighborhood of the closed disk of radius R; interior versions follow by slightly smaller radii.
nodes.example: On the half-radius circle, u lies between u(0)/3 and 3u(0).

patterns.why: Positive Poisson weights bound values by central averages.
Distance to the boundary controls comparison constants.

nodes.name: Schwarz reconstruction from the real part
nodes.intuition: Boundary values of one harmonic component determine its analytic partner up to an imaginary constant.
nodes.conditions: f holomorphic in a neighborhood of the closed unit disk; u=Re f and |z|<1.
nodes.example: Constant real boundary data produce a constant real part throughout the disk.

patterns.why: Boundary real values determine an interior analytic function.
Harmonic conjugation supplies the missing imaginary component.

nodes.name: Finite Blaschke product
nodes.intuition: Place prescribed zeros inside the disk while maintaining unit modulus on its boundary.
nodes.conditions: N finite nonnegative integer, θ real; multiplicities come from repeated aj. For N>1 the map is generally not an automorphism.
nodes.example: B(z)=z^N has an N-fold zero and winds the boundary N times.

patterns.why: One disk factor supplies each zero.
Every factor has unit boundary modulus.

nodes.name: Runge polynomial approximation for a hole-free compact set
nodes.intuition: Analytic functions near a compact set can be built from polynomials when the complement has no holes.
nodes.conditions: K compact in C, C\K connected, and f holomorphic on a neighborhood of K. With holes, rational functions with appropriate pole locations are generally needed.
nodes.example: Analytic functions near a closed disk admit uniform polynomial approximation.

patterns.why: Contour contributions are approximated by simple algebraic pieces.
Approximation is uniform on the compact set.

nodes.name: Mittag–Leffler prescribed principal parts
nodes.intuition: Assemble specified local pole behavior into one global meromorphic function.
nodes.conditions: Ω a planar domain; {aj} discrete with no accumulation inside Ω; Pj finite principal parts in negative powers of z−aj. There exists a meromorphic f with exactly those principal parts and no other poles.
nodes.example: Prescribed residues at a discrete set can be realized by suitable simple-pole principal parts.

patterns.why: Local singular pieces build a global object.
Holomorphic corrections make the construction converge.

nodes.name: Weierstrass entire product factorization
nodes.intuition: An entire function is its zeros multiplied by a nonvanishing exponential, with corrections ensuring convergence.
nodes.conditions: f entire and not identically zero; nonzero zeros aj counted with multiplicity have no finite accumulation; pj can be chosen for locally uniform product convergence; g entire, m the zero order at zero.
nodes.example: A polynomial is a finite product version with constant exponential factor.

patterns.why: Zeros and a zero-free factor are separated.
Canonical factors correct divergent raw products.

nodes.name: Euler infinite product for sine
nodes.intuition: Pair opposite integer zeros to reconstruct sine as a convergent infinite product.
nodes.conditions: z complex; convergence is locally uniform on C. Pairing ±n is part of this product convention.
nodes.example: Comparing the z³ coefficient gives ∑n≥1 1/n²=π²/6.

patterns.why: Each paired zero contributes one quadratic factor.
Symmetric zeros yield even factors after removing z.

nodes.name: Entire product for reciprocal gamma
nodes.intuition: Reciprocal gamma is rebuilt from its nonpositive-integer zeros with exponential convergence corrections.
nodes.conditions: z complex; γ is Euler’s constant; product converges locally uniformly on C. The reciprocal extends entirely through gamma poles.
nodes.example: At z=0 the reciprocal has a simple zero.

patterns.why: Zeros and exponential corrections determine the entire function.
Linear exponential corrections make the product converge.

nodes.name: Hadamard factorization for finite-order entire functions
nodes.intuition: A finite growth rate restricts the unknown zero-free factor to the exponential of a polynomial.
nodes.conditions: f entire, nonzero, of finite order ρ=limsup log log M(r)/log r, M(r)=max|z|=r|f(z)|; standard constant/polynomial cases use order zero. Zeros counted with multiplicity; p=floorρ is an admissible canonical-product genus.
nodes.example: Order-one functions such as sine have only a linear exponential factor.

patterns.why: Growth order limits algebraic complexity.
Zeros plus a polynomial exponent determine the function.

nodes.name: Contour length-times-maximum bound
nodes.intuition: Total contour accumulation is bounded by path length times the largest local contribution.
nodes.conditions: γ rectifiable piecewise C¹ and f continuous on its image; a supremum version works with an appropriate bounded integrand.
nodes.example: A unit-circle integral is bounded by 2π times the maximum modulus on the circle.

patterns.why: Local magnitudes sum along a path.
Path length controls the total.

nodes.name: Wirtinger derivatives
nodes.intuition: Combine two real derivatives into operators that distinguish analytic from anti-analytic dependence.
nodes.conditions: f is C¹ for first derivatives and C² for the Laplacian identity; z=x+iy.
nodes.example: ∂barz z=0 but ∂barz zbar=1.

patterns.why: Real derivatives split into complex-linear and anti-linear parts.
Fixed linear combinations reorganize differentiation.

nodes.name: Cauchy–Pompeiu formula
nodes.intuition: Failure of boundary data alone to reproduce a function is measured by its anti-holomorphic derivative inside.
nodes.conditions: Ω bounded planar domain with positively oriented piecewise C¹ boundary, f∈C¹ on a neighborhood of its closure, z∈Ω. The area singularity is locally integrable.
nodes.example: If f is holomorphic, the area term vanishes and Cauchy’s formula returns.

patterns.why: An interior defect corrects boundary reconstruction.
Analytic and anti-analytic contributions are separated.

nodes.name: Schwarzian derivative
nodes.intuition: The Schwarzian measures local deviation from fractional linear behavior.
nodes.conditions: f locally univalent holomorphic, so f′≠0; a local identity Sf=0 characterizes Möbius transformations.
nodes.example: Every Möbius transformation has zero Schwarzian.

patterns.why: Möbius transformations form the zero-defect family.
Third-order information measures projective distortion.

nodes.name: Schwarzian composition law
nodes.intuition: Projective distortion adds under composition after the outer distortion is rescaled quadratically.
nodes.conditions: f and g locally univalent holomorphic on compatible domains.
nodes.example: Postcomposition by a Möbius map leaves the Schwarzian unchanged.

patterns.why: Distortions combine with a coordinate factor.
Möbius postcomposition contributes zero.

nodes.name: Schwarz–Christoffel polygon map
nodes.intuition: Power factors turn a straight boundary through prescribed polygon angles.
nodes.conditions: A conformal map from the upper half-plane onto a simple n-gon, with one prevertex at infinity; xj are ordered real prevertices, interior angles are παj, and branches are analytic in the upper half-plane. Prevertices and constants must be chosen to match side lengths.
nodes.example: A right-angle vertex contributes exponent −1/2.

patterns.why: Boundary turning angles determine an analytic derivative.
Local power-map turns combine multiplicatively.

nodes.name: Picard–Lindelöf local well-posedness
nodes.intuition: A uniform local bound on slope sensitivity prevents two trajectories from splitting at the same initial point.
nodes.conditions: f is continuous near (t0,y0) and locally Lipschitz in y, uniformly on a small time interval. Existence and uniqueness are local, not necessarily global.
nodes.example: For y′=y² and y(0)=1, the unique solution exists only until t=1.

patterns.why: The integral equation becomes a contraction on a short interval.
Lipschitz control limits slope sensitivity.

nodes.name: Peano local existence theorem
nodes.intuition: Continuity is enough to assemble at least one local solution, even when branching cannot be ruled out.
nodes.conditions: f maps an open neighborhood of (t0,y0) in R×Rn continuously to Rn. The theorem guarantees a solution on some time interval, with no uniqueness claim.
nodes.example: For y′=2√|y| and y(0)=0, the zero solution and delayed departures coexist.

patterns.why: Compactness extracts a solution from approximate paths.
The limit satisfies the integral equation.

nodes.name: Finite-time ODE continuation criterion
nodes.intuition: A solution of a globally defined locally Lipschitz vector field can stop in finite time only by escaping every bounded set.
nodes.conditions: Autonomous y′=f(y), f:Rn→Rn locally Lipschitz; (T−,T+) is the maximal existence interval. For a proper open domain, approaching its boundary is another obstruction.
nodes.example: y′=y², y(0)=1 gives y(t)=1/(1−t), which diverges at the finite endpoint.

patterns.why: Bounded trajectories admit a continuation point.
Local existence can restart at each finite state.

nodes.name: Bernoulli equation linearizing substitution
nodes.intuition: A power substitution converts a particular nonlinear equation into a linear one.
nodes.conditions: n≠1 is constant; p,q continuous. Work on an interval where the required powers are differentiable and y≠0; any excluded zero solutions must be checked separately.
nodes.example: For y′+y=y², setting v=1/y gives v′−v=−1.

patterns.why: A power coordinate removes the nonlinear term.
The transformed equation obeys superposition for its homogeneous part.

nodes.name: Scalar Riccati to second-order linear equation
nodes.intuition: A logarithmic derivative converts a quadratic first-order law into a linear second-order law.
nodes.conditions: a,b continuous, c continuously differentiable and nowhere zero; u is a nonzero local solution on the interval considered. Zeros of u can produce poles of y.
nodes.example: For y′=y² use c=1 and u′′=0, giving y=−u′/u.

patterns.why: A logarithmic derivative changes equation order and linearity.
The square term cancels the squared logarithmic derivative.

nodes.name: Exact differential equation criterion
nodes.intuition: An exact equation follows the level curves of a potential function.
nodes.conditions: M,N are C1 on an open simply connected planar domain. Equality of cross-partials gives a global potential there; local potentials need only a small disk.
nodes.example: y dx+x dy=d(xy), so solutions lie on xy=C.

patterns.why: Solutions remain on a potential level.
Closed differentials integrate to path-independent changes.

nodes.name: Cauchy–Euler indicial polynomial
nodes.intuition: Power functions play the role that exponentials play for constant coefficients.
nodes.conditions: x>0, a,b real constants; repeated or complex roots require the usual logarithmic factors or real trigonometric combinations in log x.
nodes.example: x²y′′−2y=0 has solutions x² and x^(−1).

patterns.why: Power functions respect multiplicative rescaling.
t=log x converts the equation to constant coefficients.

nodes.name: Reduction of order from one known solution
nodes.intuition: One solution supplies the shape; a varying multiplier generates an independent companion.
nodes.conditions: y1 is a nonzero solution of y″+p(x)y′+q(x)y=0 on an interval where y1 never vanishes; p,q continuous.
nodes.example: For y″=0 and y1=1, the formula gives y2=x.

patterns.why: A second solution is a known shape times an unknown multiplier.
Integrating the Wronskian relation supplies the multiplier.

nodes.name: Frobenius series at a regular singular point
nodes.intuition: A power factor captures a singular scale while an ordinary series supplies corrections.
nodes.conditions: For x²y″+xp(x)y′+q(x)y=0, p,q are analytic near 0, p0=p(0),q0=q(0). At least one Frobenius solution exists locally on x>0; resonant roots may require logarithms for the other solution.
nodes.example: The Bessel indicial roots are r=±ν.

patterns.why: The leading exponent captures the singular behavior.
Higher coefficients are determined by a recurrence.

nodes.name: Green kernel for the interval Dirichlet problem
nodes.intuition: The inverse of a differential operator is assembled from responses to point loads.
nodes.conditions: L>0, 0≤x,s≤L; u solves −u″=f with u(0)=u(L)=0, for example for continuous f. The derivative of G jumps by −1 across x=s.
nodes.example: For f=1, u=x(L−x)/2.

patterns.why: Individual point responses superpose.
The kernel is chosen to vanish at both endpoints.

nodes.name: Sturm–Liouville nodal count
nodes.intuition: Higher eigenmodes have more internal sign changes.
nodes.conditions: Regular scalar self-adjoint equation −(py′)′+qy=λwy on [a,b], p∈C1 positive, q,w continuous with w>0, and Dirichlet endpoints; yn is a nonzero nth eigenfunction.
nodes.example: For −y″=λy on (0,π), yn=sin(nx) has n−1 interior zeros.

patterns.why: Distinct weighted eigenmodes are orthogonal.
Ordering eigenvalues orders the number of oscillations.

nodes.name: Fundamental solution of minus the Laplacian
nodes.intuition: A radial point-source response is harmonic away from its source and carries one unit of total flux.
nodes.conditions: Distributional identity on Rn for n≥2; |S^(n−1)| is the area of the unit sphere. The sign convention is −Δ.
nodes.example: In three dimensions Φ(x)=1/(4π|x|).

patterns.why: Rotations force a radial response.
A small enclosing sphere detects the unit source.

nodes.name: Dirichlet Green representation for Poisson
nodes.intuition: Separate the influence of interior forcing from boundary values using a kernel adapted to the boundary.
nodes.conditions: Smooth bounded Ω, sufficiently regular solution −Δu=f with boundary u=g; G vanishes on the boundary and satisfies −ΔyG(x,y)=δx. The normal is outward.
nodes.example: If f=0, only the boundary integral remains.

patterns.why: Interior sources and boundary data contribute separately.
Normal kernel derivatives transfer boundary values into the domain.

nodes.name: Weak and strong harmonic maximum principles
nodes.intuition: A harmonic function averages its neighbors, so a strict isolated interior peak is impossible.
nodes.conditions: Ω bounded and connected, u∈C2(Ω)∩C(closure Ω), Δu=0; x0 is interior for the strong statement. The minimum version follows by changing sign.
nodes.example: Boundary temperatures between 0 and 1 force an equilibrium temperature in the same range.

patterns.why: An interior value equals averages over nearby spheres.
Boundary extrema control the entire interior.

nodes.name: Hopf boundary point lemma for harmonic functions
nodes.intuition: A nonconstant harmonic function reaching a boundary maximum must approach it with a nonzero outward slope.
nodes.conditions: Ω has an interior tangent ball at x0; u harmonic in Ω and C1 up to x0, with a strict boundary maximum over the interior. ν is the outward unit normal at a smooth boundary point.
nodes.example: For u=x1 on a ball, the rightmost boundary point has positive outward derivative.

patterns.why: Boundary geometry controls the sign of a derivative.
A strict maximum forces a first-order boundary slope.

nodes.name: Weyl lemma for distributional harmonic functions
nodes.latex: u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega),\quad\Delta u=0\text{ in }\mathcal D^{\prime}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u=\widetilde u\ \text{a.e.},\ \widetilde u\in C^\infty(\Omega)
nodes.intuition: A very weak harmonic equation automatically repairs the function into a smooth harmonic representative.
nodes.conditions: Ω open in Rn; distributional Δu=0 means ∫uΔφ=0 for every compactly supported smooth φ. Equality is almost everywhere because L1 functions ignore null sets.
nodes.example: A locally integrable candidate with zero distributional Laplacian is an ordinary smooth harmonic function after changing a null set.

patterns.why: Mollification connects weak equations to smooth solutions.
Harmonic averaging is preserved by smoothing.

nodes.name: Caccioppoli interior energy estimate
nodes.intuition: Interior derivative energy is bounded by function size in a slightly larger region.
nodes.conditions: 0<r<R, concentric balls with closure BR contained in Ω, and u weakly harmonic on BR. Cn depends only on dimension.
nodes.example: A buffer of thickness R−r pays for differentiating a cutoff.

patterns.why: Derivative size is controlled by nearby function size.
A surrounding buffer shields the interior estimate.

nodes.name: Interior H2 estimate for Poisson
nodes.intuition: Two weak derivatives become square integrable when the Laplacian has square-integrable forcing.
nodes.conditions: Ω′ has compact closure in a bounded open Ω, f∈L2(Ω), and u∈H1(Ω) is a weak solution. C depends on the domains; this is an interior estimate and asserts no boundary smoothness.
nodes.example: Rough boundaries can obstruct global H2 regularity while this interior conclusion still holds.

patterns.why: Finite differences recover second weak derivatives.
Regularity is gained away from the boundary.

nodes.name: Method of images for a Dirichlet half-space
nodes.intuition: An opposite reflected source cancels the potential on a flat boundary.
nodes.conditions: n≥2, x,y in the upper half-space xn>0, and Φ is the fundamental solution of −Δ. This kernel vanishes on xn=0.
nodes.example: Equal distances to y and y* on the boundary make the two terms cancel.

patterns.why: Reflection makes boundary distances equal.
Two signed point responses superpose.

nodes.name: Compatibility and uniqueness for Neumann Poisson data
nodes.intuition: Net interior forcing must balance outward boundary flux; an additive constant remains invisible.
nodes.conditions: Smooth bounded connected Ω and sufficiently regular data/solution. With appropriate regularity the compatibility condition gives a solution unique up to an additive constant; a zero-mean constraint fixes it.
nodes.example: For zero normal flux, the source f must have mean zero.

patterns.why: The integrated source is balanced by boundary flux.
Adding a constant changes neither Laplacian nor normal derivative.

nodes.name: Heat semigroup Lp contraction
nodes.intuition: A normalized positive smoothing kernel cannot increase the global Lp size.
nodes.example: The sup norm cannot increase because every new value is a weighted average of old values.

patterns.why: The kernel has nonnegative unit mass.
Heat evolution composes by adding times.

nodes.name: Heat-kernel derivative smoothing bound
nodes.intuition: Diffusion pays inverse powers of time to turn rough data into smooth functions.
nodes.conditions: t>0, integer multi-index α, 1≤p≤q≤∞, f∈Lp(Rn); C depends on n,p,q,α. The equation uses diffusivity one.
nodes.example: With p=q, each spatial derivative costs a factor proportional to t^(−1/2).

patterns.why: Diffusive width √t fixes every time exponent.
Positive-time evolution improves regularity instantly.

nodes.name: Parabolic maximum principle
nodes.intuition: A heat subsolution cannot create a new temperature peak after the initial time without boundary input.
nodes.conditions: Ω bounded, T>0, u continuous on the closed cylinder and C2 in space/C1 in time inside, with ut−κΔu≤0 and κ>0. Boundary values are understood on the parabolic boundary.
nodes.example: Zero initial and boundary data force a heat solution to remain zero by applying the principle to ±u.

patterns.why: The parabolic boundary includes initial time as well as spatial sides.
Diffusion suppresses new interior maxima.

nodes.name: Heat flow in Dirichlet eigenmodes
nodes.intuition: Each spatial eigenmode fades independently, with finer modes typically fading faster.
nodes.conditions: Smooth bounded Ω, zero Dirichlet boundary, κ>0, f∈L2(Ω); eigenfunctions form an orthonormal L2 basis. The expansion converges in L2 and attains f in L2 as t↓0. The inner product is conjugate-linear in the first slot.
nodes.example: On (0,π), sine mode sin(jx) is multiplied by exp(−κj²t).

patterns.why: The initial field splits into orthogonal spatial modes.
Each coefficient obeys its own exponential decay law.

nodes.name: Finite speed of wave propagation
nodes.intuition: A disturbance can influence only points reached by a cone of finite slope.
nodes.conditions: Classical solution utt=c²Δu on Rn, c>0, t≥0, with initial displacement f and velocity g compactly supported. The same support result extends to energy solutions.
nodes.example: Data vanishing on Bct(x) cannot influence (t,x).

patterns.why: Euclidean distance and elapsed time define the dependence cone.
Local energy balances bound how far a disturbance travels.

nodes.name: Kirchhoff formula for three-dimensional waves
nodes.intuition: A three-dimensional wave samples expanding spherical shells of its initial data.
nodes.conditions: t>0,c>0, smooth initial f=u(·,0),g=ut(·,0) on R3, for example compactly supported. The measure is area on the unit sphere, whose total is 4π.
nodes.example: Constant f and zero g give the same constant solution.

patterns.why: Spherical means organize propagation.
The sampling shell expands at speed c.

nodes.name: Bromwich inversion of the Laplace transform
nodes.intuition: Recover a time function by superposing complex exponentials along a vertical frequency line.
nodes.conditions: For example f is piecewise C1 and of exponential order a on [0,∞), γ>a, and t>0 is a continuity point; symmetric truncation is used. At a jump, suitable one-sided regularity gives the midpoint value.
nodes.example: F(s)=1/(s+a) inverts to exp(−at).

patterns.why: A transform is reconstructed from its complex-frequency data.
Complex exponentials combine growth and oscillation.

nodes.name: Laplace method at a nondegenerate interior minimum
nodes.intuition: Strong exponential weighting concentrates almost all contribution near the smallest phase value.
nodes.conditions: λ→+∞, finite [a,b], φ∈C2 has a unique minimum at interior x0 with φ″(x0)>0; g continuous and g(x0)≠0. These sufficient assumptions give the leading ratio asymptotic.
nodes.example: For φ=x²/2, x0=0, the leading scale is √(2π/λ).

patterns.why: A quadratic phase approximation controls the peak.
Rescaling distance by √λ reveals a Gaussian limit.

nodes.name: One-dimensional stationary phase
nodes.intuition: Rapid oscillations cancel except near a point where phase temporarily stops changing.
nodes.conditions: λ→+∞; a∈C∞c(R), φ smooth and real near its support, with exactly one stationary point x0 there and φ″(x0)≠0.
nodes.example: A positive quadratic phase contributes the phase factor exp(iπ/4).

patterns.why: The local quadratic phase sets amplitude and phase shift.
Nonstationary regions cancel to higher order.

nodes.name: Watson lemma for endpoint Laplace asymptotics
nodes.intuition: A large Laplace parameter magnifies only the local endpoint expansion.
nodes.conditions: s→+∞ real, α>0, f has the stated asymptotic expansion as t↓0 and is locally integrable with at most exponential growth at infinity. The resulting series is asymptotic, not necessarily convergent.
nodes.example: For f(t)=1/(1+t), the expansion yields 1/s−1/s²+2!/s³−⋯.

patterns.why: Endpoint asymptotic coefficients determine large-parameter behavior.
Exponential damping suppresses the remote tail.

nodes.name: Lebesgue differentiation theorem
nodes.intuition: Zoomed local averages recover an integrable function at almost every point, even when it is discontinuous.
nodes.conditions: f∈L1loc(Rn); balls are Euclidean and the conclusion is with respect to Lebesgue measure. Values on a null set can be chosen arbitrarily.
nodes.example: The density of a measurable set is 0 or 1 at almost every point by applying the theorem to its indicator.

patterns.why: Shrinking neighborhood means reveal the point value.
Almost-everywhere recovery survives weak regularity.

nodes.name: Cumulative distribution function
nodes.intuition: A distribution can be stored as the running total of probability to the left of a moving threshold.
nodes.conditions: X is real valued; a<b. Every CDF is nondecreasing, right-continuous, with limits 0 and 1 at the two infinities.
nodes.example: A fair die has F(3)=1/2.

patterns.why: Each threshold includes all probability already passed.
The function records a complete one-dimensional law.

nodes.name: Generalized quantile function
nodes.intuition: Read the cumulative plot sideways: a probability level asks which threshold first reaches it.
nodes.conditions: F is any real CDF and 0<u<1; this generalized inverse also handles jumps and flat intervals.
nodes.example: For an exponential law, Q(u)=-log(1-u)/λ.

patterns.why: Uniform probability coordinates become outcome coordinates.
A single uniform draw generates the desired marginal law.

nodes.name: Probability integral transform
nodes.intuition: A continuous observation's own percentile has no preferred location on the probability scale.
nodes.conditions: X has a continuous CDF; atoms require randomized ranks and invalidate this unmodified statement.
nodes.example: Correctly calibrated continuous predictive percentiles should be uniform.

patterns.why: The CDF removes the original marginal scale.
All continuous marginal laws share the same percentile law.

nodes.name: Survival and hazard relation
nodes.intuition: Hazard measures the instantaneous failure rate among those still present; accumulated hazard determines remaining survival.
nodes.conditions: T≥0 is absolutely continuous, S(0)=1, and S(t)>0 on the interval considered; f is its density.
nodes.example: Constant hazard λ gives exponential survival exp(-λt).

patterns.why: Integrating instantaneous hazard gives total exposure.
Multiplicative survival becomes additive cumulative hazard.

nodes.name: Density of an order statistic
nodes.intuition: The kth ranked value needs k−1 observations below it and the rest above it.
nodes.conditions: X1,…,Xn are iid with absolutely continuous CDF F and density f; 1≤k≤n.
nodes.example: The maximum of n independent uniform(0,1) draws has density n x^(n−1).

patterns.why: The factorial factor counts allocations below and above the selected value.
Rank changes a marginal law into a different sampling law.

nodes.name: Multinomial distribution
nodes.intuition: One total count is divided among several mutually exclusive outcomes.
nodes.conditions: n independent categorical trials; pj≥0, sum pj=1; nj are nonnegative integers summing to n; use 0^0=1.
nodes.example: Counts of six faces in repeated die rolls follow a multinomial law.

patterns.why: The coefficient counts orderings with prescribed category totals.
Category counts must add to the fixed number of trials.

nodes.name: Dirichlet distribution
nodes.intuition: Random proportions share a fixed total; concentration parameters describe both their preferred balance and variability.
nodes.conditions: αj>0; pj>0, sum pj=1; density uses the first k−1 simplex coordinates.
nodes.example: With all αj=1 the distribution is uniform on the probability simplex.

patterns.why: Proportions always sum to one.
Expected category weight is αj/α0.

nodes.name: Lognormal distribution
nodes.intuition: Additive Gaussian variation on a log scale becomes multiplicative variation on a positive scale.
nodes.conditions: σ>0 and μ real; logarithms are natural. The mean is exp(μ+σ²/2), not exp(μ).
nodes.example: A geometric Brownian motion at a fixed positive time is lognormal.

patterns.why: Exponentiation converts additive noise into multiplicative factors.
The 1/x factor is the logarithm's Jacobian.

nodes.name: Chi-squared distribution
nodes.intuition: Squared independent standard Gaussian coordinates turn random displacement into random energy.
nodes.conditions: Zi iid N(0,1) and integer ν≥1 for the sum representation; the density defines the law for any real ν>0.
nodes.example: The squared length of a two-dimensional standard Gaussian vector is χ² with two degrees of freedom.

patterns.why: Squares combine Gaussian coordinates into an energy.
Independent squared coordinates add degrees of freedom.

nodes.name: Student t distribution
nodes.intuition: Dividing a Gaussian quantity by an uncertain estimate of scale adds heavier tails.
nodes.conditions: Z∼N(0,1), V∼χ²ν are independent and ν>0; mean needs ν>1 and variance needs ν>2.
nodes.example: At ν=1 this is the standard Cauchy distribution.

patterns.why: The denominator introduces additional scale uncertainty.
As ν grows, the estimated scale concentrates near one.

nodes.name: F distribution
nodes.intuition: A ratio of independent estimates of variance measures how unusually large one source of variation is relative to another.
nodes.conditions: d1,d2>0; U,V independent. Both degrees-of-freedom divisors are essential.
nodes.example: The square of a tν variable follows F(1,ν).

patterns.why: Normalizing each energy by its degrees of freedom puts them on a common scale.
Both numerator and denominator come from Gaussian squared lengths.

nodes.name: Weibull distribution
nodes.intuition: A power-law change of the clock lets failure risk rise, fall or remain constant with age.
nodes.conditions: Shape k>0 and scale λ>0; density is h(t)S(t) for t>0.
nodes.example: k=1 is exponential; k>1 gives increasing hazard.

patterns.why: A power of time sets how ageing changes risk.
Cumulative hazard is the power (t/λ)^k.

nodes.name: Pareto distribution
nodes.intuition: A fixed proportional increase in the threshold always removes the same fraction of the remaining tail.
nodes.conditions: xm>0, α>0; displayed moment formula for real r<α. Moments of order r≥α diverge.
nodes.example: Doubling the threshold multiplies the survival probability by 2^(−α).

patterns.why: Tail ratios depend on threshold ratios rather than absolute units.
Heavy tails create a precise cutoff between finite and infinite moments.

nodes.name: Cauchy distribution
nodes.intuition: Rare huge observations remain strong enough that averaging does not squeeze the distribution toward a center.
nodes.conditions: Location x0 real, scale γ>0; the ordinary expectation and variance do not exist. Characteristic function uses E exp(itX).
nodes.example: The mean of iid standard Cauchy observations is itself standard Cauchy.

patterns.why: Cauchy sums rescale linearly rather than by a square root.
Multiplying characteristic functions exposes stability under averaging.

nodes.name: Laplace distribution
nodes.intuition: Two exponential tails meet at a sharp center, making absolute deviations the natural measure of mismatch.
nodes.conditions: μ real, b>0; mean μ and variance 2b². This is a probability distribution, distinct from the Laplace transform.
nodes.example: With fixed b, fitting μ by likelihood minimizes the sum of absolute deviations.

patterns.why: Negative log density is proportional to absolute error.
Equal exponential tails extend on both sides of the location.

nodes.name: Wishart Gaussian scatter distribution
nodes.intuition: A scalar sum of squares becomes a matrix of accumulated cross-products, recording energy in every direction.
nodes.conditions: Zi iid Np(0,Σ), Σ positive definite, integer n≥1. W is singular almost surely when n<p; no nonsingular density is asserted then.
nodes.example: A centered normal sample's scatter matrix has Wp(Σ,n−1) distribution.

patterns.why: Outer products store every directional squared projection.
Independent scatter contributions add.

nodes.name: Conditional multivariate Gaussian
nodes.intuition: Observing correlated coordinates shifts the best prediction linearly and removes the uncertainty explained by them.
nodes.conditions: (X,Y) jointly Gaussian; ΣYY positive definite. The remaining covariance may be singular; it does not depend on y.
nodes.example: For standard correlated scalars, X|Y=y has mean ρy and variance 1−ρ².

patterns.why: The residual is uncorrelated, hence Gaussian-independent, from Y.
Completing a block quadratic separates observed and residual parts.

nodes.name: Gaussian integration by parts
nodes.intuition: Multiplication by a Gaussian coordinate can be exchanged for a derivative inside an expectation.
nodes.conditions: f is absolutely continuous, E|f'(Z)| and E|Zf(Z)| finite, with vanishing boundary term f(x)e^(−x²/2) at both infinities.
nodes.example: Taking f(z)=z³ gives E Z⁴=3 E Z²=3.

patterns.why: Coordinate multiplication and differentiation are paired under Gaussian averaging.
The Gaussian log density has derivative −z.

nodes.name: Wick–Isserlis Gaussian moment formula
nodes.intuition: Every centered Gaussian even moment is assembled by pairing coordinates; no extra higher-order interactions are needed.
nodes.conditions: Xi are jointly centered real Gaussian variables, possibly repeated or degenerate. P2 is the set of pair partitions; odd moments vanish.
nodes.example: E[X²Y²]=Var(X)Var(Y)+2Cov(X,Y)².

patterns.why: Each high-order moment splits into products of pairwise covariances.
Pair partitions enumerate the possible contractions.

nodes.name: First Borel–Cantelli lemma
nodes.intuition: If the total probability budget of later failures is finite, failures eventually stop almost surely.
nodes.conditions: An are events in one probability space. Independence is unnecessary; the conclusion concerns infinitely many occurrences.
nodes.example: Failure probabilities bounded by 1/n² imply only finitely many failures almost surely.

patterns.why: Summability controls the entire remaining tail of events.
Tail union probabilities shrink to zero.

nodes.name: Second Borel–Cantelli lemma
nodes.intuition: Independent fresh chances with an infinite total probability budget cannot all dry up after a finite time.
nodes.conditions: An are mutually independent events; divergence alone is insufficient for arbitrarily dependent events.
nodes.example: Independent trials with success probability 1/n succeed infinitely often almost surely.

patterns.why: Independence keeps later opportunities genuinely fresh.
Products of avoidance probabilities tend to zero.

nodes.name: Kolmogorov zero–one law
nodes.intuition: An event unaffected by every finite initial segment of an independent sequence cannot retain an intermediate probability.
nodes.conditions: Xn are mutually independent. The displayed intersection is the tail sigma-algebra; no identical-distribution assumption is needed.
nodes.example: Convergence of an independent random series is a tail event and has probability zero or one.

patterns.why: Discarding finitely many coordinates leaves tail events unchanged.
A tail event is independent of every finite block and ultimately of itself.

nodes.name: Convergence in probability
nodes.intuition: For any fixed error tolerance, the chance of exceeding it eventually becomes negligible.
nodes.conditions: Xn and X are real random variables on one probability space; this need not give convergence along every sample path.
nodes.example: A Bernoulli sample proportion converges in probability to its success probability.

patterns.why: Probability of each fixed-size error vanishes.
The approximation guarantee is probabilistic rather than pointwise.

nodes.name: Convergence in distribution
nodes.latex: X_n\Rightarrow X\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F_{X_n}(x)\to F_X(x)\ \text{at every continuity point of }F_X
nodes.intuition: The distributions approach one another even when individual random outcomes cannot meaningfully be paired.
nodes.conditions: Real random variables may live on different probability spaces. CDF convergence is required only at continuity points of the limit.
nodes.example: Standardized binomial sums approach a normal distribution.

patterns.why: Whole probability laws converge through their cumulative values.
Only distributional information survives; sample-path matching is absent.

nodes.name: Lp convergence of random variables
nodes.intuition: Lp convergence makes the average powered error disappear, so rare errors must also be small enough in magnitude.
nodes.conditions: Xn,X belong to Lp on a common probability space; p is finite. Larger p penalizes extremes more strongly.
nodes.example: Independent sample means with finite variance converge in L² to their common mean.

patterns.why: The error is measured by an expected powered magnitude.
A norm tending to zero strengthens probability-only control.

nodes.name: Continuous mapping theorem
nodes.intuition: A transformation preserves a distributional limit when its discontinuities do not matter to the limiting law.
nodes.conditions: Xn,X are random vectors in Euclidean spaces, g is measurable, and Dg is its discontinuity set.
nodes.example: Squaring an asymptotically standard normal statistic produces an asymptotic χ²1 statistic.

patterns.why: Limits pass through transformations continuous at almost every limiting outcome.
Distributional convergence is stable under suitable mappings.

nodes.name: Slutsky's theorem
nodes.latex: X_n\Rightarrow X,\ Y_n\xrightarrow{p}c\quad\Longrightarrow\quad X_nY_n\Rightarrow cX,\quad X_n+Y_n\Rightarrow X+c
nodes.intuition: A factor whose uncertainty vanishes can be replaced by its constant limit in a distributional calculation.
nodes.conditions: Real random variables; c deterministic. Division also holds when c≠0. Independence of Xn and Yn is unnecessary.
nodes.example: A consistent standard-error estimate can replace the unknown scale in a CLT pivot.

patterns.why: A concentrating nuisance factor behaves as a fixed coefficient.
Distributional and probability limits combine when one limit is constant.

nodes.name: Lévy continuity theorem
nodes.intuition: Convergence of all oscillatory probes identifies a limiting probability law, provided no mass escapes.
nodes.conditions: φn are characteristic functions on R^d. Their pointwise limit must be continuous at zero; necessarily φ(0)=1.
nodes.example: Multiplying characteristic functions and taking a quadratic limit proves many central limit theorems.

patterns.why: Oscillatory transforms encode complete probability laws.
Continuity at zero ensures the transform limit corresponds to a probability measure.

nodes.name: Berry–Esseen bound
nodes.intuition: The central limit approximation has a measurable error budget; heavy third moments make convergence slower.
nodes.conditions: Xi iid, E Xi=μ, Var Xi=σ²>0, finite third absolute centered moment. C is a universal finite constant.
nodes.example: For bounded Bernoulli variables away from p=0 or 1, CDF error is O(n^−1/2).

patterns.why: The standardized third moment is dimensionless.
A finite-sample bound quantifies approach to the Gaussian law.

nodes.name: Lindeberg triangular-array CLT
nodes.intuition: Many unequal small contributions still make Gaussian noise when no large contribution carries a lasting fraction of the variance.
nodes.conditions: Each row contains independent centered variables with finite variances; sn²=sumk Var(Xnk)>0. The displayed Lindeberg condition holds for every ε>0.
nodes.example: Bounded centered triangular arrays satisfy the condition when their maximal magnitude is o(sn).

patterns.why: Total fluctuations split among row-wise independent contributions.
The Lindeberg cutoff measures each contribution against total standard deviation.

nodes.name: Sub-Gaussian moment bound
nodes.intuition: A variable need not be Gaussian to have fluctuations whose exponential moments are bounded by a Gaussian envelope.
nodes.conditions: X integrable; σ²≥0 is a variance proxy, not necessarily the actual variance. The bound must hold for every real t.
nodes.example: A variable in [a,b] is sub-Gaussian with proxy (b−a)²/4.

patterns.why: Exponential moments compare tails through a quadratic exponent.
The Gaussian-shaped quadratic controls deviations at every exponential tilt.

nodes.name: Bernstein inequality for bounded sums
nodes.intuition: Small deviations depend on actual variance, while very large deviations also feel the maximum size of one summand.
nodes.conditions: Xi independent, centered, |Xi|≤M almost surely, M>0, t≥0; 0<v<∞. If v=0, the sum is identically zero and its tails can be handled directly.
nodes.example: Rare Bernoulli successes can concentrate more sharply than a range-only Hoeffding estimate suggests.

patterns.why: Variance controls the near-mean quadratic exponent.
The linear Mt term describes the large-deviation scale.

nodes.name: Bennett inequality
nodes.intuition: A sharper exponential calculation preserves the transition from Gaussian-size fluctuations to rare large upward deviations.
nodes.conditions: Independent centered Xi≤M almost surely, M>0; v=sum E Xi² is finite and positive; t≥0.
nodes.example: Expanding h(u) near zero recovers the variance-controlled Gaussian exponent.

patterns.why: The convex function h records the optimized exponential tilt.
The tail exponent retains a logarithmic large-deviation shape.

nodes.name: Cantelli one-sided variance bound
nodes.intuition: Knowing which side matters gives a sharper variance-only bound than treating both tails together.
nodes.conditions: E X=μ and Var X=σ²<∞. No independence or density assumptions are needed.
nodes.example: At two standard deviations above the mean, the bound is 1/5.

patterns.why: A shifted square is optimized to target only the upper tail.
The entire guarantee comes from the first two moments.

nodes.name: Paley–Zygmund lower bound
nodes.intuition: A nonnegative quantity with a substantial mean and controlled second moment cannot be tiny almost all the time.
nodes.conditions: X≥0 almost surely and 0<E X²<∞, with E X>0.
nodes.example: A second-moment argument can prove a random combinatorial count is positive with nonzero probability.

patterns.why: The ratio of squared first moment to second moment measures concentration of mass.
The result gives a lower probability bound from moment data.

nodes.name: Efron–Stein variance inequality
nodes.intuition: A function cannot fluctuate much if independently replacing any one input usually changes it only a little.
nodes.conditions: Xi independent, f(X) square-integrable; X^(i) replaces Xi by an independent copy with its same distribution.
nodes.example: For f=sum Xi, the inequality is an equality and recovers the variance sum.

patterns.why: Resampling one coordinate isolates its contribution to variability.
Squared input-replacement effects bound output variance.

nodes.name: McDiarmid bounded-difference inequality
nodes.intuition: Many individually harmless inputs cannot easily combine into a large surprise, even when the output is nonlinear.
nodes.conditions: Xi independent; changing only coordinate i changes f by at most ci everywhere on the support; t≥0.
nodes.example: An empirical average of [0,1] values has ci=1/n and exponent −2nt².

patterns.why: Coordinate-wise influence controls a nonlinear total.
Squared sensitivity sizes determine the effective fluctuation scale.

nodes.name: Azuma–Hoeffding martingale bound
nodes.intuition: A fair evolving estimate still concentrates when each surprise is bounded, even though the surprises need not be independent.
nodes.conditions: Mi is a real martingale and |Mi−M(i−1)|≤ci almost surely for deterministic ci; t≥0.
nodes.example: An adapted game with bounded fair increments has exponentially unlikely large gains.

patterns.why: Conditional fairness replaces independence of increments.
The bound adds squared limits on successive surprises.

nodes.name: Kolmogorov maximal inequality
nodes.intuition: The final variance budget also controls the chance that any earlier partial sum crossed a fixed boundary.
nodes.conditions: Xi independent, centered and square-integrable; t>0. The maximum is over the entire finite sequence of partial sums.
nodes.example: The inequality controls maximal fluctuations in proofs of strong laws.

patterns.why: All partial sums share one total variance budget.
First boundary crossing identifies which paths need to be counted.

nodes.name: Cramér large-deviation principle
nodes.latex: I(x)=\sup_t\{tx-\log\mathbb E e^{tX_1}\},\quad -\inf_{A^\circ}I\le\liminf_n\frac1n\log\Pr(\bar X_n\in A)\le\limsup_n\frac1n\log\Pr(\bar X_n\in A)\le-\inf_{\overline A}I
nodes.intuition: Rare sample means have an exponential cost determined by the cheapest tilt that makes them typical.
nodes.conditions: Xi iid real; their MGF is finite on a neighborhood of zero. A is Borel; infimum of the empty set is infinity.
nodes.example: For N(μ,σ²) observations the rate is (x−μ)²/(2σ²).

patterns.why: The rate function is the convex conjugate of the cumulant generator.
Probabilities are described on the logarithmic scale n.

nodes.name: Le Cam Poisson approximation
nodes.intuition: Many rare independent opportunities behave almost like a Poisson count; the squared probabilities measure collisions with the rare-event approximation.
nodes.conditions: Bi independent Bernoulli(pi); dTV is supremum over events, equivalently half the L1 probability difference.
nodes.example: Binomial(n,λ/n) has approximation error at most λ²/n.

patterns.why: Rare-event scaling makes the approximation error vanish.
The target Poisson mean adds the individual success probabilities.

nodes.name: Wald's random-sum identity
nodes.intuition: A fair stopping rule changes how many increments are collected without changing the expected reward per included increment.
nodes.conditions: Xi iid integrable; N is a nonnegative integer stopping time for their natural filtration and E N<∞. These ensure absolute integrability of the stopped sum.
nodes.example: Expected total reward up to a stopping time equals expected count times mean reward.

patterns.why: Expected reward per included increment stays constant.
A stopped sum is expanded using indicators that the next increment is included.

nodes.name: Variance of an independent random sum
nodes.intuition: Total uncertainty splits into noisy items and uncertainty about how many items there are.
nodes.conditions: Xi iid with finite second moment; N independent of the entire sequence, nonnegative integer valued, with finite second moment. An empty sum is zero.
nodes.example: For Poisson N with mean λ, variance of the compound sum is λ E X1².

patterns.why: Within-count noise and between-count variation contribute separately.
Fluctuating counts multiply the square of the item mean.

nodes.name: Sklar's copula representation
nodes.intuition: Separate the shape of each variable from the way their percentiles move together.
nodes.conditions: F is a joint CDF with marginal CDFs Fj. C is a CDF on [0,1]^d with uniform marginals; it is unique when all Fj are continuous.
nodes.example: Independence corresponds to C(u)=the product of the coordinates.

patterns.why: Marginal laws and dependence are represented separately.
Each coordinate is moved to its cumulative probability scale.

nodes.name: Fréchet–Hoeffding copula bounds
nodes.intuition: Marginal probabilities alone already restrict how large or small an intersection can be.
nodes.conditions: C is a d-dimensional copula and u∈[0,1]^d. The upper bound is a copula in every dimension; the lower-bound function is a copula only for d=2.
nodes.example: For two uniforms, (U,U) attains the upper bound and (U,1−U) the lower bound.

patterns.why: Extreme couplings bound all intermediate dependence structures.
An intersection cannot exceed the probability available in any marginal.

nodes.name: Statistical risk
nodes.intuition: Judge a data-dependent decision by averaging its loss over repeated datasets from a specified truth.
nodes.conditions: A statistical model Pθ, measurable decision rule δ, and nonnegative measurable loss L; risk may be infinite.
nodes.example: With squared error, risk is the estimator's mean squared error.

patterns.why: Loss is averaged over the sampling distribution.
Different decision rules can be compared under one explicit objective.

nodes.name: Bayes action by posterior expected loss
nodes.intuition: After observing data, weight each possible consequence by the posterior and choose the smallest expected loss.
nodes.conditions: A proper prior and well-defined posterior are given; a measurable minimizing action exists. Integrated losses must be defined, possibly nonnegative extended values.
nodes.example: Squared-error loss selects the posterior mean; zero–one loss for a finite parameter set selects a posterior mode.

patterns.why: Posterior probabilities weight possible consequences.
The best action depends on the chosen loss, not just on a likely parameter.

nodes.name: Bayes classifier and irreducible error
nodes.intuition: At each input, choose the most likely label; the remaining conditional probability is unavoidable classification error.
nodes.conditions: A finite label set, measurable conditional class probabilities, and zero–one loss. Ties can be broken measurably.
nodes.example: If class probabilities are (0.7,0.2,0.1), minimum conditional error is 0.3.

patterns.why: Each input gets the label minimizing its conditional error.
Uncertainty remaining after observing X sets the best possible accuracy.

nodes.name: Quantiles minimize pinball loss
nodes.intuition: Charging underestimates and overestimates differently moves the best prediction from the center to a chosen percentile.
nodes.conditions: X integrable and 0<τ<1. Atoms can give nonunique minimizers; the displayed interval condition handles them.
nodes.example: At τ=1/2 this is half absolute error, so every median minimizes it.

patterns.why: The target statistic changes when the loss changes.
One-sided slopes bracket zero exactly at a τ-quantile.

nodes.name: Minimax statistical risk
nodes.intuition: Choose a procedure whose worst supported truth hurts as little as possible.
nodes.conditions: A specified model class Θ, sample experiment and nonnegative loss; the infimum may not be attained. This is a statistical decision criterion.
nodes.example: For one observation Y∼Nd(θ,σ²I) and squared error, the usual estimator has constant risk dσ².

patterns.why: The order infimum over procedures then supremum over truths fixes the criterion.
Priors supply lower bounds by averaging risks below their worst value.

nodes.name: James–Stein shrinkage estimator
nodes.intuition: Several noisy coordinates can borrow strength from a common center, lowering total squared error even when the true means are unrelated.
nodes.conditions: Y∼Nd(θ,σ²I), d≥3, known σ²>0; squared Euclidean loss. Define the estimator arbitrarily at Y=0, a probability-zero event.
nodes.example: With d=5 and ||Y||²=12σ², all coordinates are multiplied by 3/4.

patterns.why: A common shrinkage factor shares evidence about signal magnitude across coordinates.
Controlled bias lowers total risk despite each coordinate's unbiased alternative.

nodes.name: Stein's unbiased risk estimate
nodes.intuition: Training residuals underestimate prediction error; the estimator's sensitivity supplies an exact average correction for Gaussian noise.
nodes.conditions: Y∼Nd(θ,σ²I), known σ²; δ weakly differentiable with integrable derivative terms and squared error, and boundary conditions permitting Gaussian integration by parts.
nodes.example: For δ(Y)=aY, the divergence is ad, giving a directly computable shrinkage-risk estimate.

patterns.why: Divergence measures how much fitted output reacts to perturbing its own data.
The correction is unbiased after averaging over Gaussian noise.

nodes.name: Minimal sufficient statistic criterion
nodes.intuition: Two datasets can be compressed together exactly when their relative likelihood carries no parameter information.
nodes.conditions: A dominated model with positive densities on a common support; T measurable. The criterion characterizes minimal sufficiency up to model-null sets.
nodes.example: For iid Poisson data, equal sample sums give parameter-independent likelihood ratios.

patterns.why: The statistic retains exactly the likelihood distinctions relevant to θ.
Datasets are partitioned into classes with proportional likelihood functions.

nodes.name: Completeness of a statistic
nodes.latex: \bigl[\mathbb E_\theta g(T)=0\ \forall\theta\bigr]\quad\Longrightarrow\quad g(T)=0\quad P_\theta\text{-a.s. for every }\theta
nodes.intuition: A complete statistic has no nontrivial function that averages to zero for every possible truth.
nodes.conditions: The implication is required for all measurable g with Eθ|g(T)|<∞ for every θ. Completeness is a property of a family of distributions.
nodes.example: A Poisson count with parameter ranging over all positive values is complete.

patterns.why: No nonzero parameter-invisible mean-zero adjustment remains.
The expectation operator has no nontrivial common null direction on functions of T.

nodes.name: Lehmann–Scheffé theorem
nodes.latex: T\text{ complete sufficient},\quad \mathbb E_\theta g(T)=\tau(\theta)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad g(T)\text{ is the unique UMVU estimator of }\tau
nodes.intuition: Once all information is compressed into a complete statistic, an unbiased estimate built from it cannot be improved in variance.
nodes.conditions: T complete and sufficient; g(T) square-integrable for every θ. Uniqueness is up to almost sure equality for every model distribution.
nodes.example: The sample mean is the unique UMVU estimator of a Poisson mean.

patterns.why: Variance is minimal within the class of unbiased estimators.
Sufficiency removes irrelevant noise; completeness removes alternative unbiased summaries.

nodes.name: Basu's theorem
nodes.latex: T\text{ complete sufficient},\quad A\text{ ancillary}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad T\perp A
nodes.intuition: A complete summary of parameter information is independent of statistics whose entire distribution is parameter-free.
nodes.conditions: A is ancillary, meaning its law is the same for every θ; T is complete and sufficient for the same model.
nodes.example: In a normal location family with known variance, the sample mean is independent of centered residual statistics.

patterns.why: Parameter information separates from parameter-free sampling variation.
Sufficiency and completeness turn lack of parameter dependence into independence.

nodes.name: Fisher information under reparameterization
nodes.intuition: Information about a coordinate changes with its units and directions, exactly like a quadratic measurement of small displacements.
nodes.conditions: Differentiable parameter map θ(η) in a model with square-integrable scores; J has compatible dimensions. Invertibility is needed only for a true coordinate change.
nodes.example: For η=log σ, information rescales by (dσ/dη)²=σ² in the scalar case.

patterns.why: Scores transform by the transpose Jacobian.
The information matrix transforms as a metric tensor.

nodes.name: Asymptotic normality of a regular MLE
nodes.intuition: Near the true parameter, a smooth likelihood is approximately quadratic and its random slope is approximately Gaussian.
nodes.conditions: Iid data; consistent interior MLE; differentiable score with a CLT, mean zero and positive definite covariance I; normalized Hessian converges locally uniformly to −I.
nodes.example: The exponential rate MLE 1/mean has asymptotic variance λ²/n.

patterns.why: Linearizing the score equation transfers its Gaussian noise to parameter error.
Likelihood curvature rescales score fluctuations.

nodes.name: Sandwich covariance for estimating equations
nodes.latex: \sum_i\psi(X_i,\widehat\theta)=0,\quad \sqrt n(\widehat\theta-\theta_0)\Rightarrow N(0,A^{-1}BA^{-\top}),\ A=\mathbb E\partial_\theta\psi,\ B=\mathbb E[\psi\psi^\top]
nodes.intuition: Noise in an estimating equation is filtered through its sensitivity on both sides of the covariance.
nodes.conditions: Iid data; E ψ(X,θ0)=0, finite second moments; consistent root; A nonsingular; a locally uniform derivative LLN justifies linearization.
nodes.example: Heteroskedastic regression uses residual score variability between inverse design-sensitivity factors.

patterns.why: Inverting the local estimating equation converts score errors into parameter errors.
Covariance transforms on both sides, producing the sandwich.

nodes.name: Wald test for smooth restrictions
nodes.intuition: Measure the estimated violation of a hypothesis in units of its own uncertainty.
nodes.conditions: Under g(θ0)=0, sqrt(n)(θhat−θ0)⇒N(0,V); Vhat consistent; g differentiable with derivative G of row rank r and GVGᵀ positive definite.
nodes.example: For one scalar restriction, this is the square of its asymptotic z statistic.

patterns.why: The inverse covariance measures distance from the null in uncertainty units.
A derivative transfers parameter uncertainty to restriction uncertainty.

nodes.name: Rao score test
nodes.intuition: Test whether the likelihood still has an unusually strong slope at the proposed parameter.
nodes.conditions: Simple null θ=θ0 in a d-dimensional iid regular model; score CLT and nonsingular information In=nI. Formula has no nuisance parameters.
nodes.example: A Bernoulli success-rate score test compares the observed proportion with the null proportion.

patterns.why: The likelihood slope detects a local departure from the null.
Information normalizes the score's squared length.

nodes.name: Confidence sets by test inversion
nodes.intuition: Keep every parameter value that its own level-α test would not reject.
nodes.conditions: For each θ, the rejection indicator φθ has Eθ φθ≤α; the inverted set is measurable. Randomized tests require their auxiliary randomization in the sample.
nodes.example: Inverting two-sided normal mean tests yields the usual confidence interval.

patterns.why: Tests and confidence regions are two views of the same acceptance sets.
The confidence set collects null values compatible with the observed statistic.

nodes.name: Bonferroni familywise correction
nodes.intuition: Divide one overall false-alarm allowance among all the questions being asked.
nodes.conditions: m≥1 tests; every true-null p-value is super-uniform. Dependence among tests is unrestricted; V counts false rejections.
nodes.example: With 20 tests and familywise α=0.05, each threshold is 0.0025.

patterns.why: Individual error allowances add to the overall budget.
The total type-I-error allocation stays within α.

nodes.name: Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery control
nodes.intuition: Allow more discoveries when many p-values are convincing while controlling the expected fraction of false discoveries.
nodes.conditions: Independent p-values with super-uniform true-null p-values; m tests. If the defining set is empty reject none. R is total rejections.
nodes.example: The rule controls an expected fraction, not the chance that every reported finding is true.

patterns.why: The controlled quantity is the expectation of the false-discovery proportion.
The rank-dependent threshold adapts to the number of discoveries.

nodes.name: Permutation randomization test
nodes.intuition: Compare the observed statistic with values obtained by relabeling data in ways the null model treats as interchangeable.
nodes.conditions: A finite transformation group G leaves the null distribution invariant; the full orbit, including identity, is used. The nonrandomized p-value is conservative with ties.
nodes.example: Under equal iid group distributions, permuting group labels tests a difference in means.

patterns.why: Null-valid transformations preserve the data's law.
The tail rank among transformed datasets becomes a p-value.

nodes.name: Fisher exact test distribution
nodes.intuition: After fixing row and column totals, count which table allocations remain possible under independence.
nodes.conditions: A is the upper-left cell of a 2×2 table under the null odds ratio 1; margins fixed or conditioned upon. Only feasible integer a are included.
nodes.example: Summing the displayed probabilities over a chosen tail gives an exact one-sided test.

patterns.why: Possible allocations with fixed margins are counted combinatorially.
Conditioning keeps both row and column totals fixed.

nodes.name: Kolmogorov–Smirnov one-sample statistic
nodes.intuition: Find the largest discrepancy between an observed cumulative curve and a proposed distribution.
nodes.conditions: Iid observations under a fully specified continuous null CDF F0; z>0. Fitting null parameters from the same data changes the reference law.
nodes.example: Testing a fully specified uniform law gives the same null distribution as testing a fully specified normal law.

patterns.why: A supremum distance measures the worst cumulative mismatch.
The probability integral transform removes the continuous null's shape.

nodes.name: Dvoretzky–Kiefer–Wolfowitz inequality
