nodes.intuition: One exponential bound covers the entire empirical cumulative curve, despite infinitely many possible thresholds.
nodes.conditions: Xi iid real with any CDF F; n≥1 and ε>0. No continuity assumption on F is needed.
nodes.example: A confidence band half-width is sqrt(log(2/α)/(2n)).

patterns.why: The entire empirical CDF concentrates uniformly.
A single band simultaneously bounds every threshold probability.

nodes.name: Glivenko–Cantelli theorem
nodes.intuition: Repeated sampling eventually learns every threshold probability at once.
nodes.conditions: Xi iid real with CDF F; Fn is their empirical CDF. This is a uniform almost sure statement, stronger than pointwise laws of large numbers.
nodes.example: An empirical CDF converges uniformly even when the true distribution has atoms.

patterns.why: The worst error across all thresholds tends to zero.
Every CDF value is an average of indicators from the same sample.

nodes.name: Asymptotic distribution of a sample quantile
nodes.intuition: An empirical percentile is unstable when the cumulative curve is flat near the target.
nodes.conditions: Xi iid; 0<τ<1; qτ is unique; F differentiable near qτ with continuous density f(qτ)>0. qhat is the empirical generalized quantile.
nodes.example: For a standard normal sample median, asymptotic variance is π/(2n).

patterns.why: Inverting the local CDF slope divides fluctuation by f(qτ).
The density at the target converts probability error into outcome error.

nodes.name: Unbiased U-statistic
nodes.latex: U_n=\binom nm^{-1}\sum_{1\le i_1<\cdots<i_m\le n}h(X_{i_1},\ldots,X_{i_m}),\qquad \mathbb E U_n=\mathbb E h(X_1,\ldots,X_m)
nodes.intuition: Average the same symmetric calculation over every subset of the required size, spreading information evenly across observations.
nodes.conditions: Xi iid; h symmetric and integrable; integers 1≤m≤n. Terms share data and are generally dependent.
nodes.example: With m=2 and h(x,y)=(x−y)²/2, the U-statistic is the unbiased sample variance.

patterns.why: All equally sized subsets contribute equally.
Relabeling observations leaves the statistic unchanged.

nodes.name: Jackknife variance estimate
nodes.intuition: Remove each observation in turn and measure how much the estimate reacts to losing one data point.
nodes.conditions: n>1; θhat(−i) fits the same procedure to n−1 observations. Consistency needs smooth asymptotically linear behavior and can fail for nonsmooth statistics such as raw quantiles.
nodes.example: For the sample mean the jackknife variance equals s²/n.

patterns.why: Delete-one sensitivity approximates the influence of individual observations.
Squared sensitivity is accumulated into a variance estimate.

nodes.name: K-fold cross-validation
nodes.intuition: Let each observation take a turn as an unseen exam question for a model trained on the other folds.
nodes.conditions: Disjoint folds partition the data; each fit excludes its validation fold, including preprocessing and tuning internal to that fit. Iid prediction requires an appropriate sampling split.
nodes.example: Five-fold validation evaluates models trained on roughly 80% of the data.

patterns.why: The sample is divided into complementary training and validation roles.
Held-out losses are pooled over all observations.

nodes.name: Leave-one-out shortcut for linear smoothers
nodes.intuition: A point that strongly pulls its own fitted value needs a larger correction when pretending it was held out.
nodes.conditions: Squared loss; ordinary least squares or ridge with fixed penalty and linear hat matrix H; Hii≠1 and each deleted fit exists. Arbitrary data-adaptive smoothers need not obey the shortcut.
nodes.example: High-leverage observations get residual inflation by 1/(1−Hii).

patterns.why: Diagonal leverage quantifies a datum's influence on its own fit.
Full-data fitting and self-influence separate algebraically.

nodes.name: Akaike information criterion
nodes.intuition: Reward fit while charging for the optimism gained by estimating parameters on the same data.
nodes.conditions: Compare likelihoods for the same observations and base measure; k is the number of freely estimated parameters. The 2k optimism justification is asymptotic for regular correctly specified fixed-dimensional models.
nodes.example: Adding one parameter must improve maximized log likelihood by more than one to reduce AIC.

patterns.why: Observed fit and complexity correction are added separately.
The criterion approximates expected predictive log-loss comparison.

nodes.name: Bayesian information criterion
nodes.intuition: A flexible model spreads prior support over more parameter volume, creating a sample-size-dependent evidence penalty.
nodes.conditions: Same observations and likelihood measure across models; regular fixed-dimensional iid models with locally positive smooth priors and interior nonsingular likelihood peaks for the evidence approximation.
nodes.example: At n=100, one extra parameter costs log(100)≈4.61 BIC units.

patterns.why: Posterior concentration volume shrinks like n^(−k/2).
The score approximates negative twice log marginal evidence up to bounded terms.

nodes.name: Bayes factor
nodes.intuition: Evidence compares each model after averaging over the parameter values it predicted before seeing the data.
nodes.conditions: Proper within-model priors; finite marginal likelihoods with positive denominator; common data measure. Arbitrarily normalized improper priors do not define a Bayes factor.
nodes.example: A Bayes factor of 4 multiplies prior model odds by 4.

patterns.why: Each likelihood is integrated over its model's prior.
Data update model odds by an evidence ratio.

nodes.name: Jeffreys prior measure
nodes.intuition: Allocate prior mass by distinguishability of nearby distributions instead of equal numerical parameter increments.
nodes.conditions: Regular identifiable model with positive definite Fisher information. The measure may be improper; posterior propriety and any model-evidence use must be checked separately.
nodes.example: For a Bernoulli probability, the prior is Beta(1/2,1/2).

patterns.why: The density transforms correctly under smooth one-to-one reparameterizations.
Fisher information supplies a local volume element.

nodes.name: Dirichlet–multinomial posterior update
nodes.intuition: Observed category counts add to prior pseudo-counts while preserving the same probability-simplex geometry.
nodes.conditions: αj>0, fixed finite categories, categorical sampling conditionally iid given p, and counts sum to n.
nodes.example: The next-label predictive probability is (αj+Nj)/(α0+n).

patterns.why: Prior and data counts add coordinate by coordinate.
Posterior predictions blend prior proportions with empirical proportions.

nodes.name: Gamma–Poisson posterior update
nodes.intuition: Counts add to the evidence numerator, while observation exposure adds to the rate denominator.
nodes.conditions: Gamma uses shape α>0 and rate β>0; exposures ti≥0 known; counts conditionally independent. At ti=0 the count must be zero.
nodes.example: The posterior mean is (α+total count)/(β+total exposure).

patterns.why: Events and exposure contribute separate additive sufficient statistics.
Multiplying conjugate exponential forms updates exponents and rates.

nodes.name: Kaplan–Meier survival estimator
nodes.intuition: Multiply the observed survival fractions at successive event times, updating who is still eligible to fail.
nodes.conditions: Independent subjects with noninformative right censoring; tj distinct event times, dj failures, nj at risk just before tj>0. Follow-up supports estimation only over observed risk sets.
nodes.example: If one of ten and then two of eight at-risk subjects fail, estimated survival is (9/10)(6/8).

patterns.why: Conditional survival fractions multiply over time.
Each risk set accounts for those remaining under observation.

nodes.name: Nelson–Aalen cumulative hazard estimator
nodes.intuition: Add estimated local failure exposure instead of multiplying local survival fractions.
nodes.conditions: Independent subjects and noninformative right censoring; tj event times, dj failures and nj>0 at risk immediately before tj.
nodes.example: When every dj/nj is small, exp(−Hhat(t)) is close to Kaplan–Meier survival.

patterns.why: Hazard increments add across event times.
Cumulative hazard approximates negative log product survival.

nodes.name: Cox proportional-hazards partial likelihood
nodes.intuition: At each failure, compare the subject with everyone still at risk; the common baseline hazard cancels from that competition.
nodes.conditions: Independent subjects, proportional hazards, conditionally noninformative right censoring, and no tied event times for this formula. R(ti) is the risk set just before ti.
nodes.example: A unit covariate increase multiplies hazard by exp(β), assuming other covariates fixed.

patterns.why: A common unknown baseline cancels in conditional relative hazards.
Multiplying risk-set contributions yields an estimable coefficient objective.

nodes.name: Kernel density estimator
nodes.intuition: Replace each observed point mass by a small normalized bump, then average the bumps.
nodes.conditions: Real observations, h>0, and nonnegative kernel K with integral one. Iid sampling is assumed for standard statistical properties.
nodes.example: A Gaussian kernel creates a mixture of equal-width Gaussian bumps centered at the data.

patterns.why: Each observation contributes an equally weighted local density.
The 1/h factor preserves unit mass as bump width changes.

nodes.name: Kernel density bias–variance bandwidth law
nodes.intuition: Narrow bumps reduce smoothing bias but leave noisy spikes; wide bumps trade detail for stability.
nodes.conditions: Iid real data; h→0 and nh→∞; symmetric bounded compactly supported probability kernel; f has bounded continuous second derivative with f''∈L². R(g)=∫g² and μ2(K)=∫u²K(u)du.
nodes.example: Balancing leading terms gives bandwidth of order n^−1/5.

patterns.why: Integrated error splits into variance and squared smoothing bias.
Opposite powers 1/(nh) and h⁴ create the optimal bandwidth scale.

nodes.name: Nadaraya–Watson regression
nodes.intuition: Predict locally by letting nearby observations vote more strongly than distant ones.
nodes.conditions: h>0, nonnegative kernel K, positive denominator; paired observations. To target E[Y|X=x], use iid sampling with integrable responses and appropriate smoothing conditions.
nodes.example: A box kernel averages responses whose inputs lie in a neighborhood of x.

patterns.why: Normalized distance-dependent weights form a local mean.
Input proximity determines which observations contribute most.

nodes.name: Quantile regression
nodes.intuition: Fit a conditional percentile surface by charging residuals differently on its two sides.
nodes.conditions: 0<τ<1; finite design and responses; rho is the pinball loss. Minimizers may be nonunique. A linear conditional quantile is a modeling assumption.
nodes.example: At τ=0.5 this is least absolute deviations regression.

patterns.why: An asymmetric convex objective targets a chosen conditional quantile.
Piecewise-linear residual costs reduce sensitivity to extreme magnitudes.

nodes.name: Huber loss
nodes.intuition: Treat small discrepancies like Gaussian noise but stop letting one extreme residual exert an arbitrarily large force.
nodes.conditions: δ>0; real residual r. The loss is convex and continuously differentiable but not twice differentiable at ±δ.
nodes.example: A residual ten times the threshold has the same derivative magnitude as a residual twice the threshold.

patterns.why: Large errors have bounded slope and therefore bounded residual influence.
A quadratic center joins smoothly to linear tails.

nodes.name: M-estimation objective and equation
nodes.intuition: Define an estimator by the total discrepancy it minimizes, then balance the resulting forces when differentiability permits.
nodes.conditions: The minimizer exists; the displayed first-order equation additionally assumes an interior differentiable optimum. It is necessary, not generally sufficient, without convexity.
nodes.example: Negative log likelihood, squared error and Huber loss give different M-estimators.

patterns.why: Statistical estimation is expressed as minimizing an empirical objective.
Individual observations contribute additive discrepancy or score terms.

nodes.name: Elastic net regression
nodes.intuition: Combine a preference for sparse coefficients with a preference for sharing weight across correlated directions.
nodes.conditions: Finite real design; λ1,λ2≥0. If λ2>0 the coefficient objective is strongly convex and the minimizer is unique. Intercepts, if exempted, are handled separately.
nodes.example: λ2=0 gives lasso; λ1=0 gives ridge with the corresponding normalization.

patterns.why: Two penalties express distinct preferences in one convex objective.
The quadratic penalty supplies strict curvature even with dependent columns.

nodes.name: Regression hat matrix and leverage
nodes.intuition: Regression projects the response vector onto the span of available predictor patterns.
nodes.conditions: X is n×p with full column rank. Hii is leverage; it depends on the design, not on y.
nodes.example: With only an intercept, every fitted response is the sample mean and each leverage is 1/n.

patterns.why: Fitted and residual vectors occupy perpendicular subspaces.
The p-dimensional fitted subspace distributes p units of total leverage.

nodes.name: Frisch–Waugh–Lovell residualization
nodes.intuition: To measure a predictor block's added contribution, first remove everything the other block can already explain.
nodes.conditions: [X1 X2] has full column rank. Residualize both the response and X2 against X1; residualizing only the response is insufficient.
nodes.example: An adjusted slope is obtained by regressing residualized outcomes on residualized predictor values.

patterns.why: Residualization removes components in the nuisance predictor subspace.
A joint regression is split into nuisance and remaining contributions.

nodes.name: Generalized linear model mean–variance structure
nodes.intuition: Keep a linear predictor while allowing response means, distributions and variances appropriate to counts, categories or positive outcomes.
nodes.conditions: One-parameter exponential-dispersion family with regular differentiation of its normalizer; a chosen invertible link g on the mean domain. Observations usually conditionally independent.
nodes.example: Poisson regression uses log μ=xᵀβ and variance μ.

patterns.why: Differentiating the log normalizer generates mean and variance.
The link maps a constrained mean scale to a linear predictor.

nodes.name: Gaussian linear discriminant analysis
nodes.intuition: When classes share the same Gaussian shape, common quadratic terms cancel and only linear comparisons remain.
nodes.conditions: Class-conditional X|Y=k∼N(μk,Σ), shared positive definite Σ, priors πk>0; zero–one classification loss.
nodes.example: For two classes, the decision boundary is a hyperplane normal to Σ^−1(μ1−μ0).

patterns.why: Equal covariance matrices make quadratic x terms cancel.
The discriminant chooses the largest posterior class score.

nodes.name: Partial correlation from precision
nodes.intuition: Remove the linear effects of all other variables before measuring how two residuals move together.
nodes.conditions: A random vector has finite second moments and positive definite covariance Σ. The formula gives linear partial correlation; zero implies conditional independence only for jointly Gaussian variables.
nodes.example: A zero off-diagonal precision entry marks a missing conditional-dependence edge in a Gaussian graphical model.

patterns.why: Shared effects from the remaining variables are removed by projection.
Residual correlations describe what remains after linear adjustment.

nodes.name: F test for nested Gaussian linear models
nodes.intuition: Compare improvement from extra fitted directions with the unexplained variation per remaining direction.
nodes.conditions: Fixed nested full-rank design spaces of dimensions p0<p1<n; q=p1−p0; independent N(0,σ²) errors; the smaller mean model is true under H0.
nodes.example: Testing one additional coefficient gives the square of its t test statistic.

patterns.why: Additional fitted and remaining residual subspaces are perpendicular.
Independent Gaussian sums of squares form the F ratio.

nodes.name: Gaussian regression prediction interval
nodes.intuition: A new outcome is uncertain both because the fitted mean is uncertain and because the new observation brings fresh noise.
nodes.conditions: Full-rank fixed X, n>p; Gaussian iid errors of variance σ²; independent new response at fixed x0 with the same variance; s²=RSS/(n−p).
nodes.example: The leading 1 is omitted for a confidence interval for the conditional mean, not for a new response.

patterns.why: Parameter estimation error and new observation noise contribute separate variances.
The design covariance determines uncertainty at the new input.

nodes.name: Covariate adjustment for average treatment effect
nodes.latex: \mathbb E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=\mathbb E_X\!\left[\mathbb E(Y\mid A=1,X)-\mathbb E(Y\mid A=0,X)\right]
nodes.intuition: Compare treatment groups at the same observed background, then average those comparable contrasts over the target population.
nodes.conditions: Binary treatment; consistency Y=Y(A); conditional exchangeability (Y(0),Y(1)) independent of A given X; positivity 0<P(A=1|X)<1 almost surely; integrable outcomes.
nodes.example: Randomization makes exchangeability hold without adjustment when treatment assignment is independent of potential outcomes.

patterns.why: Within-background contrasts are standardized to one population distribution.
Identification depends on observed X blocking treatment-outcome confounding.

nodes.name: Inverse propensity weighting identity
nodes.intuition: Give underrepresented treatment-background combinations more weight so each group represents the same target population.
nodes.conditions: Consistency, conditional exchangeability and positivity as in covariate adjustment; integrable potential outcomes. Finite variance requires stronger overlap and moment conditions.
nodes.example: With treatment probability 1/4, each treated outcome receives weight 4 in its treatment mean.

patterns.why: Unequal selection probabilities are compensated by inverse weights.
Reweighting changes the represented covariate distribution.

nodes.name: Doubly robust treatment-effect score
nodes.intuition: Start from an outcome prediction, then correct it using weighted residuals from the outcomes actually observed.
nodes.conditions: Under causal identification assumptions, Eψ equals the average treatment effect if either e is the true propensity or both ma are true outcome means; weights and terms must be integrable. Estimated nuisances need additional inference conditions.
nodes.example: If both outcome regressions are correct, each weighted residual has conditional mean zero even with a misspecified positive propensity.

patterns.why: A model-based contrast and residual correction handle complementary errors.
At the true nuisances, first-order perturbations in either component cancel.

nodes.name: Markov transition kernel
nodes.intuition: One object moves observables backward by conditional averaging and moves probability distributions forward.
nodes.conditions: K(x,·) is a probability measure for each x and K(·,A) measurable for each measurable A; f bounded measurable, μ a probability measure.
nodes.example: A finite transition matrix is the case K(i,{j})=Pij.

patterns.why: The same kernel acts oppositely on functions and measures.
Kf is the expected next observable from the present state.

nodes.name: Finite Markov chain time-average theorem
nodes.intuition: One long dependent trajectory samples each state in its stationary proportion.
nodes.conditions: Finite irreducible Markov chain with stationary distribution π; any real f and any initial state. Aperiodicity is not needed for this time-average conclusion.
nodes.example: A deterministic two-state alternation spends half its time in each state despite having no pointwise distributional limit.

patterns.why: Averages along one path equal stationary averages.
Persistent dependence still permits an almost sure long-run limit.

nodes.name: Finite Markov chain convergence theorem
nodes.intuition: After enough transitions, the distribution forgets the starting state.
nodes.conditions: P is a finite irreducible aperiodic transition matrix; π is its unique stationary distribution. Periodicity can prevent this limit.
nodes.example: Adding a positive chance of staying in each state removes periodic oscillations from an irreducible finite chain.

patterns.why: Repeated transition operators approach a common limiting distribution.
The limiting law is the invariant probability vector.

nodes.name: Total variation distance between laws
nodes.intuition: Measure the largest probability discrepancy that any yes-or-no event can expose.
nodes.conditions: P,Q probability measures on one measurable space; p,q densities with respect to a common dominating μ, such as P+Q.
nodes.example: For Bernoulli(p) and Bernoulli(q), total variation is |p−q|.

patterns.why: The metric measures the strongest event-level distinction.
It quantifies how distinguishable two probability laws are.

nodes.name: Coupling characterization of total variation
nodes.intuition: Try to realize two laws together so their outcomes agree as often as possible.
nodes.conditions: X∼P and Y∼Q on a common standard Borel state space; the infimum is over all joint laws with those marginals and is attained by a maximal coupling.
nodes.example: Coupling two Bernoulli variables with one uniform draw makes disagreement probability |p−q|.

patterns.why: Choose a joint construction minimizing mismatch.
Distributional distance becomes an achievable probability of unequal outcomes.

nodes.name: Dobrushin contraction coefficient
nodes.intuition: If every pair of states produces similar next-step distributions, one transition must erase part of the difference between starting laws.
nodes.conditions: P is a finite row-stochastic matrix; μ,ν probability row vectors. α(P)≤1; a strict one-step contraction needs α(P)<1.
nodes.example: Identical transition rows give α=0 and erase all initial information in one step.

patterns.why: Repeated strict contraction gives geometric forgetting.
Overlapping transition mixtures smooth differences between input laws.

nodes.name: Total variation mixing time
nodes.intuition: Ask how many steps suffice to make every starting state look stationary to any event-level test.
nodes.conditions: Finite irreducible aperiodic chain; 0<ε<1; t is an integer. Mixing concerns the distribution, not independence of consecutive samples.
nodes.example: An independent sampler with every row equal to π mixes in at most one step.

patterns.why: A qualitative limit is converted into an accuracy-dependent time.
The threshold controls the most distinguishing event.

nodes.name: Kac mean return-time identity
nodes.intuition: A state visited during a fraction π(i) of steps has average spacing 1/π(i) between visits.
nodes.conditions: Finite irreducible Markov chain; start at i; return is strictly after time zero. Periodicity is allowed.
nodes.example: A state with stationary probability 0.1 has mean return time ten steps.

patterns.why: Visits to a state regenerate future return cycles.
Long-run visit frequency is reciprocal to average cycle length.

nodes.name: Dirichlet form of a reversible chain
nodes.intuition: A Markov step dissipates variation most strongly when connected states carry very different observable values.
nodes.conditions: Finite chain reversible with stationary π; weighted inner product is sum πi fi gi; f real.
nodes.example: Constant observables have zero energy because all edge differences vanish.

patterns.why: Energy is a weighted sum of squared differences.
Detailed balance turns directed transition flows into symmetric conductances.

nodes.name: Spectral bound on reversible mixing
nodes.intuition: Every nonconstant eigenmode fades at its own rate; the slowest absolute eigenvalue controls the remaining memory.
nodes.conditions: Finite irreducible aperiodic reversible chain with at least two states; eigenvalues ordered with λ1=1; t≥0 integer.
nodes.example: An eigenvalue close to −1 causes slowly damped alternation, which explains the absolute value.

patterns.why: The initial discrepancy splits into orthogonal eigenmodes.
Powers of nontrivial eigenvalues quantify forgetting.

nodes.name: Metropolis–Hastings acceptance rule
nodes.intuition: Correct an easy proposal's directional bias so accepted traffic balances under the desired target law.
nodes.conditions: A proper target π known up to a constant; proposal density or mass q with a common reference measure. At π(x)q(y|x)>0 use the formula; zero-target proposals reject. Invariance alone does not ensure mixing.
nodes.example: Symmetric random-walk proposals reduce the ratio to π(y)/π(x).

patterns.why: Forward and reverse accepted target flows match.
The acceptance ratio corrects proposal bias without evaluating the target normalizer.

nodes.name: Gibbs conditional resampling
nodes.intuition: Replace one coordinate by a fresh draw consistent with the others, preserving the whole joint target distribution.
nodes.conditions: A proper joint target with available regular conditional laws. Coordinate updates preserve π; convergence additionally needs irreducibility and appropriate recurrence or mixing conditions.
nodes.example: A bivariate Gaussian sampler alternates draws from its two conditional normal laws.

patterns.why: A sequence of invariant coordinate updates remains invariant.
Each update samples uncertainty remaining after conditioning.

nodes.name: Integrated autocorrelation and effective sample size
nodes.intuition: Repeated similar samples provide less averaging precision than fresh independent samples; negative correlations can instead improve precision.
nodes.conditions: Stationary real sequence with 0<σY²<∞ and absolutely summable autocorrelations. Effective-size expression assumes τint>0 and is an asymptotic variance comparison, not a count of independent draws.
nodes.example: For an AR(1)-type correlation ρk=r^k, |r|<1, τint=(1+r)/(1−r).

patterns.why: All lagged covariances contribute to average uncertainty.
Dependence changes the precision gained per sample.

nodes.name: Acceptance–rejection sampling
nodes.latex: Y\sim q,\ U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1),\quad \text{accept if }U\le\frac{p(Y)}{M q(Y)};\qquad Y\mid\text{accepted}\sim p
nodes.intuition: Generate points under an easy envelope and retain exactly the fraction needed to carve out the target density.
nodes.conditions: p,q normalized densities, p≤Mq almost everywhere with finite M≥1; U independent of Y. Accepted fraction is 1/M.
nodes.example: A uniform envelope can sample a bounded density on a compact interval.

patterns.why: Acceptance cuts the target shape out of an enveloping region.
Independent uniform thinning corrects the proposal density.

nodes.name: Importance sampling identity and estimator
nodes.intuition: Visit useful regions more often, then discount each visit by how much it was oversampled.
nodes.conditions: p absolutely continuous with respect to q, E_p|f|<∞; Xi iid q. The estimator is unbiased; finite variance additionally requires ∫f²p²/q<∞.
nodes.example: Shift a Gaussian proposal toward a rare tail and compensate with the density ratio.

patterns.why: A change of probability measure is paid for by a likelihood ratio.
Weighted proposal observations estimate a target expectation.

nodes.name: Self-normalized importance sampling
nodes.intuition: When the target's total mass is unknown, estimate both the weighted quantity and its normalization from the same draws.
nodes.conditions: Xi iid q, target p proportional to nonnegative ptilde supported where q>0; 0<Eq w<∞ and Eq(w|f|)<∞. A positive denominator is required; the estimator is consistent but generally biased at finite n.
nodes.example: Posterior expectations can be estimated without evaluating the evidence normalizer.

patterns.why: Normalized nonnegative weights sum to one.
A ratio of two laws of large numbers cancels the unknown constant.

nodes.name: Optimal linear control variate
nodes.intuition: Subtract the predictable part of simulation noise using another quantity whose mean is already known.
nodes.conditions: X,Y square-integrable with positive variances; E Y known and c fixed independently of the draws used for the displayed unbiasedness. Data-estimated coefficients require separate bias analysis.
nodes.example: A simulation output strongly correlated with a known analytic approximation can be estimated much more precisely.

patterns.why: Optimal subtraction leaves a residual uncorrelated with the control.
The coefficient minimizes a quadratic variance function.

nodes.name: Antithetic sampling variance
nodes.intuition: Pair a random draw with its reflected counterpart so opposite errors can cancel.
nodes.conditions: U uniform(0,1), f(U) square-integrable. Variance improves over two independent draws when the covariance is negative; monotone f is a sufficient condition.
nodes.example: For f(u)=u, the paired estimator is identically 1/2.

patterns.why: Reflection preserves the uniform marginal distribution.
A carefully dependent pair can average more accurately than independent draws.

nodes.name: Stratified Monte Carlo and allocation
nodes.intuition: Guarantee representation of each region, then spend extra draws where probability mass and within-region variability are largest.
nodes.conditions: Known finite partition probabilities ph; independent iid samples within each stratum, nh>0; σh² finite. The displayed interior allocation formula assumes phσh>0 for every stratum and minimizes variance for a fixed total under continuous allocation and equal sampling cost.
nodes.example: Proportional allocation removes randomness in how many samples land in each region.

patterns.why: The expectation splits across a known partition.
Sampling effort is allocated by each stratum's marginal variance contribution.

nodes.name: Sequential importance weights for particle filtering
nodes.latex: w_t^{(i)}\propto w_{t-1}^{(i)}\frac{p(y_t\mid x_t^{(i)})p(x_t^{(i)}\mid x_{t-1}^{(i)})}{q(x_t^{(i)}\mid x_{t-1}^{(i)},y_t)},\quad \widehat\pi_t=\sum_i\bar w_t^{(i)}\delta_{x_t^{(i)}}
nodes.intuition: Carry many possible hidden states forward, reward those that explain the next observation, and replicate promising particles when weights become uneven.
nodes.conditions: State-space model with Markov transitions and conditionally independent observations; proposal covers target support. Formula is before resampling; resampling resets ancestor weights as appropriate. Finite particles give an approximation.
nodes.example: Using the transition itself as proposal leaves the new likelihood as the incremental weight.

patterns.why: The posterior approximation is updated one observation at a time.
Normalized particle weights approximate conditional expectations.

nodes.name: Continuous-time Markov generator matrix
nodes.intuition: Replace per-step transition probabilities with instantaneous traffic rates between states.
nodes.conditions: Finite time-homogeneous continuous-time Markov chain; off-diagonal qij≥0 and finite, row sums zero. Holding time in i is exponential with rate −qii when positive.
nodes.example: A two-state chain has Q=[[-a,a],[b,−b]].

patterns.why: I+hQ is the first-order transition approximation.
Zero row sums preserve total probability.

nodes.name: Kolmogorov equations for a finite chain
nodes.intuition: Local transition rates assemble into a linear differential equation for the full probability distribution.
nodes.conditions: Finite generator Q; P(0)=I and probability row vector p(0). The two matrix equations are backward and forward forms; Q commutes with its own exponential.
nodes.example: A two-state law relaxes exponentially at rate a+b.

patterns.why: Probability evolves by a linear system.
The semigroup composes successive time intervals.

nodes.name: Uniformization of a finite Markov chain
nodes.intuition: Run a discrete Markov chain at a common Poisson clock, allowing harmless self-transitions when a state needs fewer real jumps.
nodes.conditions: Finite generator Q and ν>0 with ν≥maxi(−qii), so P is stochastic. The series converges absolutely for every t≥0.
nodes.example: A chain with escape rates at most 5 can be driven by a Poisson clock of rate 5.

patterns.why: Continuous evolution is a Poisson mixture of discrete-step evolutions.
The matrix exponential factors into scalar Poisson weights.

nodes.name: Stationary law of a birth–death process
nodes.intuition: Each neighboring pair balances upward and downward traffic, so probabilities are built by successive rate ratios.
nodes.conditions: Irreducible nonexplosive process on nonnegative integers; births λn>0, deaths μn>0 for n≥1 and μ0=0; displayed normalizing sum finite.
nodes.example: Constant birth λ and death μ give a geometric stationary law when λ<μ.

patterns.why: The ratio of neighboring stationary masses determines the whole law.
Local balance makes every neighboring probability flow cancel.

nodes.name: Stationary M/M/1 queue
nodes.intuition: One server can balance arrivals only when average service capacity exceeds incoming work; delay rises sharply near that boundary.
nodes.conditions: Poisson arrivals rate λ>0, iid exponential service rate μ>λ, independent arrival/service processes, one FIFO server and unlimited waiting room. L counts jobs in the system; W includes service time.
nodes.example: At λ=1 and μ=2, mean population and mean sojourn time are both 1 in their respective units.

patterns.why: Stationary occupancy balances arrival and departure rates.
The gap μ−λ determines the mean time scale.

nodes.name: Little's queueing law
nodes.intuition: Average occupancy equals entry rate times average time spent inside.
nodes.conditions: A stationary stable system with finite admitted-arrival rate λ and finite arrival-average sojourn time W; L is mean number present. Use consistent system boundaries and count the same population in all three quantities.
nodes.example: An arrival rate of 3 jobs/minute and average stay of 4 minutes imply 12 jobs present on average.

patterns.why: Each admitted job contributes its time inside to accumulated occupancy.
Time-average population equals arrival-average duration times rate.

nodes.name: Renewal equation
nodes.intuition: After the first renewal, the process restarts and the remaining time contains a fresh copy of the same counting problem.
nodes.conditions: Iid strictly positive interarrival times with CDF F; N(t) counts completed arrivals after time zero. The integral is Lebesgue–Stieltjes.
nodes.example: Exponential interarrivals solve the equation with m(t)=λt.

patterns.why: Condition on the first waiting time to restart the process.
The convolution-like integral combines first arrival and remaining evolution.

nodes.name: Renewal reward theorem
nodes.intuition: Long-run reward per unit time is average reward per cycle divided by average cycle duration.
nodes.conditions: Iid pairs (Ti,Ri), Ti>0, 0<E Ti<∞, E|Ri|<∞; N(t) counts completed cycles. Reward and duration may be dependent within a cycle.
nodes.example: Expected working time divided by expected work-plus-repair cycle length gives long-run availability.

patterns.why: Separate laws of large numbers for rewards and durations form a ratio.
Renewal cycles reset the statistical experiment.

nodes.name: Equilibrium residual lifetime
nodes.intuition: An observer arriving at a random time is more likely to land inside a long interval than a short one.
nodes.conditions: Stationary renewal process with positive interarrival T and 0<E T<∞; R is forward time to the next event. The mean formula is extended-valued if E T²=∞.
nodes.example: Equal-probability intervals of lengths 1 and 9 give mean forward wait 4.1, exceeding half the ordinary mean interval 2.5.

patterns.why: Random-time observation length-biases which intervals are seen.
Tail integration turns interval lengths into residual-time probabilities.

nodes.name: Galton–Watson extinction probability
nodes.intuition: The population dies out exactly when every child's independent descendant population dies out.
nodes.conditions: Start from one ancestor; each individual has iid nonnegative integer offspring K, finite almost surely. q is the eventual extinction probability.
nodes.example: For K=0 or 2 with equal probabilities, q=1; for K identically 1, q=0 despite mean offspring 1.

patterns.why: Self-similar descendant survival creates a fixed-point equation.
The offspring PGF averages the extinction probabilities of all children.

nodes.name: Galton–Watson mean and normalized martingale
nodes.intuition: Divide out expected population growth and the remaining population size becomes a conditionally fair process.
nodes.conditions: Z0=1; iid offspring K with 0<m=E K<∞; Fn records the first n generations. Convergence need not preserve mean without additional integrability.
nodes.example: Even with m>1, extinction can occur and the normalized limit can be zero.

patterns.why: Dividing by m^n removes deterministic expected growth.
Each generation conditionally has m times the current population.

nodes.name: Doob Lp maximal inequality
nodes.latex: \mathbb E\!\left[\max_{0\le k\le n}|M_k|^p\right]\le\left(\frac p{p-1}\right)^p\mathbb E|M_n|^p,\qquad p>1
nodes.intuition: Control the largest excursion of an entire fair process using only a moment of its final value.
nodes.conditions: Mk is a real discrete-time martingale on 0,…,n with E|Mn|^p<∞. The displayed constant requires p>1.
nodes.example: For p=2, the expected squared maximum is at most four times the final second moment.

patterns.why: Crossing a threshold links a path maximum to future conditional expectations.
Maximal control helps turn endpoint estimates into process-level convergence.

nodes.name: Discrete Doob decomposition
nodes.intuition: Separate each observed change into what was predictable just before it and its mean-zero surprise.
nodes.conditions: Xn is an integrable adapted discrete-time process. M is a martingale with M0=X0; A is predictable. If X is a submartingale, A is nondecreasing.
nodes.example: A random walk with drift decomposes into its linear drift plus a centered martingale.

patterns.why: Predictable drift and unpredictable innovation sum to the process.
Predictability is defined relative to the chosen filtration.

nodes.name: L1-bounded martingale convergence
nodes.intuition: A fair process with bounded expected magnitude cannot oscillate forever across fixed intervals.
nodes.conditions: Real discrete-time martingale. This alone gives almost sure convergence; L1 convergence and preservation of E M0 require uniform integrability.
nodes.example: Nonnegative martingales converge almost surely but may lose expectation in the limit.

patterns.why: Moment control rules out endlessly many fixed-size upcrossings.
Finite-time fairness can fail to preserve expectation at the limiting exchange.

nodes.name: Brownian quadratic variation
nodes.intuition: Brownian increments shrink, yet their squared contributions accumulate into a nonzero clock.
nodes.conditions: Standard Brownian motion on [0,t]; deterministic partitions with mesh tending to zero. Almost sure convergence holds along dyadic partitions; arbitrary mesh convergence here is in L².
nodes.example: The sum's variance is 2 sumk(Δtk)², which tends to zero.

patterns.why: Tiny squared fluctuations add to elapsed time.
Brownian increment size is of order square root of the time step.

nodes.name: Itô product rule
nodes.intuition: Two rough processes share an extra product change from their simultaneous fluctuations.
nodes.conditions: X,Y continuous semimartingales; [X,Y] is their quadratic covariation. For Itô diffusions driven by the same scalar Brownian motion, d[X,Y]=σXσY dt.
nodes.example: With X=Y=W, d(W²)=2W dW+dt.

patterns.why: Products of noise increments survive as covariation.
Product change separates into two first-order terms and shared roughness.

nodes.name: Brownian exponential martingale
nodes.intuition: Subtract half the accumulated noise energy to keep an exponentiated stochastic integral fair.
nodes.conditions: On a fixed finite horizon T, H progressively measurable and satisfies Novikov's condition E exp(1/2∫0^T Hs²ds)<∞. Then Z is a true martingale for t≤T.
nodes.example: For constant H=θ, exp(θWt−θ²t/2) has mean one.

patterns.why: An additive stochastic integral becomes a multiplicative positive process.
The quadratic correction preserves expected total weight.

nodes.name: Girsanov Brownian drift change
nodes.intuition: Reweight whole paths so what looked like systematic drift under one probability law becomes fair Brownian motion under another.
nodes.conditions: W Brownian under P; finite T; θ progressively measurable with E_P exp(1/2∫0^T θs²ds)<∞. Then WQ is Brownian under Q on [0,T].
nodes.example: A constant tilt θ changes Brownian path drift by −θ under the new measure.

patterns.why: The change is of probability measure, not of the sample paths themselves.
A stochastic exponential is the path likelihood ratio.

nodes.name: Itô–Stratonovich drift conversion
nodes.intuition: Changing how noise increments are sampled changes the deterministic drift needed to describe the same process.
nodes.conditions: Scalar continuous diffusion with sufficiently regular coefficients, b continuously differentiable, and stochastic integrals well defined; displayed coefficients have no explicit time dependence.
nodes.example: dX=X∘dW corresponds to dX=(X/2)dt+X dW and solution X0 exp(Wt).

patterns.why: Two integral conventions require different drift coefficients.
Variation of the noise amplitude creates the half-derivative correction.

nodes.name: Strong existence and uniqueness for Lipschitz SDEs
nodes.intuition: A drift and noise rule that do not amplify nearby states too quickly determine a unique path from the given initial state and noise.
nodes.conditions: b,σ measurable in time, globally Lipschitz in state uniformly on each finite horizon and of linear growth; X0 is square-integrable and F0-measurable. There is a unique continuous adapted strong solution.
nodes.example: The Ornstein–Uhlenbeck coefficients b(x)=−θx and constant σ satisfy the assumptions.

patterns.why: Successive approximations converge to the integral-equation solution.
Lipschitz bounds control the difference between candidate solutions.

nodes.name: Diffusion infinitesimal generator
nodes.intuition: A diffusion acts on observables through local drift plus the curvature-sensitive spreading caused by noise.
nodes.conditions: Time-homogeneous nonexplosive Itô diffusion dX=b(X)dt+σ(X)dW; f is C² and in the generator domain, for example compactly supported with appropriate continuous coefficients.
nodes.example: Standard d-dimensional Brownian motion has generator one-half the Laplacian.

patterns.why: The generator gives the first-order change of an expected observable.
Noise covariance contracts with the observable Hessian.

nodes.name: Kolmogorov backward equation for a diffusion
nodes.intuition: Predict a future observable by evolving a function of the present starting state.
nodes.conditions: Time-homogeneous nonexplosive diffusion; f in the generator domain and u sufficiently C1 in time and C2 in space for the classical equation. Without this smoothness use the semigroup formulation.
nodes.example: For Brownian motion, expected future observables solve the heat equation with diffusivity 1/2.

patterns.why: Observables evolve backward relative to forward probability-density evolution.
The Markov semigroup links nearby prediction horizons.

nodes.name: Feynman–Kac representation
nodes.intuition: A linear evolution with local killing can be computed by averaging terminal values over random paths with survival weights.
nodes.conditions: Nonexplosive diffusion with generator L; bounded continuous V,g. Any bounded C1,2 solution whose Itô integral is a true martingale has this representation; the expectation is not automatically a classical solution without regularity.
nodes.example: With V=0 and Brownian X, this is Gaussian averaging for the heat equation.

patterns.why: Solutions are expected path-weighted terminal data.
The potential is integrated along each path before exponentiation.

nodes.name: Brownian reflection principle
nodes.intuition: Reflect the part of a path after its first boundary hit to pair paths ending below the boundary with paths ending above it.
nodes.conditions: Standard Brownian motion starting at zero, t>0 and a>0. This exact formula is for zero drift.
nodes.example: The running maximum at time t has the same distribution as |Wt|.

patterns.why: Reflected post-hit Brownian increments preserve their law.
A first boundary hit turns a path event into an endpoint event.

nodes.name: Brownian first-passage density
nodes.intuition: Reaching a fixed level is almost certain, but occasional extremely long waits make the average waiting time infinite.
nodes.conditions: Standard Brownian motion starting at zero and a>0. τa is finite almost surely yet E τa=∞.
nodes.example: Doubling the target level multiplies the hitting-time scale by four.

patterns.why: The stopping time records first arrival at a boundary.
Brownian square-root displacement implies quadratic hitting-time scaling.

nodes.name: Brownian bridge
nodes.intuition: A Brownian path is pinned to a prescribed endpoint by removing the part linearly explained by that endpoint.
nodes.conditions: Standard Brownian W, fixed T>0, 0≤s,t≤T. B is centered Gaussian with B0=BT=0; it is not adapted to W's original past filtration in this construction.
nodes.example: Its variance t(1−t/T) is largest halfway through the interval.

patterns.why: The endpoint-correlated component is subtracted from each coordinate.
Both endpoints are fixed while interior values remain random.

nodes.name: Tanaka's local-time formula
nodes.intuition: A corner in the absolute-value function accumulates a correction whenever Brownian motion revisits that corner.
nodes.conditions: One-dimensional Brownian W; a real. Local time is normalized by ∫0^t g(Ws)ds=∫g(a)Lt^a da; sign(0) may be set to zero.
nodes.example: At a=0, absolute Brownian motion is a martingale term plus its increasing local time at zero.

patterns.why: Local time measures accumulated contact with one spatial level.
Smooth approximations to a kink produce a concentrated second-derivative correction.

nodes.name: Lévy characterization of Brownian motion
nodes.latex: M_0=0,\quad M\text{ continuous local martingale},\quad[M]_t=t\quad\Longrightarrow\quad M\text{ is standard Brownian motion}
nodes.intuition: Continuity, conditional fairness and the correct accumulated noise clock already determine Brownian behavior.
nodes.conditions: Real process adapted to a filtration satisfying the usual conditions; M is a continuous local martingale with quadratic variation exactly t almost surely.
nodes.example: The stochastic integral of a predictable ±1 process against Brownian motion is Brownian relative to the same filtration.

patterns.why: Predictable sign changes preserve the Brownian law through its quadratic clock.
The local-martingale condition is relative to the given filtration.

nodes.name: Compensated Poisson martingale integral
nodes.intuition: Subtract predictable arrivals from the counting process; the remaining jump surprises integrate like orthogonal noise.
nodes.conditions: Poisson process of rate λ>0 in a filtration where its future increments remain independent; H predictable with E∫0^t Hs²ds<∞.
nodes.example: For H=1, Var(Nt−λt)=λt.

patterns.why: A count splits into predictable intensity and centered jump noise.
Disjoint compensated increments have zero covariance.

nodes.name: Campbell moments for a Poisson point process
nodes.intuition: Random point contributions average according to spatial intensity, and independent Poisson placement gives a particularly simple variance.
nodes.conditions: Poisson point process or random measure with intensity Λ; real measurable f with ∫|f|dΛ and ∫f²dΛ finite. Multiplicities are counted.
nodes.example: For an indicator of a finite-intensity region, both mean and variance equal that region's intensity.

patterns.why: Point contributions integrate against an intensity measure.
Independent Poisson counts make variance add locally.

nodes.name: Convex set
nodes.intuition: Every straight journey between two allowed points stays allowed.
nodes.conditions: Subset C of a real vector space; the empty set is conventionally convex. The condition concerns all pairs and all t in [0,1].
nodes.example: A Euclidean ball and an affine half-space are convex; a circle's boundary is not.

patterns.why: All two-point mixtures remain in the set.
Straight segments describe the feasible geometry.

nodes.name: Epigraph characterization of convexity
nodes.intuition: A function is convex exactly when all the space above its graph forms a convex solid.
nodes.conditions: Extended-real function f:R^d→(−∞,+∞]; its effective domain is included through the inequality f(x)≤t.
nodes.example: Minimizing a convex function can be written as minimizing t subject to (x,t) lying in its epigraph.

patterns.why: A functional inequality becomes closure of a set under mixtures.
A graph acquires an extra coordinate representing an upper bound.

nodes.name: Perspective of a convex function
nodes.latex: g(x,t)=t\,f(x/t),\quad t>0;\qquad f\text{ convex}\Longrightarrow g\text{ convex}
nodes.intuition: Separate the amount of a resource from its per-unit value while preserving convex tradeoffs.
nodes.conditions: Convex f on a convex domain; g is defined where t>0 and x/t lies in that domain. Boundary t=0 requires a separately specified closed extension.
nodes.example: The perspective of ||x||² is ||x||²/t, a convex quadratic-over-linear function for t>0.

patterns.why: The extra variable records total scale separately from normalized coordinates.
Rescaled mixture weights preserve the convexity inequality.

nodes.name: Support function of a set
nodes.intuition: Ask how far the set reaches when viewed in each linear direction.
nodes.conditions: Nonempty C⊆R^d; the value may be +∞ for unbounded sets. The support function is convex and positively homogeneous even when C is not convex.
nodes.example: For the Euclidean ball of radius r centered at zero, σC(y)=r||y||₂.

patterns.why: Directions describe a set through extremal linear evaluations.
Supporting hyperplanes measure directional extent.

nodes.name: Extended-real indicator of a constraint
nodes.intuition: Encode a hard constraint as an infinite penalty so that one optimization language handles both.
nodes.conditions: C⊆R^d and the objective is interpreted in extended-real arithmetic. This 0/+∞ indicator differs from a probability event's 0/1 indicator.
nodes.example: The proximal map of δC is Euclidean projection when C is nonempty, closed and convex.

patterns.why: Feasibility becomes an additive objective term.
Forbidden points are excluded by infinite cost.

nodes.name: Strong separation of disjoint convex sets
nodes.latex: \exists a\ne0,\alpha<\beta:\quad \langle a,x\rangle\le\alpha<\beta\le\langle a,y\rangle\quad(x\in C,\ y\in D)
nodes.intuition: Two suitably closed convex regions that do not touch can be distinguished by a linear measurement with a positive gap.
nodes.conditions: Nonempty disjoint convex subsets C,D⊆R^d; C compact and D closed suffice. Mere disjointness of arbitrary convex sets need not give a positive gap.
nodes.example: A point outside a closed convex set can be separated using the direction from its closest point in the set.

patterns.why: A linear certificate witnesses geometric infeasibility.
Convexity prevents the regions from winding around each other.

nodes.name: Farkas alternative for linear feasibility
nodes.latex: \text{Exactly one: }\quad \exists x\ge0:Ax=b\quad\text{or}\quad\exists y:A^\top y\ge0,\ b^\top y<0
nodes.intuition: Either nonnegative ingredients build the target, or one linear test proves that no such recipe can work.
nodes.conditions: Real matrix A∈R^{m×n}, b∈R^m; vector inequalities are componentwise. This alternative needs no strict feasibility assumption.
nodes.example: If every column of A has nonnegative first coordinate but b has negative first coordinate, y=e₁ is an infeasibility certificate.

patterns.why: Feasible points and separating certificates are mutually exclusive alternatives.
The constraints and certificates are linear evaluations.

nodes.name: Fenchel–Moreau biconjugation
nodes.intuition: A closed convex function can be reconstructed from every affine lower support it admits.
nodes.conditions: Proper lower-semicontinuous convex f:R^d→(−∞,+∞]. For more general functions, the biconjugate may instead describe a closed convex relaxation.
nodes.example: The absolute-value function is recovered by maximizing xy over slopes |y|≤1.

patterns.why: Switching between points and supporting slopes twice recovers the function.
Closed convex geometry is exactly what affine supports can reconstruct.

nodes.name: Infimal convolution
nodes.intuition: Split a target into two components and choose the cheapest division of labor.
nodes.conditions: Extended-real functions on R^d for which the displayed sum is defined; convex f,g give a convex result. Finiteness, closedness and attainment require additional conditions.
nodes.example: With f=δC and g=δD, the result is the extended-real indicator of the Minkowski sum C+D.

patterns.why: A total x is divided as y+(x−y).
An infimum chooses the best split.

nodes.name: Conjugate of an infimal convolution
nodes.intuition: A common price makes the two components of a split optimization separate.
nodes.conditions: Proper functions f,g on R^d with their infimal convolution proper; extended-real conjugates are allowed. No claim of primal attainment is needed.
nodes.example: Combining quadratic costs by optimal splitting turns into adding reciprocal-curvature quadratic conjugates.

patterns.why: A shared dual variable prices both summands.
Independent suprema add after the variable split.

nodes.name: Moreau envelope and its gradient
nodes.intuition: Allow a point to move a little while charging for distance, producing a smooth version of a possibly sharp objective.
nodes.conditions: Proper lower-semicontinuous convex f on R^d and λ>0. The minimizer is unique, the envelope finite and continuously differentiable, and its gradient is 1/λ-Lipschitz.
nodes.example: The envelope of absolute value is a scaled Huber loss.

patterns.why: A regularized local minimization defines the smoothed value.
Squared distance supplies unique minimizers and a Lipschitz gradient.

nodes.name: Moreau primal-dual decomposition
nodes.intuition: A proximal point and a scaled dual proximal residual divide the same vector into complementary roles.
nodes.conditions: Proper lower-semicontinuous convex f on R^d and λ>0; prox_h minimizes h plus half squared distance.
nodes.example: For f=||·||₁, soft thresholding plus clipping to the dual ℓ∞ ball reconstructs x.

patterns.why: Primal regularization and conjugate constraints describe complementary pieces.
The vector splits into a point and a scaled residual.

nodes.name: Firm nonexpansiveness of a proximal map
nodes.intuition: A convex proximal step cannot amplify differences, and its displacement obeys a stronger angle constraint.
nodes.conditions: Proper lower-semicontinuous convex f on R^d; λ>0. In particular ||P(x)−P(y)||≤||x−y||.
nodes.example: Projection onto a closed convex set is firmly nonexpansive by taking f to be its extended-real indicator.

patterns.why: Output distances are bounded by an input-output inner product.
Nonexpansive geometry supports stable fixed-point iterations.

nodes.name: Monotone set-valued operator
nodes.intuition: The output never changes in a direction that opposes the change in input.
nodes.conditions: A:R^d⇉R^d may be set-valued. Maximal monotonicity additionally means its graph cannot be enlarged while preserving this inequality.
nodes.example: The subdifferential of a proper closed convex function is maximal monotone.

patterns.why: An inner-product angle inequality governs pairs of graph points.
Convex subgradients are the central optimization example.

nodes.name: Resolvent of a maximal monotone operator
nodes.latex: J_{\lambda A}=(I+\lambda A)^{-1},\qquad A=\partial f\Longrightarrow J_{\lambda A}=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}
nodes.intuition: Solve one implicit balance equation to convert a possibly multivalued relation into a stable single-valued update.
nodes.conditions: Maximal monotone A on finite-dimensional Euclidean space and λ>0. Its resolvent is everywhere defined and firmly nonexpansive.
nodes.example: For A(x)=Mx with symmetric M≥0, the resolvent is (I+λM)⁻¹x.

patterns.why: Zeros of A are fixed points of its resolvent.
Inverting an implicit relation turns a force into a point update.

nodes.name: Baillon–Haddad gradient inequality
nodes.intuition: For a smooth convex landscape, the gradient's change must align with the displacement strongly enough to control its size.
nodes.conditions: Convex differentiable f:R^d→R with L-Lipschitz gradient and L>0. Lipschitz continuity without convexity is insufficient.
nodes.example: For f(x)=L||x||²/2, equality holds.

patterns.why: Convexity strengthens a gradient norm bound into an angle inequality.
The gradient difference is controlled in the displacement direction.

nodes.name: Polyak–Łojasiewicz gradient domination
nodes.intuition: A large objective error must leave a detectable slope, so a small gradient certifies near-optimal value.
nodes.conditions: Differentiable f bounded below by attained minimum f*, globally L-Lipschitz gradient and the displayed PL inequality with 0<μ≤L. Rate for xk+1=xk−∇f(xk)/L; convexity is not required.
nodes.example: Rank-deficient least squares can satisfy PL despite lacking strong convexity in every parameter direction.

patterns.why: Gradient size bounds remaining objective error.
Geometric contraction follows from sufficient decrease.

nodes.name: Projected gradient mapping
nodes.latex: G_\alpha(x)=\frac{x-\Pi_C(x-\alpha\nabla f(x))}{\alpha},\qquad G_\alpha(x)=0\iff\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle\ge0\ \forall y\in C
nodes.intuition: Measure the part of the gradient step that survives the feasibility constraint.
nodes.conditions: Nonempty closed convex C⊆R^d, x∈C, differentiable f and α>0. The zero condition is first-order stationarity; it implies global optimality if f is convex.
nodes.example: At the minimizer of f(x)=x on [0,∞), the ordinary gradient is 1 but the projected gradient mapping is zero.

patterns.why: Stationarity is adapted to feasible directions.
A boundary can block an otherwise nonzero descent direction.

nodes.name: Nonconvex gradient-descent stationarity bound
nodes.intuition: Repeated decreases cannot consume more objective value than is available, so some iterate must have a small slope.
nodes.conditions: Differentiable f:R^d→R with L-Lipschitz gradient, L>0 and finite infimum. This bounds a gradient norm, not distance to a global minimum.
nodes.example: To find an iterate with gradient norm at most ε, the bound requires K≥2L(f(x0)−inf f)/ε².

patterns.why: Per-step decreases sum to a finite objective budget.
A finite average of squared gradients forces one small term.

nodes.name: Nesterov accelerated gradient scheme
nodes.intuition: Use carefully scheduled extrapolation to make past progress help the next gradient evaluation.
nodes.conditions: Convex differentiable f with L-Lipschitz gradient, L>0 and a minimizer x*. Initialize y0=x0,t0=1. This scheme gives f(xk)−f*≤2L||x0−x*||²/(k+1)² for k≥1.
nodes.example: The worst-case convex objective rate improves from order 1/k for ordinary gradient descent to order 1/k².

patterns.why: A scalar recurrence coordinates extrapolation across steps.
An accelerated potential controls the objective error.

nodes.name: FISTA for composite convex objectives
nodes.intuition: Combine a smooth gradient, a nonsmooth proximal correction, and an acceleration schedule.
nodes.conditions: F=f+g; f convex differentiable with L-Lipschitz gradient, g proper closed convex, L>0, and a minimizer exists. Start x0∈dom g,y0=x0,t0=1; objective gap is O(1/k²), but individual values need not decrease.
nodes.example: For least squares plus an ℓ₁ penalty, each accelerated step ends with soft thresholding.

patterns.why: Smooth and nonsmooth objective pieces receive different updates.
Extrapolation reuses the previous displacement.

nodes.name: Frank–Wolfe conditional gradient
nodes.intuition: Find the best feasible point for a linearized objective, then blend toward it.
nodes.conditions: Nonempty compact convex C, differentiable f on a neighborhood of C, x0∈C and 0≤γk≤1. The formula defines a feasible method; convergence rates additionally need smoothness and suitable step choices.
nodes.example: On a simplex, the linear oracle selects a coordinate vertex, so iterates are sparse mixtures of selected vertices.

patterns.why: A linear oracle approximates the objective at the current point.
A convex combination preserves feasibility.

nodes.name: Frank–Wolfe optimality gap
nodes.latex: g_{\rm FW}(x)=\max_{s\in C}\langle\nabla f(x),x-s\rangle,\qquad0\le f(x)-f_*\le g_{\rm FW}(x)
nodes.intuition: The largest feasible linearized improvement is a computable upper bound on how much objective value remains to gain.
nodes.conditions: Convex differentiable f on a neighborhood of nonempty compact convex C; x∈C and f*=min_C f.
nodes.example: The same linear oracle that produces a Frank–Wolfe direction also produces its stopping certificate.

patterns.why: A linear lower bound certifies the primal objective gap.
A computable directional improvement bounds unknown suboptimality.

nodes.name: Projected dual ascent
nodes.intuition: Raise the price of violated inequalities and lower prices when constraints are comfortably satisfied.
nodes.conditions: L(x,λ)=f(x)+λᵀg(x), constraints g≤0, λk≥0, αk>0 and an attained finite Lagrangian minimum at each step. Convergence needs additional step-size and regularity assumptions.
nodes.example: If a resource constraint exceeds its budget, its multiplier increases at the next update.

patterns.why: Multipliers optimize the concave dual objective.
Current constraint residuals adjust future prices.

nodes.name: Augmented Lagrangian for equality constraints
nodes.intuition: Combine constraint prices with a quadratic charge for disagreement, then revise prices using the remaining residual.
nodes.conditions: Equality-constrained problem Ax=b, ρ>0. In the method of multipliers, xk+1 minimizes Lρ(·,λk); convergence is not guaranteed for arbitrary nonconvex problems.
nodes.example: The extra quadratic term penalizes infeasibility while vanishing at every feasible point.

patterns.why: A multiplier update prices residual constraint error.
A squared residual stabilizes the primal minimization.

nodes.name: Alternating direction method of multipliers
nodes.intuition: Let two objective blocks solve separate subproblems and use a shared residual to coordinate their agreement.
nodes.conditions: Problem min f(x)+g(z) subject to Ax+Bz=c; fixed ρ>0. Standard two-block convergence assumes proper closed convex objectives, a saddle point and attained subproblem minima; more than two naive blocks need not inherit it.
nodes.example: Splitting lasso with x=z separates a quadratic solve from soft thresholding.

patterns.why: Separate blocks handle distinct objective terms.
The scaled multiplier accumulates their disagreement.

nodes.name: Douglas–Rachford splitting
nodes.intuition: Reflect through one proximal solution, correct using the other, then average the effect.
nodes.conditions: Proper closed convex f,g on R^d, γ>0, and a solution of 0∈∂f(x)+∂g(x). The shadow pk converges to a minimizer; z itself is an auxiliary variable.
nodes.example: For two closed convex sets with nonempty intersection, the two proximal maps are projections.

patterns.why: The auxiliary iteration seeks a fixed point whose shadow solves the inclusion.
Two subdifferentials are treated through separate resolvents.

nodes.name: Chambolle–Pock primal-dual splitting
nodes.latex: \begin{aligned}y^{k+1}&=\operatorname{prox}_{\sigma g^*}(y^k+\sigma K\bar x^k),\\x^{k+1}&=\operatorname{prox}_{\tau f}(x^k-\tau K^\top y^{k+1}),\\\bar x^{k+1}&=2x^{k+1}-x^k\end{aligned}
nodes.intuition: Alternate primal and dual proximal corrections while a linear operator passes disagreement between their spaces.
nodes.conditions: Minimize f(x)+g(Kx) with proper closed convex f,g on finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces and an existing saddle point. Set x̄0=x0 and τ,σ>0 with τσ||K||²<1.
nodes.example: Image denoising can place pixel fidelity in f and a gradient penalty in g(Kx).

patterns.why: Conjugation turns g(Kx) into a saddle problem.
Separate proximal maps avoid directly inverting a composite penalty.

nodes.name: BFGS Hessian approximation update
nodes.latex: B_{k+1}=B_k-\frac{B_ks_ks_k^\top B_k}{s_k^\top B_ks_k}+\frac{y_ky_k^\top}{y_k^\top s_k},\quad s_k=x_{k+1}-x_k,\ y_k=\nabla f(x_{k+1})-\nabla f(x_k)
nodes.intuition: Use the observed change in gradient to repair a curvature model along the latest step.
nodes.conditions: B_k symmetric positive definite, s_k≠0 and y_kᵀs_k>0. The update remains positive definite and satisfies B_{k+1}s_k=y_k; convergence claims require further hypotheses.
nodes.example: For a one-dimensional quadratic, one nonzero secant step recovers its exact second derivative.

patterns.why: Gradient differences reveal curvature along a displacement.
A rank-two matrix change updates the local quadratic model.

nodes.name: Exact trust-region subproblem conditions
nodes.intuition: A local quadratic model is optimized only within a radius where it is trusted, including directions of negative curvature.
nodes.conditions: Real symmetric B and Δ>0. A feasible p is a global minimizer exactly when some λ satisfies the displayed conditions; B itself need not be positive semidefinite.
nodes.example: At a saddle with zero gradient and negative curvature, the optimal step can lie on the boundary instead of staying at zero.

patterns.why: A shifted Hessian certifies global minimization of the constrained quadratic.
The multiplier distinguishes interior and radius-limited solutions.

nodes.name: Armijo sufficient-decrease condition
nodes.intuition: Accept a step when it earns a specified fraction of the improvement predicted by the local slope.
nodes.conditions: f continuously differentiable, p a descent direction with ∇f(x)ᵀp<0, α>0 and 0<c1<1. Sufficiently small positive steps satisfy this condition; backtracking contracts α by a fixed factor in (0,1).
nodes.example: For gradient descent p=−∇f(x), the required decrease is c1α||∇f(x)||².

patterns.why: A directional derivative predicts the required improvement.
A line search chooses an acceptable step length.

nodes.name: Wolfe line-search conditions
nodes.latex: \begin{aligned}f(x+\alpha p)&\le f(x)+c_1\alpha\nabla f(x)^\top p,\\\nabla f(x+\alpha p)^\top p&\ge c_2\nabla f(x)^\top p,\qquad0<c_1<c_2<1\end{aligned}
nodes.intuition: Require both enough decrease and enough flattening along a downhill direction.
nodes.conditions: Continuously differentiable f, descent direction p, α>0. If f is bounded below along the search ray, acceptable Wolfe steps exist. These are the weak Wolfe conditions.
nodes.example: With s=αp and y=∇f(x+αp)−∇f(x), the curvature condition guarantees yᵀs>0.

patterns.why: Directional slopes check whether the step is still too short.
Value and slope conditions jointly control line search.

nodes.name: Natural gradient direction
nodes.latex: v_{\rm nat}=-I(\theta)^{-1}\nabla L(\theta)=\arg\min_v\left\{\nabla L(\theta)^\top v+\tfrac12v^\top I(\theta)v\right\}
nodes.intuition: Measure the size of a parameter move by how much it changes the probability model.
nodes.conditions: Differentiable objective L and a regular statistical model with finite positive-definite Fisher information I(θ). The tangent direction is invariant under smooth invertible reparameterization; a finite coordinate Euler step need not be.
nodes.example: For a normal location model with known variance σ², the natural gradient scales the ordinary gradient by σ².

patterns.why: Fisher information sets the local statistical metric.
A metric-corrected tangent direction respects reparameterization.

nodes.name: Diagonal AdaGrad update
nodes.intuition: Coordinates with a long history of large gradients take smaller future steps.
nodes.conditions: Gradient or subgradient vectors gt, η>0 and numerical safeguard ε>0; this is an unconstrained diagonal version. Regret and convergence guarantees require boundedness and assumptions on the objective sequence.
nodes.example: A rarely active feature keeps a larger effective learning rate than a frequently active coordinate.

patterns.why: Past squared gradients build a coordinatewise scale.
Each coordinate receives its own adaptive step size.

nodes.name: Adam moment-corrected update
nodes.intuition: Smooth the gradient and its squared magnitude separately, then use their ratio to scale each update.
nodes.conditions: m0=v0=0, 0≤β1,β2<1, α,ε>0; squaring, square roots and division are coordinatewise. Bias correction removes zero-initialization bias for stationary moments; the formula alone gives no universal convergence guarantee.
nodes.example: At the first step, the bias-corrected estimates are g1 and g1 squared.

patterns.why: Exponential moving averages summarize recent first and second moments.
A coordinatewise second-moment scale normalizes the update.

nodes.name: Variance-reduced finite-sum gradient
nodes.latex:
v_i(x)=
abla f_i(x)-
abla f_i(\widetilde x)+
abla f(\widetilde x),\quad f= rac1n\sum_{j=1}^n f_j,\quad\mathbb E_i v_i(x)=
abla f(x)
nodes.intuition: Correct a noisy component gradient by subtracting its remembered value and adding back the exact average at that snapshot.
nodes.conditions: Differentiable finite-sum objective, i sampled uniformly from {1,…,n} independently conditional on x and snapshot x̃. This establishes unbiasedness; algorithmic rates require smoothness and step schedules.
nodes.example: When x=x̃, every sampled estimator equals the full gradient at the snapshot, so sampling variance is zero.

patterns.why: The estimator splits into a difference plus a known average.
A correlated correction reduces sampling noise.

nodes.name: Online projected-gradient regret bound
nodes.intuition: Even without knowing future losses, projected gradient updates can approach the performance of the best fixed decision in hindsight.
nodes.conditions: Nonempty closed convex feasible set of diameter at most D>0; convex losses with chosen subgradients gt of norm ≤G>0. Update xt+1=ΠC(xt−ηgt), x1∈C; bound holds for every fixed u∈C.
nodes.example: Average regret is at most DG/√T under the displayed horizon-dependent step size.

patterns.why: One-step distance inequalities telescope across the sequence.
Performance is compared with one hindsight comparator.

nodes.name: Logarithmic barrier and central-path gap
nodes.intuition: Stay inside the feasible region while increasing pressure toward the true objective, with reciprocal slacks acting as prices.
nodes.conditions: Differentiable convex f,gi, constraints gi(x)≤0, strictly feasible domain and an attained stationary barrier minimum for t>0; unconstrained except for these inequalities. The resulting dual certificate yields the gap.
nodes.example: Increasing t tenfold reduces the certified barrier suboptimality m/t tenfold.

patterns.why: The logarithm diverges when a strict constraint approaches its boundary.
Inverse slacks generate feasible multipliers and a known duality gap.

nodes.name: Semidefinite programming form
nodes.latex: \min_{X\in\mathbb S^n}\langle C,X\rangle\quad\text{subject to }\langle A_i,X\rangle=b_i,\quad X\succeq0,\qquad\langle A,X\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(A^\top X)
nodes.intuition: Optimize linearly over matrices that represent nonnegative quadratic energies.
nodes.conditions: Real symmetric data C,Ai; X≽0 means vᵀXv≥0 for all v. This is a convex optimization model; strong duality requires an appropriate qualification such as strict feasibility.
nodes.example: Restricting X to diagonal matrices recovers nonnegative variables in linear programming.

patterns.why: The positive-semidefinite cone is convex.
A matrix constraint controls every associated quadratic form.

nodes.name: Second-order cone programming form
nodes.latex: \min_x c^\top x\quad\text{subject to }\|A_i x+b_i\|_2\le d_i^\top x+e_i,\quad Fx=g
nodes.intuition: Keep Euclidean magnitudes below affine budgets while optimizing a linear cost.
nodes.conditions: Real compatible matrices and vectors. Each constraint is the preimage of a Lorentz cone, so its right side is necessarily nonnegative at feasible points.
nodes.example: Least-squares norm minimization becomes an SOCP by minimizing t subject to ||Ax−b||₂≤t.

patterns.why: Norm constraints bound distances or vector magnitudes.
Affine preimages preserve convex cone feasibility.

nodes.name: Empirical risk minimization
nodes.intuition: Choose a rule by minimizing its average observed loss, hoping that this average represents future cases.
nodes.conditions: Measurable loss and predictors with well-defined expectations; the training sample is usually iid from the target distribution. An exact minimizer must exist for the displayed argmin; empirical success alone does not imply generalization.
nodes.example: Squared-loss empirical risk over linear predictors gives ordinary least squares.

patterns.why: Training risk is the arithmetic mean of individual losses.
A hypothesis is selected by minimizing the observed average.

nodes.name: Regularized empirical risk
nodes.intuition: Balance fitting observed examples against a cost for the complexity or size of the fitted rule.
nodes.conditions: λ≥0, specified loss, hypothesis class and penalty; existence and uniqueness depend on them. The numerical meaning of λ changes if the loss is a sum rather than an average.
nodes.example: An ℓ₂ penalty on regression coefficients gives ridge; an ℓ₁ penalty gives lasso.

patterns.why: Two objectives are combined through a tradeoff parameter.
Fit and complexity contribute separate costs.

nodes.name: Finite-class uniform generalization bound
nodes.intuition: Testing many candidate rules costs only a logarithm of their number in the sample-size requirement.
nodes.conditions: A fixed finite nonempty class H, iid sample of size n and measurable losses in [0,1]; ε>0. The class cannot be freely chosen after looking at the same sample.
nodes.example: It suffices that n≥log(2|H|/δ)/(2ε²) to make every empirical risk ε-accurate with probability at least 1−δ.

patterns.why: The number of candidate rules enters through a union bound.
Bounded-loss concentration controls each rule's sample average.

nodes.name: Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension
nodes.intuition: Count how many sample locations can receive every possible binary labeling from the model class.
nodes.conditions: Class H of binary-valued functions on a set X; A ranges over finite subsets of X. The value is an integer or infinity; shattering concerns existence of a suitable set, not all sets of that size.
nodes.example: Thresholds on the real line have VC dimension 1; intervals have VC dimension 2.

patterns.why: Capacity is measured by realizable label patterns.
Shattering measures how many independent binary choices the class can encode.

nodes.name: Sauer–Shelah growth bound
nodes.intuition: A class that cannot freely label d+1 points has only polynomially many patterns on larger samples.
nodes.conditions: Binary class H of VC dimension d; ΠH(n) is the largest number of labelings on n points. The first sum uses binomial coefficients zero above n; the final bound requires n≥d≥1.
nodes.example: For line thresholds, the exact growth is n+1, matching the d=1 binomial sum.

patterns.why: Binomial coefficients count the limited family of patterns.
Finite shattering dimension replaces exponential growth by polynomial growth.

nodes.name: VC uniform-convergence bound
nodes.intuition: An infinite model class can behave like a finite collection once restricted to the observed and comparison samples.
nodes.conditions: Binary classification with 0/1 loss, iid sample of size n, ε>0 and a class satisfying the standard measurability condition for the supremum; otherwise use outer probability. Constants here are a conservative classical version.
nodes.example: Combining with Sauer–Shelah gives an error scale of order sqrt((d log(n/d)+log(1/δ))/n) when n≥d.

patterns.why: Only the label patterns on a finite doubled sample need counting.
The deviation shrinks when sample size dominates effective capacity.

nodes.name: Empirical Rademacher complexity
nodes.intuition: Measure how well the function class can align with random signs on this particular sample.
nodes.conditions: Fixed sample S=(Z1,…,Zn), nonempty real function class and independent symmetric signs. Assume the supremum measurable and integrable; this convention uses no absolute value and a factor 1/n.
nodes.example: A single fixed function has empirical Rademacher complexity zero because its random signed average has mean zero.

patterns.why: Independent signs supply a pure-noise fitting target.
The supremum chooses the member best aligned with that noise.

nodes.name: Rademacher generalization bound
nodes.intuition: The capacity to fit random noise on the sample bounds how optimistic the sample average may be.
nodes.conditions: Fixed measurable class F of [0,1]-valued loss functions; iid sample size n and 0<δ<1. The displayed simultaneous bound holds with probability at least 1−δ; R(f)=E f(Z).
nodes.example: Two classes of equal parameter count can receive different bounds because their sample-specific Rademacher complexities differ.

patterns.why: Random-sign fitting quantifies statistical flexibility.
A complexity term and a concentration term control generalization.

nodes.name: PAC-Bayes Bernoulli-KL bound
nodes.intuition: A data-chosen distribution over predictors pays for how far it moves from a prior fixed before seeing the data.
nodes.conditions: Finite hypothesis and observation spaces, losses in [0,1], iid sample n≥8, prior P independent of S, 0<δ<1. With probability ≥1−δ the bound holds for all Q≪P; risks average over h∼Q and kl is Bernoulli relative entropy in nats.
nodes.example: A concentrated posterior around a low-loss group can be certified if its KL cost relative to the prior is modest.

patterns.why: KL measures the cost of specializing the prior.
Both training and population loss average over randomized predictors.

nodes.name: Uniform stability implies expected generalization
nodes.intuition: If replacing one training example barely changes any prediction loss, reusing the training data creates little average optimism.
nodes.conditions: S and S′ have size n and differ in one observation; deterministic measurable learning rule A, iid data and integrable loss. The stated bound is on the expected signed gap, not a high-probability or expected-absolute-gap bound.
nodes.example: Strongly regularized convex learning algorithms often have replacement stability of order 1/n under Lipschitz loss assumptions.

patterns.why: Replacing a sample by an independent copy compares training and test roles.
