Small sensitivity can force the average generalization gap to vanish.

nodes.name: Hard-margin support vector machine
nodes.intuition: Choose a separating hyperplane with the widest empty buffer between the two classes.
nodes.conditions: Finite sample xi∈R^d, yi∈{−1,1}, both classes present and linearly separable. The canonical functional margin is fixed at 1; the distance between the two supporting planes is 2/||w||.
nodes.example: Only observations touching the optimal margin need nonzero dual multipliers.

patterns.why: Minimizing ||w|| maximizes the geometric margin.
The learning problem is a convex quadratic program.

nodes.name: Soft-margin SVM and hinge loss
nodes.intuition: Permit violations of the ideal margin but charge linearly for their size.
nodes.conditions: Finite binary-labeled sample and C>0; the intercept b is unpenalized. This equals the slack-variable program with ξi≥0 and yi(wᵀxi+b)≥1−ξi.
nodes.example: A correctly classified point can still incur hinge loss if it lies within the margin.

patterns.why: Hinge loss is a maximum of two affine functions.
A penalty trades margin width against violations.

nodes.name: Kernel soft-margin SVM dual
nodes.intuition: Express the classifier through weighted training examples and pairwise similarities.
nodes.conditions: Positive-semidefinite kernel k, finite labels ±1, C>0, unpenalized intercept and the soft-margin primal. Prediction uses sign(Σi αiyi k(xi,x)+b).
nodes.example: For a linear kernel, w=Σi αiyi xi.

patterns.why: Lagrange multipliers become coefficients of training examples.
The classifier is a finite expansion in kernel sections.

nodes.name: Positive-semidefinite kernel
nodes.intuition: A similarity function is a valid kernel when it behaves like an inner product in some feature space.
nodes.conditions: Real symmetric k on X×X; the quadratic inequality must hold for every finite choice of points and real coefficients. This is equivalent to a Hilbert-space feature representation.
nodes.example: k(x,x′)=(1+xᵀx′)² is the inner product of suitable constant, linear and quadratic features.

patterns.why: Similarity is represented as feature-space geometry.
Every finite Gram matrix must be positive semidefinite.

nodes.name: Representer theorem
nodes.intuition: Although the hypothesis space may be infinite, an optimum needs only components visible at the training points.
nodes.conditions: Reproducing-kernel Hilbert space H; Φ depends only on the displayed evaluations and Ω is strictly increasing. The implication assumes a minimizer exists; nondecreasing Ω guarantees an in-span minimizer when one exists, not necessarily every minimizer.
nodes.example: Kernel ridge regression searches finitely many coefficients despite using an infinite-dimensional Gaussian kernel space.

patterns.why: An invisible orthogonal component increases norm without altering training values.
Solutions expand in the finite span of data-centered kernels.

nodes.name: Kernel ridge regression
nodes.intuition: Fit a weighted collection of data-centered similarities, shrinking unstable directions of the Gram matrix.
nodes.conditions: Real positive-semidefinite kernel, λ>0; objective is n⁻¹Σi(yi−f(xi))²+λ||f||H² with no separate intercept. K+nλI is invertible even if K is singular.
nodes.example: With a linear kernel, this is ridge regression written in sample coordinates.

patterns.why: The solution can be expressed in sample coefficients instead of feature coefficients.
A regularized Gram matrix determines the squared-loss solution.

nodes.name: Gaussian process
nodes.intuition: Specify a random function by requiring every finite list of its values to form a Gaussian vector.
nodes.conditions: Mean function m and positive-semidefinite covariance kernel k; finite-dimensional laws must be consistent, as this construction ensures. Sample-path continuity or differentiability requires additional kernel regularity.
nodes.example: Brownian motion is a zero-mean Gaussian process with k(s,t)=min(s,t) for s,t≥0.

patterns.why: Uncertainty is placed on entire functions through compatible finite marginals.
Means and covariances determine all finite Gaussian laws.

nodes.name: Gaussian-process regression posterior
nodes.intuition: Observed values pull the predicted function through covariance, while subtracting the part of uncertainty those observations explain.
nodes.conditions: Zero-mean GP prior, yi=f(xi)+εi with independent N(0,σ²) noise independent of f, σ²>0. Formulas describe latent test values; predicting noisy observations adds σ²I.
nodes.example: The posterior mean equals kernel ridge prediction when nλ=σ² and the kernel is the same.

patterns.why: Predictions are covariance-weighted linear combinations of observations.
Conditioning subtracts explained covariance via a Schur complement.

nodes.name: Gaussian-process log marginal likelihood
nodes.intuition: A covariance model is rewarded for explaining the data and charged for spreading probability over a large volume.
nodes.conditions: Zero-mean Gaussian-process observations with independent Gaussian noise and positive-definite C. Nonzero means replace y by y−m; kernel parameters affect both the fit and determinant terms.
nodes.example: A very flexible covariance can reduce the quadratic mismatch but pays through its log determinant.

patterns.why: The Mahalanobis term measures covariance-adjusted data mismatch.
The determinant controls Gaussian normalization and model evidence.

nodes.name: Gaussian radial-basis kernel
nodes.intuition: Two inputs are similar when their distance is small relative to a chosen length scale.
nodes.conditions: x,x′∈R^d, ℓ>0 and σf²≥0. The squared-exponential kernel is positive semidefinite; it is a covariance/similarity function rather than a normalized probability density over x.
nodes.example: Doubling all input coordinates and doubling ℓ leaves every kernel value unchanged.

patterns.why: Similarity decays with squared Euclidean distance.
The length scale defines what counts as a nearby input.

nodes.name: Affine-activation neural layer
nodes.intuition: Mix input features linearly, shift their thresholds, then apply a nonlinear response.
nodes.conditions: Compatible real matrix/vector dimensions and a specified activation σ, usually applied coordinatewise. Stacking purely affine layers without nonlinearities is still an affine map.
nodes.example: Choosing σ(t)=max(0,t) produces a piecewise-affine layer.

patterns.why: Layers compose simple transformations into a richer map.
Each layer begins with an affine feature mixture.

nodes.name: Backpropagation through dense layers
nodes.intuition: Pass loss sensitivities backward through each operation, reusing intermediate values from the forward computation.
nodes.conditions: a^(ℓ+1)=Wℓh^(ℓ)+bℓ, h^(ℓ)=σ(a^(ℓ)), and δ^(ℓ)=∂L/∂a^(ℓ). Scalar differentiable loss and differentiable activations at the evaluated points; nonsmooth points require a convention and need not have an ordinary derivative.
nodes.example: A weight derivative is the downstream sensitivity times the upstream activation.

patterns.why: The chain rule traverses a composed computational graph.
Transpose Jacobians pull output sensitivities back to inputs.

nodes.name: Rectified linear unit
nodes.intuition: A gate blocks negative input and passes positive input unchanged.
nodes.conditions: Real z; the derivative at zero does not exist. The convex subdifferential at zero is [0,1], and implementations choose a convention for backpropagation.
nodes.example: ReLU(z)−ReLU(−z)=z exactly.

patterns.why: Positive and negative parts can represent a signed quantity.
The function is linear on each side of one kink.

nodes.name: Softmax cross-entropy gradient
nodes.latex: p_j=\frac{e^{z_j}}{\sum_ke^{z_k}},\qquad L=-\sum_j y_j\log p_j,\qquad\frac{\partial L}{\partial z_j}=p_j-y_j
nodes.intuition: The learning signal is predicted probability minus target probability.
nodes.conditions: Finite real logits, target vector yj≥0 summing to1, and natural logarithms. The derivative is with respect to logits; one-hot labels are a special case.
nodes.example: For a one-hot correct class c, its gradient is pc−1 while other class gradients equal their predicted probabilities.

patterns.why: Log-sum-exp cancels the exponential normalization cleanly.
A coding-style cross-entropy loss yields a probability residual.

nodes.name: Inverted dropout
nodes.intuition: Randomly omit features during training while rescaling the survivors to preserve their conditional mean.
nodes.conditions: Keep probability 0<q≤1, masks independent of h and usually independent across coordinates; the formula uses inverted scaling during training. Nonlinear network outputs need not equal their expectation when masks are removed.
nodes.example: With q=1/2, each retained activation is doubled and each omitted activation is zero.

patterns.why: Random masks perturb the feature representation.
Rescaling preserves each activation's conditional mean.

nodes.name: Mini-batch normalization
nodes.intuition: Put the current batch on a common scale, then learn a useful shift and rescaling.
nodes.conditions: Applied to one feature across a batch of m≥1 observations; ε>0 and learned γ,β. This uses divisor m, not the unbiased sample-variance divisor m−1. Inference commonly uses stored population-moment estimates.
nodes.example: For γ=1,β=0, the normalized batch has mean zero and variance vB/(vB+ε).

patterns.why: Batch moments supply a local mean and variance.
Centering and rescaling change feature coordinates.

nodes.name: Scaled dot-product attention
nodes.intuition: Each query forms a data-dependent weighted average of value vectors using its similarity to keys.
nodes.conditions: Q∈R^{nq×dk}, K∈R^{nk×dk}, V∈R^{nk×dv}, dk≥1; row-wise softmax has finite logits. Masked rows must retain at least one allowed key.
nodes.example: Identical logits in a row give the arithmetic mean of that row's available value vectors.

patterns.why: Softmax weights are nonnegative and sum to one.
Similarity computation, normalization and value aggregation compose.

nodes.name: Sigmoidal universal approximation
nodes.intuition: Enough shifted and tilted copies of one nonlinear response can approximate any continuous shape on a bounded cube.
nodes.conditions: Continuous sigmoidal σ with limits0 at −∞ and1 at +∞; finite-dimensional unit cube, real coefficients and an unrestricted finite width N. The theorem gives existence, not efficient training, sample complexity or an economical width.
nodes.example: The logistic activation satisfies these hypotheses; a single affine layer does not have this approximation property.

patterns.why: A target is approximated by a finite sum of simple ridge functions.
The approximation is uniform as the chosen network becomes sufficiently rich.

nodes.name: k-means distortion objective
nodes.intuition: Represent each observation by its nearest prototype and minimize total squared replacement error.
nodes.conditions: Finite points xi∈R^d and integer1≤k≤n; the centroids are unconstrained real vectors. The objective is generally nonconvex in all centroids together.
nodes.example: For k=1, the unique centroid is the arithmetic mean.

patterns.why: Each fixed cluster is represented by its mean.
Squared distances measure the cost of replacing data by prototypes.

nodes.name: Lloyd assignment-and-centroid iteration
nodes.intuition: Alternate sending each point to its nearest center and moving each center to its group's average.
nodes.conditions: Finite Euclidean data, specified tie-breaking and nonempty updated clusters; empty clusters need a separate reinitialization or retention rule. Each exact block step cannot increase distortion, but global optimality is not guaranteed.
nodes.example: Starting from two centers, each pass alternately changes the partition and the two means.

patterns.why: Assignments and centers update each other.
The centroid update is an exact arithmetic mean.

nodes.name: Finite Gaussian mixture model
nodes.intuition: Choose a hidden group, then draw from that group's Gaussian cloud.
nodes.conditions: Finite k, xi∈R^d and positive-definite covariance matrices for ordinary densities. A mixture of Gaussians is generally not itself Gaussian.
nodes.example: Two separated one-dimensional Gaussian components can produce a bimodal density.

patterns.why: The density is a probability-weighted mean of component densities.
A latent label decomposes the population into groups.

nodes.name: EM updates for a Gaussian mixture
nodes.intuition: Use fractional group memberships to compute weighted counts, means and covariance matrices.
nodes.conditions: Positive mixture weights and nonsingular component densities for the E-step; each Nj>0. The unconstrained covariance update may become singular and Gaussian-mixture likelihood can be unbounded, so regularization is often needed.
nodes.example: A point with responsibility0.8 contributes0.8 of an observation to that component's updated mean.

patterns.why: Responsibilities act as data-dependent weights.
Posterior assignments and parameter estimates update each other.

nodes.name: Naive Bayes classifier
nodes.intuition: Add separate pieces of class evidence after assuming the features are independent within each class.
nodes.conditions: Finite classes with positive prior mass and specified conditional feature probabilities/densities; conditional independence Xj⊥Xk given Y is a modeling assumption. Zero factors give log probability −∞ and ties require a rule.
nodes.example: Under Bernoulli feature models, word-presence evidence contributes additive class log odds.

patterns.why: Conditional independence factorizes the likelihood by feature.
Logs turn evidence products into sums.

nodes.name: k-nearest-neighbor regression
nodes.intuition: Predict by averaging the outcomes of the k observations closest to the query.
nodes.conditions: 1≤k≤n, a specified distance on inputs and deterministic or randomized tie-breaking defining exactly k neighbors. Statistical consistency needs assumptions and a growing k with k/n→0; the formula alone is only an estimator.
nodes.example: For k=n, every query receives the global response mean.

patterns.why: Prediction is a local arithmetic mean.
The metric decides which observations are comparable.

nodes.name: Decision-tree impurity decrease
nodes.intuition: A useful split makes each child group more predictable than the unsplit parent.
nodes.conditions: Empirical class proportions in a nonempty parent, two nonempty children and weights equal to child fractions. Here I is entropy in nats; other tree criteria use different impurity functions.
nodes.example: A perfectly separating split has zero child entropy, so its gain equals parent entropy.

patterns.why: A split measures reduction in class uncertainty.
Parent uncertainty is compared with the weighted child uncertainties.

nodes.name: AdaBoost exponential reweighting
nodes.intuition: Increase the influence of examples the current weak rule misses and combine the rules with confidence weights.
nodes.conditions: Binary labels and predictions ±1, positive normalized observation weights, and0<εt<1/2 for the displayed positive finite αt. Final classifier uses sign(Σt αtht(x)); the separable εt=0 case needs stopping or a convention.
nodes.example: A mistaken example's weight is multiplied by e^α while a correctly classified example's weight is multiplied by e^−α before normalization.

patterns.why: Mistakes alter the distribution used by the next learner.
Exponential loss yields a log-odds coefficient.

nodes.name: Random Fourier feature approximation
nodes.intuition: Approximate a stationary similarity by averaging a finite collection of randomly chosen oscillations.
nodes.conditions: Continuous real stationary positive-definite kernel k with k(0)=1 and spectral probability law ρ such that k(t)=Eρ cos(ωᵀt). Independent ωj∼ρ and bj∼Uniform[0,2π]; this formula uses angular frequencies.
nodes.example: For k(t)=exp(−||t||²/(2ℓ²)), sample ω∼N(0,ℓ⁻²I).

patterns.why: A finite random feature sum estimates a spectral expectation.
A nonlinear kernel is approximated by an explicit finite feature map.

nodes.name: Autoencoder reconstruction objective
nodes.intuition: Compress each example into an internal representation and train a decoder to reconstruct what matters.
nodes.conditions: Finite Euclidean data and specified encoder/decoder families. A bottleneck, regularization or corruption is needed to prevent an unrestricted identity solution; useful representations do not follow from reconstruction alone.
nodes.example: A linear rank-r encoder-decoder at a global squared-error optimum reconstructs the PCA subspace for centered data.

patterns.why: An encoder and decoder form a round trip.
A lower-dimensional code represents selected data structure.

nodes.name: Bayesian-network factorization
nodes.intuition: Build a joint distribution from local conditional rules arranged without directed cycles.
nodes.conditions: A finite directed acyclic graph and normalized conditional probability tables, or compatible conditional densities/kernels; parent sets follow a topological order. A causal interpretation requires additional assumptions beyond this factorization.
nodes.example: A first-order Markov chain factors as p(x0)∏t p(xt|xt−1).

patterns.why: Local conditionals multiply into a normalized global law.
The graph specifies which preceding variables a local rule consults.

nodes.name: Sum-product messages on a pairwise tree
nodes.latex: m_{i\to j}(x_j)=\sum_{x_i}\psi_i(x_i)\psi_{ij}(x_i,x_j)\!\!\prod_{\ell\in N(i)\setminus\{j\}}\!\!m_{\ell\to i}(x_i),\qquad p_i(x_i)\propto\psi_i(x_i)\prod_{\ell\in N(i)}m_{\ell\to i}(x_i)
nodes.intuition: Each branch sends the rest of the tree a compact summary of all possibilities it contains.
nodes.conditions: Finite discrete variables on a tree with nonnegative unary/pairwise factors and positive finite partition sum. Messages are computed after receiving all other-neighbor messages; the formulas give exact marginals. On loopy graphs, naive iteration is not generally exact.
nodes.example: For a chain, the two message directions are forward and backward marginalization.

patterns.why: Subtree summaries are built from smaller subtree summaries.
A tree separates neighboring branches once the connecting state is fixed.

nodes.name: Log-linear Markov random field
nodes.intuition: Score compatible local configurations, add their scores, and normalize the resulting global weights.
nodes.conditions: Finite discrete state spaces and finite real parameters/features on cliques C of an undirected graph. Positivity ensures the equivalence between graph separation and the appropriate Markov factorization theorem; edges need not represent causal influence.
nodes.example: Unary terms favor labels while pairwise terms favor compatible neighboring labels.

patterns.why: Clique statistics assemble a global model.
Additive scores become multiplicative positive potentials.

nodes.name: Coordinate mean-field variational update
nodes.intuition: Replace a complicated joint posterior with independent factors, letting each factor feel the averaged effect of the others.
nodes.conditions: A normalizable posterior with finite relevant expectations; restrict q to a product family. Each coordinate update is valid when the exponentiated expectation is integrable and normalized. Coordinate optima need not give the global best product approximation.
nodes.example: In conjugate models, averaging sufficient statistics often keeps each updated factor in a recognizable exponential family.

patterns.why: Other latent variables enter through expectations.
Each factor is optimized while the others are held fixed.

nodes.name: Pathwise reparameterization gradient
nodes.intuition: Keep the underlying random draw fixed while differentiating how the generated sample moves with the parameters.
nodes.conditions: Base law p0 independent of θ; almost-sure differentiability in a parameter neighborhood and an integrable dominating bound on derivatives justify exchange of gradient and expectation. The derivative on the right includes all direct and pathwise parameter dependence.
nodes.example: For Z=μ+σε with ε∼N(0,1), derivatives can pass through μ and σ while ε remains fixed.

patterns.why: Parameter dependence moves from the sampling law into a deterministic map.
The chain rule differentiates through that map.

nodes.name: Likelihood-ratio gradient of an expectation
nodes.intuition: A parameter changes an average both by changing each outcome's value and by changing how often outcomes are sampled.
nodes.conditions: Densities or masses with parameter-independent support, differentiable integrand/density and domination sufficient to differentiate under the integral; score terms integrable. Moving support may add boundary terms. No differentiability in Z is needed.
nodes.example: A constant baseline b can be subtracted from f in the score term because the expected score is zero under the same regularity.

patterns.why: Direct-value and probability-weight changes contribute separate derivatives.
Sampling converts a derivative of an expectation into an expected estimator.

nodes.name: Gaussian denoising score matching
nodes.latex: \widetilde X=X+\sigma\varepsilon,\quad \min_s\mathbb E\left\|s(\widetilde X)+\frac{\widetilde X-X}{\sigma^2}\right\|^2,\qquad s_*(u)=\nabla_u\log p_\sigma(u)
nodes.intuition: Learn a field pointing toward likely clean structure by predicting how noise displaced the observations.
nodes.conditions: X∈R^d, independent ε∼N(0,I), σ>0; pσ is the Gaussian-smoothed data density. Minimize over measurable square-integrable fields, with differentiation of the Gaussian convolution justified. The target is the spatial score of pσ, not a parameter score or the unsmoothed density's score.
nodes.example: The optimal denoised mean is E[X|X̃=u]=u+σ²s*(u).

patterns.why: The squared-loss optimum is a conditional mean of the noise target.
A log-density gradient describes local probability increase.

nodes.name: Hellinger distance
nodes.intuition: Take square roots of probabilities and compare them with Euclidean geometry.
nodes.conditions: Probability measures P,Q dominated by a common measure μ, with densities p,q. This normalized convention has0≤H≤1; some references omit the factor1/2. The result is independent of μ.
nodes.example: Distributions with disjoint supports have H=1.

patterns.why: Square-root densities lie on the unit sphere in L².
The distance is a squared norm after a nonlinear coordinate change.

nodes.name: Rényi divergence
nodes.intuition: Change the order to tune how heavily rare or large likelihood ratios contribute to distributional mismatch.
nodes.conditions: Finite alphabet, probability vectors and natural logs. For α>1, pi>0 with qi=0 gives +∞; zero-over-zero terms contribute0. For0<α<1, terms with either mass zero vanish; disjoint supports give +∞.
nodes.example: As α→1, the expression tends to KL divergence; at α=1/2 it is −2log Σ√piqi.

patterns.why: A log moment of the likelihood ratio controls the comparison.
The order parameter changes sensitivity to mass concentration.

nodes.name: Rényi entropy
nodes.intuition: Measure effective diversity while changing how strongly common outcomes dominate the count.
nodes.conditions: Finite probability vector, α>0 with α≠1 in the displayed sum, and natural logs. The value at1 is its continuous limit; zero masses contribute0.
nodes.example: H2(P)=−log Σpi² is negative log probability that two independent draws collide.

patterns.why: Exponentiating entropy gives an order-dependent effective number of outcomes.
The order controls the weight given to high-probability outcomes.

nodes.name: Jensen–Shannon divergence
nodes.intuition: Compare two distributions through a common mixture so neither is asked to explain outcomes it assigns no mass to.
nodes.conditions: Probability measures on the same measurable space, KL in nats. This equal-weight convention satisfies0≤JS≤log2 and remains finite for disjoint supports; √JS is a metric.
nodes.example: If a fair hidden coin chooses P or Q, JS is the mutual information between the coin and the observed draw.

patterns.why: A midpoint distribution provides the common reference.
The divergence measures how much one draw reveals about its source.

nodes.name: Csiszár f-divergence
nodes.intuition: Compare probability laws by applying a convex penalty to their local likelihood ratio.
nodes.conditions: P≪Q, convex f:(0,∞)→R with f(1)=0 and f(0) defined by the right limit; expectation may be +∞. General nondominated laws need an added singular-mass term, which is outside this displayed version.
nodes.example: f(t)=tlog t gives KL; f(t)=|t−1|/2 gives total variation.

patterns.why: A convex likelihood-ratio penalty yields nonnegativity by Jensen.
The likelihood ratio encodes distinguishability.

nodes.name: Pinsker inequality
nodes.intuition: Small relative entropy guarantees that every event has nearly the same probability under the two laws.
nodes.conditions: Probability measures on the same measurable space, TV=sup_A|P(A)−Q(A)| and natural-log KL; if KL is infinite the bound is vacuous. The factor changes with log base or unhalved variation conventions.
nodes.example: KL≤0.02 nats implies event probabilities differ by at most0.1.

patterns.why: An information discrepancy controls observable probability differences.
A divergence bounds a metric.

nodes.name: Chain rule for relative entropy
nodes.intuition: Total mismatch splits into disagreement about the first variable and remaining disagreement after it is known.
nodes.conditions: Finite or countable joint distributions with PXY≪QXY; conditional laws are evaluated only at x of positive PX. Extended nonnegative values are allowed, with the usual zero-mass conventions.
nodes.example: If the two models share the same conditional law of Y given X, all divergence lies in the X marginals.

patterns.why: A joint likelihood ratio factors into marginal and conditional parts.
Conditional divergence is averaged under the first model's marginal.

nodes.name: Log-sum inequality
nodes.latex: \sum_i a_i\log\frac{a_i}{b_i}\ge A\log\frac AB,\qquad A=\sum_i a_i,\quad B=\sum_i b_i
nodes.intuition: Combining categories can hide mismatch, but cannot create more of it.
nodes.conditions: Finite nonnegative ai,bi with A,B>0;0log(0/b)=0 and a log(a/0)=+∞ for a>0. Equality holds when ai/A=bi/B for every i.
nodes.example: With A=B=1, the inequality reduces to nonnegativity of KL divergence.

patterns.why: Convexity of tlog t survives weighted averaging.
Coarsening categories cannot increase distinguishability.

nodes.name: Information density
nodes.intuition: One outcome pair supplies evidence for dependence relative to an independence model.
nodes.conditions: Finite/countable variables, or jointly dominated densities with the corresponding ratio; evaluate on the joint support and use natural logs. Individual information density may be negative although its expectation is nonnegative.
nodes.example: An outcome pair rarer jointly than under independent marginals has negative information density.

patterns.why: A sample-specific log likelihood ratio quantifies evidence.
Mutual information is its joint-distribution average.

nodes.name: Conditional Shannon entropy
nodes.latex: H(X\mid Y)=-\sum_{x,y}p(x,y)\log p(x\mid y)=\mathbb E_Y H(P_{X|Y})
nodes.intuition: Average the uncertainty remaining about X after learning which value Y took.
nodes.conditions: Finite discrete variables; only positive-probability y need conditional laws and0log0=0. Natural logs give nats. This is an average number, not a random conditional entropy function.
nodes.example: If X is determined by Y, conditional entropy is zero; if they are independent, it is H(X).

patterns.why: Each conditional uncertainty is weighted by the probability of its condition.
Conditioning describes the information already available.

nodes.name: Entropy rate of a stationary source
nodes.intuition: Count fresh uncertainty per symbol after the past has already been described.
nodes.conditions: Stationary discrete-time process on a finite alphabet; both limits exist and agree. Independence is not required, and ergodicity is not needed for this equality.
nodes.example: For a stationary Markov chain, H̄=−Σi,j πiPijlogPij.

patterns.why: Past dependence reduces the fresh information in each new symbol.
A per-symbol long-block limit equals a limiting conditional quantity.

nodes.name: Shannon–McMillan asymptotic equipartition
nodes.intuition: Long typical messages have almost the same exponential probability scale, even when symbols are dependent.
nodes.conditions: Stationary ergodic finite-alphabet process; natural logs and entropy rate H̄. Without ergodicity, the limit can depend on the ergodic component rather than equal one constant.
nodes.example: For an iid source, typical block probabilities are approximately e^(−nH), and roughly e^(nH) typical messages carry most mass.

patterns.why: Normalized log likelihood settles to a constant under ergodicity.
Entropy rate governs typical message size.

nodes.name: Binary symmetric channel capacity
nodes.intuition: Each transmitted binary symbol offers one binary choice, reduced by the uncertainty of an independent flip.
nodes.conditions: Memoryless binary channel Y=X⊕N with independent Bernoulli(p) noise,0≤p≤1; capacity in nats per channel use. Divide by log2 for bits.
nodes.example: At p=1/2 the output is independent of the input and capacity is zero.

patterns.why: Capacity subtracts noise uncertainty from maximal output uncertainty.
Input-label symmetry makes the uniform input optimal.

nodes.name: Binary erasure channel capacity
nodes.intuition: A received symbol reveals its entire binary choice or explicitly announces that the choice was erased.
nodes.conditions: Memoryless binary channel that independently erases each input with probability ε∈[0,1] and otherwise returns it exactly; erasure is a distinct output symbol. Units are nats per use.
nodes.example: Erasing half of the symbols leaves capacity one-half bit per use.

patterns.why: Information is weighted by the fraction of unerased uses.
An erasure hides a symbol but does not introduce an ambiguous flipped value.

nodes.name: Water-filling for parallel Gaussian channels
nodes.intuition: Allocate power to quieter channels until all used channels have the same combined noise-plus-power level.
nodes.conditions: Parallel real memoryless additive Gaussian channels with independent noises of variances Nj>0 and total average input power P≥0. Independent Gaussian inputs attain capacity; ν is chosen to satisfy the budget. Units are nats per vector channel use.
nodes.example: A channel whose noise variance exceeds the water level receives no power.

patterns.why: A concave power-allocation problem chooses channel investments.
One multiplier equalizes marginal gain among active channels.

nodes.name: Rate-distortion function
nodes.latex: R(D)=\inf_{P_{\widehat X|X}:\ \mathbb E\,d(X,\widehat X)\le D}I(X;\widehat X)
nodes.intuition: Find the least information a reconstruction must retain to meet an average accuracy requirement.
nodes.conditions: Specified source law, reconstruction alphabet and nonnegative distortion d; infimum over conditional reconstruction laws. For finite-alphabet memoryless sources, its operational meaning is the asymptotic block-compression rate with vanishing excess tolerance.
nodes.example: At a distortion large enough for a constant reconstruction, the rate can be zero.

patterns.why: Mutual information measures retained source information.
An accuracy constraint defines the cheapest permissible representation.

nodes.name: Gaussian squared-error rate-distortion
nodes.intuition: Precision is logarithmically expensive: every fixed factor of error reduction costs the same extra information.
nodes.conditions: Memoryless real Gaussian source of variance σ²>0, real reconstructions and mean squared error distortion; nats per source symbol.
nodes.example: Reducing mean squared error by a factor4 costs one additional bit per symbol.

patterns.why: Rate depends logarithmically on variance divided by allowed error.
Squared error and Gaussian entropy yield a closed form.

nodes.name: Bernoulli Hamming rate-distortion
nodes.intuition: Retaining only approximate bits saves the entropy associated with the allowed error fraction.
nodes.conditions: Memoryless Bernoulli(p) source, binary reconstruction, distortion1{x≠x̂},0≤p≤1 and natural-log binary entropy h2 with0log0=0.
nodes.example: For a fair source, R(D)=log2−h2(D) until D=1/2; guessing a constant reaches that zero-rate error.

patterns.why: Allowed uncertainty in errors reduces the necessary retained information.
The optimal binary reconstruction law achieves the distortion budget.

nodes.name: Slepian–Wolf separate-compression region
nodes.latex: R_X\ge H(X|Y),\qquad R_Y\ge H(Y|X),\qquad R_X+R_Y\ge H(X,Y)
nodes.intuition: Two encoders can exploit correlation even when they cannot see each other's data, provided the decoder sees both messages.
nodes.conditions: Iid pairs from a fixed finite-alphabet joint distribution; separate block encoders, joint decoder and error probability tending to zero. The inequalities describe the closure of achievable rates in nats per pair.
nodes.example: If X=Y, the total rate need only equal H(X); one encoder can carry the entire description.

patterns.why: Separate messages divide responsibility for joint information.
Conditional entropies and joint entropy set the three rate constraints.

nodes.name: Information bottleneck objective
nodes.intuition: Build a compact summary that forgets details of X while preserving information useful for predicting Y.
nodes.conditions: Fixed finite-alphabet joint law PXY, specified finite representation alphabet T and β≥0. The Markov condition means T is generated from X; predictive relevance depends on the chosen Y.
nodes.example: A summary suitable for identifying a speaker need not be suitable for transcribing the words they speak.

patterns.why: Compression and predictive information are measured separately.
The parameter β trades summary compactness against retained relevance.

nodes.name: Sanov large deviations for empirical laws
nodes.intuition: An empirical distribution unlike the true one costs an exponential probability governed by relative entropy.
nodes.conditions: Iid observations on a finite alphabet with strictly positive true probabilities p; A is any Borel subset of its probability simplex, using the usual topology. Infimum of the empty set is+∞; matching interior/closure infima yields a limit.
nodes.example: For a Bernoulli sample whose empirical success rate is near q≠p, the exponent is the Bernoulli KL divergence D(q||p).

patterns.why: Relative entropy is the rate function for an unusual empirical law.
Logarithmic probabilities scale linearly with sample size.

nodes.name: Chernoff–Stein testing exponent
nodes.intuition: With one error probability held below a fixed tolerance, the other can shrink exponentially at a KL-determined rate.
nodes.conditions: Two distinct strictly positive distributions P,Q on a finite alphabet, iid samples and fixed0<α<1. A is the event of accepting P, so α controls rejection under P and β is erroneous acceptance under Q.
nodes.example: Doubling sample size approximately squares the optimal small type-II error on its leading exponential scale.

patterns.why: Relative entropy becomes an operational discrimination rate.
The optimal error is characterized through a normalized log limit.

nodes.name: Chernoff information for symmetric testing
nodes.intuition: Balance both kinds of classification mistake and choose the exponential tilt at which the two models are hardest to distinguish.
nodes.conditions: Distinct strictly positive finite-alphabet distributions, iid samples and fixed positive prior probabilities for the two hypotheses; Pe* is minimum average Bayesian error. Natural logs are used.
nodes.example: Unlike the directed KL exponent, Chernoff information is symmetric in P and Q.

patterns.why: A one-dimensional tilt parameter selects the best exponential bound.
The minimized overlap governs Bayesian testing difficulty.

nodes.name: Entropy power inequality
nodes.intuition: The effective Gaussian variance associated with entropy grows at least additively when independent noises are added.
nodes.conditions: Independent R^d-valued vectors with densities, finite second moments and finite differential entropies; natural-log h. Equality holds for nondegenerate Gaussian vectors with proportional covariance matrices.
nodes.example: For independent scalar Gaussians, entropy power equals variance and the inequality becomes variance additivity.

patterns.why: Independent contributions cannot reduce their combined entropy-power budget.
Exponentiating entropy produces a variance-like quantity.

nodes.name: de Bruijn entropy derivative
nodes.latex: \frac d{dt}h(X+\sqrt t\,Z)=\frac12J(X+\sqrt t\,Z),\qquad J(Y)=\mathbb E\|\nabla\log p_Y(Y)\|^2
nodes.intuition: The rate at which Gaussian smoothing creates entropy is measured by the roughness of the log density.
nodes.conditions: X∈R^d with finite second moment, independent Z∼N(0,I), and t>0. J is total spatial Fisher information of the smoothed density; natural-log entropy. A statement at t=0 requires additional regularity.
nodes.example: For X∼N(0,σ²I), both sides equal d/[2(σ²+t)].

patterns.why: The derivative of entropy measures infinitesimal added noise.
Spatial score energy quantifies sensitivity of the density.

nodes.name: I-MMSE identity
nodes.intuition: The extra information gained from a slight increase in signal strength equals half the estimation error still left.
nodes.conditions: Real X with finite second moment, independent standard normal Z and γ≥0, with the right derivative at zero. Mutual information is in nats; the input distribution is fixed while γ changes.
nodes.example: For X∼N(0,σ²), the MMSE is σ²/(1+γσ²), matching the derivative of (1/2)log(1+γσ²).

patterns.why: Channel information growth is tied to estimation uncertainty.
The remaining squared error uses the conditional mean predictor.

nodes.name: Mutual information of a Gaussian pair
nodes.intuition: For jointly Gaussian variables, dependence is exactly the reduction in covariance volume from independent to joint uncertainty.
nodes.conditions: Jointly Gaussian vector (X,Y) with positive-definite full covariance ΣXY and marginal covariance blocks ΣX,ΣY. The scalar formula uses correlation |ρ|<1; logs are natural.
nodes.example: Uncorrelated jointly Gaussian variables have zero mutual information and are independent.

patterns.why: The entropy difference measures dependence.
A determinant ratio compares uncertainty ellipsoids.

nodes.name: KL divergence between Gaussian laws
nodes.intuition: Separate distributional mismatch into covariance shape, mean displacement and normalization volume.
nodes.conditions: Two real d-dimensional Gaussian laws with positive-definite covariance matrices; natural-log KL. Singular Gaussian cases require support-aware formulas and may have infinite divergence.
nodes.example: With equal covariance Σ, the divergence is half the squared Mahalanobis distance between means.

patterns.why: Mean, covariance and volume terms contribute separately.
Expected log-density differences reduce to quadratic moments.

nodes.name: Maximum entropy on a half-line with fixed mean
nodes.intuition: With only a nonnegative support and an average size specified, exponential decay spreads uncertainty most.
nodes.conditions: Absolutely continuous law on [0,∞) with mean μ and well-defined differential entropy; equality exactly for density μ⁻¹e^(−x/μ) almost everywhere. Natural logs.
nodes.example: A mean-one exponential variable has maximal entropy1 nat among nonnegative continuous variables of mean1.

patterns.why: Entropy is maximized subject to a support and moment constraint.
A linear log-density matches the mean constraint.

nodes.name: Dual of finite maximum-entropy moment matching
nodes.intuition: Find the least-committed probability vector by adjusting prices until model moments match the required moments.
nodes.conditions: Finite real feature vectors Ti, target τ in the relative interior of their convex hull, and natural logs. The minimizing parameter may be nonunique along redundant feature directions, but the maximizing probability vector is unique.
nodes.example: With only normalization and no feature constraints, the optimum is uniform and the value is log m.

patterns.why: Moment constraints become coefficients of a log-partition objective.
Entropy maximization and convex moment matching describe the same optimum.

nodes.name: Local quadratic expansion of KL
nodes.intuition: Very close probability models have a quadratic information distance determined by Fisher information.
nodes.conditions: Finite observation alphabet with strictly positive probabilities that are twice continuously differentiable in a parameter neighborhood; θ interior. Natural logs; I may be singular if parameters are locally redundant.
nodes.example: For a normal location family with known variance, the corresponding exact KL is δ²/(2σ²).

patterns.why: Second-order expansion describes nearby probability laws.
Fisher information supplies a local quadratic metric when positive definite.

nodes.name: Wasserstein p-distance
nodes.intuition: Match the mass of one distribution to the other and minimize the average cost of moving matched mass.
nodes.conditions: Probability laws on R^d with finite pth moments,1≤p<∞; Π(μ,ν) is the set of joint couplings having the required marginals. The infimum is attained and defines a metric.
nodes.example: For two point masses δa and δb, Wp equals ||a−b|| for every p.

patterns.why: Distributional distance respects the geometry of sample locations.
A coupling is chosen to minimize transportation cost.

nodes.name: Kantorovich–Rubinstein duality
nodes.intuition: The cheapest transport cost equals the largest difference detectable by a function that cannot change faster than distance allows.
nodes.conditions: Probability measures on R^d with finite first moments; real1-Lipschitz functions. Constants cancel, so one may impose φ(0)=0 to make integrability explicit.
nodes.example: For point masses at a and b, a suitable distance-aligned linear function attains ||a−b||.

patterns.why: Transport plans and Lipschitz tests give equivalent primal and dual descriptions.
A Lipschitz constraint ties observable variation to movement cost.

nodes.name: Sinkhorn scaling for entropic transport
nodes.intuition: Repeatedly fix row totals and column totals of a positive transport table until both marginal budgets agree.
nodes.conditions: Strictly positive probability vectors a,b, finite real cost matrix C, ε>0 and positive initialization; division is componentwise. The transport table converges to the unique minimizer of ΣCijPij+εΣPij(logPij−1) with the stated marginals. At fixed ε this is regularized transport.
nodes.example: Uniform a,b make the scaled table have equal row and column sums.

patterns.why: Alternating row and column corrections seek consistent marginals.
An entropy penalty spreads mass and produces exponential cost weights.

nodes.name: Finite-alphabet entropy continuity bound
nodes.intuition: Changing only a small fraction of probability mass changes entropy by a controlled amount when the alphabet is fixed.
nodes.conditions: Two distributions on the same finite alphabet of size m≥2, total variation t∈[0,1], natural logs and binary entropy h2. The bound is not uniform over arbitrarily large alphabets.
nodes.example: For binary laws the bound simplifies to |H(P)−H(Q)|≤h2(t).

patterns.why: The entropy change is bounded by uncertainty about whether and how outcomes differ.
Small total variation implies entropy convergence on a fixed finite alphabet.

nodes.name: Bilateral z-transform
nodes.intuition: Encode a whole sequence by weighting each time index with a power of one complex variable.
nodes.conditions: Complex sequence on the integers; z≠0 at points of absolute convergence. The region of convergence is part of the transform and can be an annulus, possibly with boundary circles; a rational expression alone does not specify the sequence.
nodes.example: For x[n]=a^n for n≥0 and zero otherwise, X(z)=1/(1−az⁻¹) on |z|>|a|.

patterns.why: Time indices become exponents and sequence operations become algebra.
Complex exponential weighting selects growth rates and oscillations.

nodes.name: Bilateral z-transform shift rule
nodes.intuition: A delay of k samples attaches a factor representing k units of waiting.
nodes.conditions: Bilateral transform and finite integer k; equality holds at every nonzero finite z in the original absolute-convergence region. Behavior at zero or infinity can change. One-sided transforms need boundary terms.
nodes.example: A one-sample delay of the unit impulse has transform z⁻¹.

patterns.why: Translation in time has a simple representation in transform coordinates.
A reindexing of the series becomes multiplication by a monomial.

nodes.name: z-transform convolution rule
nodes.intuition: Combining all pairs of time contributions becomes ordinary multiplication of their generating expressions.
nodes.conditions: At a nonzero z where both weighted series converge absolutely, the convolution converges absolutely and the identity holds. The resulting transform can have a larger region after cancellation. This is linear convolution on all integers.
nodes.example: Two causal sequences aⁿ and bⁿ have convolution transform [(1−az⁻¹)(1−bz⁻¹)]⁻¹ in their common outer region.

patterns.why: Cascading time-invariant filters multiplies their transfer functions.
The Cauchy product collects all contributions with the same total index.

nodes.name: Discrete-time Fourier transform
nodes.intuition: An aperiodic sequence has a continuous frequency description that repeats every full turn.
nodes.conditions: Absolute summability x∈ℓ¹(Z) gives a continuous2π-periodic transform and the stated inversion. There is also an ℓ²-to-L² extension. Here ω is angular frequency per sample; this is not a finite DFT.
nodes.example: The sequence x[0]=x[1]=1, zero elsewhere, has X(ω)=1+e⁻ⁱω.

patterns.why: Discrete time pairs with a periodic continuous frequency domain.
Integer exponentials on one frequency period extract individual samples.

nodes.name: Exponential eigenfunctions of LTI filters
nodes.latex: T_h(e^{2\pi i\xi t})=\widehat h(\xi)e^{2\pi i\xi t},\qquad (T_hf)(t)=\int_{\mathbb R}h(s)f(t-s)\,ds
nodes.intuition: A time-invariant linear filter changes each pure frequency's size and phase while preserving its frequency.
nodes.conditions: Impulse response h∈L¹(R) and real ξ. The bounded complex exponential makes the displayed integral well-defined; it is a generalized frequency mode, not a square-integrable eigenvector on the whole real line.
nodes.example: A moving average suppresses frequencies whose oscillations cancel within its averaging window.

patterns.why: Commuting with time translations selects exponentials as frequency modes.
A filter acts independently on the Fourier components of a signal.

nodes.name: Noncausal Wiener filter for additive noise
nodes.intuition: Keep frequencies in proportion to how much of their observed power is expected to be signal.
nodes.conditions: Zero-mean jointly wide-sense stationary discrete-time signal S and noise N, uncorrelated at all lags, with integrable spectral densities. The formula gives the mean-square optimal noncausal linear estimator in the closed span of all observations. Set H=0 where both spectra vanish. It need not be causal or have an absolutely summable impulse response.
nodes.example: If signal and noise have equal power at a frequency, that frequency is multiplied by one half.

patterns.why: The optimal residual is orthogonal to every observation used for prediction.
Each frequency is shrunk according to its signal-to-total-power ratio.

nodes.name: Matched-filter signal-to-noise optimum
nodes.intuition: To detect a known shape in equally noisy coordinates, add the data with weights matching that shape.
nodes.conditions: Nonzero deterministic signal s∈Cⁿ and additive mean-zero noise with covariance E[NN*]=σ²I, σ>0. The criterion is output squared signal divided by noise variance; Gaussianity is unnecessary for this SNR optimum.
nodes.example: For a real pulse with samples(1,2,1), the statistic y1+2y2+y3 collects its energy; convolution implements this with a time-reversed template.

patterns.why: Only the data component parallel to the signal contributes to the matched statistic.
Cauchy–Schwarz determines the weights maximizing signal relative to noise.

nodes.name: Short-time Fourier transform
nodes.intuition: Slide a window across a signal and measure the frequencies visible within each window.
nodes.conditions: f,g∈L²(R), g nonzero, and real τ,ξ. Cauchy–Schwarz makes each displayed integral absolutely convergent. ξ is cycles per unit time. Window choice sets the time-frequency resolution.
nodes.example: A rising chirp traces a rising frequency band in |Vgf|² even though its whole-signal Fourier transform does not record when each frequency occurred.

patterns.why: The signal is compared with localized oscillatory templates.
The transform is an inner product with a translated and modulated window.

nodes.name: Continuous wavelet transform
nodes.intuition: Compare a signal with shifted copies of one shape at many zoom levels.
nodes.conditions: f,ψ∈L²(R), ψ nonzero; a∈R\{0}, b∈R. The normalization preserves the template's L² norm. The admissibility condition ∫|ψ̂(ξ)|²/|ξ|dξ<∞ is additionally needed for the usual reconstruction theorem.
nodes.example: A short oscillating feature produces a large coefficient when the template's location and scale fit it.

patterns.why: Dilation changes the template's resolution while normalization preserves its energy.
Coefficients measure agreement with a family of translated and rescaled shapes.

nodes.name: Hilbert transform and analytic signal
nodes.intuition: Build a quadrature partner for a real signal so the combined complex signal retains only positive frequencies.
nodes.conditions: Real f∈L²(R), with the Fourier transform defined using e⁻²πⁱξt and the Hilbert transform defined by its L² multiplier. The last equality is almost everywhere; a possible value at ξ=0 is irrelevant in L². A principal-value integral needs its own pointwise hypotheses.
nodes.example: In the periodic analogue, H(cos t)=sin t and cos t+i sin t=eⁱt.

patterns.why: Positive and negative frequency halves of a real signal are separated.
A real oscillation becomes a complex amplitude and phase representation.

nodes.name: Cauchy–Binet formula
nodes.intuition: A determinant of a composite sums the volume contributions from every intermediate coordinate plane.
nodes.conditions: A is m×n and B is n×m over a commutative field, with m≤n; index subsets use increasing order.
nodes.example: For B=Aᵀ, each summand is a squared maximal minor.

patterns.why: Intermediate coordinate planes contribute separately.
Subsets select which coordinates carry an m-dimensional volume.

nodes.name: Matrix determinant lemma
nodes.intuition: A rank-one change modifies volume by a single scalar factor.
nodes.conditions: A is an invertible n×n real or complex matrix; u,v are n-vectors and * denotes conjugate transpose.
nodes.example: For A=I the new determinant is 1+v*u.

patterns.why: A rank-one change is separated from the original matrix.
The determinant tracks signed or complex volume scaling.

nodes.name: Sylvester determinant identity
nodes.intuition: A coupled transformation has the same nontrivial determinant contribution whether tracked through its input or output space.
nodes.conditions: A is m×n and B is n×m over a commutative field. Neither matrix need be square or invertible.
nodes.example: A tall matrix can reduce a large determinant to one of smaller dimension.

patterns.why: The two orders describe the same coupling on different spaces.
Extra dimensions contribute only unit factors.

nodes.name: Determinant of a matrix exponential
nodes.intuition: Trace adds infinitesimal expansion rates; exponentiation turns their sum into total volume scaling.
nodes.conditions: A is any finite square complex matrix, including real matrices; no diagonalizability is assumed.
nodes.example: For a trace-zero real matrix, eᵗᴬ preserves oriented volume for every real t.

patterns.why: Products of exponential eigenvalues combine through a sum.
Zero trace gives determinant one.

nodes.name: Complex Schur triangularization
nodes.intuition: An orthonormal change of coordinates makes every complex linear map triangular, even when eigenvectors do not form a basis.
nodes.conditions: A is a finite complex square matrix; U is unitary and diagonal entries of T are the eigenvalues with multiplicity. This is an existence statement, not an algorithm.
nodes.example: A defective Jordan block is already triangular but cannot be diagonalized.

patterns.why: Unitary coordinates preserve inner-product geometry.
The triangular flag exposes successive invariant subspaces.

nodes.name: Simultaneous diagonalization of commuting Hermitian matrices
nodes.latex: AB=BA\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad A=U\Lambda U^*,\ B=U M U^*
nodes.intuition: Commuting self-adjoint measurements can be resolved in one common set of orthogonal directions.
nodes.conditions: A,B are Hermitian n×n matrices over C, or real symmetric matrices with orthogonal U; Λ and M are real diagonal.
nodes.example: Two diagonal matrices commute because each coordinate is processed independently.

patterns.why: One operator preserves the other’s eigenspaces.
A common basis splits both maps into scalar actions.

nodes.name: Eigenvalue interlacing for a principal submatrix
nodes.intuition: Removing one coordinate constrains allowable directions, trapping each new eigenvalue between two old ones.
nodes.conditions: A is n×n Hermitian, n≥2; B is a principal (n−1)×(n−1) submatrix; eigenvalues are sorted increasingly.
nodes.example: Deleting a graph vertex gives an adjacency principal submatrix with interlacing eigenvalues.

patterns.why: Rayleigh extrema are taken over restricted subspaces.
A coordinate hyperplane restricts the direction search.

nodes.name: Weyl eigenvalue bounds for a Hermitian sum
nodes.intuition: Adding B shifts every ordered eigenvalue by an amount between B’s weakest and strongest quadratic effects.
nodes.conditions: A,B are n×n Hermitian and eigenvalues are indexed increasingly, 1≤i≤n.
nodes.example: If −εI≼B≼εI, every eigenvalue shifts by at most ε.

patterns.why: Variational eigenvalue formulas compare the quadratic forms.
The bounds add Rayleigh-quotient inequalities.

nodes.name: Schur product theorem
nodes.intuition: Entrywise products preserve positive-semidefinite Gram structure by pairing the feature vectors through tensor products.
nodes.conditions: A,B are Hermitian positive-semidefinite matrices of equal finite size over R or C.
nodes.example: Multiplying two valid covariance-kernel matrices entrywise gives another positive-semidefinite matrix.

patterns.why: The product remains a nonnegative quadratic form.
Tensoring feature vectors multiplies their inner products.

nodes.name: Hadamard determinant inequality
nodes.intuition: A parallelepiped has maximal volume when its edge directions are perpendicular.
nodes.conditions: A is a real or complex square matrix with columns aⱼ. A zero column gives equality automatically; when every column is nonzero, equality holds iff the columns are pairwise orthogonal.
nodes.example: Unit-length columns give determinant magnitude at most one.

patterns.why: Perpendicular columns achieve the maximal volume.
Volume is bounded by the product of edge lengths.

nodes.name: Pfaffian and skew-symmetric determinant
nodes.intuition: A skew-symmetric determinant is the square of a signed sum over pairings. Pairing is the natural building block of an alternating bilinear form.
nodes.conditions: A is a 2n×2n skew-symmetric real or complex matrix; n≥0 and the empty Pfaffian is 1.
nodes.example: For a 2×2 matrix with upper-right entry a, the Pfaffian is a and the determinant is a².

patterns.why: Each term selects a pairing of indices.
Alternation supplies the signs and forces a square determinant.

nodes.name: Minimal polynomial of a linear operator
nodes.intuition: The shortest monic polynomial relation among powers of A generates every polynomial relation satisfied by A.
nodes.conditions: A is an endomorphism of a nonzero finite-dimensional vector space over a field; mₐ is monic of least positive degree with mₐ(A)=0.
nodes.example: A nonidentity matrix with A²=I in characteristic not two has minimal polynomial dividing (t−1)(t+1).

patterns.why: An annihilator ideal in the polynomial ring is principal.
Repeated factors reveal generalized eigenvector structure.

nodes.name: Rational canonical form
nodes.intuition: A linear map is assembled from cyclic blocks describing how repeated application acts on one starting vector.
nodes.conditions: A is a nonempty square matrix over a field; fᵢ are monic nonconstant invariant factors, C(fᵢ) their companion matrices, and the ordered invariant factors are unique.
nodes.example: A real rotation can be represented by a quadratic companion block without introducing complex eigenvalues.

patterns.why: A companion block stores a polynomial recurrence.
Invariant cyclic modules form the canonical blocks.

nodes.name: Primary decomposition of a linear operator
nodes.intuition: Coprime polynomial factors separate a linear system into independent invariant parts.
nodes.conditions: V is finite-dimensional over a field; pⱼ are distinct monic irreducible factors of the minimal polynomial and aⱼ≥1.
nodes.example: Over C the pieces are generalized eigenspaces.

patterns.why: Coprime factors isolate invariant subspaces.
Polynomial Bézout identities construct the projections.

nodes.name: Sylvester rank inequality
nodes.intuition: Composition can lose only the directions sent by B into A’s kernel.
nodes.conditions: A is m×n and B is n×p over a field. A negative lower bound remains true but uninformative.
nodes.example: Two rank n operators on an n-dimensional space have a rank n product.

patterns.why: The image of B splits into surviving and killed directions.
Dimensions bound the possible information loss.

nodes.name: Vectorization of a matrix product
nodes.intuition: A two-sided matrix action becomes an ordinary linear map on one long column of entries.
nodes.conditions: A,X,B are finite matrices over one field with compatible sizes; vec stacks columns, and T is ordinary transpose even over C.
nodes.example: A matrix-valued linear equation can be regarded as a vector-valued one.

patterns.why: Stacking entries changes the representation of the same linear operation.
Left and right actions combine through a tensor product.

nodes.name: Spectrum of a Kronecker sum
nodes.intuition: Independent additive actions on two factors produce every pairwise sum of their spectral values.
nodes.conditions: A is m×m and B is n×n over C; eigenvalues on the right include algebraic multiplicity. The symbol ⊕ here denotes Kronecker sum, not block direct sum.
nodes.example: A separable grid Laplacian has eigenvalues equal to sums of one-dimensional Laplacian eigenvalues.

patterns.why: Each factor contributes one spectral component.
Operators act independently on the two tensor factors.

nodes.name: Determinant of a Kronecker product
nodes.intuition: Each eigenvalue of one factor pairs with every eigenvalue of the other, multiplying the total volume factors repeatedly.
nodes.conditions: A is m×m and B is n×n over a commutative field.
nodes.example: For A=2I₂ and B=3I₃, A⊗B=6I₆ and both sides equal 6⁶.

patterns.why: Each determinant is repeated once for every dimension of the other factor.
Tensor multiplication combines all factor directions.

nodes.name: Dimension and top action of an exterior power
nodes.intuition: Alternating tensors keep distinct directions without ordering them twice. In top degree, every linear map acts by one scalar: its determinant.
nodes.conditions: V has finite dimension n over a field, 0≤k≤n; T is an endomorphism. Wedges of increasing basis indices form a basis.
nodes.example: In three dimensions the space of oriented area elements Λ²V has dimension three.

patterns.why: An exterior basis is indexed by k-element subsets.
Top-degree action measures oriented volume scaling.

nodes.name: Dimension of a symmetric power
nodes.intuition: Symmetric tensors remember how often each direction is selected, rather than the order of selection.
nodes.conditions: V is n-dimensional over a field, n≥1, k≥0; SymᵏV is the degree-k part of the symmetric algebra, defined as a quotient of the tensor algebra.
nodes.example: Homogeneous degree-three polynomials in two variables have four monomials.

patterns.why: Multiplicity vectors are weak compositions of k.
Permuting tensor factors does not change their symmetric class.

nodes.name: Completing the square for a quadratic polynomial
nodes.intuition: Translate a multivariable quadratic to remove its linear term and expose its center.
nodes.conditions: A is a real symmetric invertible matrix; b,x are compatible real vectors and c is real. A positive-definite A gives a unique minimum; an indefinite A need not.
nodes.example: For A=I, the center is −b/2.

patterns.why: A translation cancels all first-degree terms.
Positive definiteness turns the centered form into an explicit minimization certificate.

nodes.name: Cayley transform of a skew-Hermitian matrix
nodes.intuition: A rational change of coordinates converts an infinitesimal rotation into an exact length-preserving map.
nodes.conditions: A is a finite complex skew-Hermitian matrix, so I+A is invertible. The inverse A=(I−U)(I+U)⁻¹ is defined for unitary U without eigenvalue −1. Real skew-symmetric A gives orthogonal U.
nodes.example: A 2×2 real skew matrix produces a planar rotation by a rational formula.

patterns.why: The transform switches between skew-Hermitian and unitary descriptions.
The resulting map preserves the inner product.

nodes.name: Frobenius inner product on matrix space
nodes.intuition: Treat all matrix entries as one Euclidean vector while retaining a basis-independent trace expression.
nodes.conditions: A,B have equal finite size over R or C; singular values include multiplicity. The Frobenius norm differs from the operator norm in general.
nodes.example: An identity n×n matrix has Frobenius norm √n but operator norm one.

patterns.why: Entrywise squared magnitudes define matrix energy.
Orthogonal singular components have additive squared energy.

nodes.name: Spectral projectors by polynomial interpolation
nodes.intuition: Build a filter that is one on a chosen eigenspace and zero on every other eigenspace.
nodes.conditions: A is diagonalizable over a field; λ₁,…,λᵣ are its distinct eigenvalues. The Pⱼ need not be orthogonal unless A is normal in an inner-product setting.
nodes.example: For eigenvalues 0 and 1, the projectors are I−A and A.

patterns.why: Projectors isolate independent spectral components.
Interpolation constructs idempotents in the algebra of polynomials in A.

nodes.name: Second isomorphism theorem for groups
nodes.intuition: Taking a subgroup and then forgetting a normal subgroup removes exactly their overlap.
nodes.conditions: H≤G and N is normal in G. Then HN is a subgroup, H∩N is normal in H, and h(H∩N) maps to hN.
nodes.example: For G=Z, H=2Z and N=3Z, both quotients have order three.

patterns.why: The intersection identifies which subgroup elements disappear.
Quotient maps preserve the group operation.

nodes.name: Third isomorphism theorem for groups
nodes.intuition: Forgetting distinctions in two stages agrees with forgetting their total effect at once.
nodes.conditions: N and H are normal subgroups of G with N⊆H. The isomorphism sends (gN)(H/N) to gH.
nodes.example: Reducing integers first modulo 12 and then modulo the subgroup generated by 4 leaves Z/4Z.

patterns.why: Nested quotient maps compose.
Normality makes both quotient operations well defined.

nodes.name: Subgroup correspondence for a quotient
nodes.latex: \{H\le G:N\subseteq H\}\longleftrightarrow\{K\le G/N\},\qquad H\mapsto H/N,\quad K\mapsto q^{-1}(K)
nodes.intuition: A quotient keeps precisely the subgroups that already contain everything being collapsed.
nodes.conditions: N is normal in G and q:G→G/N is the quotient map. The correspondence preserves inclusion and normality.
nodes.example: Subgroups of Z/12Z correspond to subgroups of Z containing 12Z.

patterns.why: The subgroup lattices agree above N.
The same surviving structure has two descriptions.

nodes.name: Semidirect product
nodes.intuition: Combine two groups while allowing one factor to change how the other is viewed during multiplication.
nodes.conditions: N,H are groups and φ:H→Aut(N) is a homomorphism. The displayed law is on N×H.
nodes.example: The dihedral group combines cyclic rotations with a reflection that inverts them.

patterns.why: The second factor acts while the first factors are combined.
Automorphisms preserve N’s group law.

nodes.name: Commutator subgroup
nodes.intuition: Collect every obstruction to swapping the order of two group operations.
nodes.conditions: G is a group; angle brackets mean the subgroup generated by all displayed commutators. This subgroup is normal.
nodes.example: For S₃ the commutator subgroup is A₃.

patterns.why: Commutators generate a normal subgroup.
Conjugation preserves the collection of commutators.

nodes.name: Abelianization and its universal property
nodes.intuition: Erase exactly the noncommutative information that no abelian target can detect.
nodes.conditions: G is a group and A is an abelian group; the bijection is induced by composing with G→Gab.
nodes.example: The abelianization of a free group on r generators is Zʳ.

patterns.why: A universal quotient forces commutativity.
Every map to an abelian group factors through the same quotient.

nodes.name: Derived series and solvable groups
nodes.latex: G^{(0)}=G,\qquad G^{(k+1)}=[G^{(k)},G^{(k)}],\qquad G\text{ solvable}\iff G^{(r)}=\{e\}\text{ for some }r
nodes.intuition: Repeatedly remove the abelian part and inspect the remaining noncommutativity. Solvability means this process eventually ends.
nodes.conditions: G is any group and r is a finite nonnegative integer. Finite nonabelian groups need not be solvable.
nodes.example: S₃ has derived series S₃, A₃, {e}.

patterns.why: Each stage applies the same commutator construction.
Successive quotients are abelian.

nodes.name: Free group universal property
nodes.intuition: Choose images of generators freely; every word then has a uniquely forced image.
nodes.conditions: S is a set, G a group, and F(S) the group of reduced finite words in symbols s and s⁻¹. The bijection restricts a homomorphism to generators.
nodes.example: The free group on one generator is Z; on two generators it is noncommutative.

patterns.why: Word concatenation encodes repeated operations.
Only cancellation and the group laws are imposed.

nodes.name: Presentation by generators and relations
nodes.intuition: Start with all possible words and identify those forced equal by the declared relations.
nodes.conditions: R is a set of words in the free group F(S); double brackets denote its normal closure. Relations are imposed as words equal to the identity.
nodes.example: A cyclic group of order n has presentation ⟨a∣aⁿ=1⟩.

patterns.why: Relations specify a quotient of a free object.
Generators describe pieces and relations describe how they fit.

nodes.name: Jordan–Hölder theorem for finite groups
nodes.latex: G=G_0\triangleright G_1\triangleright\cdots\triangleright G_r=\{e\},\qquad\{G_i/G_{i+1}\}_{i=0}^{r-1}\text{ unique up to permutation and isomorphism}
nodes.intuition: Different ways of peeling a finite group into simple layers yield the same list of irreducible group factors.
nodes.conditions: Each successive subgroup is normal in the preceding one and each quotient is nontrivial simple; G is finite. The actual subgroups and their order need not be unique.
nodes.example: Any composition series of S₃ has factors C₂ and C₃.

patterns.why: Simple quotient layers are the atomic pieces.
The factor multiset is independent of the chosen series.

nodes.name: Chinese remainder theorem for rings
nodes.intuition: Independent congruence conditions split one ring into separate coordinate rings.
nodes.conditions: R is commutative with identity; I₁,…,Iᵣ is a nonempty finite family of pairwise comaximal ideals, meaning Iᵢ+Iⱼ=R for i≠j.
nodes.example: Distinct linear factors split k[x]/∏(x−aᵢ) into copies of k.

patterns.why: Comaximal pieces can be solved independently.
The isomorphism respects addition and multiplication.

nodes.name: Prime ideal quotient criterion
nodes.latex: R/\mathfrak p\text{ is an integral domain}\iff\mathfrak p\text{ is prime}
nodes.intuition: A prime ideal removes elements without creating zero divisors among the surviving nonzero classes.
nodes.conditions: R is a commutative ring with identity and p is a proper ideal; prime means ab∈p implies a∈p or b∈p.
nodes.example: (x) is prime in k[x,y], since the quotient is k[y].

patterns.why: Multiplication in a quotient detects primeness.
A zero product can arise only from a vanished factor.

nodes.name: Gauss’s lemma for primitive polynomials
nodes.latex: c(fg)\sim c(f)c(g),\qquad f\text{ primitive}:\quad f\text{ irreducible in }R[x]\iff f\text{ irreducible in }K[x]
nodes.intuition: Common factors in coefficients behave multiplicatively, so factorization over fractions can be cleared back to integral coefficients.
nodes.conditions: R is a unique-factorization domain, K its fraction field, f,g are nonzero polynomials, and c is coefficient gcd up to units. The irreducibility statement assumes f is primitive and nonconstant.
nodes.example: A primitive integer polynomial factors over Q exactly when it factors nontrivially over Z.

patterns.why: Unique factorization controls coefficient content.
Content is separated from the primitive polynomial.

nodes.name: Eisenstein irreducibility criterion
nodes.latex: p\nmid a_n,\quad p\mid a_i\ (i<n),\quad p^2\nmid a_0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a_nx^n+\cdots+a_0\text{ irreducible over }\mathbb Q
nodes.intuition: Reduction modulo a prime forces every prospective factor to have a highly restricted shape; the constant term prevents both factors from existing.
nodes.conditions: n≥1, all aᵢ are integers, aₙ≠0 and p is prime.
nodes.example: x⁵−2 is irreducible over Q using p=2.

patterns.why: Modular reduction constrains polynomial factors.
A proposed factorization contradicts constant-term divisibility.

nodes.name: Minimal polynomial and a simple field extension
nodes.intuition: An algebraic number is described by one irreducible polynomial relation; every expression in it reduces to a bounded list of powers.
nodes.conditions: α is algebraic over a field F and mα is its monic minimal polynomial. The isomorphism evaluates x at α.
nodes.example: Q(√2) has basis 1,√2 because the minimal polynomial is x²−2.

patterns.why: Evaluation turns a polynomial quotient into a field.
Remainders give unique coordinates in powers of α.

nodes.name: Primitive element theorem
nodes.latex: L/F\text{ finite separable}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad L=F(\alpha)\text{ for some }\alpha\in L
nodes.intuition: A finite separable extension with many algebraic generators can be encoded by a single well-chosen element.
nodes.conditions: L/F is a finite separable field extension. Separability is essential over imperfect fields.

patterns.why: Several generators are compressed into one primitive generator.
Separability ensures distinct embeddings can be distinguished.

nodes.name: Repeated-root criterion by a formal derivative
nodes.latex: f\text{ has no repeated roots in }\overline F\iff\gcd(f,f^{\prime})=1
nodes.intuition: A repeated zero is detected simultaneously by a polynomial and its rate-of-change polynomial.
nodes.conditions: f is a nonconstant polynomial over a field F; f′ is its formal derivative, including in positive characteristic; gcd is monic.
nodes.example: Over characteristic p, xᵖ−a has zero derivative and is inseparable unless its degree has collapsed.

patterns.why: A repeated root kills the first-order coefficient.
A gcd converts a root-multiplicity question into divisibility.

nodes.name: Localization of a commutative ring
nodes.latex: S^{-1}R=\{a/s:a\in R,\ s\in S\},\qquad a/s=b/t\iff\exists u\in S:\ u(at-bs)=0
nodes.intuition: Declare a selected set of elements invertible and allow exactly the fractions this requires.
nodes.conditions: R is commutative with identity; S is multiplicatively closed, contains 1 and does not contain 0. Zero divisors may still make R→S⁻¹R noninjective.
nodes.example: Localizing Z at all nonzero integers gives Q; localizing away from a prime gives Z₍ₚ₎.

patterns.why: Fractions reveal behavior where chosen denominators are invertible.
A universal ring map adjoins inverses.

nodes.name: Noetherian ring condition
nodes.latex: I_1\subseteq I_2\subseteq\cdots\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists N\ \forall n\ge N:\ I_n=I_N
nodes.intuition: An indefinitely growing list of algebraic constraints eventually adds nothing new.
nodes.conditions: R is a commutative ring with identity. The displayed ascending-chain condition on ideals is equivalent to every ideal being finitely generated.
nodes.example: Z and polynomial rings in finitely many variables over a field are Noetherian.

patterns.why: Ascending algebraic chains eventually stabilize exactly.
Finite ideal generators control all their consequences.

nodes.name: Hilbert basis theorem
nodes.intuition: Adding finitely many polynomial variables preserves the ability to describe every ideal using finitely many equations.
nodes.conditions: R is a commutative Noetherian ring and n is a finite nonnegative integer.
nodes.example: Every ideal of real polynomials in three variables has a finite generating list.

patterns.why: Finite-generation control survives polynomial extension.
The many-variable result follows by adjoining one variable at a time.

nodes.name: Nakayama’s lemma
nodes.intuition: A finite module cannot be entirely generated by multiples from a universally noninvertible ideal unless it is already zero.
nodes.conditions: R is commutative with identity, M a finitely generated R-module, and I an ideal inside the Jacobson radical, the intersection of maximal ideals.
nodes.example: For a local ring with maximal ideal m, elements spanning M/mM lift to generators of M.

patterns.why: The Jacobson radical controls invertibility of 1−a.
Generators can be checked after passing to a residue field.

nodes.name: Structure theorem for finitely generated modules over a PID
nodes.latex: M\cong R^r\oplus R/(d_1)\oplus\cdots\oplus R/(d_s),\qquad d_1\mid\cdots\mid d_s
nodes.intuition: Separate freely moving coordinates from coordinates constrained by divisibility relations.
nodes.conditions: R is a principal ideal domain, M a finitely generated R-module, r≥0, and dᵢ are nonzero nonunits. Rank and invariant factors are unique, the latter up to units.
nodes.example: For R=Z this describes every finitely generated abelian group, including infinite free parts.

patterns.why: Free and torsion pieces have different roles.
Divisibility orders the canonical cyclic factors.

nodes.name: Smith normal form
nodes.intuition: Independent invertible row and column changes expose divisibility relations in a matrix over a principal ideal domain.
nodes.conditions: A is an m×n matrix over a PID; P and Q are invertible over that same ring, r is the rank over its fraction field, and nonzero dᵢ are unique up to units. This is a structural theorem.
nodes.example: An integer matrix’s Smith factors describe the torsion of its cokernel.

patterns.why: Invertible operations change both domain and codomain bases.
Each nonzero diagonal entry becomes one cyclic relation.

nodes.name: Splitting a short exact sequence
nodes.intuition: If quotient data can be lifted consistently, the middle object separates into the kernel and a complementary copy of the quotient.
nodes.conditions: The sequence is exact in modules over a ring, or abelian groups; s:C→B must be a module homomorphism. The isomorphism sends (a,c) to i(a)+s(c).
nodes.example: Every short exact sequence of vector spaces splits, but 0→Z→Z→Z/2Z→0 with first map ×2 does not.

patterns.why: A section constructs a complementary submodule.
A retraction of i is an equivalent splitting condition.

nodes.name: Snake lemma
nodes.intuition: A compatible pair of exact rows transfers a failed lift into a precise connecting obstruction.
nodes.conditions: Start with a commutative diagram of short exact sequences 0→A→B→C→0 and 0→A′→B′→C′→0 with vertical module maps a,b,c. Then the displayed sequence is exact.
nodes.example: Connecting homomorphisms in homology are constructed by lifting, applying a map, and measuring the remaining class.

patterns.why: Kernels and cokernels account for every failure of injectivity or surjectivity.
The connecting map transfers an unresolved lift between ends.

nodes.name: Projective module lifting property
nodes.latex: p:E\twoheadrightarrow M,\quad f:P\to M\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\exists\widetilde f:P\to E:\ p\widetilde f=f
nodes.intuition: A projective module can lift its maps across every surjection without getting trapped by relations.
nodes.conditions: P is a module over a unital ring; the property is required for every surjective module map p and every f. Equivalently, P is a direct summand of a free module.
nodes.example: Free modules are projective; a projective module need not itself be free.

patterns.why: A universal lifting condition defines the class.
Projective modules are retracts of free modules.

nodes.name: Flat module and preservation of exactness
nodes.latex: 0\to A\to B\to C\to0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad0\to A\otimes_R M\to B\otimes_R M\to C\otimes_R M\to0
nodes.intuition: A flat module changes coefficients without introducing new failures of injectivity.
nodes.conditions: R is commutative with identity and M an R-module. Flatness means the displayed implication holds for every short exact sequence of R-modules.
nodes.example: Localizations S⁻¹R are flat R-modules.

patterns.why: Tensoring preserves all exact sequences.
Relations remain exact after changing coefficients.

nodes.name: Tor from a projective resolution
nodes.intuition: Resolve a module into free-like pieces, then measure the exactness lost when tensoring.
nodes.conditions: R is commutative with identity, M,N are R-modules, n≥0, and P•→M is a projective resolution. The result is independent of the resolution up to canonical isomorphism.
nodes.example: Tor₁^Z(Z/mZ,Z/nZ) is Z/gcd(m,n)Z.

patterns.why: A resolution replaces a module by manageable projective pieces.
Derived tensor information detects hidden torsion.

nodes.name: Ext from a projective resolution
nodes.intuition: Resolve the source before asking for maps into N; higher cohomology measures information ordinary homomorphisms miss.
nodes.conditions: R is a unital ring, M,N are left modules, n≥0, and P•→M is a projective resolution. Hom_R(P•,N) is the induced cochain complex.
nodes.example: Ext₁^Z(Z/nZ,Z)≅Z/nZ; Ext¹ classifies module extensions up to the standard equivalence.

patterns.why: Hom converts a chain resolution into a cochain complex.
Extensions become computable cohomological invariants.

nodes.name: Universal enveloping algebra
nodes.latex: U(\mathfrak g)=T(\mathfrak g)/\langle x\otimes y-y\otimes x-[x,y]\rangle
