nodes.intuition: Replace Lie brackets by ordinary noncommutative multiplication, imposing exactly the commutator relations.
nodes.conditions: g is a Lie algebra over a field; T(g) is its tensor algebra and the quotient is by the two-sided ideal generated by the displayed elements.
nodes.example: For an abelian Lie algebra, the enveloping algebra is its symmetric algebra.

patterns.why: Lie operations are encoded inside an associative algebra.
Products record repeated actions of Lie algebra elements.

nodes.name: Poincaré–Birkhoff–Witt theorem
nodes.intuition: At the level of highest degree, noncommutative Lie-algebra products behave like commuting polynomial variables.
nodes.conditions: g is a Lie algebra over a field and U(g) carries its filtration by tensor degree. For an ordered basis of g, ordered monomials form a basis of U(g).
nodes.example: For sl₂, ordered products fᵃhᵇeᶜ form a vector-space basis of its enveloping algebra.

patterns.why: A filtration separates products by their highest degree.
Commutators lower degree, leaving a commutative associated graded algebra.

nodes.name: Linear representation of a group
nodes.intuition: Turn an abstract symmetry into an invertible linear transformation so its effects can be studied with matrices.
nodes.conditions: G is a group and V a vector space over a specified field; the displayed map is a group homomorphism and sends the identity to I.
nodes.example: Permuting the coordinates of Rⁿ represents the symmetric group Sₙ.

patterns.why: The group law becomes matrix multiplication.
Every group element acts linearly on vectors.

nodes.name: Intertwining map between representations
nodes.intuition: An intertwiner translates vector descriptions while preserving every symmetry operation.
nodes.conditions: ρ:G→GL(V), σ:G→GL(W) are representations over the same field, and T:V→W is linear. Equivalence of representations requires an invertible intertwiner.
nodes.example: A change of basis intertwines a matrix representation with its conjugate representation.

patterns.why: An invertible intertwiner changes representation without changing the action.
Translation commutes with all group operations.

nodes.name: Maschke’s theorem
nodes.intuition: When division by the group order is possible, averaging turns an arbitrary complement into a symmetry-respecting one.
nodes.conditions: G is finite, V is finite-dimensional over a field k, and char(k) does not divide |G|. Without this characteristic hypothesis, invariant complements may fail to exist.
nodes.example: A real representation of a finite rotation group decomposes into invariant irreducible subspaces.

patterns.why: Averaging conjugates of a projection makes it equivariant.
Invariant complements permit complete splitting.

nodes.name: Schur’s lemma for complex representations
nodes.latex: \operatorname{Hom}_G(V,W)=0\text{ or consists of scalar multiples of an isomorphism},\qquad\operatorname{End}_G(V)=\mathbb C I
nodes.intuition: An irreducible symmetry system has no nontrivial internal linear adjustment compatible with every symmetry.
nodes.conditions: V,W are nonzero finite-dimensional irreducible complex representations of a group. Hom is zero if they are inequivalent; the scalar endomorphism conclusion uses algebraic closure of C.
nodes.example: An operator commuting with every matrix of an irreducible complex representation is scalar.

patterns.why: Commuting with every symmetry severely restricts an operator.
Invariant kernels and eigenspaces would contradict irreducibility.

nodes.name: Character of a finite-dimensional representation
nodes.intuition: Take a basis-independent summary of each symmetry matrix. Conjugate group elements receive the same summary.
nodes.conditions: ρ is a finite-dimensional representation over a field; the class-function identity holds generally. Character classification by these values will later use finite groups over C.
nodes.example: The character of a permutation representation counts the coordinates fixed by the permutation.

patterns.why: Trace ignores changes of basis and conjugation.
A character compresses an entire matrix to one scalar per group element.

nodes.name: Orthogonality of irreducible characters
nodes.intuition: Irreducible symmetry patterns behave like perpendicular frequency modes under a uniform group average.
nodes.conditions: G is finite and χᵢ are characters of inequivalent irreducible finite-dimensional complex representations.
nodes.example: For a cyclic group, the characters are roots-of-unity exponentials and this is discrete Fourier orthogonality.

patterns.why: The inner product averages over all group elements.
Distinct irreducible characters have zero overlap.

nodes.name: Sum of squared irreducible dimensions
nodes.intuition: The regular action contains every irreducible representation as many times as its dimension. Their squared sizes fill the whole group algebra.
nodes.conditions: G is finite and Ĝ indexes inequivalent irreducible complex representations.
nodes.example: S₃ has irreducible dimensions 1,1,2, whose squares sum to 6.

patterns.why: The dimensions account exactly for the group order.
The regular representation is resolved into irreducible pieces.

nodes.name: Multiplicity from a character inner product
nodes.intuition: Project a character onto an irreducible character to read off how many copies of that symmetry type occur.
nodes.conditions: G is finite and V a finite-dimensional complex representation. The resulting coefficients are nonnegative integers.
nodes.example: The three-coordinate permutation representation of S₃ is one trivial copy plus one two-dimensional standard copy.

patterns.why: Character projection isolates one irreducible component.
The projection coefficient counts multiplicity.

nodes.name: Averaging projection onto invariant vectors
nodes.intuition: Average every symmetry-transformed version of a vector; all nonsymmetric components cancel.
nodes.conditions: G is finite and ρ a representation over a field where |G| is invertible. Vᴳ consists of vectors fixed by every ρ(g). For a unitary complex representation, Pᴳ is an orthogonal projection.
nodes.example: Averaging all coordinate permutations sends a real vector to its arithmetic-mean constant vector.

patterns.why: All symmetry images receive equal weight.
The image consists exactly of common fixed vectors.
Reindexing the group sum leaves the average unchanged.

nodes.name: Complex group algebra decomposition
nodes.intuition: Fourier analysis of a finite group changes convolution into independent matrix multiplications.
nodes.conditions: G is finite; the algebra map sends ∑g a_g g to the family ∑g a_gρ(g). The direct sum is finite.
nodes.example: For a finite abelian group every block is 1×1; for S₃ there are two scalar blocks and one 2×2 block.

patterns.why: Simple matrix-algebra blocks separate irreducible symmetry types.
Group coefficients become Fourier matrices.

nodes.name: Induced representation
nodes.intuition: Replicate a subgroup representation over cosets and let the larger group move those copies coherently.
nodes.conditions: G is finite, H≤G, and W a finite-dimensional complex H-representation. G acts by left multiplication on the first tensor factor.
nodes.example: Inducing the trivial H-representation gives the permutation representation on G/H.

patterns.why: Coset representatives supply copies of W.
The balanced tensor product enforces the H-action relation.

nodes.name: Frobenius reciprocity
nodes.intuition: Extending symmetry on the source and restricting symmetry on the target give the same compatible maps.
nodes.conditions: H≤G are finite groups and W,V are finite-dimensional complex representations of H,G respectively; the isomorphism is natural.
nodes.example: The multiplicity of V in an induced representation can be calculated after restricting V to H.

patterns.why: Induction and restriction are adjoint constructions.
Equivariant maps are preserved by a natural correspondence.

nodes.name: Character of an induced representation
nodes.intuition: Only cosets stabilized by g contribute to the trace, and each contributes the corresponding subgroup action.
nodes.conditions: G is finite, H≤G, W a finite-dimensional complex H-representation, and g∈G. An empty sum is zero.
nodes.example: Inducing the trivial subgroup representation counts fixed cosets of g.

patterns.why: The summation selects stabilized cosets.
Conjugation transfers g into the subgroup.

nodes.name: Character of a tensor product
nodes.intuition: Combining two symmetry systems multiplies their character fingerprints point by point.
nodes.conditions: V,W are finite-dimensional representations of the same group over C, with diagonal action ρV(g)⊗ρW(g).
nodes.example: For one-dimensional cyclic characters, tensoring adds their frequency indices modulo the group order.

patterns.why: Two actions combine on paired tensor directions.
Expanding the product into irreducible characters records tensor-product multiplicities.

nodes.name: Dual or contragredient representation
nodes.intuition: Let a symmetry act on measurements so evaluation of a transformed vector by a transformed measurement stays unchanged.
nodes.conditions: V is a finite-dimensional representation over a field and V* its algebraic dual. The transpose here is not a conjugate transpose. For finite complex groups, the dual character is the complex conjugate character.
nodes.example: A rotation acts on linear coordinate measurements by the inverse transpose.

patterns.why: Vectors and linear measurements transform contragrediently.
The evaluation pairing is invariant.

nodes.name: Frobenius–Schur indicator
nodes.intuition: One average distinguishes whether an irreducible complex symmetry type has a symmetric, skew, or absent invariant bilinear pairing.
nodes.conditions: G is finite and χ is an irreducible complex character. Values +1, −1, 0 correspond respectively to invariant nondegenerate symmetric, alternating, or no nonzero bilinear form on that representation.
nodes.example: The quaternionic irreducible representation of the quaternion group has indicator −1.

patterns.why: The squared-group-element character is averaged uniformly.
The result detects how a representation compares with its dual.

nodes.name: Character of the regular representation
nodes.intuition: Translate the group’s own elements. A nonidentity translation fixes no basis position, so its trace vanishes.
nodes.conditions: G is finite; this is the left regular representation on the vector space with basis G, over C. The direct-sum statement is as a representation.
nodes.example: A cyclic shift of n coordinates has trace zero unless it is the identity shift.

patterns.why: Translation treats all group elements uniformly.
Every irreducible occurs with dimension multiplicity.

nodes.name: Irreducible characters form a class-function basis
nodes.latex: \#\widehat G=\#\{\text{conjugacy classes of }G\},\qquad\operatorname{Cl}(G;\mathbb C)=\bigoplus_{\rho\in\widehat G}\mathbb C\chi_\rho
nodes.intuition: One independent irreducible character is needed for each independent conjugacy-class value.
nodes.conditions: G is finite and Cl(G;C) is the space of functions constant on conjugacy classes. The irreducible characters form an orthonormal basis in the group-average inner product.
nodes.example: S₃ has three conjugacy classes and three irreducible complex representations.

patterns.why: Two different bases count the same class-function dimension.
Characters resolve any class function into perpendicular components.

nodes.name: Invariant inner product by averaging
nodes.intuition: Average the geometry itself until every group symmetry preserves it.
nodes.conditions: G is finite, ρ a finite-dimensional real or complex representation, and ⟨,⟩₀ any positive-definite inner product. The averaged form is positive definite and G-invariant.
nodes.example: Every finite subgroup of GLₙ(R) becomes orthogonal after a suitable change of basis.

patterns.why: Positive inner products are combined with equal weights.
Multiplying by a group element merely reindexes the sum.

nodes.name: Schur–Weyl decomposition
nodes.intuition: Changing vector coordinates and permuting tensor positions commute, and their irreducible structures organize each other.
nodes.conditions: V is n-dimensional over C and d≥0. GL(V) acts diagonally, S_d permutes tensor factors, SλV is the irreducible polynomial GL(V)-representation and Spλ the Specht representation.
nodes.example: For d=2, tensor square separates into symmetric and alternating parts.

patterns.why: Two commuting group actions are mutual centralizers.
Partitions index the shared irreducible blocks.

nodes.name: Hook-length formula for standard Young tableaux
nodes.intuition: A partition shape permits some orderings of labels and forbids others; local hook sizes combine into the exact global count.
nodes.conditions: λ is a partition of n≥0; fλ counts fillings of its Young diagram by 1,…,n increasing along rows and columns. h(u) counts the cell u and cells to its right and below.
nodes.example: Shape (2,1) has hooks 3,1,1, hence two standard tableaux.

patterns.why: The formula counts constrained permutations.
A product of local hook sizes supplies the normalization.

nodes.name: The Lie algebra sl₂
nodes.intuition: Three basic traceless directions close under commutators: one separates weights while the other two move between them.
nodes.conditions: Over C, take h=diag(1,−1), e with entry (1,2)=1, and f with entry (2,1)=1. Their span is sl₂(C), the traceless 2×2 matrices.
nodes.example: Direct multiplication of these three matrices verifies all three brackets.

patterns.why: A short multiplication table determines the Lie bracket.
The trace-zero space is closed under commutators.

nodes.name: Finite-dimensional irreducible sl₂ representations
nodes.intuition: All finite-dimensional complex irreducible sl₂ modules arise from homogeneous polynomials in two variables. The degree records their size.
nodes.conditions: Every finite-dimensional irreducible sl₂(C)-module is isomorphic to exactly one V_m. On degree-m polynomials, e=x∂y, f=y∂x and h=x∂x−y∂y.
nodes.example: Degree two gives the three-dimensional representation on x²,xy,y².

patterns.why: The family lists all irreducible finite-dimensional building blocks.
Two-variable degree-m monomials number m+1.

nodes.name: Schur polynomial alternant formula
nodes.intuition: Divide two alternating expressions and the signs cancel, leaving a symmetric character polynomial.
nodes.conditions: λ is a partition of length at most n, padded by zeros. The quotient formula is initially evaluated at distinct complex xᵢ and extends uniquely to a polynomial at coinciding values.
nodes.example: For λ=(1), the result is x₁+⋯+xₙ, the character of the defining representation.

patterns.why: A ratio of equally alternating determinants is symmetric.
The polynomial is the diagonal character of Sλ(Cⁿ).

nodes.name: Category axioms
nodes.latex: h\circ(g\circ f)=(h\circ g)\circ f,\qquad f\circ1_A=f=1_B\circ f
nodes.intuition: Specify objects through the transformations between them, with a consistent rule for composing transformations.
nodes.conditions: f:A→B, g:B→C and h:C→D are composable morphisms. Every object has an identity; composition must be defined on each compatible pair. Hom-collections are sets when the category is locally small.
nodes.example: Groups with homomorphisms, or vector spaces with linear maps, form categories.

patterns.why: Compatible arrows combine associatively.
Identity and composition laws are shared across subjects.

nodes.name: Functor laws
nodes.intuition: Translate objects and transformations together so that every way of composing steps remains consistent.
nodes.conditions: F assigns objects and morphisms from one category to another, with matching domains and codomains; both displayed laws hold for all compatible morphisms.
nodes.example: The fundamental-group construction sends based spaces to groups and based continuous maps to homomorphisms.

patterns.why: Translation preserves multi-step processes.
Functors preserve categorical structure.

nodes.name: Natural transformation
nodes.intuition: A systematic comparison between two translations is compatible with every allowed transformation.
nodes.conditions: F,G:C→D are functors; η assigns a morphism ηA:F(A)→G(A) to every object and obeys the displayed naturality square for every f.
nodes.example: The canonical map V→V** is natural in a vector space V.

patterns.why: The comparison does not depend on an arbitrary coordinate choice.
Either route around the naturality square agrees.

nodes.name: Opposite category
nodes.intuition: Reverse every arrow while retaining the same objects. Every categorical law then has a corresponding reversed form.
nodes.conditions: C is a category; in the composition formula the right-hand composition is taken in C with the reversed arrow directions.
nodes.example: Linear duality is naturally a functor from vector spaces with arrows reversed.

patterns.why: All morphism directions reverse together.
Composition order reverses consistently.

nodes.name: Equivalence of categories
nodes.latex: F:\mathcal C\rightleftarrows\mathcal D:G,\qquad GF\cong1_{\mathcal C},\quad FG\cong1_{\mathcal D}
nodes.intuition: Two mathematical languages describe the same objects and transformations up to consistent isomorphism.
nodes.conditions: F and G are functors, and the displayed isomorphisms are natural isomorphisms. An equivalence need not give a bijection of the raw object collections.
nodes.example: Finite-dimensional vector spaces over k are equivalent to the category with natural-number objects and matrices as arrows.

patterns.why: Different presentations encode the same structure.
Morphisms as well as objects are preserved.

nodes.name: Yoneda lemma
nodes.intuition: A natural rule acting on every map out of A is completely determined by what it does to A’s identity map.
nodes.conditions: C is locally small and F:C→Set is a covariant functor; A is an object. The inverse sends x∈F(A) to f↦F(f)(x).
nodes.example: For linear maps out of a vector space, a natural transformation can be recovered from its value on the identity operator.

patterns.why: All natural responses are determined by one universal test.
Functorial composition propagates the identity value.

nodes.name: Categorical product universal property
nodes.intuition: Giving one map into a product is exactly giving one map into each component.
nodes.conditions: A product has projections to A and B and a unique pairing map for every compatible pair of arrows from X; the displayed bijection is natural in X. Products are not assumed to exist in every category.
nodes.example: A linear map into V×W is uniquely a pair of linear maps into V and W.

patterns.why: A product-valued map separates into its components.
The mapping property determines the product up to unique isomorphism.

nodes.name: Categorical coproduct universal property
nodes.intuition: Giving a map out of an assembled sum means independently specifying its behavior on each included piece.
nodes.conditions: The coproduct includes A and B and has the displayed natural bijection for every X. It is the product construction in the opposite category.
nodes.example: Sets use disjoint union; groups use free product; vector spaces use direct sum.

patterns.why: The universal arrows of a product are reversed.
Independent input pieces determine one output map.

nodes.name: Pullback or fiber product
nodes.intuition: Pair two descriptions only when they agree on their shared observation.
nodes.conditions: The displayed formula is for functions f:A→C and g:B→C in sets. Categorically, a pullback represents pairs of arrows into A,B whose composites into C agree.
nodes.example: Pair two records exactly when their identifiers match.

patterns.why: Compatibility is an equality of composed maps.
The common condition selects compatible component pairs.

nodes.name: Pushout universal property
nodes.intuition: Glue two objects along specified copies of a shared piece, requiring maps out to agree on that overlap.
nodes.conditions: The input diagram is A←C→B. The displayed bijection uses precomposition maps into Hom(C,X), is natural in X, and characterizes a pushout when it exists.
nodes.example: In groups, amalgamated free product is a pushout.

patterns.why: This reverses the compatibility property of a pullback.
Compatible maps from glued pieces extend uniquely.

nodes.name: Equalizer universal property
nodes.intuition: Extract the largest part of a source on which two proposed transformations agree.
nodes.conditions: f,g:A→B are parallel arrows. An equalizer e:E→A has the displayed universal factoring property, natural in X. In sets E={a:f(a)=g(a)}.
nodes.example: For linear maps, the equalizer is ker(f−g).

patterns.why: A compatibility equation defines a universal subobject.
Equalizing a self-map with the identity extracts its fixed points.

nodes.name: Coequalizer universal property
nodes.intuition: Make the smallest quotient in which two parallel descriptions become indistinguishable.
nodes.conditions: f,g:A→B are parallel arrows and q:B→Q is universal among arrows identifying them. In sets, quotient B by the equivalence relation generated by f(a)∼g(a).
nodes.example: For module maps, the coequalizer is coker(f−g).

patterns.why: A coequalizer reverses an equalizer’s universal arrows.
The quotient forgets exactly the distinctions required by the relation.

nodes.name: Limit as a universal compatible cone
nodes.intuition: Package every compatible choice across a diagram into one object with no extra choices left over.
nodes.conditions: D:J→C is a small diagram in a locally small category; ΔX is the constant diagram. A limit exists exactly when the cone functor is representable as displayed.
nodes.example: An inverse limit of residues modulo pⁿ stores a compatible residue at every precision.

patterns.why: A diagram packages many linked components.
A universal mapping property enforces all compatibility equations.

nodes.name: Colimit as a universal compatible cocone
nodes.intuition: Assemble a diagram by identifying every overlap its arrows prescribe, and nothing beyond those required identifications.
nodes.conditions: D:J→C is small and C is locally small. The displayed property defines a colimit when it exists.
nodes.example: An increasing family of subsets has its union as the colimit in sets.

patterns.why: A colimit is a limit after reversing arrows.
Maps out of all pieces agree along the diagram.

nodes.name: Adjunction of functors
nodes.intuition: Move a construction from the source side of a mapping problem to a corresponding construction on the target side.
nodes.conditions: F:C→D and G:D→C are functors between locally small categories; the bijections must be natural in both C and D.
nodes.example: Tensoring by a fixed module is left adjoint to taking module homomorphisms from that module.

patterns.why: The same map is described from two opposite sides.
Naturality makes the correspondence coherent across objects.

nodes.name: Unit, counit and triangle identities
nodes.intuition: A round trip through the two sides of an adjunction cancels in the precise directions where cancellation is allowed.
nodes.conditions: F⊣G has unit η:1C→GF and counit ε:FG→1D. The equations are identities of natural transformations; η and ε need not be isomorphisms.
nodes.example: For free groups, introducing formal generators and then evaluating words returns the original free-group word.

patterns.why: Two specified round trips simplify to identity transformations.
Unit and counit are the paired directions of the adjunction.

nodes.name: Right adjoints preserve limits
nodes.intuition: A right adjoint transports compatible families without losing their universal description.
nodes.conditions: D:J→D is a small diagram with a limit and F:C→D is left adjoint to G:D→C. The canonical comparison is an isomorphism; dually, left adjoints preserve colimits.
nodes.example: Hom_R(M,−) preserves products of modules.

patterns.why: The colimit statement follows by reversing arrows.
Universal compatibility survives the right-adjoint translation.

nodes.name: Composition of adjunctions
nodes.latex: F\dashv G,\quad F^\prime\dashv G^\prime\quad\Longrightarrow\quad F^\prime F\dashv GG^\prime
nodes.intuition: Two successive translations of a mapping problem compose, with the reverse translations appearing in reverse order.
nodes.conditions: F:C→D, G:D→C, F′:D→E and G′:E→D are the indicated adjoint pairs.
nodes.example: Two successive free constructions can be compared with forgetting their structures in reverse order.

patterns.why: Natural Hom-bijections are composed.
Right-adjoint order reverses the order of left adjoints.

nodes.name: Tensor–Hom adjunction for modules
nodes.intuition: A bilinear interaction can be supplied all at once or one input at a time without changing its information.
nodes.conditions: R is commutative with identity and M,N,P are R-modules; the bijection sends f to m↦(n↦f(m⊗n)) and is natural in all arguments.
nodes.example: Integer-bilinear maps out of M×N correspond to homomorphisms out of M⊗Z N.

patterns.why: Tensoring and internal Hom occupy opposite sides of the mapping correspondence.
Partial evaluation turns a two-input map into nested one-input maps.

nodes.name: Monad unit and multiplication laws
nodes.intuition: A monad describes how to form structured expressions and how to flatten nested structure consistently.
nodes.conditions: T:C→C is an endofunctor, η:1C→T and μ:T²→T are natural transformations obeying the displayed laws.
nodes.example: The list monad inserts an item as a singleton list and flattens a list of lists.

patterns.why: Nested constructions flatten associatively.
Unit and associative multiplication are lifted to endofunctors.

nodes.name: Algebra for a monad
nodes.intuition: An algebra evaluates formal structured expressions in a way that respects insertion and flattening.
nodes.conditions: (T,η,μ) is a monad on C; A is an object and a a morphism satisfying both equations.
nodes.example: Algebras of the list monad are monoids: evaluate a list by multiplying its entries, with the empty list giving the unit.

patterns.why: Evaluation recovers familiar algebraic operations from formal expressions.
Evaluating nested expressions in stages agrees with flattening first.

nodes.name: Pointwise left Kan extension
nodes.intuition: Extend a functor to a larger context by assembling every existing piece that can map into the requested new object.
nodes.conditions: C is small, D locally small, E cocomplete, K:C→D and F:C→E. The comma category has objects arrows Kc→d and the compatible commuting morphisms.
nodes.example: Inducing group representations is an instance of extending along a subgroup inclusion.

patterns.why: The comma diagram records all compatible ways to reach d.
A colimit assembles the available pieces.

nodes.name: Exponential object and currying
nodes.intuition: A function of two inputs can be viewed as a function returning a function of the second input.
nodes.conditions: A category has the required products; an exponential Bᴬ represents the displayed natural correspondence. In sets, Bᴬ is the set of functions A→B. Not every category has all exponentials.
nodes.example: A two-argument table can be read as a list of one-argument lookup rules.

patterns.why: Evaluation reconstructs the original two-input map.
Product with A is left adjoint to exponentiation by A.

nodes.name: Galois connection between ordered sets
nodes.latex: L(p)\le q\iff p\le R(q),\qquad p\le RL(p),\quad LR(q)\le q
nodes.intuition: Translate a constraint in one ordered system into an equivalent constraint in another. Round trips give closure and interior operations.
nodes.conditions: P,Q are posets and L:P→Q,R:Q→P are monotone. This is the monotone adjunction convention; antitone Galois connections reverse one order.
nodes.example: For a function f, direct image and inverse image satisfy f(S)⊆T iff S⊆f⁻¹(T).

patterns.why: Two inequality directions encode the same constraint.
The composite RL is an idempotent closure operator.

nodes.name: Hockey-stick identity
nodes.intuition: Group subsets by their largest element: a diagonal sum becomes one larger choice.
nodes.conditions: Integers 0≤r≤n.

patterns.why: Partitions the same family by maximum element.
Discrete summation raises the binomial index.

nodes.name: Binomial inversion
nodes.latex: b_n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk a_k\iff a_n=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^{n-k}\binom nk b_k
nodes.intuition: Alternating signs undo a transform that mixes all smaller subset sizes.
nodes.conditions: Sequences in a characteristic-zero field; n≥0.
nodes.example: If b_n=2^n, inversion gives a_n=1.

patterns.why: Forward and inverse triangular transforms pair.
Subset containment controls transform coefficients.

nodes.name: Unsigned Stirling numbers of the first kind
nodes.latex: {n\brack k}={n-1\brack k-1}+(n-1){n-1\brack k},\quad x^{\overline n}=\sum_k{n\brack k}x^k
nodes.intuition: A new element either starts a cycle or joins one of the existing cycle positions.
nodes.conditions: n≥1; [0,0]=1; out-of-range values zero; rising factorial x(x+1)…(x+n−1).
nodes.example: [3,2]=3, the permutations of three objects with two cycles.

patterns.why: Insert the new label in a cycle or create a singleton.
Coefficients record permutations by cycle count.

nodes.name: Stirling change of polynomial basis
nodes.latex: x^n=\sum_k S(n,k)x^{\underline k},\quad x^{\underline n}=\sum_k s(n,k)x^k
nodes.intuition: Powers and falling factorials are two coordinate systems for polynomials.
nodes.conditions: n≥0; s(n,k)=(−1)^{n−k}[n,k]; sums from 0 to n.
nodes.example: x²=x(x−1)+x.

patterns.why: Stirling matrices convert polynomial bases.
The two triangular coefficient matrices are inverses.

nodes.name: Eulerian number recurrence
nodes.intuition: Insert the largest label and track whether the number of descents grows.
nodes.conditions: A(n,k) counts permutations of n with k descents; n≥2; A(1,0)=1; outside 0≤k<n values are zero.

patterns.why: Insertion separates descent-preserving and descent-creating positions.
Partitions permutations by local order changes.

nodes.name: Formal Lagrange inversion
nodes.intuition: Implicit recursive objects can be counted without explicitly solving their generating function.
nodes.conditions: Formal power series over a characteristic-zero field; φ(0)≠0, T(0)=0, n≥1; F any formal power series.
nodes.example: T=z(1+T)² gives [z^n]T=(1/n) binom(2n,n−1), the Catalan numbers.

patterns.why: An implicit equation encodes nested construction.
Coefficient extraction solves the recursion.

nodes.name: Exponential formula for labeled components
nodes.intuition: A labeled object made of an unordered set of connected pieces exponentiates its connected-piece series.
nodes.conditions: A labeled combinatorial class is uniquely a finite set of nonempty components; C is its component EGF, C(0)=0.
nodes.example: For set partitions C(z)=e^z−1, so the Bell-number EGF is exp(e^z−1).

patterns.why: Unique components determine the whole object.
Logarithms extract connected components.

nodes.name: Pólya cycle-index substitution
nodes.intuition: A coloring fixed by a permutation must be constant on each cycle.
nodes.conditions: Finite permutation group G acting on n positions; q colors; c_i(g) counts i-cycles. Counts colorings modulo G.
nodes.example: Rotating a triangle with two colors gives (2³+2·2)/3=4 orbits.

patterns.why: Orbit counts are averages of fixed-coloring counts.
Equivalent colorings differ only by allowed position permutations.

nodes.name: Rotational necklace count
nodes.intuition: Rotations with the same cycle lengths contribute the same fixed colorings.
nodes.conditions: n≥1 positions, q≥1 colors; only rotations identify necklaces, not reflections.

patterns.why: Divisor classes collect rotations with equal cycle structure.
Burnside averages over n rotations.

nodes.name: Gaussian binomial coefficient
nodes.intuition: Count ordered independent vectors, then divide out the different bases of each subspace.
nodes.conditions: q is a prime power; 0≤k≤n; counts k-dimensional subspaces of F_q^n. Empty product is 1.
nodes.example: There are [3,1]_2=7 lines in F₂³.

patterns.why: Each subspace has the same number of ordered bases.
Changing its basis leaves a subspace unchanged.

nodes.name: Finite q-binomial theorem
nodes.intuition: Selecting terms from a product weights subsets by the sum of their positions.
nodes.conditions: Formal polynomial identity in q,t; n≥0; Gaussian coefficients viewed as polynomials in q.

patterns.why: Product choices encode weighted subset counts.
The coefficient groups choices by size and position weight.

nodes.name: Euler pentagonal-number identity
nodes.intuition: The reciprocal partition series collapses to a sparse alternating pattern.
nodes.conditions: Formal power series, or complex |q|<1. Every coefficient depends on finitely many factors.
nodes.example: The product begins 1−q−q²+q⁵+q⁷−q¹²−q¹⁵.

patterns.why: The product is the multiplicative inverse of the partition series.
Equating coefficients yields the partition recurrence.

nodes.name: Möbius inversion on finite posets
nodes.intuition: Undo cumulative totals on any partially ordered collection.
nodes.conditions: Finite poset, values in a commutative ring; μ(x,x)=1 and sum_{x≤z≤y} μ(x,z)=0 for x<y.
nodes.example: On subsets μ(A,B)=(−1)^{|B\A|}, recovering inclusion-exclusion.

patterns.why: The Möbius kernel inverts cumulative summation.
The order determines an invertible triangular transform.

nodes.name: Incidence-algebra convolution
nodes.intuition: Compose interval-weighted relations by summing over intermediate stops.
nodes.conditions: Finite poset, or locally finite poset with finite intervals; coefficients in a commutative ring; ζ(x,y)=1 for x≤y, δ is the identity kernel.
nodes.example: For a chain, convolution is upper-triangular matrix multiplication.

patterns.why: Intermediate comparable elements are summed over.
Interval kernels form an associative algebra.

nodes.name: Lubell–Yamamoto–Meshalkin inequality
nodes.intuition: An antichain can meet each complete nested chain at most once.
nodes.conditions: A is an antichain of subsets of an n-element set: no distinct members contain one another.
nodes.example: All k-subsets attain equality because every complete chain contains exactly one.

patterns.why: Double-counts maximal chains meeting the family.
Each set receives its probability of appearing in a uniform maximal chain.

nodes.name: Sperner theorem
nodes.intuition: The widest layer of the subset lattice is its middle layer.
nodes.conditions: A is an antichain in the subsets of an n-element set.
nodes.example: For n=4, the six two-element subsets form a largest antichain.

patterns.why: Compares incomparable subsets with one cardinality layer.
Identifies the largest possible antichain size.

nodes.name: Dilworth chain-decomposition theorem
nodes.intuition: The largest mutually incomparable collection is exactly the number of ordered tracks needed.
nodes.conditions: Finite partially ordered set P; empty P has both values zero.
nodes.example: A disjoint union of three nonempty chains has width at most three, with equality if no cross-chain comparisons exist.

patterns.why: A minimum covering arrangement equals a maximum obstruction.
Partitions a poset into chains.

nodes.name: Euler trail criterion
nodes.latex: G\text{ has an Euler trail}\iff |\{v:\deg v\text{ odd}\}|\in\{0,2\}
nodes.intuition: Every visit uses an entrance and an exit, except possibly the two endpoints.
nodes.conditions: Finite undirected graph with at least one edge; all vertices incident to edges lie in one connected component. Loops count twice in degree.
nodes.example: A path has two odd endpoints; a cycle has none and admits a closed Euler trail.

patterns.why: Intermediate visits pair arriving and departing edges.
Degree parity records endpoint imbalance.

nodes.name: Bipartite graph criterion
nodes.latex: G\text{ bipartite}\iff G\text{ has no odd cycle}
nodes.intuition: Alternating two colors works precisely when no loop of steps forces a color reversal.
nodes.conditions: Finite undirected graph; a loop is an odd cycle of length one.
nodes.example: A square is bipartite; a triangle is not.

patterns.why: Parity of path lengths controls the two color classes.
A binary coloring turns adjacency into a cross-class relation.

nodes.name: Kőnig matching–cover theorem
nodes.intuition: In a bipartite graph, the largest set of disjoint pairs equals the smallest set of vertices touching all edges.
nodes.conditions: Finite bipartite graph; ν is maximum matching size and τ is minimum vertex-cover size.
nodes.example: For a star with m≥1 leaves, both values are one.

patterns.why: Maximum packing equals minimum covering.
Converts two discrete optimization problems into one value.

nodes.name: Tutte perfect-matching criterion
nodes.latex: G\text{ has a perfect matching}\iff o(G-S)\le |S|\quad\forall S\subseteq V
nodes.intuition: Deleting vertices cannot leave more odd islands than those deleted vertices can pair with.
nodes.conditions: Finite undirected graph; o counts connected components of odd order; G−S deletes S and incident edges.
nodes.example: Two isolated vertices fail at S=∅ because there are two odd components.

patterns.why: Every odd component needs a distinct external matching partner.
An obstruction certificate characterizes perfect matchability.

nodes.name: Menger vertex-path theorem
nodes.intuition: Independent routes equal the smallest number of internal junctions whose removal blocks travel.
nodes.conditions: Finite undirected graph; distinct nonadjacent s,t; separators exclude s,t.
nodes.example: Two disjoint arcs around a cycle give two routes and require two internal vertex removals.

patterns.why: Path packing equals separator size.
Splitting vertices converts vertex constraints to edge capacities.

nodes.name: Turán extremal graph theorem
nodes.intuition: Avoiding a large clique is most efficiently done by dividing vertices into balanced independent classes.
nodes.conditions: Integers r≥1,n≥1; finite simple graphs; T_r(n) is the complete r-partite graph with class sizes differing by at most one.
nodes.example: For triangles, the maximum edge count is floor(n²/4).

patterns.why: Maximizes edges under a forbidden-clique constraint.
Balanced multipartite structure gives the extremizer.

nodes.name: Ramsey-number recursion
nodes.intuition: From one vertex, enough neighbors or enough nonneighbors force a smaller unavoidable pattern.
nodes.conditions: s,t≥2; R(s,t) is least N forcing an s-clique or independent t-set in every N-vertex simple graph; R(1,t)=R(s,1)=1.

patterns.why: A distinguished vertex reduces one target size.
The vertex set splits into neighbors and nonneighbors.

nodes.name: Erdős–Stone asymptotic extremal theorem
nodes.intuition: At leading quadratic scale, the chromatic number controls how many edges a forbidden pattern permits.
nodes.conditions: Fixed finite simple H with chromatic number r≥2; n→∞. For bipartite H this only states ex(n,H)=o(n²).
nodes.example: For H with chromatic number three, the leading density is n²/4.

patterns.why: Lower-order details vanish after division by n².
Many different forbidden graphs share one chromatic density.

nodes.name: Laplacian kernel and connected components
nodes.intuition: Zero energy means every edge joins equal values, so each component carries one free constant.
nodes.conditions: Finite undirected weighted graph with strictly positive edge weights; isolated vertices count as components; L=D−A.
nodes.example: A graph with three components has three independent zero eigenvectors.

patterns.why: L annihilates constants on each component.
Disconnected pieces contribute independent kernel directions.

nodes.name: Normalized graph Laplacian
nodes.intuition: Degree normalization measures variation relative to the local amount of connectivity.
nodes.conditions: Finite undirected graph with positive edge weights and no isolated vertices; D contains weighted degrees.
nodes.example: For a d-regular graph, normalized eigenvalues are ordinary Laplacian eigenvalues divided by d.

patterns.why: Degree scaling converts the weighted inner product into Euclidean coordinates.
Its quadratic form sums squared normalized edge differences.

nodes.name: Graph Cheeger inequality
nodes.intuition: A low-frequency graph mode reveals a weakly connected cut, and every weak cut produces a low-energy mode.
nodes.conditions: Finite connected undirected positively weighted graph with at least two vertices; λ₂ of normalized Laplacian; vol is sum of degrees.
nodes.example: A long cycle has a small λ₂ and admits a cut with small boundary relative to its size.

patterns.why: Cut edges compare the boundary with interior degree volume.
Relates a discrete cut minimum to a continuous spectral minimum.

nodes.name: Effective resistance from the Laplacian
nodes.intuition: Inject one unit at one vertex and remove it at another; the required potential difference is resistance.
nodes.conditions: Finite connected undirected graph; edge weights are positive conductances; L⁺ is Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse.
nodes.example: One edge of conductance c has resistance 1/c.

patterns.why: Current injection and voltage response are paired by the inverse Laplacian.
Resistance is an inverse-energy quadratic form.

nodes.name: Foster resistance identity
nodes.intuition: Edge leverage scores add up to the dimension of nonconstant vertex signals.
nodes.conditions: Finite connected loopless undirected graph with positive conductances; effective resistance between edge endpoints in the full network.
nodes.example: In a tree, every summand is one, and there are n−1 edges.

patterns.why: A sum of edge quantities equals a rank.
The Laplacian is a sum of rank-one edge matrices.

nodes.name: Random-walk commute time and resistance
nodes.intuition: Electrical difficulty of travel determines expected there-and-back duration.
nodes.conditions: Finite connected loopless undirected graph with positive conductances; walk transition p_uv=c_uv/d_u; H_uv expected first hitting time; vol(G)=sum d_u.
nodes.example: On one edge, the commute time is two steps and vol·R=2c/c=2.

patterns.why: Potential solutions also solve hitting-time equations.
An expected journey time is encoded by a deterministic network.

nodes.name: Weighted spanning-tree edge probability
nodes.intuition: An edge is used often precisely when it contributes strongly to connecting its endpoints.
nodes.conditions: Connected finite loopless undirected weighted graph; tree probability proportional to product of edge conductances.
nodes.example: Every edge of a tree has probability one; each edge of an unweighted triangle has probability 2/3.

patterns.why: A determinant-defined random tree has electrical edge marginals.
Each tree selects a connectivity basis.

nodes.name: Rooted forest determinant
nodes.intuition: Adding one root choice per tree component turns the Laplacian determinant into a forest counter.
nodes.conditions: Finite undirected weighted graph; sum over spanning forests together with one marked root per component; k(F) components.
nodes.example: For one edge of weight c, det(tI+L)=t²+2ct: two root choices for the connected tree.

patterns.why: The exponent of t tracks components.
Determinants enumerate rooted acyclic structures.

nodes.name: Matroid independence axioms
nodes.latex: \varnothing\in\mathcal I,\quad J\subseteq I\in\mathcal I\Rightarrow J\in\mathcal I,\quad |I|<|J|\Rightarrow\exists e\in J\setminus I:I\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I
nodes.intuition: Abstract independence keeps the key feature that smaller independent collections can be enlarged from larger ones.
nodes.conditions: Finite ground set E; in the exchange clause I,J∈I.
nodes.example: Independent vector subsets form a matroid; acyclic edge sets form a graphic matroid.

patterns.why: Exchange abstracts the behavior of linear independence.
Maximal independent sets provide bases.

nodes.name: Matroid rank submodularity
nodes.intuition: New independent information has diminishing returns when more elements are already available.
nodes.conditions: Finite matroid; r(S) is the maximum size of an independent subset of S.
nodes.example: For vectors, rank is dimension of their span; overlapping spans explain the inequality.

patterns.why: The shared portion must be counted only once.
Rank encodes dependence without coordinates.

nodes.name: Dual matroid rank
nodes.intuition: What one basis leaves unused becomes a basis of the dual system.
nodes.conditions: Finite matroid M on E; dual bases are complements of bases of M.
nodes.example: For the uniform rank-r matroid on n elements, the dual has rank n−r.

patterns.why: Basis complements interchange selected and omitted elements.
Rank deficits quantify unavoidable omitted choices.

nodes.name: Symmetric matroid basis exchange
nodes.latex: e\in B_1\setminus B_2\Rightarrow\exists f\in B_2\setminus B_1:\ B_1-e+f,\ B_2-f+e\text{ are bases}
nodes.intuition: Two complete independent selections can trade a suitable pair without losing completeness.
nodes.conditions: Finite matroid; B₁,B₂ bases. The simultaneous exchange is stronger than the basic augmentation axiom.
nodes.example: Two spanning trees can exchange an edge across the cut created by deleting a tree edge, with an appropriate partner.

patterns.why: Changes a basis by one local replacement.
Both exchanged sets retain the same independent size.

nodes.name: Matroid intersection min–max theorem
nodes.intuition: The largest selection obeying two independence rules is limited exactly by the best split of their capacities.
nodes.conditions: Two finite matroids on the same ground set E.
nodes.example: Bipartite matchings are common independent sets of two partition matroids, one for each endpoint class.

patterns.why: A common-independent-set maximum equals a rank-partition minimum.
Combines two structural constraints.

nodes.name: Tutte polynomial by rank subsets
nodes.intuition: A single polynomial tracks how far each edge set is from spanning and how much cyclic redundancy it contains.
nodes.conditions: Finite matroid M; for a graph r(A)=|V|−c(V,A).
nodes.example: A bridge contributes x; a loop contributes y; a tree with m edges has polynomial x^m.

patterns.why: Exponents track rank deficit and nullity.
Sums over all subsets using two complementary defects.

nodes.name: Tutte duality
nodes.intuition: Duality swaps missing connectivity with excess dependence.
nodes.conditions: Finite matroid M and its dual; for a connected plane graph, the dual matroid is represented by the geometric dual graph.
nodes.example: The cycle of length three has x²+x+y; its three-parallel-edge dual has y²+y+x.

patterns.why: Complementation exchanges rank deficit and nullity.
The polynomial changes only by swapping variables.

nodes.name: Chromatic polynomial from Tutte polynomial
nodes.intuition: Proper coloring is one specialization of the universal edge-subset counter.
nodes.conditions: Finite undirected graph; c(G) counts components including isolated vertices; loops make P_G identically zero.
nodes.example: For a tree on n vertices, P_G(q)=q(q−1)^(n−1).

patterns.why: Specialization extracts a coloring enumerator.
Edge deletion and contraction govern both polynomials.

nodes.name: Bases at the center of the Tutte polynomial
nodes.intuition: At the central evaluation, only subsets with neither rank deficit nor redundancy survive.
nodes.conditions: Finite matroid; powers with exponent zero evaluate to one. For a connected graph, bases are spanning trees.
nodes.example: A triangle has T(1,1)=3 spanning trees.

patterns.why: Evaluation filters exactly the bases.
Two zero defects characterize a basis.

nodes.name: Tutte matrix perfect-matching test
nodes.latex: G\text{ has a perfect matching}\iff\det A(\mathbf x)\not\equiv0
nodes.intuition: Assign each edge its own variable so matching contributions cannot accidentally cancel identically.
nodes.conditions: Finite simple graph; skew matrix A_ij=x_ij on edges for i<j, A_ji=−x_ij, zeros otherwise; polynomial over a field of characteristic not two.
nodes.example: For four vertices, the Pfaffian is x12x34−x13x24+x14x23, omitting nonexistent edges.

patterns.why: A combinatorial existence problem becomes polynomial nonvanishing.
Pfaffian monomials correspond to perfect matchings.

nodes.name: Hensel lifting of a simple root
nodes.latex: f(a)\equiv0\pmod p,\quad f^{\prime}(a)\not\equiv0\pmod p\Longrightarrow \exists!\alpha\in\mathbb Z_p:\ f(\alpha)=0,\ \alpha\equiv a\pmod p
nodes.intuition: A root with a nonzero local slope can be corrected one p-adic digit at a time.
nodes.conditions: Prime p; f∈Z_p[x]; a∈Z_p. Uniqueness is within the residue class of a modulo p.
nodes.example: x²−2 has two roots in Z₇, lifting 3 and 4 modulo 7.

patterns.why: Invertible derivative determines each next correction.
Compatible modular roots converge in the p-adic metric.

nodes.name: p-adic digit expansion
nodes.intuition: Digits extend toward higher powers because those powers become smaller in the p-adic metric.
nodes.conditions: Prime p; each nonzero x∈Q_p has a unique such expansion with integer v and a_v≠0; x∈Z_p iff v≥0.

patterns.why: Digits split a number into scale-specific pieces.
Partial sums converge under the p-adic absolute value.

nodes.name: Product formula for rational absolute values
nodes.intuition: Ordinary size and prime-divisibility sizes exactly balance for a nonzero rational number.
nodes.conditions: x∈Q×; |p|_p=p^(−1), ordinary real absolute value at infinity; only finitely many prime factors differ from one.
nodes.example: For x=12, the product is 12·2^(−2)·3^(−1)=1.

patterns.why: Total multiplicative size across all places is fixed.
Prime factorization separates local contributions.

nodes.name: Ostrowski classification on the rationals
nodes.intuition: The rationals admit only the ordinary and prime-based kinds of metric size.
nodes.conditions: Absolute values are equivalent when they induce the same topology; p is prime; trivial absolute value excluded.
nodes.example: Completion gives R for the ordinary class and Q_p for the p-adic class.

patterns.why: Classifies all inequivalent local measuring systems.
Absolute values create metrics and completions.

nodes.name: Euler prime product
nodes.intuition: A product that chooses an exponent for each prime enumerates every positive integer exactly once.
nodes.conditions: Complex s with real part greater than one; both series and product converge absolutely.
nodes.example: At s=2, multiplying geometric prime-power series reconstructs the sum of reciprocal squares.

patterns.why: Unique prime factorization gives independent prime-power choices.
A multiplicative product encodes all integers.

nodes.name: Prime number theorem
nodes.intuition: Primes become sparser, with average density near x on the scale 1/log x.
nodes.conditions: x→∞ through positive real values; π(x) counts primes≤x; asymptotic means ratio tends to one.
nodes.example: The estimate for π(10⁶) is about 72,382, compared with its exact value 78,498.

patterns.why: Relative asymptotics describe large-scale counts.
Logarithmic decay controls density across numerical scales.

nodes.name: Dirichlet character modulo q
nodes.intuition: A character replaces invertible residue classes by multiplicative complex phases.
nodes.conditions: q≥1; χ restricted to (Z/qZ)× is a homomorphism to C×, extended by zero to nonunits.
nodes.example: Modulo four, χ(1)=1, χ(3)=−1 and even arguments have value zero.

patterns.why: Values depend only on a residue class.
Multiplication is preserved as multiplication of phases.

nodes.name: Dirichlet L-series Euler product
nodes.intuition: Twisting each prime by a character sorts multiplicative arithmetic information into frequency channels.
nodes.conditions: Dirichlet character χ; complex Re(s)>1, giving absolute convergence.
nodes.example: For the principal character modulo q, primes dividing q contribute factors equal to one.

patterns.why: Complete multiplicativity splits the series into prime factors.
Characters distinguish residue-class structure.

nodes.name: Character filter for a residue class
nodes.intuition: Average all multiplicative frequencies with the correct phase to isolate one invertible residue class.
nodes.conditions: q≥1; gcd(a,q)=1; n integer; sum over all characters modulo q, extended by zero on nonunits.
nodes.example: Modulo four, odd numbers are separated by the principal character and the sign character.

patterns.why: Orthogonal characters cancel except at the selected class.
Distinct unit-group characters have zero inner product.

nodes.name: Dirichlet theorem on arithmetic progressions
nodes.intuition: Every residue class that avoids an unavoidable common divisor continues to contain primes forever.
nodes.conditions: Integers q≥1 and gcd(a,q)=1. This existence theorem alone does not assert an error term or rate.
nodes.example: There are infinitely many primes ending in each of 1,3,7,9.

patterns.why: Reduced residue classes all support infinitely many primes.
Character filters isolate one progression.

nodes.name: Jordan totient function
nodes.intuition: Exclude k-tuples whose coordinates all share a prime divisor with the modulus.
nodes.conditions: Integers n,k≥1; counts tuples in {1,…,n}^k with gcd(a₁,…,a_k,n)=1.

patterns.why: Counts jointly coprime tuples.
Prime-by-prime exclusions multiply.

nodes.name: Ramanujan sum
nodes.intuition: Adding only primitive cyclic frequencies unexpectedly produces an integer.
nodes.conditions: Positive integer q; integer n; μ is the arithmetic Möbius function.
nodes.example: For prime p, c_p(n)=p−1 if p divides n and −1 otherwise.

patterns.why: Complete root-of-unity sums vanish away from matching divisibility.
Möbius inversion selects primitive frequencies.

nodes.name: Moduli admitting primitive roots
nodes.intuition: One generator produces every invertible residue only for a restricted family of moduli.
nodes.conditions: p odd prime, k≥1; n positive; the unit group for n=1 is taken as the trivial group.
nodes.example: Modulo seven, powers of three generate all six units; modulo eight the unit group is not cyclic.

patterns.why: A modular unit group may or may not have one cyclic generator.
Prime-power structure controls cyclicity.

nodes.name: Cyclotomic factorization
nodes.intuition: Roots of unity separate into families according to their exact period.
nodes.conditions: n≥1; Φ_n is the monic polynomial whose roots are primitive n-th roots of unity; Φ_n∈Z[x] and is irreducible over Q.
nodes.example: Φ₆(x)=x²−x+1.

patterns.why: Divisors sort roots by their exact order.
Galois conjugates comprise each primitive-root family.

nodes.name: Lucas binomial congruence
nodes.intuition: Modulo a prime, binomial choices split digit by digit in base p.
nodes.conditions: p prime; n,k≥0 with base-p digits n_i,k_i; binom(a,b)=0 when b>a.
nodes.example: binom(5,2)≡binom(1,0)binom(0,1)binom(1,0)=0 modulo two.

patterns.why: Base-p digits factor the coefficient.
The same coefficient rule repeats independently at each base-p digit.

nodes.name: Kummer carry theorem
nodes.latex: v_p\binom nk=\#\{\text{carries when adding }k\text{ and }n-k\text{ in base }p\}
nodes.intuition: Prime factors in a binomial coefficient are recorded by elementary carrying operations.
nodes.conditions: p prime; integers 0≤k≤n; count every carry between adjacent digit positions.
nodes.example: binom(5,2)=10 has one factor of two; binary 010+011=101 has one carry.

patterns.why: Prime valuation is recovered from digit behavior.
Carries count uncancelled prime factors.

nodes.name: Two-square criterion
nodes.latex: n=a^2+b^2\iff v_p(n)\text{ is even for every prime }p\equiv3\pmod4
nodes.intuition: Primes of one residue type must occur in pairs before an integer can be a sum of two squares.
nodes.conditions: Positive integer n; a,b integers, allowing zero.
nodes.example: 45=3²·5 is allowed and equals 6²+3²; 21 is not.

patterns.why: Prime-power factors decide representability.
A sum of squares is a norm in the Gaussian integers.

nodes.name: Pell equation and quadratic units
nodes.intuition: One smallest expanding unit generates all positive Pell solutions by multiplication.
nodes.conditions: D positive nonsquare integer; (x₁,y₁) is the least solution with x₁>1,y₁>0; n≥1 enumerates all x,y>0 solutions.

patterns.why: Repeated multiplication generates the solution sequence.
The quadratic norm remains one.

nodes.name: Dirichlet rational approximation
nodes.latex: \forall Q\ge1\ \exists p\in\mathbb Z,\ 1\le q\le Q:\quad \left|\alpha-\frac pq\right|\le\frac1{qQ}
nodes.intuition: Two fractional parts among enough multiples must be close, producing a good rational approximation.
nodes.conditions: Real α; integer Q≥1. For irrational α, infinitely many reduced p/q satisfy |α−p/q|<1/q².
nodes.example: An irrational can always be approximated with denominator at most 100 and error at most 1/(100q).

patterns.why: Pigeonholes force two multiples into nearby fractional positions.
Closeness on the unit interval yields rational approximation.

nodes.name: Algebraic integer criterion
nodes.intuition: The correct integers inside a number field are roots of monic integer equations.
nodes.conditions: α is an algebraic number; m≥1; monicity is essential.
nodes.example: √2 is integral; 1/2 is algebraic but not integral.

patterns.why: Monic relations define rings of integers.
A monic relation expresses higher powers using finitely many lower powers.

nodes.name: Norm and trace of a field extension
nodes.intuition: Multiplication by one field element is a linear map; its volume factor and diagonal sum become arithmetic invariants.
nodes.conditions: Finite extension L/K; m_a:L→L is K-linear multiplication by a. For separable extensions, norm and trace equal product and sum over K-embeddings.
nodes.example: In Q(√d), the norm of u+v√d is u²−dv² and the trace is 2u.

patterns.why: Field multiplication becomes a linear operator over the base field.
Determinant and trace do not depend on the chosen basis.

nodes.name: Number-field discriminant
nodes.intuition: The trace pairing measures how an arithmetic basis sits inside all embeddings at once.
nodes.conditions: Number field K of degree n; ω_i a Q-basis. For an integral basis of O_K this is the field discriminant, independent of basis.
nodes.example: For K=Q(√5), the integral basis 1,(1+√5)/2 has discriminant 5.

patterns.why: The trace pairing supplies a symmetric bilinear form.
A basis change multiplies the discriminant by the square of its determinant.

nodes.name: Unique prime-ideal factorization
nodes.intuition: When element factorization fails, ideals restore a unique list of prime building blocks.
nodes.conditions: Nonzero ideal in a Dedekind domain; finitely many nonnegative exponents are nonzero. For nonzero fractional ideals exponents may be integers.
nodes.example: The ring of integers of every number field is Dedekind, so its nonzero ideals factor uniquely.

patterns.why: Prime ideals are unique multiplicative components.
Ideal arithmetic repairs failures of element factorization.

nodes.name: Ramification and residue-degree identity
nodes.intuition: A rational prime distributes its degree budget between repeated factors and larger residue fields.
nodes.conditions: Number field K; p rational prime; distinct prime ideals above p; f_i=[O_K/𝔭_i:F_p].
nodes.example: In Q(i), (2) is ramified with e=2,f=1; primes congruent to three modulo four have e=1,f=2.

patterns.why: The weighted local degrees add to the global degree.
A prime splits into local pieces.

nodes.name: Ideal class group
nodes.intuition: The class group records the obstruction to describing every ideal with a single generator.
nodes.conditions: Number field K; I_K group of nonzero fractional ideals of O_K; P_K subgroup of nonzero principal fractional ideals.
nodes.example: For Q the class group is trivial; class number one means O_K is a principal ideal domain.

patterns.why: Equivalent ideals differ by a principal scaling.
A quotient group organizes the failure of principal generation.

nodes.name: Dirichlet unit theorem
nodes.intuition: Apart from finitely many roots of unity, all units are generated by finitely many independent multiplicative directions.
nodes.conditions: Number field with r₁ real embeddings and r₂ conjugate pairs of complex embeddings; μ(K) roots of unity.
nodes.example: A real quadratic field has one independent fundamental unit; an imaginary quadratic field has only finitely many units.

patterns.why: Separates torsion and free directions.
Logarithms turn unit multiplication into a lattice in a hyperplane.

nodes.name: Minkowski convex-body theorem
nodes.intuition: A centrally symmetric body larger than a lattice’s fundamental-volume threshold must capture a nonzero lattice point.
nodes.conditions: Full-rank lattice Λ in R^n; measurable convex C with C=−C. Strict inequality suffices; equality also suffices when C is compact.
nodes.example: For Z², an origin-centered square of side greater than two necessarily contains a nonzero integer point.

patterns.why: Continuous size forces discrete points.
Lattice cells provide a multidimensional pigeonhole argument.

nodes.name: Minkowski ideal-class bound
nodes.intuition: Every ideal class has a representative below an explicit size, making a global classification finite.
nodes.conditions: Number field K of degree n with r₂ complex pairs and discriminant D_K; each ideal class contains a nonzero integral ideal 𝔞 satisfying the bound; N is ideal index.
nodes.example: For Q(i), the bound is 2/π<1.28, forcing an ideal of norm one in every class, hence class number one.

patterns.why: Provides a bounded-size representative of every class.
The bound comes from lattice covolume and convex volume.

nodes.name: Integers of a quadratic field
nodes.latex: \mathcal O_{\mathbb Q(\sqrt d)}=\begin{cases}\mathbb Z[(1+\sqrt d)/2],&d\equiv1\pmod4,\\ \mathbb Z[\sqrt d],&d\equiv2,3\pmod4.\end{cases}
nodes.intuition: Half-integer coordinates are allowed precisely when they still give integral trace and norm.
nodes.conditions: Squarefree integer d≠0,1; negative d allowed; congruences taken modulo four.
nodes.example: In Q(√5), the golden ratio is an algebraic integer even though its coefficients in 1,√5 are halves.

patterns.why: Integrality selects a lattice inside the field.
Trace and norm control the quadratic minimal polynomial.

nodes.name: Tangent vectors as derivations
nodes.intuition: A direction is a rule that differentiates every smooth observable at one point.
nodes.conditions: Smooth finite-dimensional manifold M; derivations are R-linear and satisfy the displayed Leibniz rule at p.
nodes.example: In a coordinate chart, v=sum_i v^i ∂/∂x^i at p.

patterns.why: A tangent direction records first-order behavior of functions.
Vectors act on differentials to produce directional derivatives.

nodes.name: Lie derivative via a flow
nodes.intuition: Compare a tensor with its transported version under the motion generated by a vector field.
nodes.conditions: Smooth vector field X with local flow φ_t; smooth tensor T; pullback for contravariant slots uses the inverse differential.
nodes.example: For a function f, L_X f=X(f); for a vector field Y, L_XY=[X,Y].

patterns.why: Zero Lie derivative means infinitesimal invariance under the flow.
Differentiate a family of transported objects at time zero.

nodes.name: Koszul formula
nodes.intuition: Metric compatibility and absence of torsion determine the connection completely.
nodes.conditions: Smooth Riemannian metric; X,Y,Z smooth vector fields; ∇ is the Levi-Civita connection.
nodes.example: For commuting Euclidean coordinate vectors and constant metric coefficients, every connection coefficient vanishes.

patterns.why: Pairing with every Z identifies the covariant derivative.
The formula is intrinsic and does not depend on coordinates.

nodes.name: Hodge star operator
nodes.intuition: A metric and orientation turn a k-dimensional measurement into its complementary-dimensional measurement.
nodes.conditions: Oriented n-dimensional Riemannian manifold; α,β smooth k-forms; real-valued forms and positive-definite metric.
nodes.example: In oriented Euclidean R³, *(dx)=dy∧dz.

patterns.why: Pairs k-forms with complementary-degree forms.
The metric determines magnitudes while orientation determines signs.

nodes.name: Codifferential and Hodge Laplacian
nodes.intuition: Reverse exterior differentiation using the metric adjoint, then combine both directions into an energy operator.
nodes.conditions: Oriented n-dimensional Riemannian manifold; δ is the formal L² adjoint of d on compactly supported forms. Δ_H is nonnegative under the L² pairing.
nodes.example: On functions, Δ_H f=−Δ_g f with the atlas convention Δ_g=div grad.

patterns.why: δ is the adjoint of d.
The Laplacian energy is the sum of squared d and δ norms.

nodes.name: Hodge decomposition theorem
nodes.intuition: Every differential form splits into a topological residue and two orthogonal derivative parts.
nodes.conditions: Compact oriented smooth Riemannian manifold without boundary; smooth forms; H^k=ker Δ_H. The direct sum is L²-orthogonal.
nodes.example: On a circle, the nonzero harmonic one-form dθ represents the single circulation class.

patterns.why: Harmonic, exact and coexact pieces are pairwise perpendicular.
Separates metric-dependent representatives from topological classes.

nodes.name: Poincaré lemma
nodes.intuition: Locally, the only obstruction to being a derivative is the compatibility condition dω=0.
nodes.conditions: Smooth k-form on a star-shaped open subset of R^n; k>0. More generally holds on sufficiently small coordinate neighborhoods.
nodes.example: A curl-free vector field on a ball has a scalar potential.

patterns.why: The differential-form complex is locally exact in positive degrees.
Closed forms have local potentials, while global topology may obstruct them.

nodes.name: Gauss equation for a submanifold
nodes.intuition: Intrinsic curvature combines ambient curvature with the way the submanifold bends.
nodes.conditions: Isometric immersion M into a Riemannian manifold; h normal second fundamental form; R(X,Y)Z=∇X∇YZ−∇Y∇XZ−∇[X,Y]Z.
nodes.example: For a surface in R³, K equals the product of principal curvatures.

patterns.why: Separates ambient and extrinsic contributions.
Bending enters through products of second fundamental forms.

nodes.name: Codazzi equation in Euclidean space
nodes.intuition: The bending tensor cannot vary arbitrarily; its derivatives must be mutually compatible.
nodes.conditions: Smooth isometric immersion into Euclidean space; derivative of h uses both the induced tangent and normal connections.
nodes.example: For a plane, h=0 and the equation holds identically.

patterns.why: Interchanging the first two derivative slots leaves the result unchanged.
First derivatives constrain admissible local bending.

nodes.name: Jacobi equation for geodesic variation
nodes.intuition: Curvature controls how neighboring geodesics converge or spread apart.
nodes.conditions: Smooth Riemannian manifold; γ a geodesic; J arises from a smooth variation through affinely parametrized geodesics, or is any solution of this linear equation.
nodes.example: On the unit sphere, a perpendicular Jacobi component satisfies j″+j=0.

patterns.why: Linearizes the geodesic equation around one trajectory.
Curvature controls infinitesimal separation.

nodes.name: Riemannian exponential map
nodes.intuition: A tangent arrow becomes a point by following the geodesic it launches.
nodes.conditions: γ_v starts at p with velocity v; v lies where the geodesic exists to time one. Exp is a local diffeomorphism near zero.
nodes.example: In Euclidean space, exp_p(v)=p+v.

patterns.why: Its derivative at zero identifies tangent and manifold coordinates.
Radial straight directions become geodesics.

nodes.name: Hopf–Rinow theorem
nodes.latex: (M,d_g)\text{ complete}\iff M\text{ geodesically complete}\iff\text{closed bounded subsets are compact}
nodes.intuition: For a connected Riemannian manifold, metric completeness, endless geodesics, and compactness of bounded regions coincide.
nodes.conditions: Connected finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold without boundary. Under these conditions any two points are joined by a minimizing geodesic.
nodes.example: Euclidean space is complete; the open unit ball with its Euclidean metric is not.

patterns.why: Metric Cauchy completeness becomes a geometric existence statement.
Shortest paths exist globally under completeness.

nodes.name: Bonnet–Myers diameter bound
nodes.intuition: Uniformly positive Ricci curvature forces geodesics to reconverge, limiting the size of a complete space.
nodes.conditions: Connected complete n-dimensional Riemannian manifold, n≥2. It is compact and has finite fundamental group.
nodes.example: The round sphere of radius r attains diameter πr with k=1/r².

patterns.why: A local curvature bound limits global diameter.
Curvature has inverse-length-squared units.

nodes.name: Cartan–Hadamard theorem
nodes.intuition: Without positive curvature or topological loops, geodesics never create global coordinate ambiguity.
nodes.conditions: Connected complete simply connected Riemannian n-manifold with nonpositive sectional curvature; exp is a diffeomorphism for every p.
nodes.example: Hyperbolic space is diffeomorphic to R^n despite its non-Euclidean distances.

patterns.why: A local exponential chart becomes a global chart.
Nonpositive curvature prevents conjugate-point focusing.

nodes.name: Bochner identity for functions
nodes.intuition: Differentiating gradient energy reveals both second-derivative energy and a curvature correction.
nodes.conditions: Smooth real function on a smooth Riemannian manifold; Δ_g=div grad; curvature convention as in the atlas.
nodes.example: In Euclidean space for harmonic f, half the Laplacian of gradient energy is the squared Hessian norm.

patterns.why: Squared derivative energy is related to squared second derivatives.
Commuting higher derivatives introduces curvature.

nodes.name: Bishop–Gromov volume comparison
nodes.intuition: A lower Ricci bound prevents balls from gaining volume faster than the constant-curvature comparison space.
nodes.conditions: Complete n-dimensional Riemannian manifold with Ric≥(n−1)k g; V_k(r) is ball volume in the simply connected n-dimensional space form. For k>0 take 0<r<π/√k.
nodes.example: With Ric≥0, Vol(B(p,r))/r^n is nonincreasing and Vol(B(p,r))≤ω_n r^n.

patterns.why: Normalizes volume by the comparison growth scale.
Curvature controls the size of metric balls.

nodes.name: Killing vector-field equation
nodes.intuition: Infinitesimal motions preserve lengths when their local derivative has no symmetric stretching part.
nodes.conditions: Smooth vector field on a Riemannian manifold; indices lowered with g; the local flow consists of local isometries.
nodes.example: Translations and rotations in Euclidean space are Killing fields.

patterns.why: Encodes infinitesimal metric symmetries.
The symmetric derivative detects first-order strain.

nodes.name: Bianchi identities
nodes.intuition: Curvature is constrained by cyclic cancellation, both algebraically and after differentiation.
nodes.conditions: Levi-Civita connection; first sum cycles X,Y,Z; second is an identity of endomorphism-valued tensors cycling X,Y,Z.
nodes.example: Both identities are automatic for flat Euclidean space; they constrain nonzero curvature tensors as well.

patterns.why: Cyclic permutations enforce tensor relations.
Differential compatibility leads to contracted divergence identities.

nodes.name: Curvature of a bi-invariant metric
nodes.intuition: In a group whose metric respects left and right translation, noncommutativity is exactly the source of sectional curvature.
nodes.conditions: Lie group with bi-invariant positive-definite Riemannian metric; X,Y left-invariant and linearly independent. Not every Lie group admits such a metric.
nodes.example: An abelian Lie group with an invariant flat metric has zero brackets and zero curvature.

patterns.why: Two-sided metric invariance simplifies the connection.
Lie brackets determine geometric curvature.

nodes.name: Symplectic form
nodes.latex: d\omega=0,\qquad v\mapsto\omega(v,\cdot)\text{ is an isomorphism }T_pM\to T_p^*M
nodes.intuition: An alternating pairing matches directions with covectors while satisfying a differential compatibility law.
nodes.conditions: Smooth manifold; ω a smooth closed nondegenerate two-form. Dimension is necessarily even.
nodes.example: On R^{2n}, ω=sum_i dq_i∧dp_i.

patterns.why: Nondegeneracy identifies tangent and cotangent spaces.
An alternating form provides structure distinct from a metric.

nodes.name: Darboux theorem
nodes.intuition: Every symplectic space has the same local form, regardless of global topology.
nodes.conditions: Smooth symplectic 2n-manifold; the coordinates exist near every point. They need not extend globally.
nodes.example: The sphere admits an area symplectic form but cannot have a single global Euclidean coordinate chart.

patterns.why: A coordinate choice removes all local coefficients of the symplectic form.
There are no local curvature invariants of a symplectic form alone.

nodes.name: Lagrangian submanifold criterion
nodes.intuition: A Lagrangian submanifold occupies as many directions as possible while the symplectic pairing vanishes within it.
nodes.conditions: Embedded or immersed submanifold L of symplectic M, with inclusion or immersion ι; both conditions are required.
nodes.example: The graph of df in T*Q is Lagrangian for the canonical symplectic form.

patterns.why: A Lagrangian tangent space equals its symplectic orthogonal.
Each Lagrangian tangent space is its own symplectic orthogonal, using an alternating rather than metric pairing.

nodes.name: Cohomology cup product
nodes.intuition: Cohomology classes can multiply, detecting how topological features interact rather than merely how many exist.
nodes.conditions: Singular cohomology of a space with coefficients in a commutative ring R; graded commutativity holds at the cohomology-class level.
nodes.example: On a torus, two independent degree-one classes have nonzero product in degree two.

patterns.why: Cohomology is a graded ring, not only a sequence of groups.
Products combine classes in complementary degrees.

nodes.name: Universal coefficient theorem for cohomology
nodes.intuition: Dualizing homology almost gives cohomology; a torsion correction explains the difference.
nodes.conditions: Space X, abelian coefficient group G; singular homology and cohomology. The sequence splits as groups, generally not naturally.
nodes.example: If H_{n−1} is free, the Ext term vanishes and H^n is Hom(H_n,G).

patterns.why: Cohomology tests homology through homomorphisms.
Ext records information lost by naive dualization.

nodes.name: Long exact sequence of a pair
nodes.intuition: Relative cycles may have a boundary, provided the boundary lies in the designated subspace.
nodes.conditions: Topological pair A⊆X; singular homology with one fixed coefficient group.
nodes.example: H_n(D^n,S^{n−1};Z)=Z, whose generator maps to the sphere boundary class.

patterns.why: The connecting map sends a relative interior cycle to its boundary in A.
Relative chains quotient out the subspace chains.

nodes.name: Long exact sequence of a fibration
nodes.intuition: A sphere that contracts after projection may leave a nontrivial trace in the fiber.
nodes.conditions: Pointed Serre fibration F→E→B with chosen compatible basepoints; homotopy-group exactness in positive degrees, with the usual pointed-set interpretation at degree zero.
nodes.example: The Hopf fibration S¹→S³→S² yields π₂(S²)≅π₁(S¹)≅Z.

patterns.why: Separates total-space topology into base and fiber contributions.
Lifting a disk creates a boundary sphere in the fiber.

nodes.name: Hurewicz theorem
nodes.intuition: At the first possible nontrivial dimension, sphere-based topology and cycle-based topology agree.
nodes.conditions: n≥2; X a path-connected CW complex with π_i(X)=0 for 1≤i<n. The Hurewicz map sends a sphere map to its fundamental homology class.
nodes.example: For S^n with n≥2, π_n(S^n)≅Z.

patterns.why: Relates geometric sphere maps to additive cycle classes.
Connectivity removes lower-dimensional obstructions.

nodes.name: Whitehead theorem for CW complexes
nodes.latex: f_*:\pi_n(X)\overset{\cong}{\to}\pi_n(Y)\ \forall n\ge1\Longrightarrow f\text{ is a homotopy equivalence}
nodes.intuition: For spaces built from cells, matching every sphere-based test is enough to recover the whole homotopy type.
nodes.conditions: Continuous map f between connected CW complexes; compatible basepoints. Without the CW hypothesis a weak homotopy equivalence need not be a homotopy equivalence.
nodes.example: A contractible CW complex is homotopy equivalent to a point.

patterns.why: Homotopy groups detect equivalence within the CW setting.
Cell-by-cell lifting turns local homotopy data into a global inverse.

nodes.name: Suspension isomorphism in reduced homology
nodes.intuition: Collapsing the two ends of a cylinder shifts each reduced homology feature up one dimension.
nodes.conditions: Nonempty CW complex X; unreduced suspension ΣX; n≥0; any abelian coefficient group G.
nodes.example: Suspending S¹ gives S² and shifts its Z class from degree one to degree two.

patterns.why: Suspension shifts dimension rather than numerical size.
Two contractible cones isolate the intersection contribution.

nodes.name: Cellular homology chain complex
nodes.intuition: One generator per cell can replace the enormous singular chain complex.
nodes.conditions: CW complex X with skeleta X^n; boundary maps are induced by attaching maps and connecting homomorphisms.
nodes.example: A sphere has one zero-cell and one n-cell, making its cellular homology immediate.

patterns.why: The skeletal filtration adds one dimension of cells at a time.
Chain ranks equal cell counts.

nodes.name: Excision in relative homology
nodes.intuition: Removing a region safely inside the ignored subspace does not change the relative topological information.
nodes.conditions: A⊆X and closure(Z)⊆interior(A); singular homology with abelian coefficients G; map induced by inclusion.
nodes.example: Removing an interior subdisk from the ignored annular region does not affect the corresponding relative group.

patterns.why: Only the relative interface matters after interior pieces are excised.
Small-chain subdivision makes a global comparison local.

nodes.name: Classification of connected covering spaces
nodes.intuition: A covering space is determined by which loops close after being lifted.
nodes.conditions: X path-connected, locally path-connected and semilocally simply connected; covers unbased, hence subgroups taken up to conjugacy.
nodes.example: Subgroups nZ of π₁(S¹)=Z give the n-sheeted circle covers; {0} gives its universal cover R.

patterns.why: Geometric coverings correspond to algebraic subgroups.
Changing the chosen lifted basepoint conjugates the subgroup.

nodes.name: Borsuk–Ulam theorem
nodes.intuition: A continuous assignment of n measurements to an n-sphere must agree at some opposite pair.
nodes.conditions: n≥1; antipodal points on the unit n-sphere; arbitrary continuous real-valued n-component map.
nodes.example: For n=1, some opposite points on a circle have equal scalar measurement.

patterns.why: Antipodal symmetry forces coincidence.
The conclusion is an unavoidable coincidence, related to topological obstruction methods.
