nodes.name: Euler class and zero counts
nodes.intuition: The topology of the tangent bundle accounts for the total index of unavoidable vector-field zeros.
nodes.conditions: Closed oriented smooth n-manifold; X a smooth tangent vector field with isolated zeros; e(TM)∈H^n(M;Z).
nodes.example: A sphere S² has Euler characteristic two, so a tangent field cannot be everywhere nonzero.

patterns.why: Signed zero indices equal a global invariant.
Local behavior around zeros sums to a global topological quantity.

nodes.name: Chern classes and the Whitney sum law
nodes.intuition: Characteristic classes package the twisting of complex vector bundles into multiplicative cohomology data.
nodes.conditions: Complex vector bundles of finite rank over a CW complex; c_i(E)∈H^{2i}(X;Z), zero above the rank.
nodes.example: For line bundles L,M, c₁(L⊕M)=c₁(L)+c₁(M) and c₂(L⊕M)=c₁(L)c₁(M).

patterns.why: Direct sums multiply total characteristic classes.
Cohomology-ring multiplication combines bundle invariants.

nodes.name: Stiefel–Whitney classes
nodes.intuition: Real bundles carry mod-two twisting indicators that survive without choosing an orientation.
nodes.conditions: Real rank-r vector bundle over a CW complex; w_i(E)∈H^i(X;F₂), vanish above rank. w₁=0 iff E is orientable.
nodes.example: The Möbius line bundle over S¹ has nonzero w₁.

patterns.why: Classes detect bundle twisting independent of local coordinates.
Direct sums multiply the total class.

nodes.name: Thom isomorphism
nodes.intuition: An oriented r-dimensional fiber contributes one canonical relative class and shifts cohomological degree by r.
nodes.conditions: R-oriented real rank-r vector bundle E over a CW complex; u its Thom class; D(E),S(E) disk and sphere bundles from a chosen metric; R commutative coefficient ring.
nodes.example: For a trivial bundle over a point, this is H⁰(point)≅H^r(D^r,S^{r−1}).

patterns.why: Fiber orientation provides a canonical complementary-degree class.
Separates base cohomology from the fiber contribution.

nodes.name: Chern character
nodes.intuition: Exponentiating formal Chern roots turns bundle sum and tensor product into ordinary ring operations.
nodes.conditions: Complex vector bundles over a finite CW complex; x_i formal degree-two Chern roots under the splitting principle; values in even rational cohomology.
nodes.example: ch(E)=rank(E)+c₁+(c₁²−2c₂)/2+⋯.

patterns.why: Exponentials convert sums of roots under tensor products into products.
Defines a ring homomorphism from complex K-theory to rational cohomology.

nodes.name: Compact-to-Hausdorff bijection theorem
nodes.latex: f:X\to Y\text{ continuous bijective},\ X\text{ compact},\ Y\text{ Hausdorff}\Longrightarrow f\text{ homeomorphism}
nodes.intuition: Compactness prevents a continuous one-to-one relabeling from hiding a discontinuous inverse.
nodes.conditions: Topological spaces as stated; no metrizability needed.
nodes.example: A continuous bijection from a compact interval onto its image in Euclidean space has continuous inverse.

patterns.why: Both directions of a bijection become continuous under asymmetric hypotheses.
Compact sets and closed-set behavior control inverse continuity.

nodes.name: Tychonoff compactness theorem
nodes.intuition: Even infinitely many compact coordinate constraints remain compact in the topology that inspects finitely many coordinates at a time.
nodes.conditions: Product topology; arbitrary family of compact spaces, in standard set theory with the axiom of choice. The box topology need not satisfy the conclusion.
nodes.example: The infinite binary cube {0,1}^N is compact in its product topology.

patterns.why: Products combine arbitrarily many compact factors.
Global compactness follows from compatible coordinate constraints.

nodes.name: Boolean algebra as a Boolean ring
nodes.latex: A+B=A\triangle B,\quad AB=A\cap B,\quad A^2=A,\quad A+A=0
nodes.intuition: Logical choices become arithmetic when addition means exclusive-or and multiplication means and.
nodes.conditions: Subsets of a fixed universe; symmetric difference as addition and intersection as multiplication. More generally every Boolean algebra yields a commutative Boolean ring.

patterns.why: Logical operations obey ring laws in characteristic two.
Complementation exchanges union and intersection.

nodes.name: Downward Löwenheim–Skolem theorem
nodes.latex: A\subseteq M\Longrightarrow\exists N\preccurlyeq M:\ A\subseteq N,\ |N|\le\max(|A|,|L|,\aleph_0)
nodes.intuition: A structure may have a much smaller part that preserves every first-order statement about its own elements.
nodes.conditions: First-order L-structure M; subset A; N is an elementary substructure. Uses the usual choice principles to select witnesses.
nodes.example: An infinite structure in a countable language has a countable elementary substructure containing any chosen countable set.

patterns.why: A controlled-size substructure retains elementary information.
Repeated witness selection builds an elementary closure.

nodes.name: Tarski–Vaught test
nodes.latex: N\preccurlyeq M\iff\bigl(M\models\exists x\,\varphi(x,\bar a)\Rightarrow\exists b\in N:\ M\models\varphi(b,\bar a)\bigr)
nodes.intuition: A substructure is elementary exactly when it never needs to leave home to find an existential witness.
nodes.conditions: N⊆M an L-substructure; the condition holds for every first-order formula φ and all parameter tuples a from N.
nodes.example: A subfield of an algebraically closed field must contain every needed root to satisfy even the polynomial-witness part of this test.

patterns.why: Induction on formula complexity proves elementary equivalence of evaluations.
Reduces all formulas to existential witness checks.

nodes.name: Łoś theorem for ultraproducts
nodes.intuition: A first-order statement holds in the quotient product exactly when it holds on a set of indices deemed large by the ultrafilter.
nodes.conditions: Structures M_i in one first-order language with nonempty domains; U an ultrafilter on the index set; tuples represented coordinatewise; usual choice principles.
nodes.example: An ultraproduct of fields is a field because every field axiom transfers.

patterns.why: Combines a family of structures into one quotient product.
Changing representatives on an ultrafilter-small set preserves truth.

nodes.name: Quantifier elimination for real closed fields
nodes.intuition: Existence conditions involving polynomial inequalities can be rewritten as polynomial inequalities without hidden variables.
nodes.conditions: First-order language of ordered rings; φ may contain parameters, retained in ψ; all real closed fields satisfy the equivalence.
nodes.example: Over R, ∃y(y²=x) is equivalent to x≥0.

patterns.why: Removes quantified variables while preserving the defined set.
Order and polynomial arithmetic determine all definable sets.

nodes.name: Compactness of the space of types
nodes.latex: [\varphi]=\{p:\varphi\in p\},\qquad S_n(T)\text{ is compact Hausdorff and totally disconnected}
nodes.intuition: A complete type is a fully specified collection of compatible answers about a tuple; finite questions define its neighborhoods.
nodes.conditions: Consistent first-order theory T; S_n(T) complete n-types over T; basic sets [φ] are both open and closed.
nodes.example: For dense linear orders, one-variable types over a parameter set describe consistent positions relative to those parameters.

patterns.why: Logical compactness becomes compactness of a topological space.
Formulas become clopen subsets of the space of their complete truth assignments.

nodes.name: Affine algebraic zero set
nodes.intuition: A geometric shape is the set of simultaneous solutions of a polynomial system.
nodes.conditions: Field k; ideal I⊆k[x₁,…,x_n]. Over non-algebraically-closed fields, distinct radical ideals may have the same k-points.
nodes.example: V(y−x²) is the parabola over R.

patterns.why: Polynomial equations become ideals.
The zero set encodes geometry without first choosing distances.

nodes.name: Coordinate ring of an affine algebraic set
nodes.intuition: Two polynomials represent the same observable on a shape when they agree at every point of it.
nodes.conditions: X⊆k^n an affine algebraic set; I(X) the ideal of all polynomials vanishing on X.
nodes.example: The parabola y=x² has coordinate ring k[x,y]/(y−x²)≅k[x].

patterns.why: A space is studied through its algebra of polynomial functions.
Quotienting removes equations already enforced by the space.

nodes.name: Radical of an ideal
nodes.intuition: Discard algebraic multiplicity while retaining the underlying vanishing constraint.
nodes.conditions: Ideal I in a commutative ring with identity; sqrt(I) is an ideal.
nodes.example: sqrt((x²))=(x) in k[x].

patterns.why: Power membership defines a closure on ideals.
In polynomial zero sets, replacing I by its radical leaves the points unchanged.

nodes.name: Hilbert Nullstellensatz
nodes.intuition: Over an algebraically closed field, all equations true on a zero set are exactly the power consequences of its defining ideal.
nodes.conditions: k algebraically closed; I ideal in k[x₁,…,x_n]; V uses k-valued points.
nodes.example: The zero set of x² is the origin, whose full vanishing ideal is (x).

patterns.why: Closed sets correspond contravariantly to radical ideals.
Geometric vanishing is equivalent to ideal-power membership.

nodes.name: Zariski topology
nodes.intuition: Polynomial vanishing sets become the closed sets, making algebraic constraints into a topology.
nodes.conditions: Affine n-space over a field; arbitrary intersections and finite unions of algebraic zero sets are closed.
nodes.example: On the affine line over an algebraically closed field, proper closed subsets are finite.

patterns.why: Operations on equations reverse operations on zero sets.
Ideal arithmetic generates topological operations.

nodes.name: Affine morphisms and ring homomorphisms
nodes.intuition: Mapping points forward pulls observable functions backward.
nodes.conditions: Affine algebraic varieties over an algebraically closed field k; regular morphisms; reduced finitely generated coordinate algebras.
nodes.example: The parabola parametrization t↦(t,t²) pulls x to t and y to t².

patterns.why: Geometry reverses the direction of algebra maps.
Pullback reverses the order of composed maps.

nodes.name: Prime spectrum of a ring
nodes.latex: \operatorname{Spec}R=\{\mathfrak p\subset R:\mathfrak p\text{ prime}\},\qquad V(I)=\{\mathfrak p:I\subseteq\mathfrak p\}
nodes.intuition: Treat every prime ideal as a point, including points that encode an entire irreducible region.
nodes.conditions: Commutative ring with identity; displayed V(I) are its closed sets; the zero ring has empty spectrum.
nodes.example: Spec Z contains (0) and one closed point (p) for each rational prime.

patterns.why: Prime ideals supply generalized geometric points.
Ring arithmetic determines the space.

nodes.name: Localization as an open affine patch
nodes.intuition: Making f invertible restricts geometry to the region where f does not vanish.
nodes.conditions: Commutative ring R; localization at powers of f; canonical isomorphism of affine schemes.
nodes.example: Spec k[x,x^(−1)] is the affine line with the origin removed.

patterns.why: Principal open subsets provide affine patches of the spectrum.
Inverting a function corresponds to deleting its zero locus.

nodes.name: Local ring at a geometric point
nodes.intuition: Near one point, denominators are allowed whenever they stay nonzero at that point.
nodes.conditions: Affine variety X over an algebraically closed field; p a closed point; m_p its vanishing maximal ideal; elements are germs of regular functions.
nodes.example: At zero on the affine line, 1/(1−x) belongs to the local ring, while 1/x does not.

patterns.why: Germs identify functions that agree on some neighborhood of the selected point.
The unique maximal ideal consists of functions vanishing at the point.

nodes.name: Zariski tangent space
nodes.intuition: Keep only first-order changes compatible with every defining equation.
nodes.conditions: Affine variety X=V(I)⊆k^n over an algebraically closed field; p a k-point; f lists generators of I; tangent space over k.
nodes.example: For y²=x³ at the origin, both derivatives vanish, so the tangent space has dimension two although the curve has dimension one.

patterns.why: Quotienting by m² discards second and higher orders.
Tangent vectors are dual to first-order vanishing functions.

nodes.name: Jacobian criterion for nonsingularity
nodes.intuition: At a smooth point, the first-order approximation has exactly the dimension the space actually needs.
nodes.conditions: Reduced affine variety over an algebraically closed field; p closed; equivalently rank J_f(p)=n−dim O_X,p. For smoothness over arbitrary fields additional field hypotheses matter.
nodes.example: The parabola y−x² has Jacobian rank one everywhere; the cusp is singular at the origin.

patterns.why: Compares tangent dimension with true local dimension.
Detects local geometric regularity without choosing a metric.

nodes.name: Krull dimension
nodes.intuition: Dimension counts how deeply irreducible subspaces can nest.
nodes.conditions: Commutative ring; dimension may be infinite; chains consist of prime ideals. For affine domains over a field, equals transcendence degree of the fraction field.
nodes.example: dim k[x₁,…,x_n]=n; dim Z=1.

patterns.why: Nested prime chains measure independent geometric layers.
Ideal inclusions reverse containment of irreducible closed sets.

nodes.name: Noether normalization
nodes.intuition: An affine algebraic space admits a finite projection onto a plain affine space of the same dimension.
nodes.conditions: Finitely generated nonzero integral k-algebra A; t_i∈A algebraically independent; d=trdeg_k Frac(A); finite means finitely generated as module.
nodes.example: For k[x,y]/(y²−x³−1), the subring k[x] gives a finite module generated by 1,y.

patterns.why: Separates free polynomial coordinates from finite algebraic complexity.
Integrality makes a geometric projection finite.

nodes.name: Hilbert polynomial of a projective scheme
nodes.intuition: The number of independent homogeneous observables eventually follows a polynomial whose degree records geometric dimension.
nodes.conditions: Nonempty projective scheme X=Proj A over a field, A a finitely generated standard graded algebra; d=dim X; degree depends on the chosen embedding.
nodes.example: For P^n, P(m)=binom(m+n,n).

patterns.why: Counts independent degree-m coordinate functions.
Leading polynomial growth records dimension and degree.

nodes.name: Hilbert–Serre rationality
nodes.intuition: Finite graded algebraic data forces an infinite dimension-counting series to be rational.
nodes.conditions: M finitely generated nonnegatively graded module over k[x₁,…,x_n] with variables of degree one; finite-dimensional graded pieces; Q∈Z[t]. Cancellation may lower pole order.
nodes.example: The polynomial ring itself has H(t)=1/(1−t)^n.

patterns.why: The coefficient series records graded dimensions.
Finite generation and graded exact sequences constrain coefficient growth.

nodes.name: Projective space
nodes.intuition: A point records a direction through the origin; multiplying every coordinate by the same nonzero scale changes nothing.
nodes.conditions: Field k; λ∈k×; homogeneous coordinates cannot all be zero.
nodes.example: The chart x₀≠0 becomes affine n-space by dividing all coordinates by x₀.

patterns.why: Common nonzero scaling is discarded.
Affine charts arise by normalizing a nonzero coordinate.

nodes.name: Projective homogeneous zero sets
nodes.intuition: Homogeneous equations remain meaningful when coordinates are only defined up to scale.
nodes.conditions: Homogeneous ideal I in k[x₀,…,x_n]; evaluate homogeneous generators on any nonzero representative.
nodes.example: The projective conic xz−y²=0 includes the affine parabola chart and its point at infinity.

patterns.why: Homogeneity preserves zero equations under common coordinate scaling.
Projective completion adds limiting directions to affine charts.

nodes.name: Bézout theorem for plane curves
nodes.intuition: Projective intersections conserve a total multiplicity, even when points merge or move to infinity.
nodes.conditions: Plane projective curves over an algebraically closed field with no common irreducible component; intersection multiplicities counted.
nodes.example: A line meets a nonsingular conic in two points counted with multiplicity; tangency counts twice.

patterns.why: Total intersection multiplicity is fixed by degrees.
Multiplicity corrects naive point counting.

nodes.name: Genus of a smooth plane curve
nodes.intuition: The degree of a nonsingular projective plane equation determines the curve’s intrinsic genus.
nodes.conditions: Smooth geometrically integral projective plane curve of degree d over an algebraically closed field. Singular curves require correction terms.
nodes.example: Lines and smooth conics have genus zero; smooth cubics have genus one.

patterns.why: Degree determines the number of independent regular differentials.
Polynomial degree controls an intrinsic geometric invariant.

nodes.name: Veronese embedding
nodes.intuition: Promote degree-d monomials to linear coordinates, turning certain nonlinear equations into hyperplane sections.
nodes.conditions: Integer d≥1; all degree-d monomials included exactly once; defined over any field.
nodes.example: For P¹ and d=2, [s:t]↦[s²:st:t²], with image xz=y².

patterns.why: The embedding linearizes degree-d equations in a larger coordinate space, exactly rather than approximately.
Homogeneous monomials form new projective coordinates.

nodes.name: Segre embedding
nodes.intuition: A pair of directions becomes one rank-one tensor direction.
nodes.conditions: Projective spaces over a field; image is cut out by all 2×2 minors of the coordinate matrix.
nodes.example: P¹×P¹ embeds as the quadric z00z11−z01z10=0 in P³.

patterns.why: Combines two projective factors through products of coordinates.
Rank-one tensors are characterized by determinantal equations.

nodes.name: Plücker embedding of a Grassmannian
nodes.intuition: A k-dimensional subspace is represented by its oriented volume coordinate, with overall scale forgotten.
nodes.conditions: Finite-dimensional vector space V over a field; 1≤k≤dim V; v_i any basis of W. Image consists of decomposable nonzero exterior tensors modulo scale.
nodes.example: Gr(2,4) satisfies p12p34−p13p24+p14p23=0 in P⁵.

patterns.why: A basis change only rescales the exterior product by its determinant.
Decomposable exterior tensors encode subspaces.

nodes.name: Sheaf gluing axiom
nodes.intuition: Compatible local descriptions assemble uniquely into one global description.
nodes.conditions: Presheaf of sets F on a topological space; every open cover U=union U_i; with the restriction identities, this gluing condition defines a sheaf.
nodes.example: Continuous real functions agreeing on overlaps glue to a continuous function on the union.

patterns.why: Compatible restrictions assemble a global section.
Compatible restrictions determine a section uniquely.

nodes.name: Scheme as a locally affine ringed space
nodes.intuition: Glue affine ring-based spaces along open patches while preserving their local functions.
nodes.conditions: Locally ringed space with an open cover by affine spectra and their structure sheaves; this is the definition of a scheme.
nodes.example: Projective space is a scheme covered by n+1 affine n-space charts.

patterns.why: Affine patches build global algebraic spaces.
Local rings remain part of the geometry.

nodes.name: Fiber product of affine schemes
nodes.intuition: Combining two geometric objects over a shared base combines their coordinate algebras by tensor product.
nodes.conditions: Commutative R-algebras A,B; fiber product in the category of schemes. The tensor ring can have nilpotents even if both factors are reduced.
nodes.example: Base-changing an affine scheme from R to a field k gives Spec(A⊗_R k).

patterns.why: A geometric pullback becomes an algebraic pushout.
Tensor products enforce agreement over the common base.

nodes.name: Divisors and degree on a curve
nodes.intuition: Zeros and poles balance globally on a complete curve when counted with multiplicity.
nodes.conditions: Smooth projective integral curve over an algebraically closed field; finite divisor sum; f nonzero rational function. Over a general field, degree uses residue-field weights.
nodes.example: On P¹, the coordinate t has one simple zero and one simple pole.

patterns.why: Principal divisors have equal total zeros and poles.
A rational function is analyzed point by point by its orders.

nodes.name: Riemann–Roch for curves
nodes.intuition: Allowing poles increases the number of independent functions predictably, with a correction from differentials and genus.
nodes.conditions: Smooth projective integral curve over an algebraically closed field; D divisor; K canonical divisor; ℓ(D)=dim{f rational:div(f)+D≥0} including zero; genus g.
nodes.example: On P¹, g=0 and ℓ(m∞)=m+1 for m≥0, the polynomial space of degree at most m.

patterns.why: Counts independent functions under local pole constraints.
The correction is measured by canonical differentials with complementary divisor.

nodes.name: Elliptic curve chord–tangent addition
nodes.intuition: Join two points, find the third intersection with the cubic, then reflect it to define their sum.
nodes.conditions: Nonsingular E:y²=x³+ax+b over a field of characteristic not 2 or 3; 4a³+27b²≠0; displayed formula assumes x₁≠x₂. For doubling use m=(3x₁²+a)/(2y₁) if y₁≠0; opposite points sum to the point at infinity O.
nodes.example: On y²=x³−x, points (0,0),(1,0),(−1,0) each have order two.

patterns.why: The cubic becomes an abelian group with identity O.
Incidence of lines defines addition without a distance choice.

nodes.name: Hasse bound for elliptic curves
nodes.intuition: A nonsingular cubic over a finite field has close to one point per field element, with square-root-scale fluctuation.
nodes.conditions: Elliptic curve over finite field F_q; count includes the identity point at infinity; q a prime power.
nodes.example: Over F₅, the curve y²=x³−x has eight points, within 6±2√5.

patterns.why: Bounds a finite-field solution count.
The error grows like square root of field size.

nodes.name: Frobenius polynomial of an elliptic curve
nodes.intuition: Repeated Frobenius action satisfies a quadratic law whose trace records the point count.
nodes.conditions: Elliptic curve over F_q; F the q-power Frobenius endomorphism; [m] multiplication by m; equality in End(E). On an ℓ-adic Tate module with ℓ not dividing q, characteristic polynomial is T²−tT+q.
nodes.example: If #E(F_q)=q+1, Frobenius satisfies F²+[q]=0.

patterns.why: A quadratic relation controls all Frobenius iterates.
Arithmetic point counts become endomorphism invariants.

nodes.name: Resultant detects common roots
nodes.intuition: A determinant eliminates the root variable and reports whether two polynomial constraints can share a solution.
nodes.conditions: Nonzero polynomials f,g over a field, positive degrees m,n; a_m leading coefficient of f; roots in algebraic closure counted with multiplicity; resultant is the Sylvester-matrix determinant.
nodes.example: For f=x−a and g=x−b, the resultant is a−b.

patterns.why: Product over roots turns simultaneous vanishing into one scalar.
Elimination is encoded by a coefficient determinant.

nodes.name: Buchberger criterion for a Gröbner basis
nodes.latex: G\text{ is a Gröbner basis}\iff \operatorname{rem}_G S(g_i,g_j)=0\quad\forall i<j
nodes.intuition: It is enough to resolve every pairwise clash between leading terms to make polynomial reduction globally reliable.
nodes.conditions: Finite set G of nonzero polynomials over a field, generating ideal I; fixed monomial order; S-polynomials cancel least-common-multiple leading terms; reduction remainder means full multivariate division by G.
nodes.example: For G={x−y,y²−1} with lexicographic x>y, the single S-polynomial reduces to zero.

patterns.why: Repeated leading-term reduction terminates by the monomial well-order.
Pairwise compatibility ensures every ideal leading term is generated correctly.

nodes.name: Newton's second law
nodes.intuition: A force tells a trajectory how its velocity bends in time. Giving position and velocity turns this second-order rule into an initial-value problem.
nodes.conditions: A classical point particle of constant positive mass m, observed in an inertial frame; the prescribed force must support the desired existence and uniqueness of solutions.
nodes.example: A constant force gives r(t)=r(0)+v(0)t+Ft²/(2m), component by component.

patterns.why: Acceleration is the local rate of change of velocity along the trajectory.
Integrating the force twice recovers velocity and position after fixing initial data.

nodes.name: Work–energy theorem
nodes.latex: \Delta K=\int_{\gamma}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r,\qquad K=\tfrac12m\lVert\dot{\mathbf r}\rVert^2
nodes.intuition: The part of force aligned with motion changes kinetic energy. Integrating that local energy transfer gives the total work along the actual path.
nodes.conditions: Constant positive mass in Newtonian mechanics, a differentiable trajectory satisfying Newton's law, and an integrable force along it. Path independence requires additional conservative-force assumptions.
nodes.example: A perpendicular magnetic force can curve a trajectory while doing no work and leaving its speed unchanged.

patterns.why: Work accumulates the directional force over infinitesimal displacements.
Kinetic energy is quadratic in velocity, so its derivative pairs acceleration with velocity.

nodes.name: Angular momentum and torque
nodes.latex: \mathbf L=\mathbf r\times m\dot{\mathbf r},\qquad\dot{\mathbf L}=\mathbf r\times\mathbf F
nodes.intuition: Rotational motion has its own balance equation. Only a force with a lever arm about the origin changes angular momentum about that origin.
nodes.conditions: Classical point particle of constant mass and a fixed origin in an inertial frame. A central force parallel to r has zero torque and conserves L.
nodes.example: Inverse-square gravity is radial about its source, so a planetary orbit stays in the plane perpendicular to its conserved angular momentum.

patterns.why: Vanishing torque makes angular momentum constant.
Rotational symmetry of a central potential produces this conserved quantity.

nodes.name: Hamiltonian as a velocity Legendre transform
nodes.latex: p_i=\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q_i},\qquad H(q,p,t)=\sum_i p_i\dot q_i-L(q,\dot q,t)
nodes.intuition: The same mechanics can be described using either velocities or their conjugate momenta. The subtraction changes which variables are independent while preserving the dynamics.
nodes.conditions: A smooth regular Lagrangian with invertible velocity Hessian locally, so q̇ can be solved from p. Global identification with a convex conjugate additionally requires suitable convexity and domain conditions.
nodes.example: For L=m q̇²/2−V(q), p=mq̇ and H=p²/(2m)+V(q).

patterns.why: Velocity and momentum are paired by a Legendre transform.
The state uses q and p rather than q and q̇ when the velocity map is invertible.

nodes.name: Canonical Poisson bracket
nodes.latex: \{f,g\}=\sum_i\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial q_i}\frac{\partial g}{\partial p_i}-\frac{\partial f}{\partial p_i}\frac{\partial g}{\partial q_i}\right)
nodes.intuition: Two observables interact through paired position and momentum directions. The bracket measures how one observable changes along the motion generated by the other.
nodes.conditions: Smooth real observables on a canonical phase-space chart with the standard symplectic structure. The displayed signs use the convention {q_i,p_j}=δ_ij.
nodes.example: For H=p²/(2m)+V(q), {q,H}=p/m and {p,H}=−V′(q).

patterns.why: The bracket is bilinear, antisymmetric and satisfies Jacobi and the Leibniz rule.
Each position derivative pairs with a conjugate momentum derivative.

nodes.name: Evolution of a classical observable
nodes.intuition: An observable changes because its measuring rule changes explicitly with time and because the state moves through phase space. The Poisson bracket accounts for the second contribution.
nodes.conditions: Differentiable f(q,p,t), smooth Hamiltonian H, and a trajectory satisfying canonical Hamilton equations. If f has no explicit time dependence and {f,H}=0, it is conserved.
nodes.example: Choosing f=H gives dH/dt=∂H/∂t, so an autonomous Hamiltonian conserves its own energy.

patterns.why: The chain rule differentiates an observable composed with a phase-space trajectory.
A vanishing bracket identifies conserved observables.

nodes.name: Canonical transformation criterion
nodes.intuition: A canonical change of coordinates preserves the position–momentum pairing. It can simplify a Hamiltonian without changing the geometric form of its motion equations.
nodes.conditions: A differentiable local diffeomorphism Φ on even-dimensional canonical phase space. The equation preserves the standard symplectic bilinear form; volume preservation alone is weaker in dimension greater than two.
nodes.example: The rescaling Q=a q, P=p/a is canonical for any nonzero real a.

patterns.why: The matrix J encoding the symplectic pairing is preserved.
Canonical coordinates change while Hamilton's equation structure survives.

nodes.name: Liouville's phase-volume theorem
nodes.intuition: A cloud of Hamiltonian initial states can stretch and fold, but its phase-space volume stays fixed. The conservation concerns the whole cloud, even if individual trajectories separate.
nodes.conditions: A C² Hamiltonian in canonical coordinates, a smooth flow Φ_t defined on the region considered, and no dissipative terms. Volume here is dq₁…dq_n dp₁…dp_n.
nodes.example: A harmonic oscillator rotates phase-space ellipses without shrinking their enclosed area.

patterns.why: Hamiltonian flow preserves phase-space volume.
Zero divergence means that an infinitesimal region has zero net volume flux.

nodes.name: Hamilton–Jacobi equation
nodes.intuition: An action field labels a family of classical trajectories. Its spatial slope supplies momentum, turning trajectory mechanics into a first-order partial differential equation.
nodes.conditions: A smooth Hamiltonian and a differentiable classical action solution S on a region without the singularities being crossed. Nonsmooth viscosity solutions require a separate framework.
nodes.example: For a free particle, S(q,t)=p·q−|p|²t/(2m) solves the equation with constant momentum p.

patterns.why: The action gradient gives the momentum attached to each point.
Hamiltonian dynamics and an action-generating function provide complementary descriptions.

nodes.name: Action–angle variables
nodes.intuition: An integrable system becomes uniform motion around circles after the right coordinates are chosen. Actions label invariant tori, while angles describe position on each torus.
nodes.conditions: Near a compact connected regular invariant torus of a Liouville-integrable Hamiltonian system with n independent commuting integrals. Angles are periodic modulo 2π; singular fibers are excluded.
nodes.example: For a one-dimensional harmonic oscillator, I=E/ω and its angle advances at angular rate ω.

patterns.why: Nonlinear motion simplifies to constant-speed angular motion.
The action coordinates remain fixed along a trajectory.

nodes.name: Virial theorem for a bounded mechanical system
nodes.intuition: A bounded system cannot keep increasing its position–momentum correlation forever. Averaging its derivative balances kinetic energy with the way potential energy scales in position.
nodes.conditions: Newtonian particles in a differentiable time-independent potential. The long-time averages exist and G(T)/T→0 for G=Σ r_i·p_i. For homogeneous degree-k V this yields 2⟨K⟩=k⟨V⟩.
nodes.example: A bound inverse-distance potential has degree −1, so 2⟨K⟩=−⟨V⟩.

patterns.why: A long-time average removes the derivative of a sublinearly growing quantity.
A homogeneous potential turns position times gradient into its degree times the potential.

nodes.name: Inertia tensor
nodes.intuition: The distribution of mass determines the cost of rotating in each direction. A symmetric matrix packages all directional moments of inertia into one quadratic energy.
nodes.conditions: A rigid mass distribution with finite second moments about a fixed reference point. The displayed kinetic energy is the rotational contribution about that point; translation may contribute separately.
nodes.example: For rotation about a unit axis n, the moment of inertia is nᵀIn.

patterns.why: Mass-weighted integration aggregates squared distances from rotation axes.
Rotational kinetic energy is a positive-semidefinite quadratic form in angular velocity.

nodes.name: Euler's rigid-body equations
nodes.intuition: In axes attached to the body, angular momentum changes partly because the axes themselves rotate. The cross product corrects the time derivative for that moving frame.
nodes.conditions: A rigid body with constant inertia tensor in its body frame, angular velocity ω, and applied torque about a fixed point or the center of mass with the corresponding balance assumptions.
nodes.example: In principal axes without torque, I₁ω̇₁=(I₂−I₃)ω₂ω₃, with cyclic companion equations.

patterns.why: The body frame trades a changing inertia matrix for an extra rotational derivative term.
In torque-free motion the inertial angular momentum and rotational kinetic energy are conserved.

nodes.name: Maxwell's equations in vacuum with sources
nodes.latex:
abla\cdot E=ho/\varepsilon_0,\quad
abla\cdot B=0,\quad
abla	imes E=-\partial_t B,\quad
abla	imes B=\mu_0j+\mu_0\varepsilon_0\partial_t E
nodes.intuition: Charges produce electric flux, magnetic flux has no local sources, and changing fields generate circulating fields. Together these local rules permit self-propagating electromagnetic waves.
nodes.conditions: Classical electromagnetic fields in SI units in vacuum with charge density ρ and current density j. Smooth fields are assumed in the displayed differential form; singular sources require distributions or integral forms.
nodes.example: Taking divergence of the last equation and using the first gives ∂tρ+∇·j=0.

patterns.why: Divergence and curl connect local field behavior to surface flux and loop circulation.
The equations enforce local electric-charge continuity.

nodes.name: Lorentz force
nodes.latex: \mathbf F=q(E+\mathbf v\times B),\qquad \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v=qE\cdot\mathbf v
nodes.intuition: Electric fields can speed up a charge; magnetic fields deflect its motion perpendicular to velocity. The work relation reveals the difference immediately.
nodes.conditions: Classical point charge q moving at velocity v in prescribed electromagnetic fields, in SI units. Radiation reaction and self-force are excluded from this test-particle law.
nodes.example: With a uniform magnetic field and no electric field, nonrelativistic motion perpendicular to B is circular at constant speed.

patterns.why: The magnetic cross product is perpendicular to velocity and contributes no power.
Electric and magnetic contributions superpose linearly in the field for fixed velocity.

nodes.name: Electromagnetic scalar and vector potentials
nodes.intuition: Potentials represent fields using functions whose derivatives automatically satisfy the source-free magnetic and induction equations. Multiple potential choices can encode the same measurable fields.
nodes.conditions: Sufficiently smooth potentials on a spacetime region. Recovering potentials globally from fields can have topological obstructions; locally the homogeneous Maxwell equations provide the needed compatibility.
nodes.example: In electrostatics with a time-independent vector potential, E=−∇φ.

patterns.why: Electric field splits into a scalar-gradient and time-changing vector-potential term.
The identities curl grad=0 and div curl=0 encode differential compatibility.

nodes.name: Electromagnetic gauge transformation
nodes.intuition: Changing potentials by a coordinated derivative adjustment leaves the fields unchanged. The mathematical description contains a redundancy that can be chosen for convenience.
nodes.conditions: A sufficiently smooth scalar χ and commuting derivatives in a common spacetime chart. The relation compares classical potentials for identical local electromagnetic fields; global gauge structure may be richer.
nodes.example: Adding a spatially constant scalar to an electrostatic potential changes no electric field.

patterns.why: A family of potential changes preserves the electric and magnetic fields.
Physically equivalent potentials form equivalence classes under allowed gauge changes.

nodes.name: Poynting's energy theorem
nodes.intuition: Field energy can stay in a region, flow across its boundary, or be transferred to charged matter. The equation is a local energy ledger with all three entries visible.
nodes.conditions: Classical Maxwell fields in vacuum with sources, SI units, and enough regularity for the differential identity. Material media require the appropriate constitutive and energy accounting assumptions.
nodes.example: In source-free space, integrating over a volume says its field energy decreases by the outgoing Poynting flux.

patterns.why: Storage plus outward transport equals the negative power transferred to matter.
Field energy density is quadratic in electric and magnetic amplitudes.

nodes.name: Lorentz boost along one axis
nodes.intuition: Observers in uniform relative motion mix space and time coordinates while preserving a spacetime quadratic form. A boost acts like a hyperbolic rotation rather than a Euclidean one.
nodes.conditions: Inertial frames in flat spacetime with relative velocity v along x, |v|<c, aligned transverse axes and coincident origins at t=t′=0. Transverse coordinates y,z are unchanged.
nodes.example: Writing β=tanh η gives γ=cosh η and γβ=sinh η, so collinear rapidities add.

patterns.why: A single spacetime event receives different space and time coordinates.
The indefinite spacetime quadratic form is preserved.

nodes.name: Minkowski spacetime interval
nodes.intuition: Different observers disagree about elapsed coordinate time and distance, but agree on their particular signed combination. Along a timelike path it measures the proper time recorded by an ideal clock.
nodes.conditions: Flat spacetime with the +−−− convention. The proper-time formula applies to timelike displacements; the interval is indefinite and is not a positive distance norm on all four-vectors.
nodes.example: A lightlike displacement satisfies ds²=0 even when the time and spatial displacement are nonzero.

patterns.why: The interval supplies spacetime geometry with causal rather than Euclidean distance structure.
Lorentz transformations leave ds² unchanged.

nodes.name: Relativistic energy–momentum relation
nodes.intuition: Energy and momentum are components of one spacetime object. Their invariant quadratic combination determines rest mass across inertial frames.
nodes.conditions: An on-shell isolated particle in special relativity, invariant rest mass m≥0, and the positive-energy branch for ordinary particles. Momentum is relativistic three-momentum.
nodes.example: At rest E=mc²; for a massless particle E=c|p|. For small |p|/(mc), E=mc²+|p|²/(2m)+higher terms.

patterns.why: The energy–momentum quadratic form equals the frame-invariant rest-mass term.
Expansion near zero momentum recovers the Newtonian kinetic-energy approximation.

nodes.name: Time-dependent Schrödinger equation
nodes.intuition: The Hamiltonian generates motion of a complex amplitude. Its spatial differential terms spread the amplitude while the potential changes the local phase evolution.
nodes.conditions: A nonrelativistic spinless particle, mass m>0, real scalar potential, and a self-adjoint realization of H with suitable boundary conditions. The differential equation is interpreted on its operator domain or in an appropriate weak sense.
nodes.example: An energy eigenstate φ evolves as ψ(t)=exp(−iEt/ħ)φ; its position probability density stays fixed.

patterns.why: Superpositions of solutions remain solutions for a prescribed Hamiltonian.
An eigenstate evolves by a complex exponential phase.

nodes.name: Unitary evolution generated by a Hamiltonian
nodes.intuition: A closed quantum system rotates amplitudes while preserving their inner products. The same generator governs short steps and arbitrarily long evolution.
nodes.conditions: A finite-dimensional time-independent Hermitian matrix H. For time-dependent noncommuting H(t), the simple exponential of an integral must be replaced by a time-ordered evolution.
nodes.example: If H=diag(E₁,E₂), each coordinate gains a phase exp(−itE_j/ħ) and its squared magnitude is unchanged.

patterns.why: Unitary motion preserves norms and pairwise inner products.
Time addition corresponds to multiplication of propagators.

nodes.name: Stationary Schrödinger eigenvalue problem
nodes.intuition: A stationary energy state changes only by an overall phase. Solving the spatial eigenvalue problem identifies these simple building blocks of time evolution.
nodes.conditions: Time-independent self-adjoint Hamiltonian and a normalizable eigenvector φ in its domain. Continuous spectrum may require generalized eigenfunctions and cannot always be represented by a discrete eigenbasis.
nodes.example: In a one-dimensional box of length L with Dirichlet walls, E_n=ħ²π²n²/(2mL²) for n≥1.

patterns.why: Spectral components evolve independently under a time-independent Hamiltonian.
Kinetic confinement energy scales as the inverse square of the box length.

nodes.name: Born rule for a projective measurement
nodes.intuition: Measurement probabilities are squared lengths of orthogonal components. Different outcomes partition the total probability through a resolution of the identity.
nodes.conditions: Normalized pure state ψ in a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space and mutually orthogonal projections P_a summing to the identity. This is the projective-measurement case; general POVMs use positive effects.
nodes.example: For ψ=(|0⟩+|1⟩)/√2, measurement in that orthonormal basis gives each result with probability one half.

patterns.why: Mutually orthogonal outcome subspaces have squared lengths that add.
Squared amplitudes specify outcome probabilities.

nodes.name: Expectation of a quantum observable
nodes.intuition: The expected measurement result is an ordinary weighted average once the observable's outcomes and their Born probabilities are identified. Operator notation packages that average independently of basis.
nodes.conditions: A normalized state ψ and Hermitian matrix A with spectral decomposition A=Σa aP_a in finite dimensions. The infinite-dimensional formula additionally needs the relevant domain and integrability conditions.
nodes.example: For A=diag(−1,1) and equal outcome probabilities, the expectation is zero even though zero is not a possible measurement result.

patterns.why: Eigenvalues are averaged with squared projection lengths as weights.
The inner-product expression does not depend on the chosen orthonormal basis.

nodes.name: Robertson uncertainty inequality
nodes.intuition: The spreads of two observables cannot both be arbitrarily small when their commutator has a nonzero expectation in the state. The obstruction comes from incompatible operator directions.
nodes.conditions: Hermitian matrices A,B and a normalized state ψ; ΔA²=⟨(A−⟨A⟩I)²⟩. For unbounded observables, require the state in suitable common product domains and finite variances.
nodes.example: For Pauli X,Y in a Z-up state, ΔX=ΔY=1 and |⟨[X,Y]⟩|/2=1, so equality holds.

patterns.why: Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the inner product of centered observable vectors.
The commutator extracts the antisymmetric part responsible for the lower bound.

nodes.name: Heisenberg equation of motion
nodes.intuition: The time dependence can be assigned to observables instead of states. Their commutator with the Hamiltonian plays the same organizing role as the classical Poisson bracket.
nodes.conditions: A differentiable observable family and unitary Schrödinger evolution in finite dimensions. A_H=U†AU and H_H=U†HU. Unbounded operator versions require domain control.
nodes.example: If A has no explicit time dependence and commutes with a fixed H, then A_H is constant.

patterns.why: The unitary change of picture transfers time dependence from states to observables.
Commutation with the Hamiltonian identifies constants of motion.

nodes.name: Ehrenfest equations for position and momentum
nodes.intuition: Quantum averages obey balance laws resembling classical motion. The force is averaged over the state, so nonlinear forces generally do not equal the force evaluated at the average position.
nodes.conditions: A nonrelativistic Hamiltonian p²/(2m)+V(q), a sufficiently regular evolving state with finite relevant moments, and boundary/domain conditions allowing the operator identities and integrations by parts.
nodes.example: For a quadratic potential, ∇V is affine, so the mean position follows the corresponding classical oscillator equation exactly.

patterns.why: The equation evolves expected position and momentum rather than an individual trajectory.
Affine forces commute with averaging, while nonlinear ones generally do not.

nodes.name: Schrödinger probability current
nodes.intuition: Probability moves locally instead of appearing or disappearing. A wavefunction's phase gradient carries its density through space.
nodes.conditions: A sufficiently smooth solution of the scalar Schrödinger equation with real potential and no vector potential. Conserving total probability also requires decay or boundary conditions eliminating net boundary loss.
nodes.example: For a plane wave C exp(ik·x−iωt), j=(ħk/m)|C|². Such a wave is a generalized state on all of space, not a normalizable wavepacket.

patterns.why: The local density change balances the divergence of probability flow.
An integral over a region changes only through its boundary flux.

nodes.name: Density matrix of a quantum state
nodes.intuition: A density matrix collects the predictions of a statistical mixture of pure states. Different mixtures can give the same matrix, so the matrix captures observable information rather than a unique preparation story.
nodes.conditions: A finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space, normalized vectors ψ_k and nonnegative weights p_k summing to one. Every positive-semidefinite trace-one matrix admits such a representation.
nodes.example: The qubit state I/2 is the equal mixture of either the two Z-basis states or the two X-basis states.

patterns.why: Pure-state projectors are combined by a convex weighted average.
The set of density matrices is convex, with pure-state projectors as extreme points.

nodes.name: Trace formula for mixed-state expectation
nodes.intuition: One trace simultaneously averages over both preparation uncertainty and measurement outcomes. It is linear in the state and in the observable.
nodes.conditions: A finite-dimensional density matrix ρ and Hermitian observable A. The result is real; for a POVM effect E_a, tr(ρE_a) is the outcome probability.
nodes.example: For the maximally mixed state I/d, every observable has expectation tr(A)/d, the arithmetic mean of its eigenvalues.

patterns.why: The trace computes the mixture-weighted average of pure-state expectations.
Expectations depend linearly on both the observable and the state.

nodes.name: Reduced state by partial trace
nodes.intuition: Discarding one subsystem means retaining exactly the predictions for all measurements on the other. Partial trace removes the inaccessible subsystem without choosing a particular measurement outcome.
nodes.conditions: Finite-dimensional tensor-product Hilbert space A⊗B and a joint density matrix. The equality for every operator X uniquely specifies ρ_A.
nodes.example: Either subsystem of the Bell state (|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2 has reduced state I/2, even though the joint state is pure.

patterns.why: Summing over a basis of the discarded subsystem aggregates its unresolved alternatives.
The reduced state is characterized by its pairing with every local observable.

nodes.name: Purity of a density matrix
nodes.intuition: Purity measures how concentrated the state's eigenvalue weights are. It is highest for a single pure component and lowest when every spectral direction has equal weight.
nodes.conditions: A density matrix on a d-dimensional Hilbert space. Equality at one holds exactly for rank-one states; equality at 1/d holds exactly for I/d.
nodes.example: For a qubit diagonal state diag(p,1−p), purity is p²+(1−p)².

patterns.why: Purity is the squared Euclidean norm of the spectral probability vector.
Uniform spectral weights minimize the sum of their squares at fixed total.

nodes.name: Bloch-ball representation of a qubit
nodes.intuition: A qubit state becomes a point inside a three-dimensional ball. Its direction records spin bias and its radius records purity.
nodes.conditions: A two-dimensional complex quantum state and the standard Pauli matrices. The eigenvalues are (1±|r|)/2; pure states lie on the unit sphere, while the center is maximally mixed.
nodes.example: The Z-up projector has r=(0,0,1); I/2 has r=0.

patterns.why: Positivity becomes the geometric condition that a vector lie inside the unit ball.
Identity and Pauli components form real coordinates for Hermitian two-by-two matrices.

nodes.name: Von Neumann entropy
nodes.intuition: Quantum entropy is the Shannon entropy of the state's eigenvalue weights. It describes uncertainty in the state itself, which differs from uncertainty for a particular measurement basis.
nodes.conditions: Finite-dimensional density matrix, natural logarithms, and 0 log 0=0 by continuity. Pure states have zero entropy, even though some of their measurements remain random.
nodes.example: S(I/d)=log d, while a rank-one projector has S=0.

patterns.why: Entropy measures the spread of the spectral probability distribution.
Unitary changes of basis preserve the eigenvalues and hence the entropy.

nodes.name: Schmidt decomposition of a bipartite pure state
nodes.intuition: A joint pure state can be expressed using matched orthogonal pairs. The number and weights of these paired terms reveal whether its components can be separated.
nodes.conditions: A normalized vector in a finite-dimensional bipartite tensor product. The u_j and v_j form orthonormal lists. A state is a product state exactly when its Schmidt rank is one.
nodes.example: The Bell state has two Schmidt coefficients 1/√2, so each reduced density matrix has eigenvalues 1/2,1/2.

patterns.why: A bipartite amplitude splits into orthogonal paired components.
Each side uses an orthonormal family, making the coefficients directly interpretable.

nodes.name: Kraus representation of a quantum channel
nodes.intuition: A quantum channel describes a physical transformation when some environmental information is ignored. Its matrix pieces account for alternative environmental records while preserving total probability.
nodes.conditions: A finite-dimensional linear map is a completely positive trace-preserving channel exactly when it admits this representation. The individual terms are not necessarily unitary, and a Kraus representation is not unique.
nodes.example: Dephasing in an orthonormal basis uses the basis projectors as Kraus operators, deleting coherence between different basis states.

patterns.why: The channel sums positive contributions indexed by Kraus operators.
The completeness identity ensures that trace and total probability are preserved.

nodes.name: Trace distance and optimal state discrimination
nodes.intuition: The distance between two quantum states measures how well one optimal measurement can tell them apart. Identical states force guessing, while orthogonal states can be distinguished perfectly.
nodes.conditions: Two finite-dimensional density matrices presented with equal prior probabilities, one copy available, and arbitrary two-outcome measurements. The trace norm is the sum of singular values.
nodes.example: For orthogonal pure states D=1 and success probability is one; for identical states D=0 and success is one half.

patterns.why: An operator norm becomes an operational distinguishability measure.
The formula optimizes the decision over all allowed two-outcome measurements.

nodes.name: Harmonic-oscillator ladder operators
nodes.intuition: Raising and lowering operators organize oscillator states into an algebraic ladder. The commutator fixes the spacing and the square-root coefficients that preserve normalization.
nodes.conditions: The one-dimensional quantum harmonic oscillator, ω>0, with operators on the standard common invariant domain of finite oscillator-state combinations. The commutator cannot hold for finite square matrices.
nodes.example: The normalized ground state obeys a|0⟩=0; applying a† creates successive excited states.

patterns.why: Higher oscillator states are constructed repeatedly from the ground state.
The canonical commutation relation determines the ladder algebra.

nodes.name: Quantum harmonic-oscillator spectrum
nodes.intuition: A quadratic potential produces equally spaced energy levels, with a positive ground-state energy. The state cannot have both perfectly fixed position and perfectly fixed momentum.
nodes.conditions: A one-dimensional nonrelativistic oscillator H=p²/(2m)+mω²q²/2 with m,ω>0 and the standard self-adjoint realization on L² of the real line.
nodes.example: Adjacent levels differ by ħω, while the ground state has energy ħω/2.

patterns.why: A quadratic Hamiltonian yields a solvable evenly spaced spectrum.
Applying a raising operator moves to the next energy level.

nodes.name: Quantum angular-momentum ladder
nodes.intuition: At fixed total angular momentum, a finite ladder shifts the component along a chosen axis. The coefficient vanishes at the top or bottom, closing the representation.
nodes.conditions: An irreducible unitary angular-momentum representation with j a nonnegative integer or half-integer, m=−j,…,j, J±=Jx±iJy, and normalized simultaneous eigenvectors of J² and Jz.
nodes.example: For j=1/2, raising the lower m=−1/2 state produces ħ times the upper state; raising again gives zero.

patterns.why: The total J² value is unchanged while Jz changes.
Raising and lowering generate the finite family of basis states.

nodes.name: Canonical thermal partition function
nodes.intuition: The partition function adds the statistical weights of all energy states. Once this single generating object is known, differentiating it extracts many equilibrium quantities.
nodes.conditions: A quantum canonical ensemble at T>0 with a fixed Hamiltonian whose exponential is trace class; eigenvalues are counted with multiplicity. The finite-state case is immediate; classical phase-space ensembles require their own measure normalization.
nodes.example: For two energy levels 0 and ε, Z=1+exp(−βε). Independent subsystems have a product partition function when their Hamiltonian energies add.

patterns.why: A weighted sum over energy states generates equilibrium moments through derivatives.
Boltzmann weights turn additive independent energies into multiplicative factors.

nodes.name: Energy and energy variance from log partition function
nodes.intuition: The slope of log Z gives mean energy, and its curvature gives energy fluctuations. One function therefore records both the typical value and the spread around it.
nodes.conditions: A canonical ensemble with a β-independent energy spectrum, finite relevant moments and differentiation justified under the sum or trace. β is inverse energy, equal to 1/(kBT).
nodes.example: For levels 0,ε with excited probability p, mean energy is εp and variance is ε²p(1−p).

patterns.why: The first logarithmic derivative returns an energy-weighted average.
Higher logarithmic derivatives generate connected energy cumulants with alternating signs.

nodes.name: Canonical heat capacity–fluctuation identity
nodes.intuition: How strongly energy responds to temperature is controlled by how much energy already fluctuates at equilibrium. Response and noise are two views of the same partition-function curvature.
nodes.conditions: A canonical ensemble at T>0 with fixed volume and particle number, temperature-independent microscopic energies, finite variance and justified differentiation. Other ensembles or temperature-dependent effective Hamiltonians need separate accounting.
nodes.example: A two-level system has C_V=ε²p(1−p)/(kBT²).

patterns.why: Equilibrium energy fluctuations determine a macroscopic response coefficient.
The nonnegative second derivative of log Z ensures nonnegative canonical heat capacity.

nodes.name: Canonical response as a covariance
nodes.intuition: A small field favors states with large B. Another quantity A changes according to how strongly it co-varies with B in the unperturbed weighting.
nodes.conditions: A finite classical state space, h-independent observables A,B, fixed β, and probabilities proportional to exp[−β(H₀−hB)]. The simple covariance formula is not the general noncommuting quantum response formula.
nodes.example: Setting A=B makes the susceptibility β Var(B), which is nonnegative.

patterns.why: Differentiating a normalized weighted average produces a covariance.
The external field h is conjugate to the observable B it biases.

nodes.name: Helmholtz free energy from the partition function
nodes.intuition: Free energy balances expected energy against the number of thermally available possibilities. Taking a logarithm converts independent partition-function factors into additive thermodynamic contributions.
nodes.conditions: Canonical equilibrium at positive temperature with fixed volume and particle number; U is mean energy and S is the Gibbs thermodynamic entropy. The same microscopic normalization must be used in Z and S.
nodes.example: For two noninteracting subsystems, Z_AB=Z_AZ_B and F_AB=F_A+F_B.

patterns.why: The logarithm converts a multiplicative partition function into additive free energy.
The equilibrium Gibbs distribution minimizes mean energy minus temperature times entropy.

nodes.name: Boltzmann entropy of a microcanonical shell
nodes.intuition: A macrostate can be realized by many microscopic configurations. Entropy measures the logarithmic size of that collection, making independent multiplicities additive.
nodes.conditions: A specified microcanonical shell with Ω equiprobable discrete microstates. Continuous phase-space versions need a prescribed cell size or reference measure; the shell convention matters.
nodes.example: N independent two-state spins with no energy preference have Ω=2^N and S=NkB log 2.

patterns.why: The microscopic multiplicity Ω counts compatible configurations.
Logarithms turn multiplication of independent state counts into addition of entropy.

nodes.name: Fundamental thermodynamic differential
nodes.intuition: Temperature, pressure and chemical potential are slopes of internal energy with respect to entropy, volume and particle number. The differential identifies which quantities are thermodynamically conjugate.
nodes.conditions: A differentiable equilibrium internal energy U(S,V,N) for a simple compressible single-component system, with the convention that p dV is work done by the system. Additional work modes require extra terms.
nodes.example: Holding V,N fixed gives T=(∂U/∂S)_{V,N}; holding S,N fixed gives p=−(∂U/∂V)_{S,N}.

patterns.why: The differential gives the first-order energy change from changes of state variables.
Intensive variables are derivatives paired with extensive variables.

nodes.name: A Maxwell relation from Helmholtz free energy
nodes.intuition: Two seemingly different responses agree because they are mixed derivatives of one state function. Thermodynamics inherits an exact symmetry from multivariable calculus.
nodes.conditions: A simple equilibrium system at fixed particle number with C² Helmholtz free energy F(T,V) in a single smooth phase. Derivatives at singular phase boundaries require separate treatment.
nodes.example: For an ideal gas p=NkBT/V, the relation gives (∂S/∂V)_T=NkB/V.

patterns.why: Equality of mixed partial derivatives connects two response coefficients.
The derivatives of F pair T with −S and V with −p.

nodes.name: Clapeyron coexistence slope
nodes.intuition: A phase boundary tilts because the phases differ in both entropy and volume. The slope balances those differences while their chemical potentials remain equal.
nodes.conditions: Two equilibrium phases of one substance along a differentiable first-order coexistence curve, with specific or molar entropy s and volume v using consistent normalization and Δv≠0. The latent heat is ℓ=TΔs.
nodes.example: If the higher-entropy phase also has larger volume, the coexistence pressure increases with temperature.

patterns.why: Equal chemical potentials relate temperature and pressure changes through entropy and volume.
The slope is a local first-order constraint on the coexistence curve.

nodes.name: Classical equipartition for a quadratic mode
nodes.intuition: Every independent unconstrained quadratic degree of freedom contributes the same average energy at classical equilibrium. The stiffness changes its fluctuation size rather than this mean energy contribution.
nodes.conditions: A classical canonical ensemble at T>0, a>0, x ranging over the real line, and the indicated separable quadratic contribution with convergent integrals. Quantum freezing, constraints and nonquadratic modes need other formulas.
nodes.example: Each Cartesian velocity component contributes kBT/2 to a classical ideal gas particle's mean kinetic energy.

patterns.why: The mean quadratic energy is computed under a Gaussian equilibrium density.
Quadratic energy makes each mode a Gaussian integral whose scale cancels in the mean energy.

nodes.name: Maxwell equilibrium velocity density
nodes.intuition: Thermal equilibrium gives a Gaussian distribution of velocity vectors. Directional symmetry and quadratic kinetic energy make the three Cartesian components independent with equal variance.
nodes.conditions: A nonrelativistic classical ideal gas in equilibrium at T>0, in its rest frame, with particle mass m>0. This is the vector density with respect to d³v, not the speed density, which has an additional 4πv² factor.
nodes.example: Each component has variance kBT/m and the root-mean-square speed is √(3kBT/m).

patterns.why: Thermal particle velocities fluctuate according to an equilibrium probability density.
The density depends only on |v| and is rotationally invariant.

nodes.name: Bose–Einstein and Fermi–Dirac occupations
nodes.intuition: The allowed occupancy of a quantum mode changes its average population. Bosons permit any nonnegative integer count, while a single fermionic mode permits only zero or one particle.
nodes.conditions: Noninteracting indistinguishable particles in grand-canonical equilibrium, β=1/(kBT)>0. Bosonic mode sums require μ<ε for the displayed finite mean; condensate limits must be treated separately. Mode degeneracies are counted explicitly.
nodes.example: For ε−μ≫kBT, both occupations approach exp[−β(ε−μ)], the dilute classical limit.

patterns.why: The difference arises from summing all nonnegative occupancies versus only zero and one.
Single-mode partition sums generate the mean occupation.

nodes.name: Planck blackbody spectral energy density
nodes.intuition: Blackbody radiation combines how many photon modes are available at a frequency with how much thermal energy each mode carries. The quantum occupation factor suppresses high-frequency energy.
nodes.conditions: Electromagnetic radiation in thermal equilibrium in a large three-dimensional vacuum cavity at T>0, both polarizations included, frequency ν in cycles per second. u_ν is energy per volume per unit frequency.
nodes.example: For hν≪kBT, the formula approaches the Rayleigh–Jeans density 8πkBTν²/c³.

patterns.why: A frequency-shell count supplies the electromagnetic density of states.
Frequency enters through a cubic prefactor and the dimensionless ratio hν/(kBT).

nodes.name: Ising spin Hamiltonian
nodes.intuition: A simple binary variable at each site interacts with its neighbors. Local preferences can collectively produce large-scale order, making this model a bridge between discrete structure and statistical physics.
nodes.conditions: A specified finite graph or lattice with each interacting pair counted once. J>0 favors alignment; h is a uniform field in energy units. Infinite-volume phase transitions require a thermodynamic limit and boundary conventions.
nodes.example: With two sites, h=0 and J>0, aligned states have energy −J and anti-aligned states energy +J.

patterns.why: A graph specifies pairwise couplings between binary variables.
At zero field the energy is invariant under flipping every spin.

nodes.name: Ising mean-field self-consistency
nodes.intuition: Replace each neighbor by its average spin and require the predicted average to agree with the one used in that replacement. Collective order becomes a nonlinear fixed-point equation.
nodes.conditions: Uniform ferromagnetic Ising model with coordination number z, β=1/(kBT), and the single-site mean-field approximation. This is not exact for a general finite-dimensional lattice; fluctuations and correlations are neglected.
nodes.example: At h=0 the zero-magnetization solution loses mean-field stability when βJz passes one, producing two symmetry-related nonzero branches.

patterns.why: The assumed average field must reproduce its own average magnetization.
Neighbor spins are replaced by one common mean, discarding their fluctuations.

nodes.name: Landau quartic free-energy model
nodes.intuition: A symmetric energy landscape changes shape as its quadratic coefficient crosses zero. One central minimum can split into two equivalent minima, providing a local model of spontaneous order.
nodes.conditions: An analytic phenomenological expansion in a small scalar order parameter with m↦−m symmetry at h=0, stabilized by b>0. Truncation and mean-field treatment are modeling assumptions, especially near fluctuation-dominated critical points.
nodes.example: At h=0, the minimizing m is zero when a≥0 and m=±√(−a/b) when a<0.

patterns.why: Zero field leaves the free energy unchanged under reversal of the order parameter.
Equilibrium candidates solve stationarity and must be checked for stability and global minimality.

nodes.name: Composition law for an autonomous flow
nodes.intuition: Running a time-independent system for two consecutive intervals is the same as running it for their sum. A whole family of trajectories therefore behaves like an action of time on states.
nodes.conditions: A uniquely solvable autonomous differential equation. The identities hold whenever the relevant solutions are defined; a complete flow defines an action for every real time, while a forward-only system gives a semigroup.
nodes.example: For ẋ=ax, Φ_t(x)=e^{at}x and the flow law is the exponential addition rule.

patterns.why: Successive evolution intervals compose into one longer evolution.
Complete time evolution is a group action of the additive real numbers.

nodes.name: Spectral criterion for linear asymptotic stability
nodes.intuition: Each spectral direction expands or contracts exponentially, with Jordan blocks adding polynomial factors. Strictly negative real parts make all these contributions decay.
nodes.conditions: A finite-dimensional constant real or complex matrix A and continuous-time evolution. Eigenvalues on the imaginary axis require a different test for mere stability and do not give asymptotic stability.
nodes.example: Eigenvalues −1±2i describe decaying oscillation; an eigenvalue +0.1 produces an unstable direction.

patterns.why: Jordan or spectral components separate the modes of linear evolution.
Real parts of eigenvalues set exponential growth or decay rates.

nodes.name: Strict Lyapunov criterion for asymptotic stability
nodes.intuition: A positive scalar quantity that always decreases acts as a certificate of local convergence. It can prove stability without solving the trajectories explicitly.
nodes.conditions: An equilibrium f(0)=0 of a locally Lipschitz autonomous vector field, and a C¹ positive-definite function V with strictly negative derivative on a neighborhood excluding the equilibrium. This gives local asymptotic stability; global claims need additional properness and global assumptions.
nodes.example: For ẋ=−x³, V=x²/2 gives V̇=−x⁴, proving asymptotic stability even though the linearization is zero.

patterns.why: Trajectories descend a scalar certificate, though they need not follow its gradient.
Monotone decrease near an isolated equilibrium supports convergence.

nodes.name: Continuous Lyapunov matrix equation
nodes.intuition: A stable linear system admits a quadratic energy that decreases at a prescribed positive rate. Integrating the future cost of a state constructs that energy matrix.
nodes.conditions: A real Hurwitz matrix A and symmetric Q≻0. The integral converges and is the unique symmetric P≻0 solving the equation. Conversely existence of such P,Q implies A is Hurwitz.
nodes.example: For A=−aI with a>0 and Q=I, P=I/(2a).

patterns.why: V=xᵀPx is a quadratic stability certificate.
P integrates the future weighted energy of the evolving state.

nodes.name: LaSalle's invariance principle
nodes.intuition: If a certificate only stops increasing, trajectories may settle into a whole invariant set rather than one point. The set where the decrease vanishes identifies the remaining possible long-term motion.
nodes.conditions: A locally Lipschitz autonomous system on a compact positively invariant set K, with C¹ V and V̇≤0 on K. M is the largest invariant subset of {x∈K:V̇(x)=0}; the conclusion holds for starting points in K.
nodes.example: For a damped oscillator, mechanical energy has derivative −c v². The only invariant motion with v=0 throughout is an equilibrium under the usual restoring-force assumptions.

patterns.why: The zero-dissipation set isolates motion that can persist without further energy loss.
Long-term trajectories approach the largest invariant subset of that set.

nodes.name: Hartman–Grobman local linearization
nodes.intuition: Near a hyperbolic equilibrium, a nonlinear flow has the same local topological orbit structure as its linear part. A continuous change of coordinates can reveal that similarity even when no smooth one exists.
nodes.conditions: A C¹ autonomous vector field near equilibrium x_*, with no Jacobian eigenvalue on the imaginary axis. The conjugacy is local and homeomorphic; the equation applies while the compared trajectories remain in the relevant neighborhoods.
nodes.example: A nonlinear planar saddle remains locally a saddle when its Jacobian has one negative and one positive real eigenvalue.

patterns.why: Hyperbolicity lets the linear part determine the local topological dynamics.
A homeomorphism relates nonlinear and linear trajectories.

nodes.name: Floquet decomposition for periodic linear systems
nodes.intuition: A periodic linear system separates into a repeated within-cycle motion and a steady exponential trend. Its stability can be read from what happens after one full period.
nodes.conditions: Continuous T-periodic matrix A, T>0, and an invertible fundamental matrix X. A complex matrix logarithm gives the stated T-periodic factorization; a real factorization may require period 2T. Stability is determined by the monodromy eigenvalues with the appropriate Jordan conditions.
nodes.example: For constant A, choose P=I and B=A. A multiplier of magnitude greater than one gives growth from cycle to cycle.

patterns.why: Periodic modulation and exponential growth are separated.
The monodromy matrix advances a solution by one period repeatedly.

nodes.name: Poincaré return map
nodes.intuition: Observe a continuous trajectory only when it crosses a chosen section. A closed orbit then becomes a fixed point of a lower-dimensional discrete map.
nodes.conditions: A smooth flow and a transverse local section near a periodic orbit, with a well-defined positive first-return time τ on the neighborhood considered. Tangencies or missing returns invalidate this local construction.
nodes.example: For an attracting planar limit cycle, nearby intersections with a transverse segment move toward its fixed intersection point.

patterns.why: Successive returns form a discrete iteration.
A transverse section removes the direction of motion along the orbit.

nodes.name: Derivative test for a one-dimensional map
nodes.intuition: An iteration multiplies a small error by its local slope on each step. Slopes below one in magnitude shrink errors, while larger slopes amplify them.
nodes.conditions: A C¹ real map near its fixed point. The unit-magnitude boundary is inconclusive by this test; higher-order terms or other arguments are needed there.
nodes.example: For f(x)=cos x at its fixed point, the derivative has magnitude below one, so nearby repeated cosine iteration converges.

patterns.why: The derivative approximates the next-step error multiplier.
The criterion describes stability of a point left unchanged by iteration.

nodes.name: Saddle–node bifurcation normal form
nodes.intuition: Two equilibria meet and disappear as a parameter crosses a threshold. In this orientation the positive branch attracts and the negative branch repels.
nodes.conditions: This scalar normal-form model has real parameter μ. It describes a generic local saddle–node after appropriate smooth reductions and nondegeneracy assumptions, not every possible equilibrium collision.
nodes.example: At μ<0 there is no real equilibrium; at μ=0 one nonhyperbolic equilibrium remains; at μ>0 there are two.

patterns.why: The roots of the vector field appear or disappear in pairs.
The branch separation grows like √μ near the threshold.

nodes.name: Supercritical pitchfork normal form
nodes.intuition: A symmetric central equilibrium gives way to two symmetric stable choices. The equation turns an unchanged symmetry of the rules into a choice of one asymmetric state.
nodes.conditions: The scalar model with reflection symmetry x↦−x; nonzero real branches exist for μ>0. Generic pitchfork behavior requires a symmetry or another structural constraint and the relevant nondegeneracy conditions.
nodes.example: For μ>0, zero is unstable and the two equilibria ±√μ are locally asymptotically stable.

patterns.why: Reflection symmetry forces nonzero equilibria to occur in opposite pairs.
The flow descends the quartic potential −μx²/2+x⁴/4.

nodes.name: Transcritical bifurcation normal form
nodes.intuition: Two equilibrium branches cross and exchange stability instead of disappearing. The same local state can change from attracting to repelling as the other branch takes over.
nodes.conditions: The scalar normal-form model with real x,μ. At μ=0 the branches coincide and linearization vanishes; the generic transcritical setting requires the structural conditions preserving the crossing branches.
nodes.example: The zero branch attracts for μ<0, while the x=μ branch attracts for μ>0.

patterns.why: Two persistent equilibrium branches meet and exchange stability.
The derivative μ−2x determines which branch attracts away from the crossing.

nodes.name: Supercritical Hopf normal form
nodes.intuition: An equilibrium begins to oscillate at a nonzero frequency as a stable cycle emerges around it. Polar coordinates separate amplitude selection from phase rotation.
nodes.conditions: z is complex, μ real, and ω≠0. This is a supercritical Hopf normal-form model; applying Hopf theory to another system needs a simple conjugate eigenvalue crossing, transversality and a nonzero first Lyapunov coefficient.
nodes.example: For μ>0 the attracting cycle has radius √μ and period 2π/|ω|; for μ<0 the origin attracts.

patterns.why: Amplitude and phase obey separate equations in polar coordinates.
Rotational symmetry gives equivalent phases around the cycle.

nodes.name: Logistic map
nodes.intuition: Repeated growth followed by crowding can produce equilibria, cycles and chaotic behavior depending on one parameter. A simple quadratic update need not have simple long-term motion.
nodes.conditions: The displayed parameter and state ranges keep the unit interval invariant. Discrete time is part of the model; it is not the exact time-one map of the logistic differential equation.
nodes.example: The nonzero fixed point 1−1/r exists for r>1 and attracts for 1<r<3.

patterns.why: A single nonlinear update is applied repeatedly.
The same map supports stable fixed points or more complicated attractors as its slope changes.

nodes.name: Lyapunov exponent along a one-dimensional orbit
nodes.intuition: Small perturbations multiply along an orbit. Taking logarithms turns their average exponential growth rate into an ordinary time average.
nodes.conditions: A C¹ one-dimensional map, orbit x_k=f^k(x₀), nonzero derivatives along it, and existence of the displayed limit. A positive exponent is a sensitivity indicator; by itself it does not supply every definition of chaos.
nodes.example: For the doubling map away from its coordinate discontinuity, each derivative is two and the exponent is log 2.

patterns.why: The exponent is the arithmetic mean of local logarithmic expansion rates in the long-time limit.
Logarithms convert products of derivatives into sums.

nodes.name: Van der Pol oscillator
nodes.intuition: The damping changes sign with amplitude: small oscillations gain energy while large ones lose it. This feedback can select a persistent oscillation instead of rest.
nodes.conditions: The standard dimensionless van der Pol model with μ>0. The scalar second-order equation is an autonomous planar system; statements about its limit cycle use the corresponding Liénard theory.
nodes.example: For mechanical energy E=(ẋ²+x²)/2, Ė=μ(1−x²)ẋ², showing gain at small |x| and loss at large |x|.

patterns.why: A modified energy balance reveals where the dynamics injects or removes energy.
A stable periodic cycle replaces simple convergence to the unstable origin.

nodes.name: Lotka–Volterra predator–prey equations
nodes.latex: \dot x=x(\alpha-\beta y),\qquad\dot y=y(\delta x-\gamma),\qquad I=\delta x-\gamma\log x+\beta y-\alpha\log y
nodes.intuition: Each population changes the other's growth rate, producing coupled feedback. In this idealized model a conserved quantity organizes closed trajectories in the positive quadrant.
nodes.conditions: Positive parameters α,β,γ,δ and positive populations x,y. The invariant I belongs to the basic autonomous model; harvesting, saturation, noise or parameter changes generally destroy it.
nodes.example: The coexistence equilibrium is x=γ/δ, y=α/β; differentiating I along the flow gives zero.

patterns.why: The explicit first integral remains constant along positive trajectories.
Each species' per-capita rate depends on the other species.

nodes.name: Lorenz system
nodes.intuition: Three coupled variables create feedback between growth, transfer and damping. For suitable parameters the system has irregular sensitive motion despite being deterministic.
nodes.conditions: The classical dimensionless Lorenz ODE with positive σ,ρ,β. Chaotic conclusions depend on parameter choices and a precise invariant-set analysis; the polynomial equations alone do not prove chaos.
nodes.example: Its divergence is −(σ+1+β), so phase-space volumes contract exponentially wherever the smooth flow is defined.
