patterns.why: Nonlinear cross terms couple the evolution of three state variables.
Constant negative divergence sets an exponential phase-volume contraction rate.

nodes.name: Bendixson divergence criterion
nodes.intuition: A closed trajectory cannot enclose a region whose flow expands or contracts area strictly everywhere. Boundary flux and interior divergence would contradict one another.
nodes.conditions: A C¹ planar vector field on a simply connected open region D, with divergence strictly of one sign throughout D. The criterion as stated does not apply in three dimensions or to regions with holes.
nodes.example: The linear sink ẋ=−x,ẏ=−y has divergence −2 and no periodic orbit.

patterns.why: A closed orbit has zero normal flow, which conflicts with strictly signed interior divergence.
The argument uses planar enclosed area and the topology of the region.

nodes.name: Poincaré–Bendixson theorem without equilibria
nodes.latex: \omega(x)\text{ compact, nonempty, with no equilibrium}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\omega(x)\text{ is a periodic orbit}
nodes.intuition: A bounded planar flow has strong restrictions on its long-term motion. If its limit set avoids every equilibrium, that set must be a closed orbit.
nodes.conditions: A C¹ autonomous vector field on an open subset of the plane, with a positive orbit contained in a compact subset of the domain. The stated conclusion assumes its omega-limit set contains no fixed point.
nodes.example: A compact forward trapping annulus with no equilibria contains a periodic orbit under the planar hypotheses.

patterns.why: The theorem classifies the omega-limit set approached by a trajectory.
Planar orbit geometry imposes restrictions unavailable in higher dimensions.

nodes.name: Invariant measure for a dynamical map
nodes.intuition: Individual states move while the overall distribution stays the same. Invariance is the bridge from following trajectories to computing averages over a state space.
nodes.conditions: A measurable transformation T of a probability space and measurable sets A. The integral identity holds for integrable f and characterizes measure preservation. T need not have a pointwise inverse.
nodes.example: A rotation of the circle preserves uniform angular measure even though most individual points move.

patterns.why: The probability assigned to sets is preserved under inverse images of the evolution.
Averages of observables are unchanged by composing with one evolution step.

nodes.name: Koopman operator on observables
nodes.intuition: Instead of moving points, move the functions used to observe them. This turns even nonlinear state evolution into a linear action on a typically infinite-dimensional space of observables.
nodes.conditions: A measurable measure-preserving T on a probability space, acting on L² observables. U_T is an isometry; it is unitary when T is invertible modulo null sets. Finite coordinate observables usually do not form a closed invariant subspace.
nodes.example: For uniform circle measure and T(x)=2x mod 1, the observable exp(2πikx) is sent to exp(2πi(2k)x), creating new frequencies.

patterns.why: Composition by a fixed map is linear in the observable even when the state map is nonlinear.
Dynamics can be viewed through transported observables rather than transported states.

nodes.name: Birkhoff pointwise ergodic theorem
nodes.intuition: A long time average keeps the information that the dynamics never mixes away. If the only invariant information is trivial, that time average becomes the same space average for almost every starting state.
nodes.conditions: A measure-preserving transformation of a probability space, f∈L¹, and invariant sigma-algebra I. If T is ergodic, the limit equals ∫f dμ almost everywhere. Exceptional starting points can exist.
nodes.example: For an indicator observable, the average is the fraction of visits to a set; in an ergodic system its limit is that set's probability for almost every start.

patterns.why: The theorem converts long trajectory averages into conditional averages over invariant information.
Pointwise almost-everywhere convergence is obtained despite dependence between successive observations.

nodes.name: Von Neumann mean ergodic theorem
nodes.intuition: Repeated averaging removes the changing parts of an observable and retains its invariant component. The limiting average is an orthogonal projection, giving a geometric meaning to long-term averaging.
nodes.conditions: A unitary operator U on a Hilbert space and any vector f. The fixed subspace is closed and P is its orthogonal projection. This is norm convergence, not automatically pointwise convergence of a represented function.
nodes.example: For a planar rotation with angle not a multiple of 2π, averaging successive rotated vectors converges to zero because the only fixed vector is zero.

patterns.why: Cesàro averages of successive transforms isolate the unchanging component.
The limit is the orthogonal projection onto the invariant subspace.

nodes.name: Poincaré recurrence theorem
nodes.intuition: In a finite measure-preserving system, almost every state in a region returns to that region infinitely often. The system cannot permanently send a positive fraction of finite volume into endlessly disjoint new regions.
nodes.conditions: A measure-preserving transformation on a finite measure space and a measurable set A. The theorem gives almost-everywhere recurrence, not a uniform return time, an exact return to the same point, or convergence.
nodes.example: A rotation of the circle repeatedly returns almost every point in an arc to that arc; the theorem itself does not estimate the waiting time.

patterns.why: Infinitely many disjoint positive-measure wandering copies cannot fit in finite total measure.
Preservation of measure forces repeated returns.

nodes.name: Topological conjugacy of discrete systems
nodes.latex: h\circ f=g\circ h,\qquad h\text{ a homeomorphism}
nodes.intuition: Two systems can display the same orbit structure in different coordinates. A conjugacy translates every iterate consistently rather than matching only a few trajectories.
nodes.conditions: Continuous self-maps f:X→X and g:Y→Y of topological spaces, related by a homeomorphism h:X→Y. Smoothness, metric distances and derivative growth rates need not be preserved by a mere topological conjugacy.
nodes.example: For f(x)=2x, g(y)=8y and h(x)=x³ on the real line, h(f(x))=g(h(x)).

patterns.why: The homeomorphism relabels states while preserving their evolution.
The commuting relation persists under every number of iterations.

nodes.name: Doubling map on the circle
nodes.intuition: Each step discards the first binary digit and shifts the remaining digits forward. One elementary operation connects expanding dynamics, symbolic sequences and information loss.
nodes.conditions: The circle R/Z with uniform probability measure. Binary expansions need a convention at dyadic rationals, a null set. The map is measure preserving and two-to-one, not invertible.
nodes.example: A point is fixed by T^n exactly when (2^n−1)x is an integer modulo one, giving 2^n−1 distinct fixed points.

patterns.why: Iterating the map repeatedly shifts binary digits.
One leading binary digit is lost from the current coordinate at each step.

nodes.name: Arnold's cat map
nodes.intuition: A square torus can stretch in one direction and contract in another while preserving total area. Wrapping the stretched image back onto the torus keeps the motion in a compact space.
nodes.conditions: The map on R²/Z² defined by the indicated integer determinant-one matrix. It is an invertible hyperbolic toral automorphism preserving normalized area; the torus identification is essential.
nodes.example: The eigenvalues multiply to one, with one above one and the other below one, giving reciprocal expansion and contraction.

patterns.why: Stable and unstable eigendirections split the local linear motion.
Determinant one preserves area even as shapes are strongly stretched.

nodes.name: Expected payoff of mixed strategies
nodes.intuition: Random strategies average the payoffs of pure action pairs. The average is linear in either player's probabilities when the other player's strategy is fixed.
nodes.conditions: A finite two-player normal-form game with payoff matrix A for player one, and independently randomized mixed strategies p,q on their probability simplices.
nodes.example: For matching pennies with A=[[1,−1],[−1,1]], uniform p and q give expected payoff zero.

patterns.why: The payoff is a weighted average over action pairs.
Expected payoff is affine in each player's own mixed strategy.

nodes.name: Best-response correspondence
nodes.intuition: A player chooses the most favorable strategy against the others' current choices. The answer can be a whole set when several actions tie.
nodes.conditions: A finite normal-form game and independent mixed strategies. Payoff is affine in one's own strategy, so all best mixed responses are supported on payoff-maximizing pure actions.
nodes.example: Against a fixed opponent mixture, if two pure actions tie for the highest payoff, every mixture between them is also a best response.

patterns.why: The player solves a linear maximization over a simplex.
Convex combinations of tied maximizing pure actions remain optimal.

nodes.name: Nash equilibrium
nodes.latex: u_i(\sigma_i^*,\sigma_{-i}^*)\ge u_i(\tau_i,\sigma_{-i}^*)\quad\text{for every player }i\text{ and deviation }\tau_i
nodes.intuition: Every strategy is a best response to the others. No single player can improve by changing alone, although a coordinated change might help several players.
nodes.conditions: A specified finite normal-form game, mixed strategies independently randomized, and expected utility comparison. Nash equilibrium is a mutual best-response condition, not a guarantee of fairness, efficiency or convergence of learning.
nodes.example: Uniform randomization is a Nash equilibrium in matching pennies; neither player can gain by unilaterally biasing their coin against a uniform opponent.

patterns.why: Each player's chosen strategy belongs to the response set generated by the other choices.
Each player is individually optimal with opponents held fixed.

nodes.name: Existence of mixed Nash equilibrium
nodes.latex: \text{Every finite normal-form game has some }\sigma^*\in\prod_i\Delta(A_i)\text{ that is a Nash equilibrium.}
nodes.intuition: Allowing randomized strategies fills discrete action sets into compact convex simplices. A fixed-point argument then guarantees at least one mutually consistent strategy profile.
nodes.conditions: Finitely many players, finite nonempty action sets, and real payoff values. The theorem concerns mixed equilibria; a pure equilibrium need not exist and the theorem gives no general efficient algorithm.
nodes.example: Rock–paper–scissors has no pure equilibrium, but its symmetric uniform mixture is an equilibrium.

patterns.why: A suitable continuous adjustment map on the strategy product has a fixed point.
Probability simplices provide compact convex strategy spaces.

nodes.name: Support indifference at a mixed equilibrium
nodes.intuition: A player randomizes only among actions that are equally good against the opponents. An action receiving positive weight could otherwise be replaced by a better one.
nodes.conditions: A mixed Nash equilibrium of a finite game. v_i is player i's equilibrium payoff. Equalities on the proposed support are necessary but must be accompanied by inequalities for excluded actions and valid probabilities.
nodes.example: In a two-by-two game with both actions used, an opponent's mixing probability can be found by equating the two expected pure-action payoffs, then checking all inequalities.

patterns.why: Positive probability is assigned only to payoff-maximizing actions.
The payoff level acts like the multiplier for the probability-sum constraint.

nodes.name: Correlated equilibrium inequalities
nodes.intuition: A shared recommendation device can coordinate strategies. After learning their own recommendation, each player prefers to follow it rather than switch to another action.
nodes.conditions: A probability distribution μ over joint actions of a finite game. The displayed unconditional inequalities encode incentive constraints for each recommendation, including those of zero probability without requiring division.
nodes.example: A traffic-light recommendation can correlate which of two players proceeds, creating coordinated outcomes that independent randomization cannot encode in the same way.

patterns.why: A joint distribution permits dependence between players' recommendations.
The obedience inequalities are linear constraints on μ.

nodes.name: Coarse correlated equilibrium
nodes.intuition: Before seeing any recommendation, no player wants to commit to one fixed alternative action. This is a weaker obedience requirement than checking deviations after each recommendation is revealed.
nodes.conditions: A joint action distribution in a finite game; deviations are fixed actions selected before observing a recommendation. Random fixed deviations add no extra constraints by payoff linearity.
nodes.example: Empirical joint play from players whose average external regret vanishes approaches the coarse-correlated equilibrium set in the finite-game setting.

patterns.why: Incentive comparisons are expectations over the joint play distribution.
The allowable distributions form a convex polytope defined by linear inequalities.

nodes.name: Additive epsilon Nash equilibrium
nodes.intuition: An approximate equilibrium allows only small unilateral improvements. The tolerance quantifies how far the profile is from exact mutual optimality.
nodes.conditions: A finite game, ε≥0 and additive payoff units explicitly fixed. Rescaling payoffs rescales ε, so comparisons normally use a common normalization such as payoffs in [0,1].
nodes.example: An exact Nash equilibrium is the ε=0 case. If the best unilateral gain is 0.02 in normalized payoffs, the profile is a 0.02 equilibrium.

patterns.why: The worst profitable unilateral deviation measures the approximation error.
An additive error tolerance depends on the utility scale.

nodes.name: Exact potential game
nodes.intuition: Every player's unilateral improvement changes one shared scalar by exactly the same amount. Individual incentives can therefore be tracked through a common landscape even when payoffs differ.
nodes.conditions: A finite normal-form utility game and a real function Φ satisfying the displayed identity for every unilateral action change. Cost games use the same identity with costs and descent. This is stronger than an ordinal potential.
nodes.example: Any global maximizer of an exact utility potential is a pure Nash equilibrium; any strict better-response path terminates because Φ increases over a finite set.

patterns.why: Unilateral better responses ascend a common scalar function.
Unilateral utility differences accumulate into a path-independent potential difference.

nodes.name: Rosenthal potential for congestion games
nodes.intuition: For each resource, add the cost of the first user, then the second, and so on up to current usage. This accumulated quantity changes by exactly a switching player's change in cost.
nodes.conditions: A finite unweighted congestion game, with each player selecting an allowed subset of resources and paying the sum of c_e(n_e) on used resources. The formula is an exact cost potential; weighted variants need separate conditions.
nodes.example: If one additional player joins a resource currently used by k players, its potential contribution rises by c_e(k+1), exactly the joining player's new resource cost.

patterns.why: The potential sums successive marginal congestion costs.
Strict cost-improving moves descend a finite potential landscape.

nodes.name: Wardrop equilibrium in nonatomic routing
nodes.intuition: All routes actually used by a population have minimal travel cost for that origin and destination. An infinitesimal traveler cannot improve by changing route alone.
nodes.conditions: A nonatomic routing model with fixed demands and path costs determined by aggregate edge flows. The comparison is among paths for the same origin–destination pair; a single infinitesimal user does not alter aggregate costs.
nodes.example: If two parallel roads both carry positive flow for one demand pair, their equilibrium travel times are equal.

patterns.why: Each infinitesimal traveler chooses a minimum-cost route given aggregate flow.
The resulting flow must reproduce the route costs supporting those choices.

nodes.name: Beckmann potential for nonatomic routing
nodes.intuition: Integrate each edge's travel cost over the amount of flow assigned to it. Minimizing the resulting potential balances route costs at a Wardrop equilibrium.
nodes.conditions: A finite network with fixed nonatomic demands, feasible flow polytope F, and continuous nondecreasing separable edge costs. Potential minimizers are Wardrop equilibria. This potential differs from total travel cost Σf_ec_e(f_e).
nodes.example: For c_e(z)=a_ez+b_e, the edge potential is a_ef_e²/2+b_ef_e.

patterns.why: The potential integrates marginal route-use costs.
Nondecreasing edge costs make the separable potential convex.

nodes.name: Price of anarchy for cost games
nodes.intuition: The ratio compares the worst allowed equilibrium with the best coordinated feasible outcome. It measures a possible inefficiency of decentralized incentives under a specified equilibrium concept.
nodes.conditions: A nonnegative aggregate cost C, a chosen equilibrium set E and feasible set F, with a positive finite optimum denominator and a nonempty equilibrium set. Bounds depend on the game class and solution concept.
nodes.example: A price of anarchy of 4/3 means that every equilibrium in the specified class costs at most one third more than the coordinated optimum.

patterns.why: Equilibrium cost is compared with a global feasible optimum.
A dimensionless ratio measures inefficiency independently of a common positive cost scale.

nodes.name: Smoothness bound on equilibrium cost
nodes.intuition: Bound the total cost of everyone separately switching to their part of an optimal outcome. Combining that bound with equilibrium incentives yields an aggregate efficiency guarantee.
nodes.conditions: A finite cost game with C=Σ_i c_i≥0, λ≥0, μ<1, and the displayed smoothness inequality for every relevant pair a,a*. The bound holds for pure, mixed, correlated and coarse correlated equilibria when costs and comparison are interpreted in expectation.
nodes.example: A (λ,μ)=(1,1/4) smoothness proof gives an equilibrium cost factor at most 4/3.

patterns.why: Summing individual deviation inequalities bounds the aggregate cost.
A comparison with an optimal profile produces a robust approximation factor.

nodes.name: Second-price auction payment
nodes.latex: i^*\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_i b_i,\qquad p_{i^*}=\max_{j\ne i^*}b_j,\qquad p_j=0\ (j\ne i^*)
nodes.intuition: The highest bidder wins but pays the strongest competing bid. The payment threshold is independent of the winner's own bid above that threshold, making truthful bidding weakly dominant in the standard model.
nodes.conditions: One indivisible item, at least two bidders with nonnegative private values and bids, quasilinear utility, no participation costs or externalities, and a fixed tie-breaking rule. The stated incentive conclusion depends on these assumptions.
nodes.example: With bids 10,7,4, the winning bidder pays 7. A bidder values the item relative to this threshold rather than setting their own winning price.

patterns.why: The allocation selects the maximal reported value.
The highest competing bid acts as the threshold price for winning.

nodes.name: Vickrey–Clarke–Groves externality payment
nodes.intuition: Choose the outcome with the largest reported total value and charge each participant for the loss they impose on the others. This aligns the participant's utility comparison with the social value comparison.
nodes.conditions: Finite feasible outcomes or attained optima, quasilinear utilities, independent private valuation reports and the standard pivot-payment setup. Truthfulness does not by itself guarantee budget balance or affordability.
nodes.example: For one item, the winning bidder's externality on the others is the next-highest bid, recovering the second-price auction.

patterns.why: The allocation maximizes total reported value.
Payments price the effect of one participant on other participants' attainable welfare.

nodes.name: Myerson's single-parameter payment identity
nodes.intuition: A monotone allocation rule determines its truthful payment schedule. The integral is the utility retained by the participant, leaving the remainder as payment.
nodes.conditions: A single-parameter quasilinear environment, opponents' reports fixed, nondecreasing allocation x(v) on v≥0, and zero payment at type zero. For randomized mechanisms x and p are expected allocation and payment; the characterization is truthfulness in expectation.
nodes.example: For threshold allocation x(v)=1 when v≥τ and zero otherwise, the winner pays τ.

patterns.why: Integrating allocation over types determines information rent.
The value derivative of truthful utility equals the allocated quantity.

nodes.name: Shapley value
nodes.intuition: Average a participant's added value over every possible order in which a coalition could form. This credits contributions that depend on who was already present.
nodes.conditions: A finite transferable-utility cooperative game v on all coalitions, with v(∅)=0 and n players. The interpretation assumes that the coalition worth function has been meaningfully specified.
nodes.example: In a two-player game, each player's value is the average of their standalone contribution and their contribution when joining the other player.

patterns.why: The allocation is an average marginal contribution over uniformly random arrival orders.
Factorial weights count permutations with exactly a given predecessor set.

nodes.name: Core of a transferable-utility game
nodes.latex: \mathcal C(v)=\left\{x:\sum_{i\in N}x_i=v(N),\quad\sum_{i\in S}x_i\ge v(S)\ \forall S\subseteq N\right\}
nodes.intuition: An allocation belongs to the core when it distributes the grand coalition's worth and leaves no subgroup able to secure more on its own. Coalition stability imposes a family of linear inequalities.
nodes.conditions: A finite transferable-utility game with v(∅)=0. The core can be empty; the inequalities express the assumed coalition-blocking model and unrestricted transfer of utility within a coalition.
nodes.example: If two players create value 10 together and can each earn 3 alone, core allocations satisfy x₁+x₂=10 and x₁,x₂≥3.

patterns.why: The core is an intersection of linear halfspaces with an efficiency hyperplane.
The full coalition's worth is exactly distributed among participants.

nodes.name: Nash bargaining solution
nodes.intuition: The solution balances proportional gains above a disagreement outcome. Taking logarithms turns the product of positive gains into a sum with stronger marginal weight on smaller gains.
nodes.conditions: A compact convex feasible utility set, a specified disagreement vector d, and a strictly feasible point giving every participant a positive gain. The standard axiomatic solution uses positive affine utility invariance and other bargaining axioms.
nodes.example: With two players dividing one unit and disagreement at zero, maximizing x(1−x) selects an equal split.

patterns.why: The selected feasible point maximizes the product of gains.
For positive gains, maximizing their product is equivalent to maximizing the sum of their logarithms.

nodes.name: Replicator equation
nodes.intuition: Strategies grow when their payoff exceeds the population's average payoff and shrink when it falls below average. Subtracting the mean keeps the population fractions normalized.
nodes.conditions: A finite symmetric population game with payoff matrix A and a population state in the probability simplex. This is the standard continuous-time payoff-difference convention; some models rescale time by a positive mean fitness.
nodes.example: Summing the right-hand sides gives zero, so total population share stays one and a zero-frequency strategy remains absent without mutation.

patterns.why: Each strategy's growth is measured relative to the current weighted average payoff.
Subtracting the common mean conserves the sum of population shares.

nodes.name: Evolutionarily stable strategy condition
nodes.latex: x^{\mathsf T}Ax\ge y^{\mathsf T}Ax,\quad\text{and if equality holds, }x^{\mathsf T}Ay>y^{\mathsf T}Ay\quad\forall y\ne x
nodes.intuition: A resident strategy resists a sufficiently small mutant invasion. If a mutant ties against the resident population, the second comparison checks what happens when mutants meet one another.
nodes.conditions: A finite symmetric two-player game with bilinear payoff xᵀAy and mixed strategies x,y. The displayed two-part condition is equivalent to the standard small-invasion ESS definition; ESS is stronger than symmetric Nash equilibrium.
nodes.example: A strict symmetric Nash equilibrium is evolutionarily stable because every distinct mutant already loses in the first comparison.

patterns.why: The small-mutant-fraction comparison is resolved by its leading payoff terms.
The resident strategy must be a symmetric best response to itself before invasion resistance can hold.

nodes.name: Turing-machine transition rule
nodes.intuition: A finite local rule updates a control state, one tape symbol, and the head position. Iterating this small rule over an unbounded tape models general symbolic computation.
nodes.conditions: A deterministic single-tape Turing-machine convention with finite state set Q, finite tape alphabet Γ, initial state and halting conventions specified separately. Partial transitions or a stay-put move give equivalent computability models.
nodes.example: A transition can replace a 0 by a 1, move one cell right and enter a new state; an unbounded sequence of such steps is a program execution.

patterns.why: Global computation is repeated application of a finite transition rule.
Successive local updates compose into a transformation of complete configurations.

nodes.name: Universal simulation
nodes.intuition: A program can be treated as input data for another program. One fixed interpreter can therefore simulate every machine described in the chosen effective encoding.
nodes.conditions: A standard effective encoding of Turing machines and a universal partial computable simulator U. Equality includes matching divergence when M does not halt; it does not mean simulation has zero time or memory overhead.
nodes.example: The same universal machine can simulate an addition program or a theorem-search program by receiving a different encoded machine.

patterns.why: A fixed interpreter composes with an encoded program and its input.
Programs and ordinary data share an effective symbolic representation.

nodes.name: Undecidability of the halting problem
nodes.intuition: No total algorithm can correctly predict termination for every program and input. A supposed predictor can be used to build a program whose behavior contradicts its prediction about itself.
nodes.conditions: Unrestricted Turing-computable programs with unbounded possible runtime. The result does not prohibit deciding termination for particular programs or restricted programming languages.
nodes.example: A hypothetical program that loops exactly when a predictor says that it will halt creates a contradiction when supplied its own code.

patterns.why: No total algorithm can extract correct termination information from every unrestricted program description.
Self-reference feeds an encoded program back into a universal computation.

nodes.name: Computable many-one reduction
nodes.latex: A\le_mB\iff\exists\text{ total computable }f:\ x\in A\Longleftrightarrow f(x)\in B
nodes.intuition: Translate every instance of one decision problem into an equivalent instance of another. A solver for the target would then solve the source after this translation.
nodes.conditions: Decision languages over finite effective encodings and a total computable transformation f. The equivalence must hold on every source input, not merely on yes-instances or typical examples.
nodes.example: If the halting problem reduces to B, then B cannot have a total decider, because composing that decider with the reduction would decide halting.

patterns.why: A reduction followed by a target solver forms a source solver.
Instances are re-encoded while preserving their yes/no answer.

nodes.name: Rice's semantic undecidability theorem
nodes.intuition: Any nontrivial yes/no property of what a general program computes is undecidable uniformly from its code. The property must depend on its computed function, not merely on its written syntax.
nodes.conditions: An acceptable effective enumeration of partial computable functions and a nonempty proper extensional class A. Equivalent formulations concern nontrivial properties of recognized languages. Particular inputs, restricted program classes and syntactic properties require separate analysis.
nodes.example: Whether a program computes a function defined on every input is a semantic property and is undecidable for arbitrary programs.

patterns.why: Programs are identified by the partial function they compute, abstracting away syntactic details.
Reductions embed an undecidable computation into the semantic behavior under examination.

nodes.name: Kleene's recursion theorem
nodes.intuition: Every effective transformation of program descriptions has a program whose behavior already matches its transformed version. The fixed point is in meaning, not necessarily in the literal code number.
nodes.conditions: An acceptable numbering of partial computable functions and a total computable map f on program indices. Equality is equality of computed partial functions, including their divergence sets; e=f(e) is not required.
nodes.example: A program can obtain an effective description of itself for use inside its own computation, which underlies formal self-reproducing constructions.

patterns.why: Program behavior is unchanged by a specified computable transformation of its description.
A program can refer to an encoded version of its own behavior.

nodes.name: Polynomial-time class P
nodes.intuition: A decision problem is in P when one deterministic algorithm solves every input within a polynomial worst-case time bound. The exponent may depend on the problem but not on the input size.
nodes.conditions: A fixed standard deterministic Turing-machine model and finite encodings; asymptotic time bounds absorb constant factors. Membership is an asymptotic classification and does not by itself ensure a practical small runtime.
nodes.example: Graph reachability is in P because a systematic graph search decides it in time polynomial in the input encoding length.

patterns.why: Runtime grows at most as a fixed power of input length.
Polynomial-time procedures remain polynomial-time under composition with polynomial-size outputs.

nodes.name: NP as polynomially verifiable witnesses
nodes.latex: x\in L\iff\exists y,\ |y|\le p(|x|),\ V(x,y)=1,\qquad V\text{ runs in polynomial time}
nodes.intuition: A yes-answer can be supported by a short witness that is efficiently checked. Finding such a witness is a separate task from checking one that is already supplied.
nodes.conditions: A decision language L, a polynomial witness-length bound p, and a deterministic polynomial-time verifier V. No-instances must have no accepting witness; the definition is worst-case over all inputs.
nodes.example: A satisfying truth assignment is a polynomial-size witness for a Boolean formula's satisfiability and can be checked by evaluating the formula.

patterns.why: A solution claim splits into a proposed witness and an independent checking step.
Existential search ranges over finitely many polynomial-length certificates.

nodes.name: Polynomial-time many-one reduction
nodes.latex: A\le_pB\iff\exists f\in\mathbf{FP}:\ x\in A\Longleftrightarrow f(x)\in B
nodes.intuition: An efficient translator preserves yes/no answers without hiding an expensive computation in the translation. It lets complexity upper bounds and hardness statements move between problems.
nodes.conditions: A deterministic total polynomial-time transformation f between finite input encodings; FP denotes polynomial-time computable functions. Its output length is therefore polynomially bounded by the input length.
nodes.example: If A≤pB and B∈P, then A∈P by running the translator and then B's solver.

patterns.why: Polynomial-time translation and solution compose to a polynomial-time solution.
The translation must preserve polynomial resource bounds.

nodes.name: Cook–Levin theorem
nodes.intuition: A polynomially bounded accepting computation can be encoded as a Boolean formula with locally checkable consistency constraints. Satisfiability becomes a common language for all NP verification problems.
nodes.conditions: Boolean satisfiability under standard finite formula encodings and polynomial-time many-one reductions. NP completeness means both membership in NP and the displayed reduction property; it is not a proof that SAT lacks a polynomial algorithm.
nodes.example: A computation tableau uses variables for tape symbols, machine states and head locations, with clauses checking valid neighboring time steps.

patterns.why: A complete computation is constrained by small local consistency conditions.
Machine execution is translated into logical satisfiability.

nodes.name: Deterministic time hierarchy
nodes.intuition: Sufficiently more computation time permits solving strictly more decision problems. A diagonal simulation separates the larger time budget from all machines constrained by the smaller one.
nodes.conditions: Standard multitape deterministic Turing machines and suitable time-constructible t,T≥n, with the displayed strict asymptotic gap. The logarithmic factor accounts for universal-simulation overhead in this version.
nodes.example: The theorem separates deterministic quadratic time from cubic time under these machine-model conventions.

patterns.why: A sufficiently larger asymptotic time budget changes computational power.
A universal simulator can disagree with each smaller-budget candidate on a designated input.

nodes.name: Polynomial-space class PSPACE
nodes.intuition: A computation can reuse memory even when it takes many steps. Polynomial space allows exhaustive exploration as long as the program stores only a polynomial amount at once.
nodes.conditions: Standard deterministic work-space complexity with a read-only input tape and finite decision languages. The containments do not assert that any displayed neighboring pair is unequal.
nodes.example: A polynomial-size search witness can be enumerated and checked using polynomial memory, even when there are exponentially many candidate witnesses.

patterns.why: Depth-first exploration reuses storage between branches.
The resource bound concerns memory cells rather than elapsed steps.

nodes.name: Configuration bound for space-limited computation
nodes.intuition: A machine with limited memory has only finitely many distinct instantaneous states. A deterministic halting computation cannot revisit one, or it would repeat forever.
nodes.conditions: A fixed finite-alphabet machine using O(s(n)) work space and a read-only input of length n, with s≥log n; constants absorb finite control and head positions. This counts configurations for a fixed input, not all possible programs.
nodes.example: A deterministic decider using polynomial space can be simulated within exponential time because a longer nonhalting repeated configuration would create a loop.

patterns.why: Tape contents and head positions bound the number of configurations.
A repeated deterministic configuration repeats every later transition.

nodes.name: Savitch's space simulation theorem
nodes.intuition: A nondeterministic path through configurations can be searched by recursively guessing and testing a midpoint. Time may grow enormously, but the same workspace is reused across the alternatives.
nodes.conditions: A standard read-only-input Turing-machine model and space-constructible s(n)≥log n. The simulation trades nondeterministic space for deterministic squared space, not for comparable deterministic time.
nodes.example: Reachability within at most 2^k steps can be checked by trying every possible midpoint and recursively checking two paths of length at most 2^(k−1).

patterns.why: Path existence splits into two shorter reachability questions around a midpoint.
Sequential reuse of workspace avoids keeping every search branch in memory.

nodes.name: Bounded-error probabilistic polynomial time
nodes.intuition: An algorithm may use random bits and occasionally be wrong, but it must have a uniform correctness guarantee for every input. Repetition can reduce the error without changing the polynomial-time class.
nodes.conditions: Worst-case polynomial running time, independent unbiased random bits, and a two-sided error bound on each input. Any fixed success threshold strictly above one half gives the same class by amplification.
nodes.example: A one-third error bound can be reduced exponentially by independent repeated runs and majority voting.

patterns.why: The algorithm samples internal random bits while the input remains arbitrary.
Aggregating independent outputs improves the reliability of the decision.

nodes.name: Majority-vote error amplification
nodes.latex: \Pr(\text{majority incorrect})\le e^{-r/18}\quad\text{if each independent run succeeds with probability at least }2/3
nodes.intuition: Several independent noisy decisions can be combined into a much more reliable decision. The mean fraction of successes concentrates above the majority threshold.
nodes.conditions: An odd number r of independent runs on the same fixed input, each with success probability at least 2/3. Correlated errors may defeat the bound; the guarantee is for majority voting with binary correctness indicators.
nodes.example: Taking r proportional to log(1/δ) makes the error at most δ while multiplying runtime by only that repetition count.

patterns.why: The majority threshold tests whether the mean correctness indicator exceeds one half.
Independent concentration makes error shrink exponentially in repetitions.

nodes.name: One-sided randomized polynomial time
nodes.intuition: The algorithm can miss a yes-answer but never invent one. Repeating and accepting if any run accepts amplifies detection while preserving that one-sided guarantee.
nodes.conditions: A randomized polynomial-time algorithm for a language L with the displayed per-input bounds. This convention defines RP; reversing which side is error-free defines coRP.
nodes.example: After r independent runs, a yes-instance is missed with probability at most 2^(−r), while a no-instance is still never accepted.

patterns.why: Only one kind of error is permitted by the decision rule.
The repeated algorithm accumulates positive evidence across runs.

nodes.name: Adleman's BPP-to-circuits theorem
nodes.intuition: After amplifying correctness enough, some fixed random seed works for every input of a given length. Hardwiring such a seed produces a polynomial-size circuit for that length.
nodes.conditions: Standard polynomial-time randomized computation and nonuniform polynomial-size Boolean circuit families. The proof establishes existence of a good seed for each length, not an efficient uniform method for finding those seeds.
nodes.example: If each of the 2^n inputs fails with probability below 2^(−n), a union bound shows that at least one seed has no failing length-n input.

patterns.why: A union bound ranges over all 2^n inputs of one length.
A probabilistic existence argument is converted into a fixed nonuniform object.

nodes.name: Finite-automaton acceptance
nodes.intuition: A finite automaton summarizes the entire input prefix by one of finitely many states. Reading the next symbol updates that summary through a fixed transition rule.
nodes.conditions: A deterministic finite automaton with finite states Q, alphabet Σ, start q₀, accepting states F, transition δ, and δ*(q,empty)=q. The number of states is fixed independently of input length.
nodes.example: A two-state automaton recognizes binary strings with an even number of ones by toggling states whenever it reads a one.

patterns.why: A word is processed by extending the transition rule one symbol at a time.
The current state is a finite summary of everything read so far.

nodes.name: Pumping lemma for regular languages
nodes.intuition: A long enough accepted path in a finite-state machine must repeat a state. The loop between repetitions can be removed or repeated without changing acceptance of the remaining suffix.
nodes.conditions: If L is regular, some pumping length p exists such that every w∈L of length at least p has a decomposition satisfying the formula. The decomposition exists; it is not arbitrary. The lemma's property alone is not sufficient to characterize regularity.
nodes.example: The language {0^n1^n:n≥0} violates the lemma because pumping a forced early zero block breaks equality of the two counts.

patterns.why: A repeated state creates a repeatable segment of computation.
More visited prefix positions than states force a duplicate state.

nodes.name: Myhill–Nerode equivalence
nodes.latex: x\sim_Ly\iff\forall z\in\Sigma^*:\ xz\in L\Longleftrightarrow yz\in L,\qquad L\text{ regular}\iff[\Sigma^*:\sim_L]<\infty
nodes.intuition: Two prefixes are equivalent when no future suffix can distinguish them. The minimal memory needed for recognition is exactly the number of these distinguishable future-behavior classes.
nodes.conditions: A language over a finite alphabet. The equivalence is right invariant, and finite index equals the number of states of the minimal complete deterministic automaton.
nodes.example: For parity of ones, two prefixes are equivalent exactly when they have the same parity, yielding two minimal states.

patterns.why: An equivalence relation groups prefixes by identical future acceptance behavior.
Each automaton state represents one sufficient summary of a prefix.

nodes.name: Number of Boolean functions
nodes.intuition: A Boolean function chooses one output bit independently for every possible input. There are exponentially many truth-table entries and therefore doubly exponentially many possible functions.
nodes.conditions: n labeled Boolean input coordinates and one Boolean output. This counts distinct functions, not different formulas or circuits that may compute the same function.
nodes.example: Two input bits give four input rows and therefore 2⁴=16 Boolean functions.

patterns.why: Each of the 2^n truth-table entries has two independent output choices.
A table of exponential length gives a doubly exponential number of possible contents.

nodes.name: Counting lower bound for Boolean circuits
nodes.intuition: Short circuits cannot describe every truth table because there are far too few short descriptions. Counting proves that some functions intrinsically require large circuits without identifying a particular hard function.
nodes.conditions: Boolean circuits over a fixed finite complete bounded-fan-in basis; size counts gates. The asymptotic statement concerns existence for sufficiently large n. It is a nonconstructive lower bound and does not establish such a bound for a named explicit problem.
nodes.example: Circuits of size s have at most 2^{O(s log(n+s))} descriptions, which is too small to represent all 2^{2^n} Boolean functions when s is sufficiently below 2^n/n.

patterns.why: There are fewer small circuit descriptions than Boolean functions.
Most truth tables cannot be encoded by very short computational descriptions.

nodes.name: Comparison-sorting decision-tree bound
nodes.intuition: Every comparison supplies at most one binary branch in a decision tree. To distinguish all possible input orders, the tree must have enough leaves to label every permutation.
nodes.conditions: Deterministic comparison-based sorting of n distinct keys with binary less-than outcomes. Algorithms exploiting restricted key encodings or additional operations are outside this model; average-case and randomized variants need their corresponding arguments.
nodes.example: Three distinct keys have six possible orders, so a binary comparison tree needs worst-case depth at least three.

patterns.why: The algorithm must distinguish n! possible total orders.
Each binary comparison contributes at most one bit of branch information.

nodes.name: Plain Kolmogorov description complexity
nodes.intuition: The complexity of a finite string is the length of its shortest effective description in a fixed universal language. A long regular string can have a short description, while an irregular one may need almost all its bits stated explicitly.
nodes.conditions: A fixed optimal universal partial computable description machine U and finite binary programs p and outputs x. This is plain complexity C, not prefix-free complexity K; constants depend on the chosen machine.
nodes.example: A string of n zeros has a description consisting of a short printing routine plus a description of n, so its complexity grows only logarithmically in n up to encoding overhead.

patterns.why: Description length measures algorithmic compressibility of an individual finite object.
The definition minimizes over all halting programs producing that object.

nodes.name: Kolmogorov invariance under description language
nodes.intuition: Changing a fixed description language adds at most the cost of an interpreter. This makes algorithmic complexity robust up to an additive constant, even though exact values remain language dependent.
nodes.conditions: U is an optimal universal plain description machine and M is any fixed partial computable description machine. The constant c_M depends on M and U but not on the described string x.
nodes.example: A fixed simulator prefix translates every M-program into a U-program with a bounded extra number of bits.

patterns.why: An interpreter is composed with the original program to reproduce its output.
The language-change overhead is additive rather than proportional to the object length.

nodes.name: Counting incompressible strings
nodes.intuition: There are too few short programs to compress every string. A uniformly chosen length-n string is unlikely to have a description shorter by many bits.
nodes.conditions: Plain description complexity for a fixed machine U, integers 0≤c≤n, and binary programs. Each halting program has one output; different programs may coincide on an output, which only strengthens the upper bound.
nodes.example: The fraction of length-n strings compressible by more than c bits under this strict threshold is less than 2^(−c).

patterns.why: The number of candidate short programs bounds the number of compressible outputs.
Large compression savings are rare among uniformly sampled fixed-length strings.

nodes.name: Noncomputability of exact description complexity
nodes.latex: x\longmapsto C_U(x)\quad\text{is not a total computable function}
nodes.intuition: The shortest possible program length is mathematically well defined but cannot be calculated exactly for every string by one terminating algorithm. Searching programs can improve upper bounds without recognizing that the best one has been found.
nodes.conditions: Plain Kolmogorov complexity for a fixed optimal universal description machine U. This does not prevent computable compression methods, special-case exact results or progressively improving upper approximations.
nodes.example: Dovetailing all programs can eventually find shorter descriptions, but there is no general computable signal that no still-shorter program will ever halt with the same output.

patterns.why: The global minimum ranges over a space whose halting behavior cannot be fully decided.
Upper approximations can improve without a computable exact stopping certificate.

nodes.name: Pauli matrices and their product algebra
nodes.intuition: Three small Hermitian matrices encode the geometry of a qubit. Their products combine an ordinary dot-product part with an oriented cross-product part.
nodes.conditions: The standard two-by-two complex Pauli matrices, Cartesian indices x,y,z, Kronecker delta δ and right-handed Levi-Civita symbol ε. Physical spin operators are ħσ_i/2, so their units and commutator factors differ.
nodes.example: For real vectors a,b, (a·σ)(b·σ)=(a·b)I+i(a×b)·σ; each individual Pauli matrix squares to I.

patterns.why: The matrices close under products into scalar and Pauli components.
Their product law expresses Euclidean dot and cross products in matrix form.

nodes.name: Arithmetic mean
nodes.intuition: Replace a collection by one equal value while preserving its total. It is also the balance point and the best constant approximation under squared error.
nodes.conditions: A nonempty finite list of real numbers; n is its length.
nodes.example: For 2, 4, 9 the mean is 5: three copies of 5 preserve the total 15.

patterns.why: Equal weights compress a collection to a representative value.
Averaging commutes with addition and scalar multiplication.
The mean uniquely minimizes total squared error.

nodes.name: Weighted arithmetic mean
nodes.intuition: Give each value a share of the total influence. Normalizing the weights converts masses, frequencies or probabilities into one averaging rule.
nodes.conditions: Finite real x_i, nonnegative real w_i, and sum of weights strictly positive.
nodes.example: Two units at 10 and one at 16 have weighted mean 12.

patterns.why: Normalized weights describe unequal contributions.
With weights fixed, the output is linear in the values.

nodes.name: Geometric mean
nodes.intuition: Average in logarithmic coordinates, then return to the original scale. It preserves the product instead of the sum.
nodes.conditions: Strictly positive real inputs; n >= 1. The product form extends to nonnegative inputs.
nodes.example: Growth factors 2 and 8 have geometric mean 4 because 4 squared equals 2 times 8.

patterns.why: It represents multiplicative data by equal factors.
Logarithms turn multiplication into addition.
Exponentiation reverses the log average.

nodes.name: Harmonic mean
nodes.intuition: Average reciprocals and invert. This is useful when equal amounts are accumulated at different rates.
nodes.conditions: Strictly positive real inputs and n >= 1.
nodes.example: Equal distances traveled at 30 and 60 km/h give overall speed 40 km/h.

patterns.why: Rates are combined by averaging time per unit.
The reciprocal transform converts the relevant additive quantity.

nodes.name: Root mean square
nodes.intuition: Average squared magnitudes before taking a square root. Positive and negative signals both contribute to energy.
nodes.conditions: Real inputs and n >= 1.
nodes.example: The values -3 and 3 have mean 0 but RMS 3.

patterns.why: Squares are averaged.
Energy and squared distance use the same sum of squares.

nodes.name: Power mean
nodes.intuition: A single exponent selects a whole family of means. Larger exponents give more influence to large inputs.
nodes.conditions: A finite nonempty list of n >= 1 strictly positive real inputs; p is real. The p=0 value is the continuous limit.
nodes.example: p=-1, 0, 1, 2 give the harmonic, geometric, arithmetic and root mean square means.

patterns.why: Many familiar averages become members of one family.
Take a power, average, and invert the power.

nodes.name: Arithmetic–geometric mean inequality
nodes.intuition: For a fixed sum, balancing positive entries maximizes their product. Unevenness creates the gap between arithmetic and geometric means.
nodes.conditions: Nonnegative real x_i and n >= 1; equality iff all inputs are equal.
nodes.example: A rectangle of fixed perimeter has greatest area when its side lengths are equal.

patterns.why: Concavity of log explains why averaging raises the product.
Balancing solves product maximization under a sum constraint.

nodes.name: Weighted AM–GM inequality
nodes.intuition: The same balance principle works when entries carry unequal influence.
nodes.conditions: x_i > 0, w_i >= 0, and sum w_i = 1; equality iff inputs with positive weights are equal.
nodes.example: With weights 1/4 and 3/4, 1/4 + 3x/4 is at least x to the power 3/4.

patterns.why: Unequal weights define both sides.
Apply Jensen to the concave logarithm.

nodes.name: Power mean inequality
nodes.intuition: Increasing the averaging exponent shifts attention toward larger values. This orders many inequalities at once.
nodes.conditions: A finite nonempty list of n >= 1 positive real inputs; p and q real with the continuous definition at zero. Equality iff all inputs agree.
nodes.example: H <= G <= A <= RMS is one chain in this theorem.

patterns.why: It compares entire averaging rules.
Convex powers and Jensen yield the ordering.

nodes.name: Quasi-arithmetic mean
nodes.intuition: Choose coordinates in which averaging makes sense, average there, and transform back. This unifies additive, multiplicative and reciprocal averaging.
nodes.conditions: f is continuous and strictly monotone on an interval containing all x_i; w_i >= 0, sum w_i = 1.
nodes.example: The generators x, log x and 1/x give weighted arithmetic, geometric and harmonic means; equal weights 1/n recover their ordinary forms.

patterns.why: It generalizes weighted means.
The generator f chooses the scale of comparison.
The rule is transform, combine, inverse-transform.

nodes.name: Mean as the best constant
nodes.intuition: Any constant other than the mean adds exactly one extra nonnegative error term. The mean is therefore the unique best constant in squared distance.
nodes.conditions: Real finite data, n >= 1, and real a.
nodes.example: For 2 and 6, predicting 4 costs 8; predicting 5 costs 10, an increase of 2 times 1 squared.

patterns.why: The error decomposition identifies the minimizer.
Cross terms cancel because centered deviations sum to zero.
Centered residuals are perpendicular to constant vectors.

nodes.name: Averaging as orthogonal projection
nodes.intuition: Averaging is the operation of projecting a data vector onto the line of constant vectors. The residual contains every deviation from that common level.
nodes.conditions: Euclidean space R^n, n >= 1; 1 denotes the all-ones column vector.
nodes.example: The vector (2,4,9) projects to (5,5,5); its residual (-3,-1,4) has zero sum.

patterns.why: The projection replaces every coordinate by the mean.
The residual has zero inner product with the all-ones vector.
Data splits into common level plus centered variation.

nodes.name: Center of mass
nodes.intuition: A weighted average of positions gives the point at which first moments balance. The same formula works coordinate by coordinate.
nodes.conditions: Points x_i in a finite-dimensional real affine space, nonnegative masses m_i, and positive total mass. The squared-distance interpretation uses a chosen Euclidean inner product.
nodes.example: Masses 1 at position 0 and 3 at position 4 balance at position 3.

patterns.why: Mass determines the weights.
The weighted displacement from the center sums to zero.
After choosing a Euclidean inner product, the center uniquely minimizes mass-weighted squared distance.

nodes.name: Online mean update
nodes.intuition: Correct the old average by a shrinking fraction of the new prediction error. No old data values need to be retained.
nodes.conditions: Real finite sequence, n >= 1; exact arithmetic identity, subject to rounding in computation.
nodes.example: An average 10 from four values becomes 12 after observing 20.

patterns.why: The next mean is computed from the current mean.
The gain 1/(n+1) gives the new observation its correct weight.

nodes.name: Combining group means
nodes.intuition: A mean of means is correct when each group is weighted by its size. Grouping changes the computation but preserves the underlying sum.
nodes.conditions: Nonempty finite groups of real observations, combined by concatenation; n_j is each group's positive size. To represent a dataset without duplicate observations, the groups must form a disjoint partition.
nodes.example: A group of 2 averaging 5 and a group of 8 averaging 10 combine to 9, not 7.5.

patterns.why: Group size supplies the correct weights.
Partitioning a dataset preserves its total and count.

nodes.name: Circular mean direction
nodes.intuition: Average unit vectors before recovering an angle. This respects wraparound at a full turn.
nodes.conditions: Real angles, nonnegative weights, positive weight total, and nonzero vector sum; otherwise mean direction is undefined.
nodes.example: Directions 359 degrees and 1 degree average to 0 degrees, rather than 180 degrees.

patterns.why: Directions are averaged as vectors.
Embedding angles on the unit circle handles periodicity.

nodes.name: Weighted squared-error decomposition
nodes.intuition: Weighted averaging and weighted least squares select the same center. The total error separates into irreducible spread and error from choosing the wrong center.
nodes.conditions: Finite real inputs; nonnegative weights with positive total; a real.
nodes.example: Mass-weighted center estimation and frequency-weighted data fitting use the same identity.

patterns.why: The weighted mean cancels the mixed term.
Completing the square splits the objective.
The second term proves unique minimization.

nodes.name: Sum of consecutive integers
nodes.intuition: Pair the first and last terms so each pair has the same sum. A triangular count becomes half a rectangle.
nodes.conditions: Integer n >= 0; the empty sum at n=0 is zero.

patterns.why: It counts a triangular arrangement.
Pairing k with n+1-k gives equal totals.

nodes.name: Sum of consecutive squares
nodes.intuition: Accumulating a quadratic sequence produces a cubic expression. This mirrors how integration raises polynomial degree.
nodes.conditions: Integer n >= 0.
nodes.example: The first three squares total 1+4+9=14.

patterns.why: A discrete sum accumulates the sequence.
The summands are squared magnitudes.

nodes.name: Finite geometric sum
nodes.intuition: Multiply the sum by its common ratio and subtract: almost every term cancels.
nodes.conditions: Real or complex r != 1; integer n >= 0. At r=1 the sum is n.

patterns.why: Each term is obtained by the same multiplication.
Geometric growth is discrete exponential growth.
Many stages are collapsed into a closed form.

nodes.name: Binomial theorem
nodes.intuition: Every term records how many times b was chosen from n factors. The coefficient counts all ways to make that choice.
nodes.conditions: Nonnegative integer n; commuting a and b, for example real or complex scalars.

patterns.why: Binomial coefficients count subsets of factor positions.
The polynomial is split into monomials.

nodes.name: Logarithm laws
nodes.intuition: A logarithm converts multiplication into addition and powers into scaling. This is why growth rates, likelihoods and products often simplify in log coordinates.
nodes.conditions: x,y > 0 and real a; natural logarithm. Complex principal logarithms require branch corrections.
nodes.example: A product of many probabilities becomes a sum of log probabilities.

patterns.why: Log is the inverse of exponential.
Multiplicative structure becomes additive.

nodes.name: Exponential addition law
nodes.intuition: Adding time or an exponent composes multiplicative growth. This is the basic bridge between additive and multiplicative structures.
nodes.conditions: Real or complex scalar x,y. For square matrices, the analogous identity holds when the matrices commute and can fail without commutation.
nodes.example: Growing for time x and then y has the same factor as growing for time x+y.

patterns.why: Exponential sends sums to products.
Consecutive evolution combines by addition of parameters.

nodes.name: Quadratic formula
nodes.intuition: Shift a quadratic to its center, then take a square root. The discriminant tells whether real roots are separated, repeated or absent.
nodes.conditions: Real coefficients and a != 0; real roots require b^2-4ac >= 0. Both complex roots are allowed over C.
nodes.example: x^2-5x+6=0 has roots 2 and 3.

patterns.why: Second-degree equations reduce to a centered square.
Factoring isolates the roots.

nodes.name: Completing the square
nodes.intuition: Separate a quadratic into a centered square and a constant. Its location, minimum or maximum, and roots become visible.
nodes.conditions: Real or complex a,b,c with a != 0; the minimum interpretation requires real variables and a > 0.

patterns.why: Translation removes the linear term.
For positive a, the center gives the minimum.

nodes.name: Pythagorean theorem
nodes.intuition: Perpendicular contributions add in squared length. This becomes the template for energy decomposition in inner-product spaces.
nodes.conditions: A Euclidean right triangle with legs a,b and hypotenuse c.
nodes.example: Lengths 3 and 4 at a right angle give diagonal length 5.

patterns.why: Perpendicular directions produce no cross term.
Squared lengths add.

nodes.name: Euler's formula
nodes.intuition: A complex exponential packages circular motion into one expression. Multiplication becomes addition of angles.
nodes.conditions: Real theta for the unit-circle interpretation; the identity extends to complex theta.
nodes.example: At theta=pi/2 the exponential is i.

patterns.why: Exponential growth with imaginary rate gives oscillation.
Multiplication by a unit complex number rotates without stretching.
Consecutive rotations add their angles.

nodes.name: Euler's identity
nodes.intuition: Half a turn on the complex unit circle lands at -1. This is one especially recognizable value of Euler's formula.
nodes.conditions: i^2=-1 and the usual complex exponential.
nodes.example: It encodes a rotation of 180 degrees.

patterns.why: It evaluates the complex exponential.
A half-turn exchanges opposite points.

nodes.name: Pythagorean trigonometric identity
nodes.intuition: Sine and cosine are the coordinates of a unit vector. Their squared contributions always give unit length.
nodes.conditions: Real theta for the geometric interpretation; the algebraic identity extends to complex theta.
nodes.example: At pi/4 both squares are 1/2.

patterns.why: The coordinates lie on perpendicular axes.
Rotation preserves unit length.

nodes.name: Sine addition formula
nodes.intuition: Combining two rotations mixes their horizontal and vertical components in a precise way.
nodes.conditions: Real or complex alpha,beta.
nodes.example: Choosing alpha=beta gives sin(2 alpha)=2 sin alpha cos alpha.

patterns.why: Two angle changes compose.
The imaginary part of a product gives the identity.

nodes.name: Cosine addition formula
nodes.intuition: The horizontal component of two composed rotations is the difference of two products.
nodes.conditions: Real or complex alpha,beta.
nodes.example: Choosing beta=-alpha gives cos squared alpha plus sin squared alpha equals 1.

patterns.why: Rotation angles add.
Take the real part after multiplying complex exponentials.

nodes.name: De Moivre's formula
nodes.intuition: Repeated rotation multiplies the angle. Taking roots reverses that process and exposes cyclic symmetry.
nodes.conditions: Integer n and real theta; negative powers are defined because the base is nonzero.
nodes.example: Cube a unit complex number to triple its angle.

patterns.why: Roots of unity are equally spaced rotations.
The exponential power law makes the formula immediate.

nodes.name: Complex modulus
nodes.intuition: The modulus measures the stretching part of a complex number. Multiplication combines stretches while arguments combine rotations.
nodes.conditions: Real x,y and complex z,w.

patterns.why: Modulus is Euclidean distance from zero.
Multiplicative stretches multiply.

nodes.name: Union of sets
nodes.intuition: Union turns logical 'or' into a construction on sets. Set operations provide a geometric language for logical rules.
nodes.conditions: Sets A and B in a common universe.

patterns.why: Union is associative, commutative and idempotent.
Several collections can be combined in stages.

nodes.name: Inclusion–exclusion for two sets
nodes.intuition: Add both counts, then remove the overlap counted twice. Corrections for overlap recur in counting and probability.
nodes.conditions: Finite sets A and B.
nodes.example: If two groups have 8 and 7 members with 3 in common, their union has 12.

patterns.why: Corrects duplicate counting.
Separate the two disjoint remainders and the intersection.

nodes.name: Cartesian product
nodes.latex: A\times B=\{(a,b):a\in A,\ b\in B\},\qquad |A\times B|=|A||B|
nodes.intuition: Make a joint object by choosing one component from each collection. Independent choices multiply the count.
nodes.conditions: The cardinality equation is stated for finite sets.
nodes.example: Three shirts and four trousers give twelve pairs.

patterns.why: The product rule counts independent choices.
Coordinates assemble a structured object.

nodes.name: Composition of functions
nodes.intuition: The output of one rule becomes the input to another. This gives a common language for processes, transformations and nested models.
nodes.conditions: x must be in the domain of f and f(x) in the domain of g.
nodes.example: If f(x)=x+1 and g(x)=x squared, then g(f(x))=(x+1) squared.

patterns.why: It formalizes sequential application.
Composition is associative, generally not commutative.

nodes.name: Inverse function
nodes.intuition: An inverse undoes a transformation while recovering every input uniquely. Both existence and uniqueness matter.
nodes.conditions: f:X to Y must be bijective; restricting the codomain to the image suffices for an injective f.
nodes.example: The exponential maps R bijectively to positive reals; logarithm reverses it.

patterns.why: A map and its inverse compose to do nothing.
Forward and reverse descriptions exchange inputs and outputs.
A reversible coordinate map changes the representation without losing the underlying object.

nodes.name: Equivalence relation
nodes.latex: x\sim x,\qquad x\sim y\Rightarrow y\sim x,\qquad x\sim y,\ y\sim z\Rightarrow x\sim z
nodes.intuition: Specify which distinctions are irrelevant. The resulting equivalence classes turn many representations into one abstract object.
nodes.conditions: A binary relation on a set; all three axioms must hold for all elements.
nodes.example: Integers equivalent modulo n have the same remainder.

patterns.why: Related representations share what is being preserved.
Quotient constructions start from well-defined equivalence classes.

nodes.name: Mathematical induction
nodes.intuition: Prove a starting case and a rule that carries truth to the next case. The finite successor structure then reaches every natural number.
nodes.conditions: P is a proposition about nonnegative integers; both the base and inductive step are required.
nodes.example: The sum-of-integers formula follows by adding n+1 to the n-case.

patterns.why: The proof follows the recursive structure of natural numbers.
The successor operation organizes the argument.

nodes.name: Telescoping sum
nodes.intuition: Internal changes cancel, leaving only the endpoints. This is the discrete prototype of the fundamental theorem of calculus.
nodes.conditions: Integer m <= n; a sequence in an abelian additive group, such as real numbers.
nodes.example: Summing daily changes gives the difference between final and initial totals.

patterns.why: Accumulated interior differences reduce to endpoint data.
Local changes are summed.

nodes.name: Forward finite difference
nodes.intuition: Measure change over a finite step. Dividing by the step size connects discrete differences to derivatives.
nodes.conditions: Both function values are defined; h is a chosen nonzero real step when forming a difference quotient.
nodes.example: For f(x)=x squared, the difference is 2xh+h squared.

patterns.why: Difference quotients approximate local slopes as h shrinks.
Shifts organize discrete dynamics.

nodes.name: Discrete product rule
nodes.intuition: A product's finite change splits into two contributions, with a shift in one factor. The shift is essential before taking a limit.
nodes.conditions: All displayed values are defined; scalar-valued f,g.
nodes.example: Subtract f(x)g(x) after inserting f(x+h)g(x).

patterns.why: Insert and subtract an intermediate product.
Dividing by h and taking a limit yields the differential product rule.

nodes.name: Summation by parts
nodes.intuition: Move a difference from one factor to the other while recording endpoint terms. This is discrete integration by parts.
nodes.conditions: Integers m <= n and finite scalar sequences with all displayed indices defined; an empty final sum is zero.
nodes.example: It transfers a difficult difference to a factor whose differences are simpler.

patterns.why: The difference operator transfers between paired factors with a sign change.
Endpoint contributions record the boundary.

nodes.name: Power-law scaling
nodes.intuition: A homogeneous function changes predictably under rescaling. The exponent says how the measured quantity scales.
nodes.conditions: The equation defines homogeneity of degree k on a domain closed under the allowed positive scale factors lambda.
nodes.example: Length, area and volume scale with exponents 1, 2 and 3.

patterns.why: One exponent summarizes response to a scale change.
The form of the rule is preserved under rescaling.

nodes.name: Dimensional homogeneity
nodes.intuition: Quantities can be added only when their dimensions agree; multiplying quantities multiplies their units. This constrains candidate equations before calculation.
nodes.conditions: Physical quantities with declared dimensions; these are consistency rules, not a guarantee of a physically correct model.
nodes.example: A distance cannot be added directly to a time, but speed times time has distance units.

patterns.why: Changing units imposes consistent rescaling.
Dimensions combine multiplicatively.

nodes.name: Affine combination
nodes.intuition: Combine points in a way independent of the chosen origin. Unlike a convex combination, some coefficients may be negative.
nodes.conditions: Points in a real affine space; real coefficients summing to one.
nodes.example: 2b-a extends the line segment from a through b by the same distance.

patterns.why: The coordinate expression is linear in the points.
The sum-one constraint preserves the combination under translations.

nodes.name: Convex barycentric combination
nodes.intuition: Treat coefficients as mass fractions. The result lies inside the convex hull of the contributing points.
nodes.conditions: A finite set of points in a real affine space. Coordinates are unique for an affinely independent simplex.
nodes.example: A triangle's centroid uses weights 1/3 at each vertex.

patterns.why: The coefficients are normalized nonnegative weights.
All such combinations form the convex hull.

nodes.name: Cross-ratio
nodes.intuition: A ratio of ratios survives fractional linear coordinate changes. It is a natural measure in projective geometry when ordinary distances are not preserved.
nodes.conditions: Distinct finite real or complex a,b,c,d with displayed denominators nonzero. Invariance holds for invertible fractional linear transformations T(z)=(alpha z+beta)/(gamma z+delta), with alpha delta-beta gamma nonzero. Interpret points at infinity projectively; the displayed finite formula requires finite transformed points.
nodes.example: Perspective images preserve cross-ratios of four collinear points, although lengths change.

patterns.why: Mobius transformations preserve the cross-ratio.
It detects structure independent of projective coordinates.

patterns.name: Averaging
patterns.intuition: Replace many values with a representative while preserving a chosen aggregate.
patterns.conditions: An organizing template, not a theorem applying to every member. Check each formula's own hypotheses.
patterns.example: What quantity is being preserved, and what sets the weights?
patterns.question: What quantity is being preserved, and what sets the weights?
patterns.trap: Averages in different coordinates answer different questions.

patterns.name: Linearity
patterns.intuition: Understand combinations by understanding their parts separately.
patterns.conditions: An organizing template, not a theorem applying to every member. Check each formula's own hypotheses.
patterns.example: Can I solve basis cases and combine their answers?
patterns.question: Can I solve basis cases and combine their answers?
patterns.trap: Multiplying two variable inputs usually breaks linearity.

patterns.conditions: An organizing template, not a theorem applying to every member. Check each formula's own hypotheses.

patterns.question: What is the first-order response to a small change?
patterns.trap: A good local approximation need not be accurate far away.

patterns.intuition: Build a global quantity by adding small contributions.
patterns.conditions: An organizing template, not a theorem applying to every member. Check each formula's own hypotheses.

patterns.question: What is the local contribution and what measure weights it?

patterns.question: What is the corresponding question on the other side of the pairing?

patterns.intuition: Separate contributions so they do not interfere in the chosen inner product.
patterns.conditions: An organizing template, not a theorem applying to every member. Check each formula's own hypotheses.
patterns.example: Can I choose components whose cross terms vanish?
patterns.question: Can I choose components whose cross terms vanish?
patterns.trap: Uncorrelated random variables need not be independent.

patterns.intuition: Define a desirable object as the one that best satisfies a criterion.
patterns.conditions: An organizing template, not a theorem applying to every member. Check each formula's own hypotheses.
patterns.example: What objective and constraints identify the object I want?
patterns.question: What objective and constraints identify the object I want?

patterns.name: Fixed points

patterns.question: Can the problem be rewritten as a self-consistency condition?

patterns.intuition: Generate or reason about complex objects one step at a time.

patterns.example: What information is sufficient to move to the next step?
patterns.question: What information is sufficient to move to the next step?
patterns.trap: Repeated application can diverge, oscillate or accumulate error.

patterns.conditions: An organizing template, not a theorem applying to every member. Check each formula's own hypotheses.
patterns.example: Where does the quantity flow, accumulate or remain constant?
patterns.question: Where does the quantity flow, accumulate or remain constant?

patterns.question: Which pieces make computation or structure transparent?

patterns.question: Can I count the same objects in two useful ways?

patterns.question: Is the underlying process additive in a transformed scale?

patterns.conditions: An organizing template, not a theorem applying to every member. Check each formula's own hypotheses.

patterns.question: Does averaging stay feasible and simplify the objective?

metaphors.title: A microscope with a noisy ruler
metaphors.story: Zooming in reveals a curve’s local slope, but eventually the measuring marks become too coarse for the remaining difference. The useful magnification balances geometric detail against measurement noise.
metaphors.structure: Finite differences approximate a derivative with truncation error, while subtraction and division amplify finite-precision errors.

mappings.role: The limiting slope is the ideal feature being measured.
Two nearby samples estimate the feature at a finite zoom.
The total error budget balances an O(h²) bias against an O(u/h) rounding term.

metaphors.limits: This picture assumes the model for evaluation error and sufficient smoothness; exact arithmetic has no rounding floor, and noisy data may obey a different error law.
metaphors.question: What changes if halving the sampling distance doubles the noise contribution?

metaphors.title: Distances on a stretched rubber map
metaphors.story: Imagine transferring a small circle through a rubber map: it may become a very thin ellipse. Undoing the map requires large corrections in its compressed direction.
metaphors.structure: Singular values measure directional stretching; the ratio of largest to smallest stretching controls relative sensitivity of an invertible linear solve.

mappings.role: The principal stretch directions and factors describe the deformed circle.
The ratio of extreme stretches measures how uneven the map is.
A small equation mismatch may correspond to a large positional error after undoing a compressed direction.

metaphors.limits: Conditioning concerns the problem, not the quality of a particular algorithm. The geometric explanation uses the Euclidean norm; other norms have different unit balls.
metaphors.question: Which direction could hide a large solution error behind a small residual?

metaphors.title: A repair receipt for a computed answer
metaphors.story: A mechanic hands back an answer together with a receipt showing how much the original specification had to change to make that answer exact. A tiny repair can still change the outcome greatly when the specification is sensitive.
metaphors.structure: Backward error measures a perturbation to the input problem; forward error measures the resulting output discrepancy, linked through conditioning.

mappings.role: The receipt lists the smallest admissible perturbation to A and b.
Sensitivity determines how much a small repaired specification can move the answer.
The exact inverse describes how a forcing discrepancy changes the solution.

metaphors.limits: A small backward error does not guarantee a small forward error for an ill-conditioned system. The perturbation model must specify which inputs may change.
metaphors.question: Can the computed answer be exact for a nearby problem even when it is far from the intended answer?

metaphors.title: Narrowing a search strip
metaphors.story: Two markers bracket a crossing. Inspect the middle, keep the half still containing a crossing, and repeat until the search strip is short enough.
metaphors.structure: A sign-changing interval invariant is preserved while its length decreases geometrically.

mappings.role: The midpoint test preserves a root-containing interval.
Averaging the two endpoints places the next test at the exact middle.
Repeated factors of one-half govern the interval-size sequence.

metaphors.limits: Continuity and opposite endpoint signs are essential. A narrow bracket identifies at least one root, but it does not establish that there is only one root inside.
metaphors.question: What invariant lets an iterative search discard half its candidates safely?

metaphors.title: Canceling a known blur
metaphors.story: Take two measurements whose blur follows the same predictable rule at different scales. A weighted subtraction can cancel the leading blur without knowing the true value.
metaphors.structure: Richardson extrapolation eliminates a leading error coefficient by combining two asymptotic approximations.

mappings.role: The combination cancels the common c h^p error term.
A local expansion explains why powers of the scale describe error.
